edges.note: Aramaic-speaking Christianity reached Edessa early, but by what route and hands scholars genuinely disagree.
Egyptian Christianity's origins are obscure in detail, but its second-century emergence out of the same scattered network is broadly accepted.
The desert movement grew in Alexandria’s shadow; Athanasius of Alexandria wrote the Life of Antony that carried it to the world.
Jerome and Paula toured the Egyptian ascetic settlements; the circle's practice consciously imported the desert's renunciation.
Origen's textual scholarship (the Hexapla) is the direct ancestor of Jerome's Hebrew-testing project — even as Jerome turned publicly against Origen's theology.
Jerome heard Gregory of Nazianzus teach in Constantinople and calls him his teacher.
The School of Nisibis and the Persian church carry this tradition's teaching directly onward after 410.
Basil visited Egypt; the whole Greek monastic tradition claims the desert as its root.
John Cassian carried the desert's teaching to Gaul; Benedict's Rule commends his Conferences by name.
Via Gaul (Lérins, Martin of Tours); the route is secure in outline, thinner in specifics.
Post-Chalcedon Egyptian Christianity is the direct continuation of the desert tradition.
…and of Alexandria's own catechetical tradition.
The Waldensians adhered to the Reformation in 1532; how much earlier “proto-Protestant” continuity is real versus retrospective is a live scholarly argument.
The Radical Reformation defined itself against the magisterial reformers' church-state settlement as much as against Rome.
Azusa Street's leaders and vocabulary came directly out of the Holiness movement.
Aladura and Zionist movements drew on Pentecostal currents while being genuinely African-initiated — the balance is actively studied.
The Holiness movement understood itself as recovering Wesley's own doctrine of sanctification.

The Great Schism, in each side's own documents: Humbert's bull of excommunication laid on the altar of Hagia Sophia (16 July 1054); Cerularius's synodal condemnation of the legates the following week. Process honesty: 1054 was symbolic and legate-to-patriarch, not church-to-church; the 1204 sack of Constantinople sealed the estrangement (scholars dating the real rupture there - that reading Contested); the anathemas were mutually lifted in 1965 [S].
The Black Baptist congregations (Silver Bluff c. 1773-75, First African Savannah 1788) are the Baptist parent line of the Black Church. Edge written at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
Richard Allen’s AME (1816) and AME Zion (1821) are Methodist bodies — the Methodist parent line of the Black Church. Edge written at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).

Calvin's Institutes draws explicitly and heavily on Augustine's anti-Pelagian writings (De Praedestinatione Sanctorum, Contra Julianum) for total depravity, unconditional election, and irresistible grace -- Calvin named Augustine his primary authority next to Scripture itself. A direct theological line across eleven centuries with no institutional continuity -- influence, not identity.

movements.name: Post-Apostolic House-Church Christianity
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Moderate; communal voice rich, individual interior voice thin (disclosed on its tile)
movements.floorNote: These communities lived two centuries before the Nicene Creed was written. What they confessed is part of the raw material the creed was later drawn from, not a departure from it.
movements.relationsSummary: Parent of nearly everything on the map
movements.why: It is — open for conversation now (Representative: Chloe).

entry.subtitle: Post-Apostolic House-Church Christianity
entry.tile: The house-churches of Antioch, Asia Minor, and Rome, 70 to 200 CE — the scattered gatherings that held together after the apostles were gone, connected by letters, formed around the table, still discerning who should lead and what the body's suffering truly means.

movements.longDescription: After the apostles died, Christianity had no buildings of its own, no clergy in any later sense, and no agreed list of Scriptures — it had houses. Believers gathered in a member's dining room or the back of a workshop, ate a meal together, read aloud whatever apostolic letters had reached them, and stayed connected to distant congregations by hand-carried correspondence and travelling teachers. Across these decades the shape of the church slowly emerged in practice rather than by decree: who should preside, how to receive people through baptism, what to do when a member handed in his neighbours under interrogation, what to make of the fact that faithfulness kept costing people their lives. Ignatius of Antioch wrote to churches along his route while under armed guard on the way to his own execution in Rome; Justin Martyr, teaching in a rented room above a bathhouse in the same city, wrote down what a Sunday gathering actually looked like — and both were killed for it.
voices: Ignatius of Antioch — bishop who wrote seven letters to congregations while being marched to his execution in Rome, c. 107-117
Clement of Rome — wrote from the Roman church to the Corinthians around 96 to settle a dispute over deposed leaders, the earliest Christian letter outside the New Testament
Polycarp of Smyrna — bishop who had known the apostolic generation, put to death at Smyrna around 155, his death recorded by his own congregation
Justin Martyr — a philosopher who kept teaching Christianity as a school in Rome and left the earliest detailed description of Christian Sunday worship
Most of these communities' hosts and householders are unnamed in the record — the gatherings met in the homes of people history did not bother to write down
movements.legacy: Almost everything on this map descends from these gatherings. The basic shape of Christian worship — assembling on the first day of the week, reading Scripture aloud, a shared table — was set here, along with the offices of bishop, presbyter and deacon, and the habit of reading apostolic letters in public until they became Scripture by use rather than by ruling. Their networks of hospitality between cities became the nervous system of the ancient church, and their correspondence — Clement, Ignatius, Polycarp — has been read ever since; the Didache, by contrast, was lost for centuries and recovered from a single surviving manuscript only in the 1870s.

experienceToday.text: The Dura-Europos house-church, Syria — an ordinary home converted for worship between about 233 and 256, the earliest identified Christian church building, preserved because a Roman defensive rampart buried it
Yale University Art Gallery, New Haven — the Dura-Europos baptistery wall paintings, probably the oldest surviving Christian paintings anywhere, are on display

movements.name: Alexandrian Catechetical / Christian-Platonist Tradition
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Rich (Clement, Origen); school-institution question is live scholarship
movements.floorNote: Nothing in this tradition's confession diverges from the doctrine the Nicene Creed later stated. Some of Origen's more speculative proposals — about the pre-existence of souls and the final restoration of all things — were disputed in his own lifetime and formally condemned by a church council three centuries after his death.
movements.relationsSummary: Parent of Desert Monasticism; scholarship parent of the Bethlehem Circle
movements.why: It is — open for conversation now (Representative: Theon).

entry.subtitle: Alexandrian Catechetical Tradition
entry.tile: Alexandria, c. 150 to 400 CE — a community of readers who received seekers into a life of accompanied reading, convinced that Scripture's surface is a door onto the Logos's own inexhaustible depth.

movements.longDescription: Alexandria was the ancient world's great city of libraries and lecture halls, and Christianity there took the shape the city gave everything else — a school. Teachers received enquirers, catechumens preparing for baptism, and educated pagans curious about this new philosophy, and walked them through Scripture as a text with a surface and a depth: the letter first, then the moral sense, then the spiritual meaning that opens onto the Logos himself. Clement wrote for cultivated Greeks who wanted to know whether a Christian could keep his learning; Origen, who succeeded him, produced a staggering body of commentary and the Hexapla, a six-column parallel edition of the Old Testament assembled to see what the Hebrew actually said — before falling out with his bishop and moving his teaching to Caesarea around 231. Historians still argue about how formal the whole thing was: whether Alexandria really had one continuous institution with a succession of appointed heads, as Eusebius later described it, or a looser sequence of private Christian schools whose teachers happened to be remembered together.
voices: Pantaenus — the earliest teacher named in the tradition, remembered as a converted Stoic philosopher
Clement of Alexandria — wrote for educated Greeks, arguing that philosophy had been a tutor leading toward Christ
Origen — the tradition's towering figure: commentator, textual scholar, and the first Christian to attempt a systematic account of the faith
Dionysius of Alexandria — Origen's student, later bishop, who steered the Egyptian church through persecution and plague
Didymus the Blind — blind from early childhood, taught in Alexandria for decades and was consulted by Jerome and Rufinus
movements.legacy: The Alexandrian way of reading Scripture — that the text has depths beneath its surface, and that reading it is a lifelong formation rather than an act of information-gathering — became the dominant Christian approach for over a millennium, in the East and West alike. Origen's textual scholarship set the standard for taking the original languages seriously; Basil of Caesarea and Gregory of Nazianzus compiled an anthology of his writings, and Ambrose and Jerome read him closely even when they were careful about saying so. The tradition also fed directly into Egyptian monasticism, giving the desert its intellectual vocabulary.

movements.name: Syriac Christianity (Edessa/Nisibis)
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Rich formal/doctrinal, thinner personal texture (disclosed on its tile)
movements.floorNote: This tradition holds the doctrine the Nicene Creed states. One figure inside it, the philosopher-poet Bardaisan, taught cosmological ideas his own later tradition repudiated; exactly where he stands relative to that doctrine remains an open question.
movements.relationsSummary: Parent of the Church of the East and Syriac Orthodox lines
movements.why: It is — open for conversation now (Representative: Mar Yausep).

entry.tile: Edessa and Nisibis, 200 to 410 CE — in what is now southeastern Turkey — a community shaped by persecution under Persian rule, holding together through covenant vows and typological reading of Scripture.

movements.longDescription: East of the Roman frontier, in the border cities of Edessa and Nisibis, Christianity grew up speaking Syriac — a form of Aramaic close to the language Jesus himself spoke — and it developed a character of its own before Greek theology reached it. It taught in poetry rather than philosophical prose, reading the Scriptures typologically, as a world of symbols answering one another; Ephrem the Syrian wrote hundreds of hymns that carried doctrine in metre so a congregation could sing what it believed. Its ascetics were not desert hermits but the sons and daughters of the covenant, consecrated men and women who took vows of celibacy and stayed inside the ordinary congregation, serving it. And it lived on a fault line: when the Roman emperor Jovian surrendered Nisibis to Persia in 363, Ephrem and much of the Christian community moved west to Edessa, and the churches left behind under Persian rule faced waves of persecution as a suspected foreign fifth column.
voices: Tatian — compiled the Diatessaron, a single continuous gospel woven from the four, which Syriac churches used as their standard gospel text for centuries
Bardaisan of Edessa — philosopher, astrologer and hymn-writer at the Edessan court, whose cosmological teaching the later Syriac tradition rejected while keeping his poetic form
Jacob of Nisibis — bishop of Nisibis until 338, remembered as the city's protector during Persian siege
Ephrem the Syrian — deacon, teacher and the tradition's greatest poet, who moved from Nisibis to Edessa in 363 and died caring for famine victims there
movements.legacy: This is a living inheritance, not a closed chapter. The Syriac churches that descend from it — the Assyrian Church of the East, the Syriac Orthodox Church, and the Eastern Catholic churches in communion with Rome — still worship in Syriac and still sing Ephrem's hymns. Syriac Christianity carried the faith east along the trade routes into Persia, to India, and as far as Tang-dynasty China, and Syriac translators later became the channel through which Greek philosophy and medicine passed into Arabic and eventually back to Europe. The School of Nisibis became one of the ancient world's most important centres of theological education.

experienceToday.text: Mor Gabriel Monastery, Tur Abdin, southeastern Turkey — founded in 397 and still a working monastery and the seat of the metropolitan of Tur Abdin, one of the oldest continuously inhabited Christian monasteries on earth

movements.name: Latin Pastoral-Congregational Christianity
movements.statusDescription: One of the traditions chosen for its era after a completed survey. Construction has not begun.
movements.sourcing: Rich (Cyprian's letters, Augustine's sermons to his own flock)
movements.floorNote: Nothing in this tradition's confession diverges from the doctrine the Nicene Creed states.
movements.relationsSummary: Confirmed distinct from the Imperial tradition; Donatism contests its interval
movements.why: This tradition has already been chosen: the ordinary congregational life of Latin North Africa — Cyprian steering his flock through plague and persecution, Augustine preaching to his own people at Hippo week after week, baptisms and penance and the daily care of souls under a bishop's office. Not the councils, not the controversies — the parish, long before that word existed. Construction has not yet begun.
movements.teaser: Roman North Africa, c. 240s to 430 CE — the parish before the word existed: bishops burying plague victims, preaching to the same faces every week, and deciding what to do about the people who had failed.
movements.longDescription: This is the ordinary congregational life of Latin-speaking North Africa — not the councils and not the controversies, but the week in and week out work of a bishop with a flock. Cyprian became bishop of Carthage around 248, went into hiding when the emperor Decius ordered universal sacrifice, and returned to the hardest pastoral problem of the age: what to do with the thousands of his own people who had complied and now wanted back in. He organized relief through the epidemic that still bears his name, telling his congregation to nurse pagan neighbours as well as their own, and was beheaded outside Carthage in 258. A century and a half later Augustine, bishop of Hippo Regius from 395 until his death in 430, preached to the same congregation several times a week for thirty-five years, with stenographers taking much of it down — hundreds of those sermons survive, arguing, joking, scolding and consoling actual people whose situations he knew. Between the two: catechumens under instruction, baptisms at Easter, penitents doing public penance, the care of widows and the poor, and the bishop sitting as judge in his own people's disputes.
voices: Cyprian of Carthage — bishop through persecution and plague, whose letters are the fullest surviving picture of how a third-century congregation actually ran
Pontius the Deacon — Cyprian's deacon, who wrote an account of his bishop's life and death
Augustine of Hippo — bishop of Hippo Regius for thirty-five years, and the most extensively documented working pastor of the ancient world
Possidius of Calama — Augustine's friend and fellow bishop, who wrote his biography and catalogued his works
movements.legacy: The North African church itself did not survive: the Vandals took the province in the 430s, and the Arab conquest of the seventh century ended Latin Christianity there altogether. What it left behind is the working vocabulary of Western church life. Cyprian's letters became foundational for Western understandings of the bishop's office and the unity of the church; Augustine's sermons shaped Christian preaching for well over a thousand years, and the catechumenate and penitential practice worked out in these congregations became the pattern for Western sacramental discipline. Latin Christianity's basic assumptions about what a local church is were largely formed in these two African towns.

experienceToday.text: Hippo Regius and the Basilica of Saint Augustine, Annaba, Algeria — the excavated ruins of Augustine's city lie below a nineteenth-century basilica overlooking the site, both open to visitors

movements.name: Tertullian's Voice
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Rich corpus, one man
movements.relationsSummary: Forged much of the Latin theological vocabulary; no clear home since the Cyprian/Jerome tradition-split
movements.why: A dropped voice, not a dropped tradition - on record as such. Where he belongs is an open question for a future pass.
movements.teaser: Carthage, c. 197 to 220 CE — a trained rhetorician's mind turned loose on the Christian faith, forced to invent the Latin words the West has argued in ever since.
movements.longDescription: Tertullian was the first major Christian author to write in Latin rather than Greek, which meant that a great deal of what he wanted to say had no words yet — so he made them. Trinitas, persona, substantia, sacramentum: the technical vocabulary Western Christians still use came substantially off his pen, and his formula of one substance in three persons became the standard Latin way of stating the doctrine of God. He wrote like the advocate he was trained to be: the Apology dismantling Roman slanders against Christians, Against Praxeas arguing that Father and Son are genuinely distinct, and On the Prescription of Heretics contending that heretics have no standing even to cite Scripture, since the Scriptures belong to the churches that received them. In his later years he grew steadily more rigorist — against remarriage, against flight in persecution, against what he saw as a church going soft — and aligned himself with the New Prophecy out of Phrygia, which is one reason the Latin church quoted him endlessly and never made him a saint.
voices: Tertullian of Carthage — the tradition is one man: a convert, probably a trained rhetorician, writing in Carthage from roughly 197 to 220
Cyprian of Carthage — not a follower, but Jerome reports that Cyprian read Tertullian every day and would ask for the volume by saying 'give me the master'
movements.legacy: No community descends from him — there is some evidence of a small group of followers in Carthage after his death, and nothing beyond that. His legacy is linguistic and rhetorical: the Latin words for the Trinity, and lines that entered the common speech of Christianity, most famously his claim that the blood of Christians is seed. Cyprian, Jerome and Augustine all read him closely, and the Western habit of thinking about God, the church and the sacraments in legal and forensic categories owes a great deal to a man who was never canonized and never quite belonged anywhere.

movements.name: Marcion / Marcionism
movements.statusDescription: Excluded on a stated creedal ground you can read in full. Exclusion is not a judgment of unimportance.
movements.sourcing: Substantial, almost entirely via opponents
movements.floorNote: Marcion taught two distinct gods — the creator of the Hebrew Scriptures and a higher Father revealed by Jesus — and a Christ who only appeared to have a body. Both directly contradict the creed's confession of one God, maker of all things, and a Son truly made flesh.
movements.relationsSummary: Second-century rival the proto-orthodox defined themselves against
movements.why: Excluded by the doctrinal floor - a design effect, not an evidentiary judgment, and not a judgment of unimportance. Appears plainly inside Tradition I.1's own contested milieu.
movements.teaser: Rome and across the empire, c. 140 into the 300s CE — a shipowner who concluded the God of the Hebrew Scriptures could not possibly be the Father of Jesus, and built a rival church on that conviction.
movements.longDescription: Marcion came from Sinope on the Black Sea, made a considerable fortune in shipping, and arrived in Rome around 140 where he gave the church there a very large donation. Reading Paul on law and grace, he concluded that the just, law-giving creator of the Hebrew Scriptures and the merciful Father whom Jesus revealed were simply two different beings — and that Christ, sent by the higher God into a world he had not made, could not have taken real flesh from it. In 144 the Roman church expelled him and returned his money; he replied by organizing congregations of his own, which spread fast along the trade routes he knew and endured for centuries in the East. He gave them their own Scripture: a single gospel based on Luke and ten letters of Paul, edited to remove what he judged to be Jewish corruption, together with a book called the Antitheses setting the two Gods against one another point by point. Not one line of his own writing survives — everything we have comes through the men who wrote to refute him, above all Tertullian, whose Against Marcion runs to five books.
voices: Marcion of Sinope — shipowner and organizer, who founded an alternative church with its own bishops and its own edited Scripture
Tertullian of Carthage — wrote five books Against Marcion, the fullest surviving account of what Marcion actually taught
Irenaeus of Lyons — one of the earliest to answer him, and the source for the story that Polycarp, meeting Marcion in the street, called him 'the firstborn of Satan'
Justin Martyr — wrote against him within Marcion's own lifetime, in a work now lost
movements.legacy: Marcionite churches faded in the West by roughly the fourth century and lingered considerably longer in Syria and the East, but nothing descends from them. What Marcion left behind is what he provoked: congregations that had never needed to specify which books counted as Scripture discovered that they now had to, and the confession of one God, maker of heaven and earth, whose Son truly took flesh, was hammered into its sharpest early form in argument against him. How far he actually caused the New Testament canon rather than accelerated a process already under way is still debated by historians.

movements.name: Valentinian & other Gnostic Christianities
movements.statusDescription: Excluded on a stated creedal ground you can read in full. Exclusion is not a judgment of unimportance.
movements.sourcing: Nag Hammadi gave real internal texts
movements.floorNote: Apparent-body Christology; pleroma vs. one Maker of all
movements.relationsSummary: Rivals the early traditions anathematized and were shaped by
movements.why: Excluded by the doctrinal floor. Where relevant they appear inside the traditions that defined themselves against them - as live neighbors, not defeated foils.
movements.teaser: Alexandria, Rome and far beyond, c. 120 to 300 CE — teachers who told the Christian story as a cosmic drama of a divine spark fallen into matter, and whose own books lay buried in an Egyptian jar until 1945.
movements.longDescription: Valentinus was an Alexandrian teacher who came to Rome around 136 and, according to Tertullian, was nearly elected bishop there. He and the students who carried his name — Ptolemy, Heracleon, Theodotus — taught that the visible world was made not by the highest God but by a lesser craftsman, that human beings carry within them a spark of the divine that has fallen into matter, and that Christ came to bring the knowledge that wakes it up. Along with related currents around teachers like Basilides, they mostly did not build rival churches: they sat in ordinary congregations and offered their teaching as the deeper meaning available to those ready for it, which is precisely what alarmed bishops like Irenaeus, whose five-volume Against Heresies of about 180 was written to drag the system into the open and refute it. For eighteen centuries they were known almost entirely through such opponents — until 1945, when farmers digging near Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt turned up a sealed jar of papyrus codices in Coptic, including the Gospel of Truth, giving these currents their own voice for the first time since antiquity.
voices: Valentinus — Alexandrian teacher, later in Rome, the most influential figure of these currents and possibly the author of the Gospel of Truth
Ptolemy — a Valentinian teacher whose Letter to Flora, a patient explanation of how to read the Law of Moses, survives nearly complete
Heracleon — wrote the earliest known commentary on the Gospel of John, preserved in fragments quoted by Origen
Basilides — an Alexandrian teacher of a related but distinct system, known only through hostile summaries
Irenaeus of Lyons — their most thorough opponent, whose refutation preserved much of what they taught
movements.legacy: No community survives, and none claims descent. Their trace is double. First, the shape of what became orthodox Christianity was set partly by the labour of answering them: the insistence that the one God made matter and called it good, that the Son took real flesh and rose in a real body, and that the faith is a public rule handed down openly rather than a secret reserved for initiates, were all pressed into their enduring form in this argument. Second, since 1945 the Nag Hammadi texts have been read, translated and fought over continuously, and have reshaped how modern readers picture the diversity of the earliest Christian centuries.

experienceToday.text: The Coptic Museum, Cairo — holds the Nag Hammadi codices along with the world's largest collection of Coptic Christian art, and is open to the public

movements.name: Manichaeism
movements.statusDescription: Excluded on a stated creedal ground you can read in full. Exclusion is not a judgment of unimportance.
movements.sourcing: Rich own corpus survives
movements.floorNote: Co-original dualism denies 'maker of all things'; most scholars: a distinct universal religion
movements.relationsSummary: Augustine's own former allegiance
movements.why: Excluded by the doctrinal floor, and by most modern scholarship's judgment that it is its own religion rather than a Christian movement.
movements.teaser: From Persia to the Mediterranean and on to China, from 216 CE into the centuries beyond — a prophet who set out to found the one universal religion, and whose one intact surviving temple still stands on a hillside in Fujian.
movements.longDescription: Mani was born in Mesopotamia in 216 and raised in a Jewish-Christian baptizing sect before breaking with it after what he described as revelations from his heavenly twin. He taught that reality is the battleground of two co-eternal principles, Light and Darkness, that particles of light are trapped in the material world, and that a strict ascetic discipline sets them free. Almost uniquely among founders of his era he wrote his own scriptures and had them translated deliberately, intending a faith that could absorb and supersede Christianity, Zoroastrianism and Buddhism at once — and for a time it worked, spreading from Persia across the Roman Empire and eastward along the Silk Road into Central Asia and China. His followers divided into the Elect, who kept the full discipline, and the Hearers, who supported them and lived ordinary lives; Augustine of Hippo was a Hearer for roughly nine years before his conversion, and spent much of his later career arguing against the teachers he had once sat under. Mani himself died in custody under the Persian king Bahram I in the 270s.
voices: Mani — the founder, who wrote his own scriptures rather than leaving the task to disciples, and died in a Persian prison
Faustus of Milevis — the Manichaean bishop whose teaching Augustine sought out as a young man and later refuted at length
Augustine of Hippo — a Hearer for about nine years, then the movement's most effective Latin opponent, and an unintended preserver of its arguments
movements.legacy: In the West it was hunted by emperors and by the church and had largely vanished by the sixth century, though the word 'Manichaean' survived for centuries afterwards as an insult aimed at anyone thought too fond of dualism. In the East it lasted far longer: it was for a time the state religion of the Uyghur Khaganate from the 760s, and persisted in southern China for many centuries. Because Mani wrote his own books, and because manuscripts have been recovered over the last century from Turfan in western China, from Medinet Madi in Egypt, and in the miniature Cologne Mani Codex, this is one of the few extinct ancient religions that can now be read substantially in its own words rather than only through its enemies.

experienceToday.text: Cao'an, Jinjiang, Fujian, China — long regarded as the only intact surviving Manichaean temple, with its carved image of Mani, inscribed as part of the Quanzhou UNESCO World Heritage site in 2021

movements.name: Ebionite / Nazoraean Current
movements.statusDescription: The record is genuinely disputed. This entry carries the question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Almost wholly hostile heresiological description
movements.floorNote: Some outside writers report that they denied Jesus's virgin birth and divinity; others report the opposite of the group they call Nazoraeans. Because nothing survives from these communities themselves, what they actually confessed cannot be established either way — an open question about the evidence, not a settled verdict about their doctrine.
movements.relationsSummary: Jewish-Christian continuity; rhymes with Era 9's Messianic Judaism entry
movements.why: Not built because the record cannot even establish what they themselves confessed. Held as an honest open question - deliberately not cited alongside settled exclusions.
movements.teaser: Palestine and Syria, roughly the first through fourth centuries — Jewish followers of Jesus who never stopped keeping the Law, and whose own words have not survived to tell us what they actually believed.
movements.longDescription: The first Christians were Jews, and in Palestine and Syria some communities of Jewish believers in Jesus went on keeping Torah, circumcision and the Sabbath long after the wider church had moved away from them. Later heresy-hunting writers — Irenaeus, Origen, Eusebius, Epiphanius, Jerome — describe them under two names, 'Ebionites', from the Hebrew for the poor, and 'Nazoraeans', reporting that they used their own Hebrew or Aramaic gospel, honoured James the brother of Jesus, and regarded Paul as an apostate from the Law. But those writers disagree with one another, wrote from outside and often centuries later, and had every reason to sharpen the picture; the fullest account of all, Epiphanius's Panarion, is now widely judged unreliable in its details. Not one text these communities wrote about themselves survives intact — only fragments quoted by the people refuting them — and modern scholars genuinely disagree about whether 'Ebionite' and 'Nazoraean' name two distinct groups, one group under two labels, or largely a category the heresy-hunters assembled.
voices: No leader of these communities is named in any source they produced themselves. The heresy-hunters offer only 'Ebion', a supposed founder most scholars now think never existed — invented to explain a group name that in fact meant simply 'the poor'.
movements.legacy: No community descends from them. They disappear from the record by roughly the fifth century, absorbed into the wider church or back into Judaism or simply gone, and the gospel material attributed to them survives only as quotations in the writers who opposed them. What they left behind is a question rather than an institution: they are the standing reminder that Christianity began inside Judaism, and that the separation of the two was slower, later and far more contested than a tidy account allows. Modern Messianic Jewish movements are sometimes compared to them, but no line of descent connects them.

movements.name: Montanism (the New Prophecy)
movements.statusDescription: The concern is limited primary sourcing, not that prophetic leaders were involved. Surviving evidence centers on a handful of quoted oracles from three named prophets and hostile reports; whether independent community voices survive (some Phrygian inscriptions may point that way) isn't yet resolved.
movements.sourcing: Oracles, Tertullian's advocacy, Phrygian inscriptions
movements.floorNote: What the New Prophecy confessed about God, Christ and the Spirit is not what its opponents objected to — as far as the surviving evidence shows, it held the same doctrine as the churches that condemned it. The dispute was about authority and discipline: whether new prophecy could bind the church, and how strict its common life should be.
movements.relationsSummary: Named live neighbor inside Tradition I.1's milieu
movements.why: Still investigating: the concern is limited primary sourcing (what survives runs through three named prophets and their opponents), not that prophetic leaders were involved. LIVE QUESTION on record: Phrygian inscriptions may document a wider communal ecology - the test might yield here.
movements.teaser: Phrygia in inland Asia Minor, from around 165 CE into the centuries after — a movement convinced the Spirit was still speaking, which named the village where it expected the New Jerusalem to come down.
movements.longDescription: In a Phrygian village in the middle of the second century a man named Montanus began prophesying in ecstatic speech, and two women, Priscilla and Maximilla, prophesied alongside him. They did not call themselves Montanists — that was their opponents' label. They called it simply the New Prophecy, and their claim was that the Paraclete whom Jesus had promised was speaking now, through them. What followed was less exotic than the label suggests: stricter fasting, refusal of second marriages, a readiness to face martyrdom rather than flee it, and the expectation that the New Jerusalem would descend at Pepuza in Phrygia. It spread well beyond Asia Minor — Tertullian of Carthage became its most articulate Latin advocate — and although Asian synods condemned it and later imperial law suppressed it, communities persisted for centuries. Pepuza and its neighbour Tymion, lost for well over a thousand years, were located by archaeologists in inland Turkey only in 2000.
voices: Montanus — the prophet whose name opponents attached to the movement, though its own name for itself was the New Prophecy
Priscilla and Maximilla — the two prophetesses who spoke alongside him, and whose quoted oracles are among the very few first-person Montanist words that survive at all
Tertullian of Carthage — the movement's most articulate Latin defender, and the only sympathetic writer whose work survives in quantity
The ordinary members are the gap in the record: almost everything else comes through hostile writers such as Apollonius and the anonymous author quoted by Eusebius
movements.legacy: No church descends from the New Prophecy. Imperial suppression under Justinian in the sixth century finished it, its own writings were destroyed, and what remains is a handful of quoted oracles plus a body of Phrygian gravestone inscriptions whose Montanist identity is itself argued over — which is the honest difficulty with this entry: the surviving evidence runs overwhelmingly through the three named prophets and through their enemies, and whether an independent community voice survives anywhere is not yet settled. What outlasted the movement is the set of questions it forced: whether prophecy continued after the apostles, who may authorize it, and how a church distinguishes genuine inspiration from enthusiasm. Later renewal movements down to modern Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity have repeatedly been accused of reviving it, and have occasionally claimed the comparison themselves, though no historical line connects them.

movements.name: Novatianism
movements.statusDescription: The concern is limited primary sourcing, not that a single leader was involved. Surviving evidence centers on Novatian's own rigorist stance and rival ordination; whether an independent community voice beyond his own survives in the record isn't yet resolved.
movements.sourcing: Novatian's De Trinitate is broadly orthodox; community texture thinner
movements.floorNote: Novatian's own On the Trinity is a careful and orthodox statement of Christian doctrine, and the Novatianist bishop present at Nicaea accepted the council's creed. The break was over discipline — whether the church could readmit those who had denied the faith under persecution — not over belief.
movements.relationsSummary: Rigorist parallel communion; redundancy risk vs. Donatism noted if revisited
movements.why: Still investigating: the concern is limited primary sourcing (what survives is largely Novatian's own writing plus outsiders' reports), not that a single leader was involved. Whether a broader communal tradition survives independently in the record isn't yet resolved.
movements.teaser: Rome and across the empire, from 251 CE into the centuries after — a rival church founded the day a Roman theologian decided that Christians who had denied Christ under threat could never be readmitted.
movements.longDescription: When the emperor Decius ordered every subject of the empire to sacrifice in 250, a great many Christians complied, and once the pressure lifted they wanted to come back. Novatian — the most learned theologian in the Roman church and the first there to write substantial theology in Latin — held that the church had no authority to receive them: God might forgive apostasy, but the church could not presume to. When Cornelius, who took the lenient view, was elected bishop of Rome in 251, Novatian's supporters had him consecrated as a rival bishop, one of the earliest such rival consecrations the city had seen. His congregations called themselves the Katharoi, the pure, and they spread across the empire and lasted for centuries; at the end of the fourth century they still held several churches in Constantinople and more across Phrygia and Bithynia. What stands out is how little separated them in doctrine: their bishop attended the Council of Nicaea in 325 and accepted its creed, and the council's eighth canon set out terms for receiving Novatianist clergy — terms they largely declined. Later tradition remembers Novatian himself as a martyr, though the record on that is not firm.
voices: Novatian — Roman presbyter and theologian, author of On the Trinity, consecrated rival bishop of Rome in 251
Cornelius — the bishop of Rome whose willingness to readmit the lapsed Novatian opposed
Cyprian of Carthage — sided with Cornelius, and much of what is known about the dispute comes through his correspondence
Acesius — the Novatianist bishop of Constantinople at Nicaea, to whom the historian Socrates reports Constantine said: set up a ladder, Acesius, and climb to heaven by yourself
The congregations themselves are thin in the record — their story is told almost entirely by outside historians rather than in their own surviving words
movements.legacy: No church descends from them; the last Novatianist communities faded in the East by around the seventh century. Two things outlasted the schism. The first is the doctrine sharpened against it — that the church is a hospital rather than a society of the already-perfect, and that no sin lies beyond the reach of the church's ministry of reconciliation — worked out by Cyprian in the moment and by Augustine at length afterwards, along with the graded system of public penance that grew out of exactly this argument. The second is Novatian's own On the Trinity, which was copied, read and valued in the mainstream church as a careful Latin statement of orthodox doctrine long after his party was gone, handed down in manuscripts among the works of Tertullian.

movements.name: Desert Monasticism
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Small corpus, deep on inner combat (disclosed on its tile)
movements.floorNote: The desert communities held the same Nicene faith as the churches they came out of — what set them apart was a way of life, not a different doctrine.
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Alexandria's milieu; parent of all later monasticism
movements.why: It is — open for conversation now (Representative: Papnoute).

entry.subtitle: Desert Monasticism
entry.tile: The Nile Valley and the desert of Egypt, c. 320 to 430 CE — communities who left settled village life to wage a lifelong combat against the thoughts that trouble a person from within.

movements.longDescription: Beginning in the late third century, Egyptian Christians started walking out of their villages into the desert — first alone, into caves and abandoned forts, then into loose settlements, and finally into organized communities with shared meals, shared work, and a written rule. What drew them was not escape but combat: the conviction that the real battlefield of a Christian life is inward, among the thoughts and appetites that trouble a person from within, and that learning to fight there takes a lifetime of silence, manual labour, and blunt honesty with an elder. Their teaching passed mostly in short exchanges — a younger monk asking an elder for "a word," the elder answering in a sentence — later gathered into the collections we call the Sayings of the Desert Fathers and Mothers. By the fifth century visitors from Rome, Gaul, and Palestine were coming to watch and take notes, and what they carried home became the seed of monastic life across the whole Christian world.
voices: Antony the Great — the hermit whose withdrawal into the Egyptian desert, and the biography Athanasius wrote about him, made the movement famous across the empire
Pachomius — a former soldier who gathered scattered hermits into organized communities under a common rule, and so invented communal monasticism
Amma Syncletica — one of the desert mothers, remembered for sayings on the ascetic struggle preserved alongside the men's
Evagrius Ponticus — a scholar turned monk who mapped the inner life, naming the eight troubling thoughts that became the West's seven deadly sins
John Cassian — a visitor who spent years among the Egyptian monks and carried their teaching west in Latin, where Benedict later read him
movements.legacy: Almost every later form of Christian monastic life descends from here: Benedict's Rule sends its readers to John Cassian's reports from Egypt, and the monasteries of Sinai, Athos, and the wider East trace their practice to the same source. The sayings are still read as spiritual reading in Orthodox, Catholic, and Protestant circles alike, and Evagrius's list of the eight troubling thoughts became, by way of Gregory the Great, the seven deadly sins of Western moral teaching. Some of the houses founded in that first Egyptian generation are still living communities — the Coptic monasteries of St Antony and St Paul near the Red Sea, and the cluster at Wadi al-Natrun, are inhabited by monks today.

experienceToday.text: The Monastery of Saint Anthony, Eastern Desert, Egypt — a Coptic Orthodox monastery grown up around Antony's own cave, still inhabited and open to visitors

movements.name: Donatism
movements.statusDescription: One of the traditions chosen for its era after a completed survey. Construction has not begun.
movements.sourcing: Substantial but heavily via opponents (Augustine) - a named challenge
movements.floorNote: Donatism held the same Nicene doctrine as its rivals — the dispute was about who could validly serve as clergy after the persecution, not about the Trinity, Christ's divinity, or any point of creedal belief.
movements.relationsSummary: Rival-sibling of the Latin pastoral tradition; martyr-memory identity
movements.why: This tradition has already been chosen — and it may surprise you that it's here: the churches of Roman North Africa that broke communion with their neighbors over what faithfulness under persecution required, kept their own bishops for a century, and built their identity on the memory of the martyrs. History mostly remembers them through their opponents — Augustine wrote against them, and the label "Donatist" was never their own name for themselves. That is exactly why this project chose them: a whole communion of real Christians, serious about holiness, known mainly through hostile pens, deserves to speak as itself. Construction has not yet begun.
movements.longDescription: When Rome's persecution of Christians ended in 313, the churches of North Africa split over what happened next: could bishops who had handed over Scriptures to be burned, or otherwise compromised under threat of death, still validly ordain and consecrate? The Donatists said no — only those untainted by that betrayal could carry on the church's ministry — and for roughly a century they were the majority church across much of Roman Africa, with their own bishops, their own martyrs, and a fierce insistence that holiness, not political favor, marked the true church. Their most famous opponent was Augustine of Hippo, whose writings against them are almost all that survives of their story — the Donatists rarely got to speak in their own words, and even their name was one their rivals gave them. Imperial pressure and, eventually, the Vandal invasions wore the movement down, but for a long stretch of the fourth and fifth centuries, this was simply what Christianity looked like across much of North Africa.
movements.teaser: Roman North Africa, c. 312 to 430s CE — a church of martyrs' descendants who refused to let those who had betrayed the faith under persecution lead it again, known to history mostly through the words of their fiercest opponent.

sources.work: Augustine, On Baptism, Against the Donatists
sources.note: The fullest surviving account of Donatist belief and practice is in the writings of their chief opponent.

voices: Donatus Magnus — the movement's founding bishop and namesake
Petilian of Cirta — a Donatist bishop whose own writings, now lost, survive only in Augustine's quotations of them
Tyconius — a Donatist theologian whose ideas on the church shaped Augustine's own thinking even as his own party distanced itself from him
Augustine of Hippo — the tradition's most consequential opponent, whose polemics are the main surviving record of their arguments
movements.legacy: Donatism left no continuing church of its own — its last communities disappeared under the Arab conquest of North Africa in the seventh century. But arguing against it, Augustine worked out that the church is a mixed body of saints and sinners rather than a pure remnant, and that a sacrament's validity doesn't depend on the minister's own holiness — both became foundational, lasting Western Christian doctrine. Excavated basilica ruins from Donatist-era Timgad, one of their strongholds in Roman Numidia, still stand in Algeria today — a physical trace of a communion that otherwise left no institution behind.

experienceToday.text: Timgad, Algeria — UNESCO World Heritage Roman ruins including a Donatist-era basilica

movements.name: Cappadocian Nicene Pastoral-Monastic Tradition
movements.statusDescription: One of the traditions chosen for its era after a completed survey. Construction has not begun.
movements.sourcing: Rich (Basil, the Gregories, Macrina; letters, rules, sermons)
movements.floorNote: These are among the people who wrote the creed. The language it uses for Father, Son, and Spirit is substantially theirs.
movements.relationsSummary: Trinitarian theology + charitable-ascetic pastoral practice; Jerome heard Gregory teach
movements.why: This tradition has already been chosen — one of the nine selected for this era: the communities around Basil of Caesarea, Gregory of Nazianzus, Gregory of Nyssa, and Macrina, where the words Christians still confess about the Trinity were being forged in real congregations, real letters, real grief. Nothing about it was judged too hard or too thin — it was selected on the strength of its sources; construction simply has not begun.
movements.longDescription: In the highland province of Cappadocia, through the 360s and 370s, one extended family and the friends around it did more than anyone else to settle the words Christians still use about God. Basil of Caesarea, his younger brother Gregory of Nyssa, their elder sister Macrina, and Basil's friend Gregory of Nazianzus argued their way through the hardest question of the century — whether the Son and the Spirit are God in the same sense the Father is — and did it not in the abstract but while running dioceses, burying relatives, quarrelling with each other, and feeding the hungry. Macrina turned the family estate into an ascetic household and, in her brother Gregory's account of her last days, taught him theology from her deathbed; Basil built a hospital, hostel, and workhouse complex outside Caesarea after the famine of 368, and wrote rules for communal ascetic life that still govern Eastern monasticism. Gregory of Nazianzus carried the argument in public, preaching it to the churches of Constantinople, and the creed most Christians still recite on a Sunday took its final shape at the council held there in 381, in the settlement their work made possible.
movements.teaser: Cappadocia, in the highlands of what is now central Turkey, c. 360 to 380s — one family and their friends hammering out the words Christians still say about God, in the middle of famine relief, funerals, and quarrels with each other.
voices: Basil of Caesarea — bishop, monastic legislator, and builder of the great hospital and poorhouse complex outside his city
Macrina the Younger — their elder sister, who turned the family estate into an ascetic community, and whose teaching Gregory of Nyssa recorded as hers rather than his own
Gregory of Nazianzus — the reluctant preacher whose sermons on the Trinity at Constantinople carried the argument in public
Gregory of Nyssa — Basil's younger brother, the most speculative of them, who wrote on the soul, the resurrection, and the soul's endless ascent into God
Emmelia — mother of Basil, Macrina, and Gregory, who ran the household this whole tradition grew out of
movements.legacy: Their settlement of the language — one being, three persons — became the standard grammar of Christian talk about God in East and West alike, and stands behind the creed recited in most churches on Sunday. Basil's rules for communal ascetic life remain the foundation of Eastern Orthodox monasticism, and his hospital-and-hostel complex for the sick and destitute is regularly named among the ancestors of the Christian hospital. All four are venerated as saints across the Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican, and Lutheran calendars, and Gregory of Nazianzus is one of only three figures the Eastern church calls simply "the Theologian."

movements.name: Imperial and Juridical Christianity
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutional (Eusebius, Ambrose, Leo)
movements.floorNote: This is the tradition that convened Nicaea and eventually made its creed imperial law, so its standing on the Creed is not in doubt. It is worth saying plainly, though, that this was never obvious to the people living through it: for long stretches of the fourth century the emperor's own church was Homoian rather than Nicene. The hard questions here are about power, not about doctrine.
movements.relationsSummary: Three causally-linked phases merged into one tradition (on record); must depict Homoian rivals plainly
movements.why: It is — open for conversation now (Representative: Marius).

entry.subtitle: Imperial and Juridical Christianity
entry.tile: Rome, Constantinople, and Milan, c. 312 to 451 CE — the church's first century beside a throne rather than beneath a sword, working out what the emperor's favor bought and what it could still take away.

movements.longDescription: For nearly three centuries the church had been an illegal association. Then, between Constantine's grant of toleration in 313 and Theodosius's legislation at the end of the century, it became first protected, then privileged, then the empire's official religion — and had to work out, very fast, what to do with that. Bishops found themselves hearing civil lawsuits, administering public building funds, and travelling to councils at imperial expense; emperors found themselves summoning those councils and expecting the results to hold. The terms of that unplanned bargain were tested constantly — Ambrose of Milan made Theodosius do public penance after the massacre at Thessalonica in 390, and a doctrinal letter Leo of Rome had written two years earlier to the bishop of Constantinople was read out at Chalcedon in 451 and received as settling the matter — and what the arrangement produced, canon law, church courts, a hierarchy mapped onto imperial administration, and a permanent argument about where a ruler's authority ends, outlasted the western empire itself.
voices: Constantine — the first emperor to protect and endow the church, and the first to summon a general council of its bishops
Eusebius of Caesarea — bishop and historian, who wrote the first church history and the most admiring account of Constantine's reign
Theodosius I — whose laws made Nicene Christianity the empire's official religion, and who did public penance at Ambrose's insistence
Ambrose of Milan — the bishop who set the precedent that an emperor stands inside the church rather than above it
Leo I of Rome — whose letter to the bishop of Constantinople, written in 449 and read aloud at Chalcedon in 451, was received as settling the question of Christ's two natures
movements.legacy: This is where most of what people mean by "the institutional church" was built: canon law, church courts, dioceses drawn along the empire's own administrative lines, and the assumption that a general council can settle a disputed doctrine for everybody. The argument it started — where a ruler's authority over the church ends and the church's over the ruler begins — runs on through the medieval investiture disputes, the Reformation's territorial settlements, and every later fight about established churches and their disestablishment. Its physical inheritance is still standing: the basilica, a Roman public hall rather than a temple, was the form the emperors paid for, and it remains the basic shape of church buildings across Europe.

experienceToday.text: The Archbasilica of St John Lateran, Rome — founded under Constantine in the 320s and still the cathedral church of the bishop of Rome

movements.name: Hieronymian Ascetic-Literary Christianity
movements.statusDescription: You can sit down with this tradition now.
movements.sourcing: Richest written record of the four built worlds - mostly via one prolific pen (disclosed)
movements.floorNote: Nothing here is in question on the Creed. Jerome was a combative defender of Nicene orthodoxy, and the circle's controversies were about asceticism, Origen's legacy, and the right basis for translating Scripture.
movements.relationsSummary: Built around the women's ascetic-patronage network (Paula, Marcella, Eustochium)
movements.why: It is — open for conversation now (Representative: Albina).

entry.subtitle: Hieronymian Ascetic-Literary Christianity
entry.tile: Rome and Bethlehem, c. 382 to 420 CE — a circle of scholars and ascetics who gave up wealth and rank to test Scripture's Latin translation against the Hebrew it was first given in.

movements.longDescription: In the early 380s a circle of wealthy Roman women — Marcella on the Aventine, and the widow Paula with her daughter Eustochium — began meeting to study Scripture and to live an ascetic life in the middle of the city, taking as their teacher a caustic, brilliant scholar named Jerome. Roman society found the whole arrangement scandalous: senatorial fortunes given away, aristocratic daughters refusing marriage, a priest shut up with widows over Hebrew grammar. When Jerome's protector Pope Damasus died in 384 and the hostility became unbearable, Paula and Eustochium sold their estates, sailed east, and founded monasteries at Bethlehem — a house for men, houses for women, and a hostel for pilgrims — with Jerome installed alongside to work. What came out of that arrangement was the Vulgate: a Latin Bible built book by book, against fierce criticism — the Old Testament rendered not from the Greek everyone was used to but from the Hebrew it had first been written in — and a body of letters in which the women's questions, funding, and insistence are visible on nearly every page.
voices: Jerome — the scholar and translator at the centre of it, whose Latin Bible became the West's standard text for a thousand years
Paula — the Roman widow who funded and led the move to Bethlehem and built its monasteries and pilgrim hostel
Eustochium — Paula's daughter, who took a vow of virginity as a girl in Rome and ran the Bethlehem women's houses after her mother's death
Marcella — the Aventine widow in whose household the circle began, and who kept pressing Jerome with questions about the biblical text long after he had left Rome
Rufinus of Aquileia — Jerome's old friend and fellow translator, whose bitter public quarrel with him over Origen split the wider ascetic network
movements.legacy: The Vulgate became the Bible of the Latin West for over a thousand years — the text medieval theology argued from, the text later translators worked from or against, and the text the Council of Trent declared authentic in 1546. Its principle mattered as much as its content: Jerome's insistence on going back to the Hebrew rather than resting on the Greek is the ancestor of every later "back to the sources" movement, including the Renaissance and Reformation scholarship that eventually turned on the Vulgate itself. The circle left a second, quieter pattern too — wealthy women funding, hosting, and directing serious biblical scholarship — which recurs constantly in later Christian history. And the caves beneath the Church of the Nativity in Bethlehem, where tradition places Jerome's study, are still shown to pilgrims.

experienceToday.text: Church of the Nativity and the Pilgrimage Route, Bethlehem — the UNESCO World Heritage site whose underground caves include the one long shown as Jerome's study

movements.name: Armenian Christianity (conversion era)
movements.statusDescription: Considered for its era and held for a later one — the reasons are on record.
movements.sourcing: Periods and transitions better attested than separable inner sub-traditions in this window
movements.relationsSummary: Formed via Cappadocia and Syriac Edessa
movements.why: Considered and deferred, not dropped: this era's evidence supports its story's outline more confidently than a lived inner tradition. It returns in the next era.
movements.longDescription: Armenia's own tradition holds that it was the first kingdom to adopt Christianity as its official religion, when Gregory the Illuminator — imprisoned for years in a pit, by the telling — converted King Trdat and the court around the turn of the fourth century. What followed over the next century and a half is the more remarkable part: an entire national church built from nothing, catechised at first in Greek and Syriac because Armenian had no script of its own, until the monk Mesrop Mashtots devised an alphabet around 405 and the church set about putting the Bible and the liturgy into the people's own language. That translation, made under the catholicos Sahak Partev, is still called by Armenians the Queen of Translations, and it did more than any royal decree to make Christianity Armenian rather than imported. The story of these years ends at the battle of Avarayr in 451, where Armenian nobles fought a Persian attempt to impose Zoroastrianism — a defeat on the field that became the founding story of Armenian religious identity.
movements.teaser: Armenia, c. 314 to 451 — the first kingdom to make Christianity its own, which then had to invent an alphabet before it could read the Bible in its own tongue.
voices: Gregory the Illuminator — the missionary bishop credited with converting the Armenian king and court, and the church's founding patriarch
King Trdat III — the ruler whose conversion made Armenia, by its own tradition, the first Christian kingdom
Mesrop Mashtots — the monk who created the Armenian alphabet around 405 so that Scripture and liturgy could be put into Armenian
Sahak Partev — the catholicos under whom the Armenian Bible was made, still known as the Queen of Translations
Vardan Mamikonian — commander at Avarayr in 451, killed resisting a Persian attempt to impose Zoroastrianism, and remembered ever since as a martyr
movements.legacy: This one did not end. The Armenian Apostolic Church is a living communion of several million people with a worldwide diaspora, still using the alphabet Mashtots made and the liturgical language it created. That alphabet outgrew the church that commissioned it and became the vehicle of all Armenian literature, secular as well as sacred; Armenian manuscript illumination and the carved cross-stones called khachkars grew from the same root. Avarayr is still kept as a feast, and the pattern it set — religious identity as national survival — has shaped Armenian self-understanding ever since.

experienceToday.text: Cathedral and Churches of Echmiatsin, Armenia — the mother cathedral of the Armenian Apostolic Church, begun in the early fourth century, a UNESCO World Heritage site

movements.name: Aksumite Christianity (conversion era)
movements.statusDescription: Considered for its era and held for a later one — the reasons are on record.
movements.sourcing: Same pattern as Armenia in this window; inscriptions and later narratives
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Alexandria (Frumentius consecrated by Athanasius)
movements.why: Considered and deferred, not dropped - same reason as Armenia. Ethiopia's richly documented centuries come later on the map.
movements.longDescription: The kingdom of Aksum, straddling what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea, was a Red Sea trading power with its own script and its own coinage when Christianity arrived by an almost accidental route: a young man from Tyre named Frumentius, shipwrecked and taken into the royal household, rose to be tutor and adviser, then travelled to Alexandria to ask Athanasius for a bishop — and was consecrated for the job himself, around 330. King Ezana's conversion followed, and it is legible in the most concrete way imaginable: his coins stop carrying the disc and crescent of the old religion and start carrying the cross, one of the earliest such declarations by any state anywhere. The faith took root in Ge'ez, the kingdom's own language, in which Scripture and liturgy were eventually rendered, and Frumentius's consecration bound the Ethiopian church to the Egyptian one for the next sixteen centuries. What survives from these years is mostly inscriptions, coinage, and later chronicles rather than the everyday voices of ordinary believers.
movements.teaser: Aksum, in what is now Ethiopia and Eritrea, c. 330 to 451 — a Red Sea kingdom whose conversion you can read on its own coinage, where the crescent gives way to the cross.
voices: Frumentius — a shipwrecked traveller from Tyre who became tutor at the Aksumite court and then its first bishop, remembered in Ethiopia as Abba Salama
King Ezana — the ruler whose conversion is recorded in his own inscriptions and on his coins, which change from the disc and crescent to the cross
Athanasius of Alexandria — who consecrated Frumentius, and so began the long link between the Egyptian and Ethiopian churches
movements.legacy: This became, and remains, one of the great ancient churches of the world: the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church together count tens of millions of members. It carried down a whole distinctive Christian culture — Ge'ez as a scriptural and liturgical language, a broader Old Testament canon than any other church's, drums and sistra and liturgical dance in worship, and, centuries later, the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela. The link Frumentius's consecration made with Alexandria held for roughly sixteen centuries, until the Ethiopian church received a patriarch of its own in the twentieth.

experienceToday.text: Aksum, Ethiopia — the ancient capital's stelae field, royal tombs, and Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion, a UNESCO World Heritage site

movements.name: Persian Church of the East (early)
movements.informalName: The Early Persian Church of the East
movements.statusDescription: Considered for its era and held for a later one — the reasons are on record.
movements.sourcing: Real and distinct; institutional self-identity matures after this window
movements.floorNote: The label "Nestorian" came from this church's rivals, not from itself — we judged what it actually taught from its own surviving texts, not the label its opponents pinned on it.
movements.relationsSummary: Direct heir of the Syriac tradition's Nisibis side
movements.why: Considered and deferred, not dropped: its clearest self-conscious identity matures just after this era's ceiling. First in line next era.
movements.longDescription: East of the Roman frontier, in the Persian Empire, were Christian communities that had never lived under a Christian emperor and never would — and Constantine's conversion made their position worse rather than better, since it let the Sassanian court read them as a Roman fifth column. The long persecution under Shapur II from about 340 killed clergy and laity in numbers this church remembered in a whole literature of martyr acts, its own head among them: the catholicos Shemon bar Sabbae was executed in the 340s after refusing to collect a punitive double tax from Christians to fund the war against Rome. When toleration eventually came, the church organized itself deliberately — a synod at Seleucia-Ctesiphon in 410 gave it a legal structure and a recognized head, and a further synod in 424 declared that its bishops would answer to no authority outside Persia. It worshipped in Syriac, thought in the exegetical idiom it shared with Edessa and Antioch, and was already becoming the church that would carry Christianity along the trade roads to India, Central Asia, and China.
movements.teaser: Persian Mesopotamia, to 451 — a church that never had a Christian emperor of its own, and was persecuted at home for the conversion of the one across the border.
voices: Shemon bar Sabbae — catholicos executed in the 340s after refusing to collect a punitive tax on his own people for Persia's war with Rome
Aphrahat, called the Persian Sage — whose Demonstrations, written in the 330s and 340s, are the earliest substantial witness to this church's own thinking
Marutha of Maypherqat — bishop and envoy, whose diplomacy helped make the synod of 410 possible
Isaac — the catholicos who presided at that synod, which gave the church its legal shape under Persian rule
movements.legacy: This church did not disappear. It became the Church of the East, which for centuries had the widest geographical reach of any Christian body on earth, with bishops in India, Central Asia, and Tang-dynasty China. Its descendants are living communities today — the Assyrian Church of the East and the Ancient Church of the East, along with the Chaldean Catholic Church and the Syro-Malabar Church of Kerala — and its liturgy, including the ancient eucharistic prayer of Addai and Mari, is still in use. Its Syriac scholarship also became a bridge for learning far beyond the church: translators from this world put Greek philosophy and medicine into Syriac and then Arabic, which is much of how that inheritance reached the medieval world.

movements.name: Antiochene Exegetical Christianity (Chrysostom-centered)
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Rich ordinary-lay ethical-formation material
movements.relationsSummary: Historical-literal exegesis vs. Alexandria's allegory; Theodore of Mopsuestia flag on record
movements.why: Proposed and tested; held out until its distinctiveness from the Latin pastoral tradition is demonstrated beyond geography and language. Deferred, not dropped.
movements.longDescription: Antioch was one of the largest cities of the Roman East, and the Christianity that grew there developed a distinctive habit of reading: where Alexandria hunted for the hidden spiritual sense beneath the text, Antioch's teachers insisted on what the words actually said in their own historical setting — and then pressed hard on what that demanded of the people in front of them. John Chrysostom, trained in rhetoric by the pagan orator Libanius and in Scripture by Diodore of Tarsus, preached in Antioch through the 380s and 390s to congregations of tradesmen, householders, and slaves: on money, on anger, on how you treat your servants, on the theatre and the racetrack, on almsgiving as a matter of justice rather than generosity. In 387, after the city's crowds smashed the imperial statues and Antioch waited to learn whether it would be destroyed in reprisal, he preached the sermons On the Statues to a terrified population — and the reason hundreds of his sermons survive at all is largely that people wanted to hear them again. At the end of 397 he was taken to Constantinople and made its archbishop, where he preached the same way to the imperial court, which is roughly why he died in exile in 407.
movements.teaser: Antioch, c. 350 to 430 — a school of preachers who refused to allegorize the hard sayings away, and told a city of shopkeepers and slaves exactly what the plain text asked of them.
voices: John Chrysostom — the preacher whose sermons on money, anger, and everyday cruelty earned him, from later generations, the name "golden-mouthed"
Diodore of Tarsus — his teacher, and the founder of the Antiochene habit of reading Scripture in its historical sense
Theodore of Mopsuestia — fellow student and the school's most systematic interpreter, whose Christology was condemned long after his death
Theodoret of Cyrrhus — bishop, historian, and commentator, the last great voice of the Antiochene reading
Libanius — the pagan rhetorician who trained Chrysostom, and a reminder that this Christianity was formed inside a still-classical education
movements.legacy: Chrysostom's sermons never stopped being read. They were quarried for medieval preaching, printed early and often in the Reformation era — Reformed and Lutheran preachers alike claimed him as an ancestor of expository preaching — and the eucharistic liturgy that carries his name is still the ordinary Sunday rite of the Eastern Orthodox churches. The Antiochene way of reading, insisting that a text means what it meant to those who first heard it, is the ancestor of the historical-grammatical method that later Western biblical scholarship made standard. The school's own fate was harsher: Theodore of Mopsuestia was condemned at Constantinople in 553, more than a century after his death, and much of his work survives only in Syriac translation preserved by the Church of the East.

experienceToday.text: The Patriarchal Church of St George, Istanbul — seat of the Ecumenical Patriarchate, where the relics of John Chrysostom rest after their return from Rome in 2004

movements.name: Cyrilline / Miaphysite Egyptian Tradition
movements.statusDescription: Considered for its era and held for a later one — the reasons are on record.
movements.sourcing: Viable in the earlier survey
movements.floorNote: Rejection of Chalcedon's formula, not of the Creed's content
movements.relationsSummary: Continuation of Alexandria + Desert
movements.why: On record as the natural first candidate of the next phase: its self-definition as a distinct communion crystallizes just after this era's deliberate ceiling at Chalcedon.
movements.longDescription: When the Council of Chalcedon met in 451 and defined Christ as one person "in two natures," the Egyptian church largely refused the wording — not because it thought Christ any less than fully God or fully human, but because it held to the formula Cyril of Alexandria had used against Nestorius twenty years earlier: one incarnate nature of the Word, a single united reality rather than two things described side by side. To Egyptian ears Chalcedon's language sounded like pulling Christ apart again; to Chalcedon's supporters, the Egyptian refusal sounded like collapsing his humanity. The council deposed the Alexandrian patriarch Dioscorus, imperial authority backed the Chalcedonian side, and Egypt was left with two rival hierarchies — one favoured by Constantinople, and one that most Egyptian Christians actually followed, worshipping increasingly in Coptic rather than Greek. Out of that separation came the Coptic Orthodox Church and the wider family of churches that made the same refusal.
movements.teaser: Egypt, from 451 — a church that would not say "in two natures," and became a separate communion rather than give up the words it had been taught to fight for.
voices: Cyril of Alexandria — whose formula for the unity of Christ, framed against Nestorius at Ephesus in 431, this tradition took as its standard
Dioscorus of Alexandria — his successor, deposed at Chalcedon in 451, and honoured by the Coptic Church as a confessor
Timothy Aelurus — elected patriarch by those who rejected Chalcedon, and among the first to argue the case at length
Severus of Antioch — the theologian, a generation later, who gave this position its most careful and lasting statement
movements.legacy: This is a living communion, not a closed chapter: the Coptic Orthodox Church of Egypt, together with the Armenian, Syriac, Ethiopian, Eritrean, and Indian Orthodox churches, forms the Oriental Orthodox family of tens of millions of Christians today. It preserved Coptic — the last stage of the ancient Egyptian language — as a liturgical tongue, along with a distinctive iconography, a long fasting calendar, and a monastic life descended unbroken from the desert. Modern dialogue has largely concluded that the fifth-century split was as much about vocabulary as about belief: a series of joint declarations from the 1970s onward record Oriental Orthodox, Eastern Orthodox, and Catholic representatives agreeing that they confess the same faith in Christ in different words.

experienceToday.text: The Hanging Church, Coptic Cairo — Saint Virgin Mary's Coptic Orthodox Church, built over a gate of the Roman fortress of Babylon and still in use

movements.name: Jerusalem Liturgical-Pilgrimage Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Strong - Egeria's eyewitness account plus unusually corroborating archaeology
movements.relationsSummary: Comparison-point for the Bethlehem Circle's distinctiveness on record
movements.why: A live, strong, deferred candidate: the open question was never evidence but whether it is one bounded community or a shifting population of clergy, locals, and pilgrims.
movements.longDescription: Once Constantine's builders uncovered what they took to be the tomb of Christ and raised a great church complex over it in the 330s, Jerusalem became something no other city was: a place where the events of the gospel could be commemorated on the day and at the spot they were believed to have happened. Its clergy built a liturgy out of exactly that — Palm Sunday as an actual procession down the Mount of Olives with branches in hand, the veneration of the Cross on Good Friday, an all-night vigil at the tomb at Easter — and the crowds who came to see it wrote home about what they saw. One of those visitors, a woman from the Latin west named Egeria, kept a detailed travel diary in the early 380s recording precisely what was done and when; the manuscript disappeared for centuries and was rediscovered in an Italian library in 1884, and it remains the single most valuable eyewitness account of early Christian worship anywhere. What makes this community hard to pin down is the very thing that made it distinctive: it was always part settled and part passing through — resident clergy and monks, local Christians, and a constant flow of pilgrims from every corner of the Christian world.
movements.teaser: Jerusalem, c. 325 to 450 — the one city where the gospel could be commemorated on the very day and at the very spot, and where a travelling woman wrote down exactly how it was done.
voices: Cyril of Jerusalem — bishop through much of this period, whose catechetical lectures to baptismal candidates survive nearly complete
Egeria — a western pilgrim whose diary of the early 380s is the fullest surviving eyewitness account of early Christian worship
Helena — Constantine's mother, whose visit in the 320s is bound up with the tradition of the finding of the Cross and the building of the holy sites
Juvenal — the bishop who secured Jerusalem's rank as a patriarchate at Chalcedon in 451
Melania the Elder — a Roman aristocrat who founded a monastery on the Mount of Olives and helped make the city a centre of Latin ascetic life
movements.legacy: Jerusalem's calendar became everyone's calendar. Keeping Holy Week as a sequence of days, each commemorating a specific event — the Palm Sunday procession, Maundy Thursday, the Good Friday veneration of the Cross, the Easter vigil — spread west from here, and it is still how most of the Christian world keeps Easter. So did the idea of pilgrimage itself as a Christian practice, and with it the habit of building churches that copy the shape of Jerusalem's holy places. Cyril's lectures remain a primary source for how baptism and communion were explained to newcomers in the fourth century, and Egeria's diary is read wherever early liturgy is studied.

experienceToday.text: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre, Jerusalem — the complex first consecrated in 335 over the sites of the crucifixion and the tomb, still shared between several churches and open to pilgrims

movements.name: Ambrosian Milan (standalone)
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Thin alone - substantially one bishop's confrontations
movements.relationsSummary: Folded into the Imperial-Juridical tradition as one of its three phases
