movements.why: Surveyed and found too narrowly biographical to stand alone; it lives inside the Imperial tradition by choice, not oversight.
movements.longDescription: Milan, not Rome, was the western emperors' working capital in the late fourth century, and in 374 its people acclaimed as their bishop a provincial governor named Ambrose who had not yet even been baptized. He was baptized and consecrated within a week, and spent the next twenty-three years working out — mostly in public confrontations — what a bishop could say to power. He refused to hand a basilica over to the Empress Justina's court in 386, and his congregation occupied the building for days, singing hymns he wrote to keep their spirits up; in 390 he required the emperor Theodosius to do public penance for a massacre of civilians at Thessalonica. He was also a preacher who opened up Scripture for a restless African rhetorician sitting in his congregation — Augustine, whom Ambrose baptized at Easter in 387 — and the city he shaped still carries his stamp in the rite that bears his name.
movements.teaser: Milan, 374 to 397 — an unbaptized governor acclaimed bishop by a crowd, who spent the rest of his life teaching emperors where their authority stopped.
voices: Ambrose — the governor turned bishop, hymn-writer, and the first churchman to make an emperor do public penance
Augustine of Hippo — who came to Milan as a professor of rhetoric, heard Ambrose preach, and was baptized by him at Easter 387
Monica — Augustine's mother, part of the Milanese congregation, whose deference to Ambrose's pastoral advice her son recorded
Empress Justina — regent for the young Valentinian II, and Ambrose's opponent in the struggle over the city's basilicas
Theodosius I — the emperor who submitted to Ambrose's demand for public penance after the massacre at Thessalonica in 390
movements.legacy: Milan still keeps the Ambrosian Rite — its own calendar, chant, and order of worship, distinct from the Roman Rite used almost everywhere else in the Latin church, and the largest surviving non-Roman Western rite. Hymns attributed to Ambrose are still sung, and the congregational hymn-singing he made famous during the basilica occupation had a very long afterlife. His confrontation with Theodosius became a standing precedent, cited for more than a millennium, that a Christian ruler stands under the church's discipline rather than above it — and his preaching, by Augustine's own account, is a large part of the reason the West got Augustine at all. The church he founded in the 380s still stands on its site in Milan — rebuilt in Romanesque form eight centuries later — with his remains beneath its altar.

experienceToday.text: The Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio, Milan — the church Ambrose commissioned in 379-386, where his remains still lie

movements.name: Priscillianist Asceticism
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Limited; executed leader, suppressed movement
movements.floorNote: Genuinely unclear, and worth saying so. The charges laid against Priscillian included Manichaeism and sorcery, but they were laid by hostile bishops in what became a political prosecution, and what survives of writing attributed to him does not obviously confess anything the creeds rule out. Where this movement actually stood is an open question rather than a settled verdict.
movements.relationsSummary: Iberian ascetic current
movements.why: Surveyed; eligibility questions were never resolved. An honest open case, not a rejection.
movements.longDescription: In the 370s a Spanish layman named Priscillian began teaching a severe ascetic Christianity in the western provinces — fasting, celibacy, retreat to the countryside for study and prayer, lay men and women reading Scripture together outside the bishops' supervision — and it spread fast enough to alarm the Spanish and Gallic bishops, who condemned the movement at a council in Saragossa around 380. His supporters responded by making him bishop of Ávila; his opponents accused him of Manichaeism and sorcery and carried the case to the imperial court. Around 385, at Trier, the usurping emperor Magnus Maximus had Priscillian and several companions tried and put to death — so far as anyone can tell, the first time a Christian state executed Christians over belief. It shocked people at the time: Martin of Tours and Ambrose of Milan both objected to churchmen taking a doctrinal quarrel to an executioner, and the bishops who had pressed the charges were disgraced for it.
movements.teaser: Spain and Gaul, c. 370 to 450 — an ascetic movement whose leader was tried and executed at Trier, in what appears to be the first time a Christian state put Christians to death over doctrine.
voices: Priscillian — the lay teacher, later bishop of Ávila, executed at Trier around 385
Ithacius of Ossonoba — one of the bishops who pressed the charges to the imperial court, and was later deposed for having done so
Martin of Tours — who intervened to try to stop the executions, and afterwards refused communion with the bishops who had sought them
Sulpicius Severus — the chronicler whose account of the affair is the main surviving narrative of it
movements.legacy: The movement was suppressed but not immediately extinguished: Priscillian became a martyr in the eyes of his followers, the ascetic current he represented persisted in Galicia in north-western Spain for more than a century, and a council at Braga was still condemning Priscillianism in 561. Its heaviest legacy is the precedent set against it — the execution at Trier is the point at which capital punishment for heresy enters Western Christian practice, and it was cited afterwards both as precedent and as warning. In 1885 a set of eleven anonymous treatises was identified in a Würzburg manuscript, widely thought to come from Priscillian or his circle: the first chance in fourteen centuries to hear this movement in something close to its own voice rather than through the charges laid against it.

movements.name: Pelagianism
movements.statusDescription: Named in the Step 0 record as a live future candidate or a dropped voice, with reasoning — not yet chosen, not forgotten.
movements.sourcing: Ecology too thin to build - kept on record to prove the point
movements.floorNote: The quarrel here was about grace, free will, and original sin — not about the Trinity or the person of Christ. On the questions the Nicene Creed actually settles, the Pelagians stood where their opponents stood, which is why the condemnations against them had to be framed on other grounds.
movements.relationsSummary: Augustine's great controversy-partner
movements.why: On record deliberately: it clears the floor but its surviving ecology is too thin for a lived tradition - proof that eligibility and buildability are separate tests.
movements.longDescription: Pelagius was a British-born ascetic teacher who came to Rome in the late fourth century and found the Christianity of the capital slack — people excusing their sins on the grounds that human nature simply could not do better. His answer was that God does not command the impossible: if Scripture tells you to be perfect, then you can be, and the excuse is a lie. Around that conviction gathered a movement of serious, high-minded Christians, including the combative Caelestius and later the bishop Julian of Eclanum, who pushed the argument into hard questions about infant baptism, inherited guilt, and whether grace is help or takeover. Augustine of Hippo fought them for the last twenty years of his life; the African councils condemned them in 418 and the Council of Ephesus did so again in 431, and almost everything Pelagius himself wrote survives only in fragments, in his opponents' quotations, or misfiled for centuries under another man's name.
movements.teaser: Rome and the wider Mediterranean, c. 390 to 430 — a movement built on the conviction that God never commands what a person cannot do, argued out of the church by Augustine and preserved mostly inside his rebuttals.
voices: Pelagius — the British-born ascetic teacher whose name the movement carries, though he never chose it
Caelestius — his most combative follower, whose blunt formulations brought the controversy into the open at Carthage
Julian of Eclanum — the Italian bishop who took the argument up after Pelagius fell silent, and pressed Augustine hard enough to keep him writing until he died
Augustine of Hippo — the opponent whose replies are the main reason we know what the Pelagians said at all
movements.legacy: There was never a Pelagian church, and the movement left no institution — but the argument it forced has never closed. Answering it, Augustine worked out the Western doctrines of original sin, prevenient grace, and predestination in the form that Aquinas, Luther, Calvin, and the Jansenists would all later fight over, so that a good deal of the shape of Western theology is the shape of this quarrel. "Pelagian" also survives as one of Christianity's most durable insults, thrown at anyone suspected of making salvation a matter of human effort — usually by people who have never read a line of Pelagius, since so little of him survives to read. A few of his works did come through, misattributed to Jerome and identified as his only in modern times.

movements.name: Homoian ('Arian') Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Excluded on a stated creedal ground you can read in full. Exclusion is not a judgment of unimportance.
movements.sourcing: Real corpus (Ulfila's Bible, homilies), much via opponents
movements.floorNote: This is the tradition the Nicene Creed was written against. Its teachers would say the Son is "like" the Father, but not that he is "true God from true God, of one being with the Father" — the very clauses the creed added in order to rule that position out. This map draws its boundary at that creed, so this tradition falls outside it. That is a statement about doctrine and nothing else: for long stretches of the fourth century these were the churches of the empire, and their leaders included some of the most effective missionaries and translators in Christian history.
movements.relationsSummary: For stretches of the 4th c., the imperial church itself
movements.why: Excluded by the doctrinal floor as it stands. OPEN QUESTION on record: whether to bring it in through the Constitution's own bounded exception path (A4) rather than moving the floor.
movements.longDescription: For long stretches of the fourth century, the church the emperors backed was not the one that eventually won. The Homoians — from the Greek homoios, "like" — taught that the Son is like the Father according to the Scriptures, and refused to go further and call him of one being with the Father, on the grounds that Scripture never used the word and no council should force it on anyone; they did not call themselves Arians, and that label came from opponents who wanted them tied to a man most of them had never followed. Backed by the emperors Constantius II and later Valens, and adopted at the councils of 359 and 360, this was the imperial church's official position long enough for Jerome to write that the world groaned to find itself Arian. Its most lasting work was done outside the empire: Ulfila, consecrated bishop around 341, spent his life among the Goths, made an alphabet for their language, and translated the Bible into it. Through that mission the Goths, Vandals, Burgundians, and Lombards became Christians in this form, and Homoian kingdoms ruled Italy, Spain, and North Africa for generations after the empire itself had turned Nicene — the Visigoths of Spain going over to the Nicene creed at Toledo in 589, with the Lombards of Italy the last to follow, two generations later.
movements.teaser: The Roman Empire, and then the Gothic and Vandal kingdoms, fourth to sixth centuries — for a while the imperial church itself, and the tradition that gave the Germanic peoples their first Bible.
voices: Ulfila — bishop to the Goths, who devised the Gothic alphabet and translated the Bible into it, producing the oldest substantial text in any Germanic language
Constantius II — the emperor whose backing made the Homoian formula the official position of the imperial church
Auxentius of Milan — bishop of the western imperial capital for nearly twenty years, and Ambrose's Homoian predecessor
Theoderic the Great — Ostrogothic king of Italy, who built Homoian churches in Ravenna that are still standing
Reccared — the Visigothic king of Spain whose conversion at the Third Council of Toledo in 589 ended the tradition in Spain, though the Lombards of Italy carried it on for two more generations
movements.legacy: Its own churches are gone: every Homoian kingdom eventually conformed to the Nicene creed, and no continuing community carries the tradition forward. What it left behind is more oblique. Ulfila's Gothic Bible is the foundation document of Germanic philology — the earliest substantial writing in any Germanic language — and the great silver-and-gold copy of it made for Theoderic's court survives in Uppsala. Its buildings survive too: the Arian Baptistery and Sant'Apollinare Nuovo in Ravenna were built for Homoian worship, and their mosaics are among the finest anywhere. And the Nicene Creed is itself partly the shape of the argument with them — the clauses most Christians recite each week were sharpened precisely to close the space this tradition tried to hold open.

experienceToday.text: The Arian Baptistery, Ravenna — built for Homoian worship under Theoderic, part of the UNESCO-listed Early Christian Monuments of Ravenna
The Codex Argenteus, Uppsala University Library — the "Silver Bible" of Ulfila's Gothic translation, on permanent display

movements.name: Cyrilline / Miaphysite Egyptian Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 3 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) — the Phase One record had already named it the next phase's natural first candidate. Its dissent was assessed as rejecting Chalcedon's formula rather than the Creed's content; that reading cleared the doctrinal floor, and the distinction was carried forward as a binding disclosure obligation for any future build.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich; Severus survives in Syriac translation (transmission flag); papyri give ordinary texture
movements.floorNote: Rejection of Chalcedon's formula, not the Creed's content
movements.relationsSummary: Continues Alexandria + Desert; contested sibling of the Chalcedonian and Syriac Orthodox traditions
movements.why: Phase One's own record had already put this first in line for whenever the next phase came to be built. It is the first of the era's three separated eastern communions — miaphysite Egypt, miaphysite Syria under illegality, dyophysite Persia — three different answers to Chalcedon given inside three different empires, and distinct enough that none of them stands in for the others.

sources.work: Severus of Antioch, Select Letters (ed./trans. E. W. Brooks, 2 vols, 1902-04)
sources.note: Inside voice of the anti-Chalcedonian leadership in exile in Egypt (518-538); Greek originals lost, survives in Syriac translation (matches census transmission flag); Brooks's English translation is old but standard and online.

sources.work: History of the Patriarchs of the Coptic Church of Alexandria (attrib. Severus ibn al-Muqaffa')
sources.note: The Miaphysite church's own continuous narrative of its Alexandrian patriarchs; Arabic compilation of earlier Coptic sources; ed./English trans. B. Evetts in Patrologia Orientalis 1, 5, 10 (1904-15), online at tertullian.org.

sources.work: John of Nikiu, Chronicle (trans. R. H. Charles, 1916)
sources.note: Egyptian Miaphysite bishop's world chronicle ending with the Arab conquest (642) - the era's terminus seen from inside; survives only via Ethiopic from Arabic; Charles's English translation online. Plus Coptic/Greek documentary papyri (e.g. Dioscorus of Aphrodito archive) for ordinary texture.

sources.work: W. H. C. Frend, The Rise of the Monophysite Movement (1972)
sources.note: Still the standard single narrative of the anti-Chalcedonian movement 451 onward; dated in places (terminology 'Monophysite' now avoided) but widely available.

sources.work: Stephen J. Davis, The Early Coptic Papacy (2004)
sources.note: Modern history of the Egyptian church's leadership and identity in exactly this window; accessible English monograph (AUC Press).

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 2 (Constantine to c.600), ch. 3, 'Greek Christianities' (F. W. Norris); cf. ch. 4 (D. Bundy)
sources.note: Reference-tradition anchor for eastern-Roman (incl. Egyptian) developments to c.600; [S] precise chapter fit for Miaphysite Egypt inferred from TOC, not page-verified.

movements.longDescription: When the Council of Chalcedon defined Christ in 451 as one person known in two natures, the Egyptian church heard a betrayal of Cyril of Alexandria, its greatest teacher, and refused the council's wording. Its patriarch Dioscorus was deposed at Chalcedon itself, and for the next two centuries Alexandria had two rival lines of bishops — one backed by Constantinople, one held by most Egyptians — with the Miaphysite line surviving deposition, exile and periodic imperial force. It was carried by the monasteries of the Egyptian desert and increasingly in the Coptic language rather than Greek, and for two decades it sheltered Severus of Antioch, the exiled Syrian patriarch who became the movement's great theologian. When Arab armies took Egypt in 642 the imperial pressure simply ended, and the church that had refused Chalcedon was left standing.
movements.teaser: Egypt, 451 to 642 CE — the church that refused to say Christ was known "in two natures," and paid for it with two centuries of rival patriarchs, exile and imperial pressure.
voices: Dioscorus of Alexandria — the patriarch deposed at Chalcedon in 451, remembered by his own church as its defender rather than its disgrace
Timothy Aelurus — Miaphysite patriarch of Alexandria, exiled and restored, who argued the case against Chalcedon in writing
Severus of Antioch — the exiled Syrian patriarch who spent his last twenty years in Egypt and became the movement's chief theologian
Theodosius I of Alexandria — patriarch from 535, deposed by Justinian and spending most of his episcopate in exile
Benjamin I — the patriarch who spent a decade in hiding under Byzantine persecution and returned to Alexandria after the conquest
John of Nikiu — the bishop whose chronicle records the events of 642 from inside the Egyptian church
movements.legacy: This is one of the traditions on the map that never ended: the same institution continued under Muslim rule as Coptic Christianity, and its patriarchal line runs unbroken to the Coptic Orthodox pope of Alexandria today. It gave the wider Oriental Orthodox family — Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean — its shared theological anchor in Cyril of Alexandria, and it made Coptic a liturgical language still sung in Egyptian churches every week. Its desert monasteries in the Wadi Natrun and its painted late-antique churches in Upper Egypt are still standing, and most are still in use.

experienceToday.text: The Red Monastery near Sohag, Egypt — a late-antique Coptic church whose painted sanctuary has been cleaned and relit, one of the best-preserved interiors of its kind anywhere

movements.name: Syriac Orthodox (West Syriac) Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 3 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1), with John of Ephesus's Lives named as its inside-voice strength. Its miaphysite dissent was assessed the same way as Egypt's — Chalcedon's formula, not the Creed's content — with that distinction carried forward as a binding disclosure obligation.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich; John of Ephesus's Lives is extraordinary inside-voice material
movements.floorNote: The disagreement was with Chalcedon's formula, not with the content of the Nicene Creed.
movements.relationsSummary: Heir of the Syriac tradition's Roman side (Ephrem's Edessa); Ghassanid royal patronage carried its hierarchy (Jacob Baradaeus consecrated under it)
movements.why: A whole communion built while officially illegal — its hierarchy consecrated on the move under Ghassanid royal protection rather than imperial licence, and holding until Yarmouk ended the empire's power to enforce against it. Distinct from Miaphysite Egypt not in confession but in circumstance: the same answer to Chalcedon, given from outside the law rather than from a patriarchal throne.
movements.dateRationale: End 636 (Yarmouk): imperial persecution ends and a new order begins — chosen over 638, the fall of Jerusalem; both defensible (Era 3 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: John of Ephesus, Lives of the Eastern Saints (ed./trans. E. W. Brooks, Patrologia Orientalis 17-19, 1923-26)
sources.note: 58 portraits of Miaphysite ascetics by an insider - the extraordinary inside-voice material the census flags; Syriac with facing English translation, online (archive.org / tertullian.org).

sources.work: John of Ephesus, Ecclesiastical History, Part III (trans. R. Payne Smith, 1860)
sources.note: Contemporary narrative of persecution and church-building under Justin II/Tiberius from the persecuted side; Syriac; the Victorian English translation is online; parts I-II survive only in excerpts.

sources.work: Pseudo-Zachariah Rhetor, Chronicle (trans. Greatrex, Phenix, Horn, TTH 55, 2011)
sources.note: Sixth-century Syriac Miaphysite compilation covering 451 onward, including Chalcedon's aftermath; excellent modern annotated English translation (Translated Texts for Historians).

sources.work: Volker L. Menze, Justinian and the Making of the Syrian Orthodox Church (2008)
sources.note: The standard modern account of how a separated West Syriac church actually formed (518-553), ordinations, memory, liturgy; Oxford Early Christian Studies, in print.

sources.work: W. H. C. Frend, The Rise of the Monophysite Movement (1972)
sources.note: Broad narrative frame connecting the Syrian and Egyptian anti-Chalcedonian movements; dated but standard and available.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 2, ch. 3, 'Greek Christianities' (F. W. Norris)
sources.note: Reference anchor for the eastern-Roman provinces incl. Syria to c.600; [S] chapter fit for West Syriac specifically inferred from TOC, not page-verified.

movements.longDescription: After Chalcedon, the Christians of Syria and Mesopotamia who refused the council's formula were in a harder position than their Egyptian counterparts: inside the Roman Empire, without a patriarchal throne of their own, and for long stretches under Justinian without legal standing at all. Their leader Severus of Antioch was driven from his see in 518 and wrote from exile in Egypt for twenty years. Their communities kept meeting, and their clergy kept being ordained, largely because of Jacob Baradaeus — a bishop consecrated under the protection of the Ghassanid Arab kings and of the empress Theodora, who spent decades travelling in disguise across Syria and Mesopotamia ordaining priests and bishops for a church the empire would not recognize. John of Ephesus, himself a Miaphysite bishop and one of Justinian's own missionaries, wrote down fifty-eight portraits of these people while it was happening. When the Byzantine defeat at Yarmouk in 636 ended the empire's power to enforce against them, what emerged was a separate hierarchy that had never stopped functioning.
movements.teaser: Syria and Mesopotamia, 451 to 636 CE — a church built without legal permission to exist, its bishops ordained on the move by a wandering missionary in patched rags.
voices: Severus of Antioch — patriarch of Antioch from 512 to 518 and the movement's foremost theologian, who spent his last two decades writing from exile
Jacob Baradaeus — the bishop who travelled for some thirty years ordaining clergy for an outlawed church, and whose name is the root of the label "Jacobite"
John of Ephesus — bishop, missionary and historian, whose Lives of the Eastern Saints portrays fifty-eight ascetics he knew personally
Al-Harith ibn Jabalah — the Ghassanid Arab king and Roman ally whose patronage secured the consecrations that kept the hierarchy alive
Theodora — Justinian's wife, whose protection of anti-Chalcedonian leaders at court made much of this possible
movements.legacy: The same institution is still here: it continued under Muslim rule and is today the Syriac Orthodox Church of Antioch, with congregations across the Middle East, in India and in a wide diaspora. It kept Syriac alive as a living liturgical language, and its translators preserved Greek theological works whose originals were lost — including most of Severus's own writing, which survives only in Syriac. Several of its monasteries in the Tur Abdin, in what is now south-eastern Turkey, were founded before or during this period and are still occupied.

experienceToday.text: Mor Gabriel Monastery, Tur Abdin, Turkey — founded in 397 and still a working Syriac Orthodox monastery and the seat of its metropolitan

movements.name: The Church of the East under Persia
movements.informalName: The Church of the East under Persia
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 3 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1), with the School of Nisibis statutes named as formation documents almost nowhere else has. The continuity check its floorNote framed as one to run rather than assume was actually run here — the Synod of Isaac (410) formally adopted the Nicene Creed, and the 612 bishops' statement affirms Christ's full divinity and humanity — assessed on the communion's own synodal confessions rather than on the hostile label.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich; the School of Nisibis statutes are formation documents almost nowhere else has
movements.floorNote: "Nestorian" was a name its opponents gave it. Its own synods say something different: the assembly of 410 formally adopted the Nicene Creed, and the bishops' statement of 612 affirms Christ as fully divine and fully human.
movements.relationsSummary: Direct heir of the Syriac tradition (deferred from Phase One for exactly this window); the St Thomas Christians of India sit inside its communion in this window
movements.why: Deferred by Phase One into exactly this window, and the assessment it was deferred toward has now been made. It is the era's third answer to Chalcedon and the only one worked out entirely outside Roman jurisdiction — a church that governed itself under Persian rule, held the St Thomas Christians of India inside its communion, and carried for centuries a name its opponents gave it.

sources.work: Synodicon Orientale (ed./trans. J.-B. Chabot, 1902)
sources.note: The Church of the East's own collected synods 410-775 - its constitutional self-record; Syriac with French translation only (no complete English); the indispensable institutional source.

sources.work: Adam H. Becker (trans.), Sources for the History of the School of Nisibis (TTH 50, 2008)
sources.note: First English translations of the Cause of the Foundation of the Schools, Barhadbshabba's school narratives, and related texts - the formation-culture documents the census highlights; in print (Liverpool UP).

sources.work: The Statutes of the School of Nisibis (ed./trans. A. Vööbus, 1961)
sources.note: The school's actual rule-texts (496, 602) - formation documents almost nowhere else has (per census); Syriac with English translation; older Estonian-series edition, findable in research libraries. [S] edition details from knowledge, not re-verified online.

sources.work: Adam H. Becker, Fear of God and the Beginning of Wisdom (2006)
sources.note: Standard modern study of the School of Nisibis and East Syrian scholastic culture; Penn Press, in print.

sources.work: Richard E. Payne, A State of Mixture (2015)
sources.note: How East Syrian Christians actually lived within Sasanian political culture - corrects older persecution-only narratives; UC Press, in print.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 2, ch. 4, 'Early Asian and East African Christianities' (David Bundy)
sources.note: The reference-tradition chapter covering Christianity beyond the Roman frontier incl. the Persian church; verified in vol. 2 TOC.

movements.longDescription: In 424 the bishops of the Persian Empire declared that their catholicos at Seleucia-Ctesiphon answered to no bishop beyond their own frontier — a church living under a Zoroastrian shah, deliberately independent of the Roman world and its councils. It gave a different answer to the question of Christ than either Chalcedon or the Miaphysites, following the tradition of Theodore of Mopsuestia in holding firmly to the distinctness of his divinity and his humanity, and its opponents fixed the name "Nestorian" on it. Its intellectual centre was the School of Nisibis, which had written statutes governing the students' day, their lodging and their discipline — formation documents of a kind almost nothing else this early has left. Its communion stretched far beyond Mesopotamia: the St Thomas Christians of India belonged to it. When the Sasanian empire fell to Arab armies by 651, the church carried straight on under new rulers and kept expanding eastward.
movements.teaser: Persian Mesopotamia, 424 to 651 CE — a self-governing church outside every Christian empire, with a theological school run by written statutes and a communion reaching as far as India.
voices: Narsai — the poet-theologian who led the school at Edessa until conflict drove him out around 471, and refounded its teaching at Nisibis — where the rest of Edessa's masters joined him when the emperor closed that school in 489
Barsauma of Nisibis — the metropolitan who secured the school's place and pressed the church's independence from Roman jurisdiction
Mar Aba I — a convert from Zoroastrianism who became catholicos in 540, reorganized the church's law, and was imprisoned and exiled for it
Babai the Great — abbot and theologian who gave the church its settled language about Christ in the early seventh century
Henana of Adiabene — head of the school at Nisibis whose teaching split it and drove students away, a controversy the school's own documents record
movements.legacy: The same institution continued without a break into the following centuries, when it became the most geographically extended Christian body in the world — its missions reaching Central Asia and China along the Silk Road. Its Indian branch, the St Thomas Christians of Kerala, is the ancestor of several churches worshipping there today, and its heirs survive as the Assyrian Church of the East and the Chaldean Catholic Church. Along the way its scholars translated Greek medicine, philosophy and logic into Syriac, work later carried on into Arabic — one of the routes by which Greek learning reached the wider medieval world.

experienceToday.text: Nusaybin, Turkey — the fourth-century church of Mar Yakup still stands in ancient Nisibis, the frontier city whose school trained this church's clergy

movements.name: Armenian Christianity after Avarayr
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 3 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — rich historiography and liturgy, held back by an access limit: the Book of Letters is verified only in Armenian editions, with no full English translation. Its end date was corrected at the gate from 531, which matched no event, to 554 (Dvin II, the formal rejection of Chalcedon).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: rich historiography and liturgy; thinner ordinary interior texture
movements.relationsSummary: Formed via Cappadocia + Edessa; rejects Chalcedon at Dvin
movements.why: Deferred by Phase One into exactly this window, which is where Armenia's confessional self-definition seals: from Avarayr to Dvin II in 554, the council at which the church formally set itself outside Chalcedon. One of the era's distinct national-church stories, and the one whose uniqueness was never the question.
movements.dateRationale: End 554 (Dvin II: formal rejection of Chalcedon) — corrects a data error; the old 531 matched no event. Alt 640 (Arab arrival) on record (Era 3 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Elishe (Ełishē), History of Vardan and the Armenian War (trans. R. W. Thomson, 1982)
sources.note: The classic inside account of Avarayr (451) and its martyr-theology of covenant; Harvard Armenian Texts and Studies 5; standard annotated English translation, online at archive.org.

sources.work: Łazar P'arpec'i, History of the Armenians (trans. R. W. Thomson, 1991)
sources.note: The other fifth-century narrative of Avarayr and the 480s Vahan revolt, more sober than Elishe; Thomson's English translation is standard.

sources.work: Girk' T'łt'oc' (Book of Letters)
sources.note: The Armenian church's own dossier of doctrinal correspondence, incl. its sixth-century rejection of Chalcedon (Dvin councils); Classical Armenian editions (Tiflis 1901, Jerusalem 1994) - no full English translation; access via excerpts in Garsoian/Sarkissian (transmission flag).

sources.work: Karekin Sarkissian, The Council of Chalcedon and the Armenian Church (1965)
sources.note: Accessible standard account (by an insider-scholar) of why and how the Armenian church came to reject Chalcedon; older but still the usual English entry point.

sources.work: Nina Garsoian, L'Eglise armenienne et le grand schisme d'Orient (CSCO 574, 1999)
sources.note: The definitive scholarly treatment of the Armenian schism with translations of key Book of Letters documents; French only - a real access barrier.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 2, ch. 4, 'Early Asian and East African Christianities' (David Bundy)
sources.note: Reference chapter covering Armenia among the non-Roman Christianities; verified in vol. 2 TOC.

movements.longDescription: In 451, while the Roman world's bishops met at Chalcedon, Armenia's nobles met the Persian army at Avarayr rather than accept an imposed return to Zoroastrian worship. They lost the battle and their commander, Vardan Mamikonian, but the resistance went on until Persia conceded the right to remain Christian in 484 — and the Armenian church came to read that defeat as a covenant sealed in martyrdom rather than as a loss. Absorbed in that struggle, Armenia had sent no bishops to Chalcedon; when it did take up the council's formula it judged it too close to dividing Christ, and at the second council of Dvin in 554 the church formally set itself outside Chalcedon. By then it had a Bible and a liturgy in an alphabet barely fifty years old, and a body of historical writing — Elishe's and Lazar's accounts of the war — that fixed the story it has told about itself ever since.
movements.teaser: Armenia, 451 to 554 CE — a church that fought a battle for the right to stay Christian in the same year the empire held the council it would spend a century declining to accept.
voices: Vardan Mamikonian — the commander killed at Avarayr in 451, remembered as a saint rather than as a casualty
Elishe — the historian whose account of Avarayr made it a covenant story, and still the classic Armenian telling
Lazar Parpetsi — the other fifth-century historian of the war and of the revolt of the 480s, soberer than Elishe
Vahan Mamikonian — Vardan's nephew, whose revolt won the settlement of 484 and who rebuilt the cathedral at Etchmiadzin
Nerses II — the catholicos who presided at the second council of Dvin in 554, where the church formally rejected Chalcedon
movements.legacy: The Armenian Apostolic Church that came out of this period is still the church of Armenia and of Armenians everywhere, and the same institution continued through the medieval Bagratid centuries into the present. Avarayr is still kept as a feast and Vardan and his companions are still counted among its saints. Its stone-vaulted, domed churches became a distinctive architectural tradition studied well beyond the Caucasus, and the alphabet devised to carry its Bible remains the alphabet of the Armenian language.

experienceToday.text: Etchmiadzin Cathedral, Vagharshapat, Armenia — the mother church of the Armenian Apostolic Church, whose core was rebuilt in 483-4 by Vahan Mamikonian

movements.name: Chalcedonian Monasticism - Judean Desert & Gaza
movements.informalName: The Monks of the Judean Desert and Gaza
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 3 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) — assessed as the era's richest inside voice, on Cyril of Scythopolis's dated Lives and Barsanuphius and John's roughly 850 letters of direction to ordinary people. Sinai was routed into this world at the Freeze rather than given its own entry, and the end was set to 614, the Persian sack the sources themselves mourn.
movements.sourcing: RICH - Cyril of Scythopolis's dated lives; Barsanuphius & John's ~850 letters of direction to ordinary people
movements.relationsSummary: Direct heir of Desert Monasticism; feeds Sinai (Climacus) and all later Orthodox practice
movements.why: Its inside-voice evidence is the richest in the era and among the best anywhere in the atlas. Monasticism elsewhere survives mostly in its rules — what a house meant to do; here it survives in letters of direction, which record what ordinary people actually asked and what they were actually told back. The era's Eastern monastic world against the Benedictines' Western one: cell-and-letters rather than rule-and-community, distinct in texture and in what each left behind.
movements.dateRationale: End 614 (Persian sack of Jerusalem; Strategius's inside account) — the destruction the sources themselves mourn (Era 3 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Cyril of Scythopolis, Lives of the Monks of Palestine (trans. R. M. Price, intro. J. Binns, 1991)
sources.note: Dated, sober lives of Euthymius, Sabas and the Judean Desert founders - the census's 'dated lives'; Cistercian Studies 114, in print.

sources.work: Barsanuphius and John, Letters (trans. John Chryssavgis, FOTC 113-114, 2006-07)
sources.note: The ~850 letters of spiritual direction to monks and ordinary laypeople in Gaza the census highlights; first complete English translation (CUA Press), in print - verified.

sources.work: John Moschus, The Spiritual Meadow (trans. John Wortley, 1992)
sources.note: Anecdotes gathered across Palestinian and Sinai monasticism right at the era's end (c.600); Cistercian Studies 139, in print; anecdotal genre needs tier care.

sources.work: Yizhar Hirschfeld, The Judean Desert Monasteries in the Byzantine Period (1992)
sources.note: Archaeological synthesis of the actual monasteries - diet, water, cells; complements the texts materially; Yale UP.

sources.work: Jennifer Hevelone-Harper, Disciples of the Desert: Monks, Laity, and Spiritual Authority in Sixth-Century Gaza (2005)
sources.note: Modern study built directly on the Barsanuphius correspondence - spiritual direction of ordinary people; Johns Hopkins UP.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 2, ch. 27, 'Asceticism and monasticism, I: Eastern' (Samuel Rubenson)
sources.note: Reference-tradition chapter for eastern monasticism to c.600; chapter title/author verified.

movements.longDescription: In the ravines between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea, and in the villages around Gaza, monastic settlement multiplied in the century after Chalcedon into something like a second population — laurae where hermits lived apart through the week and gathered on Sundays, and communal houses holding hundreds. What makes this world unusually visible is that its own paperwork survives: Cyril of Scythopolis's carefully dated lives of Euthymius, Sabas and their successors, and roughly 850 letters from two recluses near Gaza, Barsanuphius and John, answering monks, married couples, sick people and local officials one question at a time. These were firm supporters of Chalcedon, and they were pulled hard into the empire's doctrinal fights, including the purge of Origenist teaching in the 550s that split their own houses. The Persian army's sack of Jerusalem in 614 tore through the desert monasteries, and the survivors wrote down what had been lost.
movements.teaser: The Judean desert, Gaza and Sinai, c. 450 to 614 CE — monks whose surviving letters record not only what a rule required, but what ordinary people actually asked and what they were told back.
voices: Euthymius the Great — the founder whose Judean desert laura set the pattern others followed, died in 473
Sabas — founder in 483 of the monastery that still bears his name, and for decades the desert monks' representative to emperors and patriarchs
Cyril of Scythopolis — the monk-biographer whose dated lives are the reason this world can be reconstructed at all
Barsanuphius and John — two recluses near Gaza, known as the Old Men, who answered some 850 letters of direction without leaving their cells
Dorotheus of Gaza — their disciple, whose teaching on humility and bearing with others became standard reading in later monasteries
John Moschus — who travelled the Palestinian and Sinai monasteries around 600, collecting the stories the monks told about one another
movements.legacy: A great deal of what Eastern Orthodox monasticism still does comes from here. The liturgical order associated with Sabas's monastery underlies Orthodox worship to this day; the Ladder of Divine Ascent, written at Sinai just after this period, is still read aloud in Orthodox monasteries every Lent; and Dorotheus of Gaza remains standard spiritual reading. Two of the houses standing in this window — Mar Saba in the Judean desert and Saint Catherine's at Sinai — are still inhabited, among the oldest continuously occupied Christian communities anywhere.

experienceToday.text: Mar Saba, in the Kidron valley between Bethlehem and the Dead Sea — founded by Sabas in 483 and inhabited by monks almost continuously since

movements.name: Early Benedictine / Italian Monasticism
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 3 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1), on the Rule and Gregory the Great's 850-plus letters, with the Dialogues flagged as needing tier care. The Three Chapters dissent was routed to the Byzantine Imperial entry added at the same gate — its actual opponent — rather than housed here.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: the Rule, Gregory the Great's 850+ letters; Dialogues need tier care
movements.relationsSummary: Receives the desert via Cassian; parent of the whole Latin monastic line
movements.why: The parent of the whole Latin monastic line — what Cassian carried west from the desert takes durable institutional form here, in a Rule that later Western monasticism kept returning to. Set beside Gregory the Great's correspondence, the era's Latin church can be read from two sides at once: how it ordered a single house, and how it tried to govern a world.

sources.work: The Rule of St Benedict (RB 1980, ed. Timothy Fry)
sources.note: The movement's constitutive text; RB 1980 gives Latin, English, and commentary and is the standard study edition; countless cheap translations also exist.

sources.work: The Rule of the Master (trans. Luke Eberle, 1977)
sources.note: The longer rule Benedict abbreviated and humanized - essential comparison text for what is distinctive in RB; Cistercian Studies 6.

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Dialogues, Book II (Life of Benedict) (trans. O. Zimmerman, FOTC 39)
sources.note: The only narrative of Benedict's life, written c.593; hagiographic - needs the tier care the census flags (plus the Francis Clark authorship debate, now mostly rejected but worth noting).

sources.work: Gregory the Great, Letters (trans. John R. C. Martyn, 3 vols, 2004)
sources.note: The 850+ letters the census cites - day-to-day governance of the Italian church 590-604; complete English translation (PIMS); expensive but in research libraries.

sources.work: R. A. Markus, Gregory the Great and His World (1997)
sources.note: Standard modern portrait of Gregory's Italy - the world early Benedictine monasticism inhabited; Cambridge UP paperback.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 2, ch. 28, 'Asceticism and monasticism, II: Western' (Marilyn Dunn)
sources.note: Reference-tradition chapter for western monasticism incl. Benedict and the Master; chapter title/author verified.

movements.longDescription: Benedict of Nursia left Rome for a cave at Subiaco and ended up, around 529, founding a monastery on the hill of Monte Cassino, in an Italy being torn apart first by the Gothic wars and then by the Lombard invasions. What he left behind was a rule: seventy-three short chapters on prayer, work, sleep, food, guests, discipline and the election of an abbot, much of it adapted from an older and harsher text but shortened, moderated, and written with an eye for what ordinary people could actually sustain. A generation later Gregory the Great, a monk before he was a pope, wrote the only account we have of Benedict's life, and governed the Italian church through a correspondence of more than 850 letters that shows the same world from the other side — famine, plague, refugees, Lombard armies, and the daily management of a church trying to hold itself together.
movements.teaser: Italy, c. 500 to 604 CE — a short, practical rule for a single household of monks, written while the peninsula was being fought over, that ended up organizing Western monastic life for fifteen centuries.
voices: Benedict of Nursia — author of the Rule and founder of Subiaco and Monte Cassino, died around 547
Scholastica — Benedict's sister, remembered in Gregory's account as leading a community of women nearby
Gregory the Great — pope from 590 to 604, monk, the only narrator of Benedict's life, and the writer of more than 850 surviving letters
The anonymous author of the Rule of the Master — the longer, older rule Benedict abbreviated; the writer's name is unknown
movements.legacy: The Rule became the standard for Western monasticism: Carolingian reformers made it the norm across the Frankish empire, and it stands behind the Cluniacs, the Cistercians, the Trappists and the Benedictine congregations that keep it today. Its vocabulary of stability, obedience and moderation, and its ordering of a day around fixed hours of prayer, reached far beyond the cloister into Western habits of work and time. Monte Cassino itself was destroyed repeatedly — by Lombards, by Saracens, by earthquake, and by Allied bombing in 1944 — and rebuilt every time; monks live there now.

experienceToday.text: The Abbey of Monte Cassino, Italy — Benedict's own foundation of around 529, destroyed and rebuilt many times over and again a working monastery

movements.name: Merovingian Gallic Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 3 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1), assessed as the era's only ordinary-parish window: Caesarius's sermons to half-pagan congregations and Gregory of Tours's shrine-world. Its 620 end was left standing as soft but nearby, with the Edict of Paris (614) recorded as an alternative.
movements.sourcing: Rich and unusually ORDINARY - Caesarius's sermons to half-pagan congregations; Gregory of Tours's shrine-world
movements.relationsSummary: Receives Martin of Tours's line; parent of Carolingian Christianity
movements.why: The era's only ordinary-parish window. Almost every other Era 3 entry sees Christianity from inside a monastery, a court, or a council; this one sees it from a rural congregation that has not entirely stopped doing what it did before — the half-converted lay religion the atlas otherwise has very little means of reaching.

sources.work: Gregory of Tours, The History of the Franks (trans. Lewis Thorpe, 1974)
sources.note: The era's great narrative of kings, bishops and shrines from inside Gaul; cheap Penguin Classics translation; standard Latin edition MGH SRM I.1.

sources.work: Gregory of Tours, miracle books - Glory of the Martyrs, Glory of the Confessors, Life of the Fathers (trans. Raymond Van Dam / Edward James, TTH, 1985-91)
sources.note: The shrine-world the census highlights: relics, healings, ordinary pilgrims; all in affordable Liverpool TTH English translations.

sources.work: Caesarius of Arles, Sermons (trans. M. M. Mueller, FOTC 31/47/66, 3 vols, 1956-73)
sources.note: Preaching to half-pagan congregations (census's phrase) c.500-542 - rural superstition, almsgiving, basic catechesis; complete English translation in Fathers of the Church.

sources.work: William E. Klingshirn, Caesarius of Arles: The Making of a Christian Community in Late Antique Gaul (1994)
sources.note: Standard modern study of how a bishop actually tried to Christianize ordinary society; Cambridge UP.

sources.work: Yitzhak Hen, Culture and Religion in Merovingian Gaul, A.D. 481-751 (1995)
sources.note: Counterweight reading: argues Merovingian lay culture was more Christianized than Caesarius's complaints suggest; Brill.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 2, ch. 1, 'Western Christianities' (Winrich Lohr)
sources.note: Reference-tradition chapter for the Latin West incl. Gaul to c.600; chapter title/author verified in vol. 2 TOC.

movements.longDescription: When the Frankish king Clovis accepted baptism as a Nicene Christian around the turn of the sixth century, he brought his people into the same church as the Gallo-Roman bishops rather than into the Homoian one most other barbarian kings held — and the Gaul that resulted is one of the few places in this era where ordinary parish religion can actually be overheard. Caesarius, bishop of Arles, preached short, blunt, repeatable sermons at people who came to church and also consulted soothsayers, kept the old feast days, and slipped out before the sermon. Gregory of Tours, writing two generations later, filled book after book with the shrines, relics and cures that structured everyday devotion, alongside a famously unsparing narrative of Frankish kings murdering one another. Queens became founders — Radegund walked out of a royal marriage to establish a convent at Poitiers — and poets wrote hymns for their relics. It is a Christianity that is fully established and only half converted at the same time, and it says both things about itself out loud.
movements.teaser: Gaul, c. 480 to 620 CE — a church of relics, healings and Frankish kings, preaching to congregations who still stopped at the old shrines on the way home.
voices: Clovis — the Frankish king whose baptism aligned his kingdom with the Nicene bishops rather than with his Homoian neighbours
Caesarius of Arles — bishop from 502 to 542, whose surviving sermons complain in detail about what his congregations actually did
Caesaria — his sister, first abbess of the women's monastery at Arles for which he wrote a rule
Radegund — a Thuringian princess taken as a Frankish queen, who left the court to found the convent of the Holy Cross at Poitiers
Gregory of Tours — bishop from 573, historian of the Franks and cataloguer of the shrine-world of Gaul
Venantius Fortunatus — the poet at Radegund's convent whose hymns to the Cross are still sung
movements.legacy: The same institution continued directly into Carolingian Christianity, which reformed and reorganized it rather than replacing it. Its shrine culture set the pattern for Western pilgrimage, and its partnership of Frankish crown and Gallic bishops became a working model for church and kingdom across medieval Europe. Venantius Fortunatus's Vexilla Regis and Pange Lingua Gloriosi are still sung in Holy Week. Most of its buildings are gone, but a few survive — the baptistery at Poitiers, and sarcophagi and crypts scattered across France.

experienceToday.text: The Baptistère Saint-Jean in Poitiers, France — reputed to be the oldest Christian building in the country, with its original fourth-century baptismal pool and a collection of Merovingian sarcophagi

movements.name: Insular / Irish Monastic Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 3 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — Patrick's own two writings are the anchor, and the later hagiography was flagged as needing discipline. Its c. 450 start, one year before the era boundary, was recorded as boundary rounding on a 'c.'-dated start rather than as an anomaly.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: Patrick's own two writings; Columbanus's rules; penitentials; later hagiography needs discipline
movements.relationsSummary: Contested line from Gallic/Eastern asceticism; parent of Anglo-Saxon Christianity
movements.why: A monastic Christianity that grew up outside the imperial frame shaping every other Western entry in this era, and then sent its own missionaries back into it — Iona and Northumbria are in its region line for that reason. Patrick's two surviving writings are a rare thing this early: a first-person account of a mission from the man who made it. The penitentials add what few sources give at all — the ordinary failings of ordinary communities, itemised.

sources.work: Patrick, Confessio and Epistola ad milites Corotici (ed. Bieler; multiple translations; confessio.ie)
sources.note: The only two certainly authentic voices from fifth-century Ireland (census: 'Patrick's own two writings'); Royal Irish Academy's confessio.ie gives text, translations and manuscript images free online.

sources.work: Columbanus, Letters, Rules and Penitential (ed./trans. G. S. M. Walker, Sancti Columbani Opera, 1957)
sources.note: The Irish peregrinus's own words c.590-615, incl. his monastic rules; Latin with facing English (Scriptores Latini Hiberniae 2); reprinted, and texts online via CELT.

sources.work: Adomnan, Life of St Columba (trans. Richard Sharpe, 1995)
sources.note: Iona's own account of its founder (d. 597), written c.700 - close but retrospective, needs the hagiography discipline the census flags; excellent annotated Penguin translation.

sources.work: The Irish Penitentials (ed./trans. Ludwig Bieler, 1963)
sources.note: Finnian, Cumméan and kin - the tariffed-penance documents that show pastoral practice on the ground; Latin/English (Scriptores Latini Hiberniae 5); library access.

sources.work: T. M. Charles-Edwards, Early Christian Ireland (2000)
sources.note: The standard scholarly synthesis for the whole window incl. Iona and the paschal controversy to 664; Cambridge UP paperback.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 2, ch. 2, 'Germanic and Celtic Christianities' (Knut Schaferdiek)
sources.note: Reference-tradition chapter covering Celtic (incl. Irish/British) Christianity to c.600; chapter title/author verified.

movements.longDescription: Ireland was never Roman, and the church that took root there in the fifth century organized itself accordingly — around monasteries and their abbots rather than around city bishops, with monastic families and founder-saints anchoring whole regions. Patrick's two short surviving letters, a defence of his own life and a furious protest at the enslavement of his converts, are the only certainly authentic voices from the beginning, and they are startlingly personal. Two things it produced were absorbed by the wider church: peregrinatio, the practice of leaving home permanently for God's sake, which sent Columba to Iona in 563 and Columbanus into Gaul and Italy, where he founded Luxeuil and Bobbio and argued with Frankish kings; and the penitentials, handbooks assigning particular penances to particular sins, which quietly turned confession into something private and repeatable. Its own way of calculating Easter and its distinctive tonsure eventually collided with Roman practice, and at Whitby in 664 the Northumbrian king ruled against the Irish reckoning.
movements.teaser: Ireland, Iona and Northumbria, c. 450 to 664 CE — a Christianity that grew up outside the Roman Empire, organized itself around abbots instead of cities, and then sent its monks back across Europe as voluntary exiles.
voices: Patrick — a Romano-British captive turned missionary bishop, whose Confessio and Letter to Coroticus are the only certainly authentic fifth-century Irish voices
Brigid of Kildare — founder-saint of one of Ireland's great monastic churches, though everything written about her comes long afterwards
Columba — the noble-born founder of Iona in 563, from which the Irish mission reached into Pictland and Northumbria
Columbanus — the peregrinus whose letters and rules survive, founder of Luxeuil in Gaul and Bobbio in Italy, died in 615
Aidan — the monk sent from Iona in 635 who founded Lindisfarne and evangelized Northumbria
Adomnán — abbot of Iona, biographer of Columba, and promoter of a law protecting non-combatants
movements.legacy: Irish monasticism reshaped continental Christianity: Columbanus's foundations seeded dozens of monasteries across Gaul and Italy, and Iona-trained missionaries carried the faith into Northumbria and beyond. The penitential handbooks written here spread through the Frankish church and stand behind the private, repeatable confession that became normal Western practice. Its scriptoria produced the insular manuscript style that culminates in the Book of Kells, and the high crosses and round towers of Irish monastic sites are among the most recognizable Christian monuments anywhere. Iona, Clonmacnoise and Glendalough are all still visited, and Iona has a working religious community again.

experienceToday.text: Iona Abbey, Isle of Iona, Scotland — on the site Columba founded in 563; the medieval abbey church is restored and in use, and the island is still a place of pilgrimage

movements.name: Aksumite Christianity
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 3 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 3 Step 0 run and tiered Marginal/deferred (Tier 3) — real and important, but thin for interior texture in this window, with the richer Ethiopian centuries coming later. Its start was corrected at the gate from 330, which duplicated its Era 2 predecessor's window, to 451; the 615 end was adopted as the weaker of the candidates and disclosed as such. The Najran martyrs and Kaleb's Himyar intervention were routed inside this world's story at the Freeze, with pre-Islamic Arabian Christianity flagged as a future completeness question.
movements.sourcing: Thin-to-moderate for interior texture in this window (inscriptions, early manuscripts, archaeology)
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Alexandria; parent of the medieval Ethiopian flowering; the Najran martyrs (523) and Kaleb’s Himyar intervention (c. 525) live inside this world’s story (routed at the Era 3 Freeze; pre-Islamic Arabian Christianity flagged as a future completeness question)
movements.why: Deferred by Phase One, and the question it was deferred toward has now been weighed: how much of Aksum's own early voice survives inside this particular window. Not a great deal — inscriptions, early manuscripts, archaeology — and the richer Ethiopian centuries come later. It holds a place because an African kingdom-church with this reach, intervening across the Red Sea and later sheltering the first hijra, is not something the map can leave blank.
movements.dateRationale: Start 451: the era-2 conversion entry owns 330-451 and continuesAs this entry — corrects a duplicated window. End 615 (first hijra to Aksum), a weaker candidate, disclosed (Era 3 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Ezana inscriptions and Aksumite royal epigraphy (RIE; trans. in Munro-Hay, Aksum, and elsewhere)
sources.note: The kingdom's own words - Ezana's shift to Christian formulae, later Kaleb-era texts; scattered scholarly editions (Recueil des inscriptions de l'Ethiopie), no single accessible English corpus. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: The Garima Gospels (Abba Garima Ge'ez gospel manuscripts)
sources.note: Radiocarbon-dated c.5th-7th c. - the earliest Ethiopic gospel books and witnesses to the Ge'ez Bible translation itself; studied and illustrated in McKenzie & Watson, The Garima Gospels (2016) - verified.

sources.work: Cosmas Indicopleustes, Christian Topography, esp. bk 2 (trans. J. W. McCrindle, 1897)
sources.note: Outside eyewitness who copied the Monumentum Adulitanum at Adulis c.520s and describes Aksumite trade-world Christianity; old English translation online.

sources.work: Stuart Munro-Hay, Aksum: An African Civilisation of Late Antiquity (1991)
sources.note: Standard synthesis of Aksumite history and archaeology incl. Christianization; full text has circulated free online.

sources.work: David W. Phillipson, Foundations of an African Civilisation: Aksum and the Northern Horn (2012)
sources.note: The current archaeological synthesis, updating Munro-Hay - matches the census's note that this window is carried by inscriptions, manuscripts, archaeology; James Currey, in print.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 2, ch. 4, 'Early Asian and East African Christianities' (David Bundy)
sources.note: Reference chapter covering Ethiopia among the non-Roman Christianities; verified in vol. 2 TOC.

movements.longDescription: Aksum had been Christian since the fourth century, and in the period after Chalcedon it was a serious Red Sea power with its own coinage, its own script, and its Bible being translated into Ge'ez. Tradition credits the spread of monasticism and much of that translation work to the Nine Saints, monks said to have come from the Roman east around the turn of the sixth century. In 523 the Jewish king of Himyar, across the water in Yemen, massacred the Christians of Najran; the Aksumite king Kaleb crossed the Red Sea in about 525, destroyed his kingdom, and for a few decades Aksum ruled southern Arabia. Its church stayed in communion with Alexandria and shared its refusal of Chalcedon. Evidence from inside this particular window is thin — inscriptions, a few very early gospel books, archaeology — but the kingdom was still substantial enough in 615 that Muhammad sent his first followers to its king for protection.
movements.teaser: Ethiopia and Eritrea, 451 to 615 CE — a Christian kingdom on the Red Sea that sent an army across the water to avenge a massacre, and later gave shelter to the first Muslim refugees.
voices: Kaleb — the Aksumite king who crossed to Himyar around 525 in response to the killing of the Christians of Najran
The Nine Saints — monks remembered as arriving from the Roman east and spreading monasticism and Ge'ez scripture; their story reaches us only through much later Ethiopian tradition
Cosmas Indicopleustes — a travelling merchant-monk who copied an inscription at the Aksumite port of Adulis in the 520s and described the Christian trade world of the Red Sea
The martyrs of Najran — the Christians killed in Himyar in 523, whose deaths were reported across the Christian world and drew Aksum into war
movements.legacy: The same institution continued without interruption and is today the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, one of the largest of the Oriental Orthodox communions, alongside its Eritrean counterpart. Ge'ez, the language its Bible was translated into in this period, is still its liturgical language, and its scriptural canon preserves books — Enoch, Jubilees — that no other church kept. The Garima Gospels, radiocarbon-dated to roughly these centuries and still held at a monastery in Tigray, are among the oldest illustrated Christian manuscripts to survive anywhere.

experienceToday.text: The Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion at Axum, Ethiopia — on the site of the kingdom's original cathedral, beside the Aksumite stelae field

movements.name: Georgian Christianity
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 3 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 3 Step 0 run and tiered Marginal/deferred (Tier 3) — thin-to-moderate overall, though its Jerusalem-linked lectionary was singled out as an unusual liturgical strength. Its end was set to 609 (Dvin III, the break with Armenia), with the sources' 607/609–10 split disclosed rather than smoothed over.
movements.sourcing: Thin-to-moderate; liturgical evidence unusually strong (Jerusalem-linked lectionary); earliest text is a martyrdom
movements.relationsSummary: Jerusalem and Armenian lines; takes the Chalcedonian side (609)
movements.why: The Caucasus's other national church, and the one that chose the other side — at Dvin III its communion broke with Armenia and stayed Chalcedonian, which is why the region needs two entries rather than one. Its record is thin overall but unusually strong in an area most churches leave dark: a Jerusalem-linked lectionary showing what was actually prayed, in a century where most traditions survive chiefly in what was argued.
movements.dateRationale: End 609 (Dvin III: break with Armenia; sources split 607/609-10) — its own communion realigns. Start 330 precedes the era; the standing rule is an open gate question (Era 3 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Iakob Tsurtaveli, The Martyrdom of Queen Shushanik (trans. in D. M. Lang, Lives and Legends of the Georgian Saints, 1956)
sources.note: The earliest surviving original Georgian text (c.476-83) - exactly the census's 'earliest text is a martyrdom'; Lang's English translation verified (1956, reprinted); confirms the Armenian-Georgian-Persian frontier world.

sources.work: The Conversion of Kartli cycle / Life of St Nino (trans. in Lang 1956; scholarly trans. C. B. Lerner, 2004)
sources.note: Georgia's own conversion narrative; the surviving redactions are later (7th-10th c.) than the era, so use with retrospection flags. [S] Lerner edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: The Old Georgian Jerusalem Lectionary (ed./Latin trans. M. Tarchnischvili, CSCO 188-189, 204-205, 1959-60)
sources.note: The unusually strong liturgical evidence the census flags - Georgian preservation of Jerusalem's 5th-8th c. worship; edition verified; Georgian/Latin only, no English translation (access barrier).

sources.work: Stephen H. Rapp Jr., The Sasanian World through Georgian Eyes (2014)
sources.note: Leading modern treatment of early Georgian historiography and its Iranian-frontier Christian identity; Ashgate/Routledge, expensive but standard.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 2, ch. 4, 'Early Asian and East African Christianities' (David Bundy)
sources.note: Reference chapter covering Georgia among the Caucasus Christianities; verified in vol. 2 TOC.

movements.longDescription: The kingdom of Kartli, in what is now eastern Georgia, became Christian in the fourth century through the preaching of a woman the tradition calls Nino, and then spent three centuries holding that identity on a frontier where Persia had every reason to prise it loose. Its oldest surviving book, written in the 470s or 480s, is the account of Shushanik — an Armenian princess married to the local ruler, who abandoned Christianity for Zoroastrianism and imprisoned and beat his wife until she died rather than follow him. Georgia developed its own alphabet, its own monasteries, and an unusually rich liturgical life: Georgian manuscripts preserve the worship of fifth- to eighth-century Jerusalem more fully than any Greek source does. In 609, at the third council of Dvin, its church broke with Armenia and took the Chalcedonian side — which is why the two neighbouring Caucasian churches have belonged to different communions ever since.
movements.teaser: The Caucasus, c. 330 to 609 CE — a church on the Persian frontier whose earliest surviving book is the story of a queen beaten to death for refusing to follow her husband out of the faith.
voices: Nino — the woman Georgian tradition credits with the kingdom's conversion, known through narratives written centuries later
Shushanik — the martyred queen whose death in the 470s is the subject of the oldest surviving work of Georgian literature
Iakob Tsurtaveli — her chaplain, who wrote that account, and Georgia's first named author
Vakhtang Gorgasali — the fifth-century king remembered for reorganizing the church and pressing its independence
Kyrion I — the catholicos who led the break with the Armenian church at the third council of Dvin in 609
movements.legacy: The Georgian Orthodox Church that emerged is still the church of Georgia, and the same institution continued through the medieval revival centuries into the present. Its choice in 609 placed it permanently in the Eastern Orthodox family rather than with its Armenian neighbour. Its greatest bequest to everyone else is almost accidental: because Georgian scribes translated and kept Jerusalem's liturgical books, scholars can now reconstruct how the holy city actually worshipped in late antiquity largely from Georgian manuscripts. And churches built at the very end of this period, like Jvari above Mtskheta, are still standing almost unaltered.

experienceToday.text: Jvari Monastery above Mtskheta, Georgia — built between about 590 and 605 and surviving nearly unchanged; part of a UNESCO World Heritage site

movements.name: Nubian Christianity
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 3 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 3 Step 0 run and tiered Marginal/deferred (Tier 3), and named an honest hard case: substantially archaeological, with the run sharpening that its one narrative conversion source is an outside Syrian voice rather than its own. Its end was corrected at the gate from an unexplainable 623 to 652, the Baqt treaty that fixed Christian Nubia's terms under Islam.
movements.sourcing: Thin for inside voice: substantially archaeological (Faras murals, Qasr Ibrim texts)
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Egypt - both rival communions' missions at once
movements.why: An honest hard case: real, important, and known mostly through walls and graves rather than through its own letters — the Faras murals and the Qasr Ibrim texts carry what no narrative from inside it does. Even its one conversion account is an outside Syrian voice. It holds a place because a Christian kingdom on the Nile that negotiated its own terms under Islam is not something the map can leave blank, and the honest way to include it is to say plainly how little of it speaks for itself.
movements.dateRationale: End 652 (Baqt treaty: the settlement fixing Christian Nubia's terms under Islam) — corrects an unexplainable 623; straddles one era boundary, allowed (Era 3 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: John of Ephesus, Ecclesiastical History, Part III, bk 4 (trans. R. Payne Smith, 1860; online tertullian.org)
sources.note: The near-contemporary narrative of Nobadia's conversion (Julian 543, Longinus 569-80s) told from the Miaphysite mission's side - verified online; note it is an outside (Syrian) voice, per census 'thin for inside voice'; cf. John of Biclarum for the rival Chalcedonian claim on Makuria.

sources.work: Faras cathedral excavations and murals (K. Michalowski, Faras publications, 1960s-70s)
sources.note: The material inside-voice: bishops' portraits, painted liturgy, bishop lists from the rescued cathedral; publications scattered (Polish/French/German series; murals split Warsaw/Khartoum museums).

sources.work: Qasr Ibrim excavation texts (Egypt Exploration Society reports and text editions)
sources.note: Documentary and liturgical finds from the fortress-cathedral site; mostly later than this era but anchoring the tradition's texture; specialist publications only.

sources.work: Derek A. Welsby, The Medieval Kingdoms of Nubia (2002)
sources.note: The standard accessible synthesis of Christian Nobadia/Makuria/Alwa from conversion onward - verified (British Museum Press).

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 2, ch. 4, 'Early Asian and East African Christianities' (David Bundy)
sources.note: Reference chapter whose scope includes Nubia; verified in vol. 2 TOC. No dedicated Cambridge chapter for Christian Nubia in this era exists.

movements.longDescription: Christianity reached the Nubian kingdoms south of Egypt through competing missions in the 540s — a Miaphysite priest named Julian sent with the empress Theodora's backing, and a Chalcedonian effort sent with Justinian's — and the story of that race survives only because a Syrian bishop, John of Ephesus, wrote it down from the winning side. What Nubia itself left is not narrative but walls. The cathedral at Faras, built a few generations later,, buried in sand and rescued before the Aswan dam flooded the region, gave up a list of its bishops and more than a hundred painted figures: Nubian bishops, kings and queens, saints, some with dark faces and some pale, in a style nobody had seen before. When Arab armies pushed south after taking Egypt, Nubian archers held them at Dongola, and in 652 the two sides signed the Baqt — a treaty of exchange rather than of conquest, which left Christian Nubia standing on its own terms.
movements.teaser: The Nile in what is now Sudan, 543 to 652 CE — three Christian kingdoms whose clearest surviving face comes from a cathedral's painted walls, from the centuries just after this one, which stopped an Arab army and then negotiated their own terms.
voices: Julian — the Miaphysite missionary who reached Nobadia in 543; his mission is known only through John of Ephesus's account
Longinus — his successor, consecrated bishop for Nubia, who went on to bring Christianity to the southern kingdom of Alodia around 580
John of Ephesus — the Syrian bishop who recorded these missions; he is an outside voice, and Nubia left no narrative of its own conversion
The bishops of Faras — a list of their names and a wall of their portraits survive from the cathedral, though almost nothing they said or wrote does
movements.legacy: Christian Nubia outlasted this window by many centuries and only faded in the later Middle Ages; no Nubian church continues today. What survives is largely visual, and it is remarkable: the Faras murals, rescued from the rising waters of Lake Nasser in the 1960s and now divided between museums in Warsaw and Khartoum, are one of the great surviving bodies of medieval African painting. Documents from the fortress-cathedral at Qasr Ibrim show a church writing in Greek, Coptic and Old Nubian at once. And the Baqt held, in one form or another, for centuries — an unusually durable settlement between a Christian state and its Muslim neighbour.

experienceToday.text: The Faras Gallery at the National Museum in Warsaw — the only permanent European exhibition of medieval Nubian wall paintings, rescued from the Faras cathedral before it was flooded

movements.name: Gothic, Vandal & Lombard Homoian Christianity
movements.informalName: The Gothic, Vandal and Lombard Churches
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future Step 0 to answer — stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Real corpus; Vandal persecution of Nicenes documented by its victims
movements.floorNote: These churches held the Homoian creed agreed at Rimini and Constantinople in 359 and 360: the Son is like the Father, but not described as sharing the Father's very being in the way the Nicene Creed says. That places them outside the Nicene definition the rest of this map works from, and how they should be treated here is an open question that has not been settled.
movements.relationsSummary: Ulfila's line; entire post-Roman kingdom churches; scope extended to Lombard Arianism (568-c. 680) at the Era 3 gate
movements.why: Excluded by the floor as it stands (per the Phase One record's reasoning); whether the Constitution's bounded exception path should apply is a live, unresolved question.
movements.dateRationale: End c. 680: Lombard Arianism's effective end (last Arian kings 660s-671; conversion complete by c. 700 — disclosed). Scope + end extension approved (Era 3 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: The Gothic Bible of Ulfila (Codex Argenteus etc.; ed. Streitberg)
sources.note: The tradition's founding artifact - scripture in Gothic; substantial NT portions survive; texts freely online (Wulfila Project); the Skeireins John-commentary fragments add a rare slice of Gothic exegesis.

sources.work: Auxentius of Durostorum, Letter on the life and creed of Ulfila (trans. in P. Heather & J. Matthews, The Goths in the Fourth Century, TTH 11, 1991)
sources.note: The Homoian church's own memory of its apostle, with his creed - preserved in the Dissertatio Maximini; affordable English translation with commentary.

sources.work: Victor of Vita, History of the Vandal Persecution (trans. John Moorhead, TTH 10, 1992)
sources.note: The census's 'documented by its victims': Nicene account of Vandal Homoian coercion in Africa (429-489); hostile witness - read against the grain for Homoian church life; affordable TTH translation.

sources.work: Acts of the Third Council of Toledo (589)
sources.note: The tradition's endpoint: Reccared and the Gothic bishops formally abandon Homoian Christianity; Latin in Vives, Concilios visigoticos (1963); English excerpts in sourcebooks - no standard complete English translation. [S] translation status from knowledge.

sources.work: Robin Whelan, Being Christian in Vandal Africa: The Politics of Orthodoxy in the Post-Imperial West (2018)
sources.note: The key modern corrective - reconstructs Homoian Christianity as a functioning church with clergy, texts and arguments, not a caricature; UC Press, verified.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 2, ch. 2, 'Germanic and Celtic Christianities' (Knut Schaferdiek)
sources.note: Reference-tradition chapter by the leading specialist on Gothic (Homoian) Christianity; chapter title/author verified.

movements.longDescription: Most of the peoples who took over the western Roman provinces — Goths, Vandals, Burgundians, and later the Lombards — were Christians before they arrived, but of a kind the Nicene churches did not recognize: Homoian, holding that the Son is like the Father rather than of one being with him. Their tradition went back to Ulfila, the fourth-century missionary bishop who devised an alphabet for Gothic and translated most of the Bible into it, and it worked as a real church, with clergy, liturgy, scripture in the vernacular, and arguments of its own. In Vandal Africa it was the persecuting party, exiling and maiming Nicene bishops in a campaign its victims documented in detail. In Ostrogothic Italy it lived alongside the Catholic church in separate buildings, some of which still stand in Ravenna. Where it ended, it ended two ways. In Africa and Ostrogothic Italy it was destroyed by Byzantine reconquest. In Spain and among the Lombards it ended by conversion: the Visigothic king Reccared brought his kingdom over at the third council of Toledo in 589, and the last Arian Lombard kings gave way in the seventh century.
movements.teaser: Iberia, Italy and North Africa, 451 to c. 680 CE — the churches of the post-Roman kingdoms, with their own Gothic Bible and their own bishops, on the losing side of the argument that fixed the Creed.
voices: Ulfila — the fourth-century Gothic bishop who created a written form of Gothic and translated the Bible into it
Auxentius of Durostorum — his pupil, whose letter preserves both Ulfila's creed and his church's memory of him
Geiseric and Huneric — the Vandal kings of Africa whose coercion of the Nicene church was recorded by its victims
Theodoric the Great — Ostrogothic king of Italy, who built Arian churches in Ravenna without dismantling the Catholic ones
Victor of Vita — a Nicene bishop and hostile witness, whose History of the Vandal Persecution is the fullest account of this church in power
