Reccared — the Visigothic king who renounced Homoian Christianity at the third council of Toledo in 589, taking his kingdom with him
movements.legacy: Nothing continues this tradition today: it ended in conversion, and its buildings were reconsecrated rather than destroyed. What it left is physical and textual. The Gothic Bible, surviving mainly in the silver-and-purple Codex Argenteus at Uppsala, is by far the largest body of text in any early Germanic language and the foundation of Germanic philology — historians of English and German still work from it. In Ravenna the Arian Baptistery and Theodoric's palace church survive with their mosaics, including a panel where the Gothic court figures were later scrubbed out of the picture. And the crossing of Visigothic Spain at Toledo in 589 set the shape of Iberian Christianity for the next century.

experienceToday.text: The Arian Baptistery in Ravenna, Italy — built for Theodoric's Gothic church around 500 and still standing with its mosaic dome, part of a UNESCO World Heritage site

movements.name: The Byzantine Imperial Church (Justinianic)
movements.statusDescription: Added at the Era 3 gate (Mark, 2026-08-02) — proposed by the Era 3 Step 0 run as the era's largest completeness gap.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutional: conciliar acta (Constantinople II, 553), Justinianic legislation, Procopius, Romanos's kontakia; interior lay texture thinner than its documents
movements.relationsSummary: The rival context for Miaphysite Egypt and the Syriac Orthodox; hosts the Three Chapters dissent internally; the empire whose favor and pressure every Era 3 world negotiates
movements.why: The era is titled 'Monks and Empires' and the empire's own church had no entry — the Era 3 Step 0 completeness sweep's headline gap, approved at the gate. Tier 1 on sourcing.
movements.dateRationale: 451 (Chalcedon, the council its emperors enforced) to 622 (era end; the empire's church continues into Era 4's Byzantine story — succession pairing is a future A4/Era 4 question) (Era 3 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: For nearly two centuries after Chalcedon, the church of the eastern Roman Empire was inseparable from the empire itself: emperors summoned its councils, legislated for its clergy and monasteries, appointed and deposed its patriarchs, and treated doctrinal unity as a condition of political order. Justinian pushed this furthest — rebuilding Hagia Sophia in under six years, codifying Roman law with the church written into it, and in 553 calling a council to condemn the writings of three long-dead theologians, two of whom Chalcedon itself had cleared, in the hope of winning back the Miaphysites. It did not work: the condemnation alienated much of the Latin West without reconciling Egypt or Syria, and each attempted formula produced a fresh schism instead. The same church, in the same years, produced Romanos the Melodist, whose sung sermons in verse are among the finest poetry in Greek, and sent missionaries as far as the Nile kingdoms.
movements.teaser: Constantinople and the imperial Mediterranean, 451 to 622 CE — a church whose emperor built Hagia Sophia, wrote its law and summoned its councils, and still could not make it agree.
voices: Justinian — emperor from 527 to 565, who legislated for the church as thoroughly as for the state and summoned the council of 553
Theodora — his wife, who used her position to shelter the anti-Chalcedonian leaders his policy was pressing
Romanos the Melodist — a deacon from Syria whose verse sermons set to music are still sung in Orthodox worship
Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus — the mathematician-architects who designed Hagia Sophia
Menas — the patriarch of Constantinople who inaugurated the new Hagia Sophia with Justinian in December 537
Vigilius — the pope brought to Constantinople and pressured for years over the condemnation of the Three Chapters
movements.legacy: The same institution continued unbroken into the Byzantine centuries that followed, and is the direct ancestor of the Eastern Orthodox churches today. The pattern set here — emperor and patriarch as two authorities within one Christian commonwealth — became the model Byzantium exported to the Balkans and to Russia. Hagia Sophia stood as the largest church in the world for nearly a thousand years and changed what a church building could be. Justinian's legislation fed into Orthodox canon law, and the hymns of Romanos are still sung. Its harder legacy is the divisions its pressure helped harden: the separations of 451 were still unhealed when the empire lost Egypt and Syria altogether.

experienceToday.text: The Basilica of San Vitale in Ravenna, Italy — completed in 547, with the mosaic portraits of Justinian and Theodora facing each other across the sanctuary

movements.name: The Church of Caucasian Albania
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 3 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Added at the Era 3 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Thin: Movses Daskhurantsi's later history, canons of Aghuen, palimpsest fragments of the Albanian script
movements.relationsSummary: The third Caucasus church beside Armenia and Georgia; absorbed into the Armenian catholicosate after 705
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep as the third Caucasus church. Tier 3 signal (sourcing floor); awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: c. 451 to 705 (absorption into the Armenian catholicosate) (Era 3 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: Beside Armenia and Georgia there was a third Christian kingdom in the Caucasus: Albania, in what is now Azerbaijan and southern Dagestan, with its own royal line, its own bishops and its own alphabet. It held a council at Aghuen in the late fifth century that issued canons on clergy, marriage and what the nobility owed the church, and it produced a history — compiled from earlier material by a writer known as Movses Daskhurantsi — that is very nearly all the narrative it left. Pressed between Persian, Byzantine and then Arab power, and between the competing alignments of its Armenian and Georgian neighbours, it lost its independent standing in 705, when its catholicosate was placed under the Armenian church. Its written language was effectively lost for more than a thousand years, until palimpsests found at Saint Catherine's Monastery on Sinai in 1996 turned out to preserve Caucasian Albanian scripture beneath later Georgian text.
movements.teaser: The eastern Caucasus, c. 451 to 705 CE — a third Caucasian church with its own alphabet and its own canons, whose written language could not be read again until a chance discovery at Sinai in 1996.
voices: Vachagan III — the king remembered for convoking the council at Aghuen and for building churches, at the start of this window
Movses Daskhurantsi — the compiler credited with the History of the Caucasian Albanians, very nearly the only narrative this church left
Viroy — the seventh-century catholicos who, according to that history, went out to negotiate with invading forces on his people's behalf
Beyond these few names the record is thin: much of what is known about this church comes to us second-hand, through Armenian sources
movements.legacy: No church continues under this name — after 705 its structures were absorbed into the Armenian catholicosate and its separate identity dissolved into its neighbours'. The Udi people of Azerbaijan are generally regarded as descendants of its Christian population. Its most striking survival was invisible until recently: the palimpsests recovered at Sinai in 1996 preserved its alphabet and its scripture, letting scholars begin to reconstruct a language and a liturgy that nobody had been able to read for over a millennium.

movements.name: Latin African Christianity under Byzantium
movements.statusDescription: Added at the Era 3 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: Ferrandus and Facundus (Three Chapters resistance), Victor of Tunnuna, conciliar records; ordinary texture thin
movements.relationsSummary: Nicene Africa restored after the Vandal century; heir of the Era 1-2 African tradition; a principal voice in the Three Chapters resistance
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: the last century and a half of ancient African Christianity had no entry. Tier 2-3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 533 (Byzantine reconquest of Africa) to c. 698 (fall of Carthage) (Era 3 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: When Belisarius destroyed the Vandal kingdom in 533, the Nicene church of Roman Africa came out of a century of persecution and was restored to its buildings and its bishoprics — and within twenty years it was the most stubborn opposition Justinian faced anywhere in his own empire. When he condemned the Three Chapters to appease the Miaphysites, the African bishops refused: Facundus of Hermiane wrote twelve books against it, Reparatus of Carthage was deposed and exiled, and the chronicler Victor of Tunnuna spent years in prison and exile for the same refusal. Africa stayed a place where theology got argued at full volume — Maximus the Confessor spent formative years here, and African councils in 646 rejected the empire's next attempted compromise about the wills of Christ. Then Arab armies reached Carthage in the 690s, and the ancient African church, the church that had given Latin Christianity Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine, was finished within a few generations.
movements.teaser: Byzantine North Africa, 533 to c. 698 CE — the church Justinian's armies restored, which promptly told him he was wrong, and went on arguing until the conquest ended the argument.
voices: Facundus of Hermiane — the bishop whose twelve books in defence of the Three Chapters are the fullest African argument against Justinian's policy
Reparatus of Carthage — primate of Africa, deposed and exiled for refusing to sign
Victor of Tunnuna — bishop and chronicler, repeatedly imprisoned and exiled for the same refusal, who recorded it from inside
Ferrandus of Carthage — a deacon whose canon collection and letters of advice show the practical working life of the restored church
Maximus the Confessor — the theologian who spent years in Africa and helped shape the councils of 646 that rejected the imperial doctrine of a single will in Christ
movements.legacy: This church left no successor. Latin Christianity in North Africa dwindled after the conquest and had effectively disappeared by the later Middle Ages — the only major region of the ancient Christian world to vanish so completely. But it handed on its refusal: its resistance over the Three Chapters hardened a Western conviction that an emperor could not settle doctrine by decree, and its part in the argument over Christ's wills fed straight into the council of 680-681 that closed it. Its earlier centuries had already given the Latin church Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine; what this last century added was a demonstration that a provincial church could tell an empire no. The ruins of Carthage and of dozens of African basilicas remain.

experienceToday.text: The archaeological site of Carthage, Tunisia — a UNESCO World Heritage site whose remains include the basilicas and cisterns of the late antique Christian city

movements.name: Nicene Visigothic Iberia
movements.statusDescription: Added at the Era 3 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate-rich: the Toledo councils' acta ([S] English access unverified), Isidore of Seville, Braulio's letters, Visigothic liturgy
movements.floorNote: No question - III Toledo (589) is the kingdom's own Nicene turn
movements.relationsSummary: The Homoian kingdom that crossed to Nicaea from inside; Isidore's church; ends at 711
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: the one kingdom-church whose own council chose the Creed. Tier 2-3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: c. 560 to 711 (the conquest); III Toledo (589), the kingdom's own Nicene turn, is the hinge inside (Era 3 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: The Visigoths ruled Spain as Homoian Christians for over a century, in uneasy coexistence with the Nicene population they governed — until King Reccared announced his own conversion and, at the third council of Toledo in 589, brought the Gothic bishops with him. Nothing quite like it happened anywhere else: a kingdom's own church council formally abandoned its creed and adopted its subjects'. What followed was one of the more remarkable intellectual efforts of the early Middle Ages. Isidore of Seville set out to gather what survived of classical learning into a single encyclopaedia, and his circle — his brother Leander, Braulio of Zaragoza, Ildefonsus of Toledo — produced letters, liturgy, histories and rules around him. The councils of Toledo worked as something between a synod and a parliament, legislating for church and kingdom together, and their record also includes a harsh and escalating body of law against Spain's Jews. All of it ended abruptly with the Muslim conquest of 711.
movements.teaser: Visigothic Spain, c. 560 to 711 CE — the one barbarian kingdom whose own council voted to change its creed, and then governed itself through its bishops until the conquest.
voices: Reccared — the king who renounced Homoian Christianity and carried his kingdom's bishops with him at Toledo in 589
Leander of Seville — bishop, the king's ally in that conversion, and author of a rule for his sister's convent
Isidore of Seville — bishop from about 600, whose Etymologiae compiled classical learning for a world losing it, and who presided at the fourth council of Toledo in 633
Braulio of Zaragoza — Isidore's correspondent and editor, whose letters give an unusually personal view of this church at work
Ildefonsus of Toledo — bishop and writer whose devotion to the Virgin shaped later Spanish piety
Hermenegild — a king's son who converted against his Arian father, rebelled, and was executed in 585; later venerated as a martyr
movements.legacy: The same institution continued under Muslim rule as the Mozarabic Christianity of al-Andalus. Its liturgy went with it: the Mozarabic rite, formed in this period, is still celebrated in a chapel of Toledo Cathedral. Isidore's Etymologiae became one of the most copied books of the Middle Ages and served for centuries as the standard reference work of the Latin West — he is sometimes called the last scholar of the ancient world. The councils of Toledo left a large body of canon law that shaped later Western practice, and it was in Visigothic Spain that the Filioque clause first entered official use in the Creed. Several of its churches — small, sharply cut, horseshoe-arched — still stand in northern Spain.

experienceToday.text: The church of San Juan Bautista at Baños de Cerrato, Palencia, Spain — commissioned by King Recceswinth in 661 and still bearing its dedication stone

movements.name: British and Welsh Christianity
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 3 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Added at the Era 3 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Thin: Gildas's De Excidio is the anchor; saints' lives late; archaeology growing
movements.relationsSummary: The church the Anglo-Saxon invasions displaced - distinct from Irish Christianity, older than the Gregorian mission it later met; rejected Augustine's authority (603) and did not conform at Whitby (664)
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: real, distinct, and thin - an honest Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate. End c. 768: the Welsh church's own adoption of the Roman Easter (Elfoddw) - its distinct-practice identity closes on its own realignment, not at Whitby 664, a borrowed hinge the Round 2 review caught (the British church did not conform there).
movements.dateRationale: c. 451 to c. 768 (Elfoddw: the Welsh church's own adoption of the Roman Easter — not Whitby 664, which it did not attend) (Era 3 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: Britain had been Christian under Roman rule, and when the province fell away and Anglo-Saxon settlers took the east, that church did not vanish — it survived in the west: in Wales, Cornwall, the north-west, and across the sea in Brittany, which British emigrants gave its name. Its own record is thin and largely furious. Gildas, writing around the 540s, delivered a book-length denunciation of British kings and clergy for the sins he believed had brought the Saxon catastrophe on them. Its life ran through monastic schools and founder-saints whose names still sit on Welsh parishes — David, Illtud, Teilo, Cadoc — and through inscribed memorial stones that are among the few hard traces of the period. When Augustine of Canterbury arrived from Rome and met British bishops around 603, they declined to accept his authority or to join his mission to the Saxons who had displaced them; they were not at the synod of Whitby in 664 either. The Welsh church came round to the Roman dating of Easter on its own, around 768.
movements.teaser: Wales, western Britain, Cornwall and Brittany, c. 451 to 768 CE — the old British church, pushed west by Saxon settlement, which declined to recognize Rome's missionary and kept its own Easter for another century and a half.
voices: Gildas — the monk whose On the Ruin of Britain, written around the 540s, is the only substantial contemporary British voice from this period
Illtud — the teacher whose monastic school in Glamorgan is remembered as training a generation of British saints
David — the ascetic bishop, died around 589, who became the patron saint of Wales
Samson of Dol — the British bishop who crossed to Brittany, and the subject of an unusually early life
Elfoddw — the Welsh churchman credited with bringing his church to the Roman dating of Easter around 768
movements.legacy: There is no separately continuing British church: its dioceses were gradually drawn into the wider Western church, and the Welsh bishops came under Canterbury's authority in the twelfth century. What it left is written across the landscape — the llan- place names of Wales mark its churchyards, its founder-saints are still the dedications of Welsh and Cornish parishes, and its inscribed memorial stones survive in numbers. Gildas's account, for all its fury, became the foundation of what later writers thought they knew about post-Roman Britain, reaching Bede and everyone after him. And Brittany, settled from Britain in these centuries, kept both a Celtic language and a cluster of British saints' cults that are still there.

experienceToday.text: St Davids Cathedral, Pembrokeshire, Wales — the present building is medieval, but it stands on the site of the monastery David founded in the sixth century, and holds his shrine

movements.name: The Church of the East on the Silk Road
movements.informalName: The Church of the East on the Silk Road
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 4 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — the census's own word for its sourcing, spectacular fragments over long silent stretches, was left standing rather than softened. Its floor check was run in this era's own window: Timothy I's Apology before al-Mahdi defends the divinity of Christ in the patriarch's own words, alongside the synodal record cited for II.3.
movements.sourcing: Uneven: spectacular fragments (Xi'an stele, Dunhuang/Turfan texts) over long silent stretches
movements.floorNote: 'Nestorian', the label most often attached to this church, was given to it by opponents rather than chosen by itself. Its own synods and its own patriarchs confess Christ as divine — Timothy I argues exactly that in his account of debating the caliph — even though its way of describing how divinity and humanity are joined in Christ differs from the formula agreed at Chalcedon in 451.
movements.relationsSummary: Continuation of II.3 - the map's longest single lineage line (Edessa to Xi'an)
movements.why: The map's longest single lineage line — Edessa to Xi'an, one communion carried the width of Asia as far as a Chinese imperial capital. It is also where that reach documentably closes: the Huichang edict of 845 laicized foreign clergy and the Tang church stops being visible. What the entry cannot do is join its own high points to each other; a good deal of what lies between them is reconstruction, and that is stated rather than smoothed over.
movements.dateRationale: End 845 (Huichang edict laicizes foreign clergy — the Tang church's documented end); the Persia/Central-Asia continuation is disclosed, and the oft-cited 987 extinction report was not verified and is not used (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Xi'an ('Nestorian') Stele, 781 CE — trans. in M. Nicolini-Zani, The Luminous Way to the East (OUP, 2022)
sources.note: The community's own public self-presentation in Tang China (history, theology, imperial patronage). Newly annotated English translation in Nicolini-Zani; older full translation in P. Y. Saeki, The Nestorian Documents and Relics in China (1937), on archive.org [S: Saeki edition details from knowledge, not re-verified this session].

sources.work: Dunhuang and Turfan Christian ('Jingjiao') texts — trans. in Nicolini-Zani, The Luminous Way to the East (OUP, 2022)
sources.note: The Chinese-language Christian texts themselves (sutras, hymns, catechetical documents) — the 'spectacular fragments' the census names. Nicolini-Zani gives the current richly annotated English translations of the Tang-era corpus; verified via OUP/reviews.

sources.work: Timothy I, Apology before the Caliph al-Mahdi (trans. A. Mingana, Woodbrooke Studies 2, 1928)
sources.note: Patriarchal inside voice of the church that ran the Silk Road missions (Timothy I, r. 780-823); free online at tertullian.org. His letters also report missions to Turks and Tibetans [S: the letters' critical edition (Heimgartner, CSCO, Syriac with German translation) from knowledge; no complete English].

sources.work: Wilhelm Baum & Dietmar W. Winkler, The Church of the East: A Concise History (RoutledgeCurzon, 2003)
sources.note: The standard one-volume English history of the whole tradition, including the Central Asian and Chinese expansion; verified. Fills the 'long silent stretches' with the institutional frame.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 3: 'Beyond empire I: Eastern Christianities from the Persian to the Turkish conquest, 604-1071' (Igor Dorfmann-Lazarev)
sources.note: Chapter title/author verified in the vol. 3 TOC (Noble & Smith, 2008). The era's reference-tradition anchor for the eastern churches beyond Byzantium.

movements.longDescription: A Syriac-speaking church whose bishops sat in Persia had, by the seventh century, sent monks the whole width of Asia: in 635 a missionary the Chinese records call Alopen reached the Tang capital of Chang'an and was received at the imperial court, and toleration for his religion was proclaimed three years later. What that mission looked like is known mostly through a handful of extraordinary survivals — above all a stone stele erected in 781, inscribed in both Chinese and Syriac, narrating a century and a half of what it calls the Luminous Religion in China, and caches of Christian manuscripts recovered at Dunhuang and Turfan. Between those bright points lie long silences, and much of what is said about the stretches in between is reconstruction rather than record. The reach closes visibly in 845, when an imperial edict aimed at foreign religions ordered clergy out of their monasteries and the Chinese church stops appearing in the sources — though the same communion carried on in Persia and Central Asia.
movements.teaser: Persia to Tang China, c. 635 to 845 — one Syriac-speaking communion stretched the whole width of Asia, remembered now through a stone stele at Xi'an and manuscripts found in desert caves.
voices: Alopen — the Syriac missionary whom Chinese records name as reaching the Tang capital in 635
Timothy I — patriarch in Baghdad from 780 to 823, who appointed bishops for the church's most distant provinces and defended the divinity of Christ in his account of debating the caliph al-Mahdi
Adam (Jingjing) — the priest named on the Xi'an stele as the author of its Chinese text
movements.legacy: In China itself nothing carried through: no community there can be traced across the gap between the ninth century and the arrival of much later missions, and what remains is archaeological — the stele, the Dunhuang and Turfan manuscripts, and Christian gravestones scattered across Central Asia. The communion that sent them did not end, though. The Church of the East continued from its Mesopotamian heartland and would reach east again under the Mongols. This is the furthest east any church of these centuries is known to have reached, and the clearest case of a Christianity that genuinely flourished and then left almost nothing behind but stone.

experienceToday.text: The Xi'an Stele, Beilin Museum (the Forest of Steles), Xi'an — the 781 monument recording Christianity's first arrival in China, still on display

movements.name: Melkite Arabic Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 4 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) — John of Damascus, Abu Qurrah and On the Triune Nature of God give it a moderate-to-rich base, and the run named it unique as the first church to think in Arabic. Its end was set at the gate to 1009, al-Hakim's razing of the Holy Sepulchre in the entry's own heartland.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: John of Damascus at Mar Saba; Theodore Abu Qurrah's Arabic apologetics
movements.relationsSummary: Heir of II.5; the first church to think in Arabic
movements.why: The first church to think in Arabic. Chalcedonian Christianity in Palestine and Syria did not merely survive the conquest — it changed working language and began arguing its own faith in the language of the people now governing it, something no tradition in the atlas had yet had to do. Its heartland is the same monastic world Era 3's Judean Desert entry covers, continuing under an entirely new order.
movements.dateRationale: End 1009 (al-Hakim razes the Holy Sepulchre, 18 Oct 1009 — the entry's own heartland) (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: John of Damascus, Three Treatises on the Divine Images (trans. Andrew Louth, SVS Popular Patristics)
sources.note: The Mar Saba theologian the census names, writing under the caliphate; Louth's translation verified as the standard English version [S: 2003 publication year not confirmed in search results this session]. His Fount of Knowledge includes the first Christian theological account of Islam.

sources.work: Theodore Abu Qurrah, works (trans. John C. Lamoreaux, Library of the Christian East, BYU Press, 2005)
sources.note: First English translation of nearly the complete corpus of the first major Christian theologian writing in Arabic (bishop of Harran, c. 810); verified. Exactly the census's 'Arabic apologetics.'

sources.work: On the Triune Nature of God (early Melkite Arabic apology, Sinai Arabic 154, 8th c.)
sources.note: One of the oldest surviving Christian texts composed in Arabic — the tradition learning to 'think in Arabic' in real time. [S: edition/translation details (M. D. Gibson, Studia Sinaitica VII, 1899, partial English) from knowledge, not re-verified this session.]

sources.work: Sidney H. Griffith, The Church in the Shadow of the Mosque (Princeton, 2008)
sources.note: The standard modern account of Arabic-speaking Christianity under early Islam, with the Melkites at its center; verified.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 9: 'Christians under Muslim rule' (Sidney H. Griffith)
sources.note: Chapter title/author verified in the vol. 3 TOC. Direct chapter fit for this movement.

movements.longDescription: When the Arab conquests cut Palestine and Syria off from Constantinople, the Chalcedonian Christians of those provinces — Melkites, 'the emperor's people', as their neighbours labelled them — found themselves a minority under a new government and, within a few generations, doing something no church had done before: praying, arguing and writing theology in Arabic. Their intellectual heart was the monastic world of the Judean desert, above all the monastery of Mar Saba, where John of Damascus, from a family that had served in the Muslim administration, wrote the great defence of religious images that Byzantine emperors could not silence because he lived beyond their reach. A generation later Theodore Abu Qurrah was writing theology in Arabic for a mixed audience of Christians and Muslims, and anonymous works such as the treatise now called On the Triune Nature of God were explaining the Trinity in the vocabulary of the world around them. The window closes hard in 1009, when the caliph al-Hakim ordered the Church of the Holy Sepulchre razed.
movements.teaser: Palestine and Syria, c. 700 to 1009 — the first Christians to argue their faith in Arabic, writing from desert monasteries that lay beyond any emperor's reach.
voices: John of Damascus — monk of Mar Saba, whose defence of icons was written from outside the empire that was destroying them
Theodore Abu Qurrah — bishop of Harran, the first Christian theologian we can name who wrote in Arabic
The unnamed author of On the Triune Nature of God — an eighth-century writer whose explanation of the Trinity is among the earliest Christian theology in Arabic
movements.legacy: Arabic-speaking Chalcedonian Christianity did not stop here: the same communion continues in the Greek Orthodox patriarchates of Antioch and Jerusalem and, after an eighteenth-century division, in the Melkite Greek Catholic Church. John of Damascus's defence of images became the settled theology of icons for the whole Orthodox world — he was vindicated by name at the council that restored them in 787 — and his systematic Exposition of the Orthodox Faith was translated into Latin and read by Western theologians for centuries afterward. Mar Saba, where he wrote, is still a working monastery.

experienceToday.text: Mar Saba, Judean Desert near Bethlehem — the monastery where John of Damascus wrote, still inhabited by monks (women may enter only the tower at the gate)

movements.name: Coptic Christianity under Early Islam
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 4 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2): the History of the Patriarchs is institutionally strong, while ordinary interior texture stays thin inside this window. Its end was set to 1013, the escalation of al-Hakim's Egyptian persecution — the same event-complex as the Melkite end, seen from Egypt.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: History of the Patriarchs strong institutionally; ordinary interior texture thinner in this window
movements.relationsSummary: Continuation of II.1
movements.why: The continuation of Miaphysite Egypt through the centuries that decided what Egyptian Christianity would become — a church that entered this window governing its own affairs and left it governed by others. The atlas needs the transition itself and not only its endpoints, and that is what this entry holds. Its institutional record carries that story well; the ordinary life underneath it stays largely out of reach inside this window.
movements.dateRationale: End 1013 (al-Hakim's Egyptian persecution escalates 1004-1013; alt 1004 on record) — the same event-complex as the Melkite end, seen from Egypt (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: History of the Patriarchs of the Coptic Church of Alexandria (attrib. Severus ibn al-Muqaffa'; ed./trans. B. Evetts, Patrologia Orientalis)
sources.note: The church's own institutional memory across the conquest and after — the census's named strong institutional source. English translation free online at tertullian.org (verified in the Era 3 research pass; same edition covers this window).

sources.work: John of Nikiu, Chronicle (trans. R. H. Charles, 1916)
sources.note: Miaphysite bishop's narrative of the 642 conquest itself — the hinge event of this entry. Ethiopic-via-Arabic transmission; translation online (verified in the Era 3 pass).

sources.work: Apocalypse of Pseudo-Samuel of Qalamun
sources.note: Coptic-tradition lament over Arabization and language loss — rare interior texture for the thinner ordinary-voice window the census flags. [S: date debated (anywhere 8th-11th c.) and edition details (Ziadeh, Arabic with French translation) from knowledge, not verified this session.]

sources.work: Maged S. A. Mikhail, From Byzantine to Islamic Egypt (I.B. Tauris, 2014)
sources.note: Current standard monograph on exactly this transition (religion, identity, politics after the conquest); verified.

sources.work: Mark N. Swanson, The Coptic Papacy in Islamic Egypt, 641-1517 (AUC Press, 2010)
sources.note: Institution-focused companion built directly on the History of the Patriarchs; verified.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 9: 'Christians under Muslim rule' (Sidney H. Griffith)
sources.note: Chapter verified in the vol. 3 TOC; direct fit.

movements.longDescription: Egypt's miaphysite Christians had spent the century before the Arab conquest under Byzantine pressure for refusing the Council of Chalcedon; when Arab armies took Alexandria in 641-42 their patriarch Benjamin came out of hiding and was restored to his see. What followed was the long transition that made the Coptic church what it still is — no longer persecuted for its confession but taxed and governed as a protected minority, shifting gradually from Coptic into Arabic, and beginning the long, centuries-long drift toward minority status that conversions would eventually bring. Its own record of those years, the History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria, follows the church bishop by bishop with unusual care, though it says far more about patriarchs and taxes than about ordinary Egyptian Christians. The window ends with the persecution under the caliph al-Hakim in the early eleventh century, the harshest single episode the community had yet faced.
movements.teaser: Egypt, 642 to 1013 — a church that walked out of Byzantine persecution into Muslim rule, and over four centuries began the long slide from being the country's uncontested majority toward the minority it is now — a shift historians place mostly later, and argue about still.
voices: Benjamin I — the patriarch who emerged from hiding after the conquest and was restored to Alexandria
Severus ibn al-Muqaffa' — tenth-century bishop of Ashmunayn associated with the History of the Patriarchs, who wrote theology in Arabic for a church losing its own language
Pseudo-Samuel of Kalamun — the unknown author of an apocalypse written under a famous monk's name, grieving that Egyptian Christians were giving up Coptic for Arabic
movements.legacy: The same church is still there. Its institutions continued unbroken into the Fatimid and Mamluk centuries and on into the present-day Coptic Orthodox Church of Alexandria, one of the largest Christian bodies in the Middle East. What was set in these centuries is the pattern that has defined it since — a minority church organised around its monasteries and its patriarch, using Coptic in worship long after Arabic became the language of everything else.

experienceToday.text: The Hanging Church (St Virgin Mary's Coptic Orthodox Church), Old Cairo — built over a gate of the Roman fortress and long the patriarch's own church, open to visitors

movements.name: Anglo-Saxon Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 4 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1), assessed as the era's best-documented conversion-to-mission arc, with the Boniface circle's letters — Leoba's among them — carrying women's own correspondence. Its end was set to 793 (Lindisfarne, the break its own sources mourn), and its 597 start, which precedes the era, stands under the start-before-era standing rule adopted at this gate.
movements.sourcing: Rich for the era: Bede; Boniface circle's letters including women's correspondence (Leoba)
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Benedictine + Irish lines converging at Whitby; parent of the Carolingian reform
movements.why: No other church in the era can be watched turning from mission field into missionary sender in this much detail — England had been converted within living memory when it began sending its own people back onto the continent the faith had come from. Two Era 3 lines meet in it, the Benedictine and the Irish, and it hands on directly to Carolingian reform. Rare for this period, some of its letters are women's own: Leoba writes in the Boniface circle under her own name, not through a chronicler's summary.
movements.dateRationale: End 793 (Lindisfarne, 8 Jun 793 — the canonical break in the entry's own monastic world). Start 597 precedes the era boundary and stands under the start-before-era standing rule (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English People (ed./trans. Colgrave & Mynors, Oxford Medieval Texts, 1969; Penguin trans. also in print)
sources.note: The census's named anchor — the single richest narrative source of the era in the West; standard edition verified, cheap translations everywhere.

sources.work: The Letters of St Boniface (trans. Ephraim Emerton, 1940; repr. Columbia, 2000 with introduction by T. F. X. Noble)
sources.note: The Boniface circle's correspondence, including the women's letters (Leoba to Boniface) the census names; verified.

sources.work: C. H. Talbot, The Anglo-Saxon Missionaries in Germany (1954): Lives of Willibrord, Boniface, Sturm, Leoba, Lebuin + the Hodoeporicon of Willibald
sources.note: English translations of the mission-circle hagiography, including Rudolf of Fulda's Life of Leoba — the fullest portrait of an Anglo-Saxon woman religious; verified, on archive.org.

sources.work: Henry Mayr-Harting, The Coming of Christianity to Anglo-Saxon England (3rd ed. 1991)
sources.note: The classic synthesis of the conversion and the converging Roman/Irish streams (the census's Whitby convergence); verified.

sources.work: John Blair, The Church in Anglo-Saxon Society (Oxford, 2005)
sources.note: The modern ground-level account (minsters, landscape, ordinary practice) — counterweight to great-men narrative; verified.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 5: 'Germanic Christianities, 600-1100' (Lesley Abrams)
sources.note: Chapter title/author verified in the vol. 3 TOC; covers the Anglo-Saxon world.

movements.longDescription: Christianity reached the English twice over and from two directions — from Rome in 597, when Augustine landed in Kent, and from Ireland by way of Iona, whose monks founded Lindisfarne and evangelised Northumbria — and at the Synod of Whitby in 664 the two traditions had to settle publicly which calendar and which customs the English church would keep. What grew out of that settlement was a church with an extraordinary appetite for learning: Bede, writing at Jarrow, finished in 731 the history that is still the main source for the whole period, and monasteries like Whitby, under the abbess Hild, trained bishops. Within a century of being a mission field, England was sending missionaries of its own back across the Channel — Willibrord to Frisia, Boniface into Germany, and with them women such as the abbess Leoba, whose one surviving letter comes down under her own name. The window closes on 8 June 793, when Viking raiders sacked Lindisfarne and a different age began.
movements.teaser: England, 597 to 793 — converted within living memory, and already sending its own monks and nuns back across the Channel to convert the continent the faith had come from.
voices: Augustine of Canterbury — led the Roman mission that landed in Kent in 597
Aidan — Irish monk from Iona who founded Lindisfarne and evangelised Northumbria
Hild of Whitby — abbess of a double house of men and women that trained five bishops, and host of the Synod of Whitby in 664
Bede — monk of Jarrow, whose Ecclesiastical History of the English People, finished in 731, is the era's indispensable record
Boniface — the West Saxon missionary who reorganised the church in Germany and was killed in Frisia in 754
Leoba — abbess in Boniface's circle; one surviving letter, and four lines of Latin verse, are all that come down from her in her own name
movements.legacy: The same church continued: this story runs straight on into the late Anglo-Saxon church that survived the Viking wars and was rebuilt under Alfred and the reforming bishops. Beyond that succession, it left the books. The Lindisfarne Gospels and the Codex Amiatinus came out of these monasteries; Bede's history shaped how the English told their own story for a thousand years and gave the Western world the habit of dating years from the Incarnation; and the mission into Germany reorganised the continental church so thoroughly that the Carolingian reform grew directly out of it.

experienceToday.text: Lindisfarne Priory, Holy Island, Northumberland — the site raided in 793, with its Anglo-Saxon stonework, cared for by English Heritage

movements.name: Carolingian Reform Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 4 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on its institutional richness. The census's note that its ordinary voice is mostly inferred was sharpened rather than contradicted — Dhuoda's Handbook was named a genuine lay voice, though an aristocratic one. Its dates were anchored at the gate to 751 (Pippin's anointing) and 888, when the reform's imperial carrier fragments.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally; ordinary voice mostly inferred from what people were told
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Anglo-Saxon + Gallic lines; parent of Cluny
movements.why: A real question rides on this entry: whether it is a lived tradition or a policy tradition. Almost everything that survives from it is what people were told — capitularies, corrected liturgies, schoolbooks — so its institutional richness is exactly what makes the ordinary interior hard to see. It holds a place because that problem is worth showing plainly, not because it has been solved.
movements.dateRationale: Start 751 (Pippin's anointing); end 888 (death of Charles the Fat — the reform's imperial carrier fragments) (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Admonitio generalis (789) and related capitularies — trans. in P. D. King, Charlemagne: Translated Sources (1987)
sources.note: The reform program in its own words — what people were told, which the census says is where the ordinary voice must be inferred from; King's translation verified.

sources.work: Alcuin of York, letters (trans. S. Allott, Alcuin of York: His Life and Letters, 1974)
sources.note: The reform's chief architect's working correspondence. [S: Allott translation details from knowledge, not verified this session; selections also in standard sourcebooks.]

sources.work: Dhuoda, Handbook for William (trans. Carol Neel, CUA Press, 1991)
sources.note: A lay noblewoman's own religious counsel to her son (843) — a genuine ordinary-lay voice inside the reform world; verified. Mild nuance to the census's 'ordinary voice mostly inferred': one real lay voice survives (aristocratic, so the census claim stands for the non-elite).

sources.work: Rosamond McKitterick, The Frankish Church and the Carolingian Reforms, 789-895 (Royal Historical Society, 1977)
sources.note: The standard study of the reform as a pastoral program, arguing it reached further down than 'policy tradition' skeptics allow — speaks directly to the census's lived-vs-policy question; verified.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3 (Noble & Smith, 2008) — Carolingian material
sources.note: [S] No single dedicated Carolingian chapter identified in the TOC this session; coverage runs through Part I ch. 5 (Abrams, 'Germanic Christianities') and the thematic chapters (e.g. ch. 13 'Asceticism and its institutions', Helvétius & Kaplan — chapter verified). Precise chapter assignment left to era review.

movements.longDescription: When Pippin was anointed king in 751 and his son Charlemagne built an empire across western Europe, they treated the condition of the church as a matter of government: schools attached to cathedrals and monasteries, corrected copies of Scripture and the liturgy, one monastic rule for the whole realm, and decrees ordering that every priest be able to explain the Creed and the Lord's Prayer to his people in words they could understand. Scholars were imported to run it, Alcuin of York above all, and the clear round script their scriptoria developed — Carolingian minuscule — is the ancestor of the letters you are reading now. Almost everything that survives, though, is what people were told rather than what they thought: the reform is documented from the top down, and its ordinary interior life has to be inferred from its own instructions. One striking exception is a lay voice, Dhuoda, a noblewoman writing a handbook of faith and conduct for her absent son in the 840s. The imperial framework that carried the reform broke apart after 888.
movements.teaser: Francia, 751 to 888 — an empire that treated the correcting of the church's books, schools and worship as an act of government, and left behind the handwriting we still read by.
voices: Charlemagne — the ruler who made the reform of the church an instrument of government
Alcuin of York — the English scholar brought in to run the court school and oversee the correction of texts
Benedict of Aniane — the monk who pressed a single rule across the empire's monasteries
Dhuoda — a noblewoman whose handbook of faith, written for her son, is one of very few lay voices to survive from the period
Hincmar of Reims — archbishop and canon lawyer who pressed the reform's claims even against kings
movements.legacy: Its institutional line runs on into the papal reform of the eleventh century and through that into the Latin church of the whole later Middle Ages. Its most durable legacies are practical: Carolingian minuscule, which Renaissance humanists took as their model and which therefore stands behind modern printed type; corrected texts of the Bible and the Roman liturgy that stayed standard for centuries; and the cathedral and monastic schools that were the seed-bed of the medieval universities. The chapel Charlemagne built at Aachen is still standing and still in use.

experienceToday.text: The Palatine Chapel, Aachen Cathedral, Germany — Charlemagne's own chapel, consecrated in 805 and Germany's first UNESCO World Heritage Site

movements.name: Iconophile Byzantine Monasticism
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 4 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) — the era's defining theological struggle seen from inside, on Theodore the Studite's corpus and the Nicaea II acta, with an access limit noted: Theodore's roughly 550 letters have no complete English translation. Iconoclast Christianity was routed rivals-inside the imperial entry added at the same gate, as the rival that ran the palace, leaving this entry its named hostile-quotation problem.
movements.sourcing: Rich: Theodore the Studite's huge pastoral corpus; iconoclast side survives only in hostile quotation (named problem)
movements.relationsSummary: Heir of Greek monastic lines; parent of Athonite monasticism
movements.why: Iconoclasm is the argument that defines the era's Greek East, and this entry stands inside it — on the monastic side, since for two long stretches icon-rejection was what the palace enforced. That is why the census houses the iconoclast establishment in the imperial entry, as the rival that ran the state, and leaves this one its own named problem: the side it argued against survives almost wholly in the words of its opponents. What comes out of it is Athonite monasticism and a settled Orthodox theology of the image.

sources.work: John of Damascus, Three Treatises on the Divine Images (trans. Andrew Louth, SVS Popular Patristics)
sources.note: The foundational iconophile theology, written from Mar Saba outside imperial reach; Louth translation verified as standard [S: 2003 year not confirmed this session]. Shared item with the Melkite entry — the two movements genuinely overlap here.

sources.work: Theodore the Studite, On the Holy Icons (trans. Catharine Roth, SVS Press, 1981); Letters (ed. Fatouros, CFHB 31, 1992)
sources.note: Roth's translation of the icon treatises verified. Access caveat on the census's 'huge pastoral corpus': the ~550 letters exist in Fatouros's Greek edition with German summaries — no complete English translation (verified absence via search); only selections translated. Deepens, does not contradict.

sources.work: The Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea (787) (trans. Richard Price, TTH 68, Liverpool, 2018)
sources.note: The iconophile victory documents, first full English translation with commentary; verified. Also the main vehicle for the hostile-quotation survival of the iconoclast side (the census's named problem — the 754 Horos survives only as refuted excerpts here).

sources.work: Life of Stephen the Younger (ed./French trans. M.-F. Auzépy, 1997)
sources.note: The premier iconophile martyr-life (monastic milieu, Bithynia). [S: edition details from knowledge; French only, no complete English — access flag.]

sources.work: Leslie Brubaker & John Haldon, Byzantium in the Iconoclast Era, c. 680-850 (Cambridge, 2011)
sources.note: The standard modern history; verified. Caution flag for builders: it is deliberately revisionist (argues persecution was far more limited than iconophile sources claim), i.e. it presses hard on exactly the hostile-quotation problem the census names.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 2: 'The emergence of Byzantine Orthodoxy, 600-1095' (Andrew Louth)
sources.note: Chapter title/author verified in the vol. 3 TOC; the iconoclast controversy sits at its center.

movements.longDescription: Twice over a century and more, the Byzantine court tried to purge Christian worship of images, and both times the strongest organised resistance came from the monasteries. The monks argued that because God had genuinely become a human being who could be seen, he could be depicted — that refusing the image was, in the end, refusing the Incarnation — and they paid for the argument: Stephen the Younger was killed in 765, and Theodore, abbot of the great Stoudios monastery in Constantinople, was beaten, imprisoned and exiled more than once while still producing letters, talks to his monks, and treatises on the holy icons. Images were restored once at the Council of Nicaea in 787 and finally in 843, a day the Orthodox churches still keep as the Triumph of Orthodoxy. One thing is worth knowing about the story as we have it: the winning side wrote the record, and the iconoclasts' own case survives almost entirely in quotations made by the people refuting it.
movements.teaser: Constantinople and Bithynia, 726 to 843 — monks who argued that a God who had taken a human face could be painted, and were beaten, exiled and killed for saying so.
voices: John of Damascus — whose three treatises in defence of images, written safely outside the empire, gave the movement its theology
Stephen the Younger — a monk killed in 765, remembered as the persecution's most famous martyr
Theodore the Studite — abbot of Stoudios, the movement's organiser and most prolific writer, repeatedly exiled
Empress Irene — under whose regency the Council of Nicaea restored the icons in 787
Patriarch Nikephoros — deposed and exiled for refusing the second imperial iconoclasm, and a major writer against it
Empress Theodora — whose regency ended iconoclasm for good in 843
movements.legacy: The same monastic tradition continues directly as Athonite monasticism and, through it, the wider Orthodox monastic world. Its theology of the image became settled Orthodox doctrine: it is the reason icons look the way they do and are treated the way they are in Orthodox churches today, and the Sunday of Orthodoxy, kept every year on the first Sunday of Lent, is a liturgical commemoration of how this argument ended. Theodore's reorganisation of Stoudios also shaped later Byzantine and Slavic monastic rules well beyond his own house.

movements.name: Cyrillo-Methodian Slavic Christianity
movements.informalName: The Mission of Cyril and Methodius
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 4 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), with its vernacular-scripture argument named as what makes it distinct — the translations themselves stand as evidence, alongside the vitas and Hrabar's defense. Its end was corrected at the gate from 950, which matched no event, to 916 (the death of Clement of Ohrid, last of the mission's own generation).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: vitas, the translations themselves as evidence
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Byzantium; parent of Kievan Rus' Christianity
movements.why: An argument about vernacular scripture that left its own evidence behind — the translations themselves, and an alphabet made so that a people could read Scripture in their own tongue. Hrabar's defense of Slavonic letters is a rare thing in the atlas: a tradition arguing on its own behalf that its language is fit for worship. Everything in the Slavic Orthodox line, Kievan Rus' first, descends from what was made here.
movements.dateRationale: End 916 (death of Clement of Ohrid, last of the mission's own generation) — corrects a data error; the old 950 matched no event. Alt 885/886 (Moravian expulsion) on record (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Life of Constantine and Life of Methodius (trans. Marvin Kantor, Medieval Slavic Lives of Saints and Princes, Michigan Slavic Translations 5, 1983)
sources.note: The two vitas the census names — the mission's own memory of itself; facing-page Old Church Slavonic and English; verified, full text free online (kroraina.com/promacedonia.org).

sources.work: Chernorizets Hrabar, On the Letters (O pismenech)
sources.note: The first-generation defense of the Slavic alphabet against the 'trilingual' objection — the mission's program argued from inside. English in K. Petkov, The Voices of Medieval Bulgaria (Brill, 2008) [S: Petkov volume verified to exist, but its inclusion of this text not page-verified this session].

sources.work: The earliest Slavonic liturgical/biblical manuscripts (e.g. Kiev Folia) as direct evidence of the translation program
sources.note: The census's 'the translations themselves as evidence' item made concrete. [S: specialist paleographic editions; details from knowledge — access is via facsimile/scholarly literature, not reader-friendly translation.]

sources.work: A. P. Vlasto, The Entry of the Slavs into Christendom (Cambridge, 1970)
sources.note: Standard English survey of Slavic Christianization with full Cyrillo-Methodian coverage; verified.

sources.work: Francis Dvornik, Byzantine Missions among the Slavs (1970)
sources.note: The classic study of the mission in its Byzantine and papal politics. [S: not re-verified this session; standard work.]

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 6: 'Slav Christianities, 800-1100' (Jonathan Shepard)
sources.note: Chapter title/author verified in the vol. 3 TOC; direct fit.

movements.longDescription: In 863 two brothers from Thessaloniki — Constantine, better known by his monastic name Cyril, and Methodius — were sent from Constantinople to Moravia at its ruler's request, and did something unusual for their day: rather than teach in Greek or Latin, they devised an alphabet for the Slavic language and translated the Scriptures and the liturgy into it. The idea was fought hard, by clergy who held that God could properly be worshipped only in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, and the brothers travelled to Rome to argue the case, where the pope approved the Slavonic books. After Methodius died in 885 their disciples were driven out of Moravia and carried the work south, where Clement and Naum built schools at Ohrid and Preslav that turned it into a permanent literature — and where the alphabet now called Cyrillic took the shape it still has. A monk writing under the name Hrabar defended the new letters in a short, sharp treatise: a rare case of a tradition arguing publicly, in its own words, that its language was fit for worship.
movements.teaser: Moravia to Ohrid, c. 863 to 916 — two brothers who made an alphabet so that a people could hear the gospel in the language they actually spoke.
voices: Cyril (Constantine the Philosopher) — the scholar who devised the Glagolitic alphabet and began the Slavonic translations
Methodius — his brother and archbishop, who carried the work on for sixteen years after Cyril's death
Clement of Ohrid — disciple who founded the school at Ohrid after the mission was expelled from Moravia, and died there in 916
Naum — fellow disciple, who worked at Preslav and later at Ohrid
Chernorizets Hrabar — the monk whose treatise On the Letters defended writing and worshipping in Slavonic
movements.legacy: Almost everything downstream of it in the Slavic Orthodox world begins here. The tradition continues directly into the Christianity of Kievan Rus' and through that into the Russian, Ukrainian, Serbian and Bulgarian churches; Church Slavonic is still the liturgical language of much of Orthodox Christianity, and the Cyrillic alphabet — named for one brother though shaped by their successors — is used by hundreds of millions of people. Cyril and Methodius are venerated as saints in both East and West, and in 1980 the Catholic Church named them co-patrons of Europe.

experienceToday.text: The Church of Saints Clement and Panteleimon, Plaošnik, Ohrid, North Macedonia — Clement's own foundation and burial place, rebuilt on its excavated site

movements.name: Kievan Rus' Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 4 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — the Primary Chronicle and the Paterik are later compilations needing tier care, with Hilarion's Sermon (c. 1049) named as the in-window native voice. Its end was corrected at the gate from an unexplained 1068 to 1054, the death of Yaroslav the Wise, which also resolved a mismatch between its date string and its numbers.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich just past this era (Kyiv Caves Paterik, chronicle - later compilations, tier care)
movements.relationsSummary: Child of III.7; parent of the whole Russian line
movements.why: The founding arc of the entire Russian line, contained inside roughly two generations — from the conversion of 988 to Yaroslav's death at the era boundary itself. A very large share of later Orthodox Christianity traces back through this short window, which is why the atlas carries it as its own world rather than as a note on Byzantium. What it cannot yet supply is much testimony written while it was actually happening.
movements.dateRationale: End 1054 (death of Yaroslav the Wise, Feb 1054 — the founding arc closes at the era boundary itself) — corrects an unexplained 1068 and the string/number mismatch (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: The Russian Primary Chronicle, Laurentian text (trans. S. H. Cross & O. P. Sherbowitz-Wetzor, Mediaeval Academy, 1953)
sources.note: The conversion narrative (Vladimir's investigation of faiths, 988 baptism); verified. Compiled early 12th c. from earlier material — the census's 'later compilations, tier care' flag applies squarely.

sources.work: Ilarion of Kiev, Sermon on Law and Grace (trans. Simon Franklin, Sermons and Rhetoric of Kievan Rus', Harvard Library of Early Ukrainian Literature, 1991)
sources.note: The first great native voice (metropolitan of Kiev, c. 1049) — inside the census's era window, theology of the newly baptized nation; verified.

sources.work: The Paterik of the Kievan Caves Monastery (trans. Muriel Heppell, Harvard, 1989)
sources.note: The census's named source; first complete English translation, verified. 13th-c. compilation reaching back to the mid-11th-c. foundation — tier care exactly as the census says.

sources.work: Simon Franklin & Jonathan Shepard, The Emergence of Rus, 750-1200 (Longman, 1996)
sources.note: The standard English history of the period, source-critical about the chronicle; verified.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 6: 'Slav Christianities, 800-1100' (Jonathan Shepard)
sources.note: Chapter verified in the vol. 3 TOC; Shepard is also co-author of the standard secondary above — direct fit.

movements.longDescription: In 988 Prince Vladimir of Kyiv was baptised and had his people baptised with him — an act of state that the Rus' chronicle later dressed in one of the great stories of medieval Christianity: envoys sent out to sample the religions who reported that in Hagia Sophia at Constantinople they had not known whether they stood in heaven or on earth. Within two generations there was a Christian culture to match the decision. Vladimir's son Yaroslav built his own St Sophia in Kyiv and filled it with mosaics; a monastery in the caves above the Dnieper became the school of Rus' monasticism; and around 1049 a native churchman, Ilarion — whom Yaroslav would make the first native-born metropolitan two years later — preached a Sermon on Law and Grace that is the first substantial theology written by a Rus' author. The window is short, barely two generations, but almost the whole later history of Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian Christianity runs back through it. Most of what tells the story was written down afterwards, by monks looking back.
movements.teaser: Kyiv and Novgorod, 988 to 1054 — two generations in which a prince's baptism became a cathedral, a monastery and a literature, and the Slavic north became Christian.
voices: Olga of Kyiv — Vladimir's grandmother, baptised a generation before the conversion of the realm
Vladimir the Great — the prince whose baptism in 988 converted Rus'
Yaroslav the Wise — his son, builder of St Sophia in Kyiv and patron of its first Christian book culture
Ilarion of Kyiv — first native-born metropolitan, author of the Sermon on Law and Grace
Antony and Theodosius of the Caves — founders of the Kyiv Caves Monastery, the mother house of Rus' monasticism
Boris and Gleb — Vladimir's murdered sons, the first saints the Rus' church canonised of its own
movements.legacy: The same church continued without a break into the Kievan Rus' of the following two centuries and, through it, into the Russian, Ukrainian and Belarusian Orthodox churches — the largest body of Orthodox Christians in the world traces its founding to these two generations. It also left things you can still stand in front of: St Sophia in Kyiv keeps its eleventh-century mosaics and frescoes, the Caves Monastery is still a monastery, and Boris and Gleb, venerated as 'passion-bearers' who would not raise a hand against their own brother, became a model of holiness distinctive to the Slavic churches.

experienceToday.text: Saint Sophia Cathedral and the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, Kyiv — the eleventh-century cathedral with its original mosaics and the caves monastery, together a UNESCO World Heritage Site

movements.name: Mozarabic Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 4 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) — moderate in sourcing but vivid at the martyrs' crisis, where Eulogius and Alvarus speak inside a live communal argument about assimilation and provoked martyrdom. The run named it distinct on audience grounds as a church arguing with itself under Islam; its end was set to 1031, when its whole political frame ended with the Caliphate of Córdoba.
movements.sourcing: Moderate but vivid at the martyrs' crisis - Eulogius and Alvarus are real voices in a live communal argument
movements.relationsSummary: Heir of post-589 Iberia; a community arguing with itself about provoked martyrdom
movements.why: A church arguing with itself, out loud, about how much of a Muslim world a Christian may live inside — and both sides of that argument reach us. Some in Córdoba defended the martyrs who provoked their own executions; other Christians in the same city thought them wrong and said so. Very few entries in the atlas preserve an internal disagreement about assimilation in the words of the people actually having it.
movements.dateRationale: End 1031 (fall of the Caliphate of Cordoba — the entry's whole political frame ends) (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: The Eulogius Corpus (trans. Kenneth Baxter Wolf, TTH 71, Liverpool, 2019)
sources.note: First complete English translation of Eulogius of Cordoba (Memoriale sanctorum, Documentum martyriale, Liber apologeticus martyrum) — the census's named 'real voice in a live communal argument'; verified.

sources.work: Paulus Alvarus, Indiculus luminosus and letters
sources.note: The lay half of the census's named pair — the argument for the martyrs and the famous lament over young Christians preferring Arabic. [S: no complete English translation; access via excerpts in Colbert (1962) and Coope/Wolf — status from knowledge, not verified this session.]

sources.work: Chronicle of 754 (trans. K. B. Wolf, Conquerors and Chroniclers of Early Medieval Spain, TTH 9)
sources.note: A Latin Christian voice from al-Andalus at the start of the entry's window — sets the conquest-era baseline before the martyrs' crisis. [S: TTH edition details from knowledge, not re-verified this session.]

sources.work: Kenneth Baxter Wolf, Christian Martyrs in Muslim Spain (Cambridge, 1988)
sources.note: Standard study of the martyrs' movement; author verified via the TTH volume above [S: free full text online at libro.uca.edu from knowledge].

sources.work: Jessica A. Coope, The Martyrs of Cordoba: Community and Family Conflict in an Age of Mass Conversion (Nebraska, 1995)
sources.note: Reads the crisis as a communal argument about assimilation and conversion — precisely the census's framing of 'a community arguing with itself'; verified.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 9: 'Christians under Muslim rule' (Sidney H. Griffith)
sources.note: Chapter verified in the vol. 3 TOC; cf. ch. 8 (Kennedy, 'The Mediterranean frontier') for the political frame.

movements.longDescription: After 711 most of Iberia's Christians lived under Muslim rule, kept the old Visigothic liturgy, and — as generations passed — increasingly spoke, wrote and thought in Arabic. In the 850s that quiet accommodation broke open in Córdoba, where some four dozen Christians were executed after publicly denouncing Islam, many of them going out of their way to provoke the sentence. The community then argued with itself about what had happened: the priest Eulogius wrote the martyrs up as heroes and was executed himself in 859; his friend Paulus Alvarus complained bitterly that young Christians were mastering Arabic poetry while their Latin decayed; and other Christians, including bishops assembled in council, judged that the martyrs had thrown their lives away. Very little of the community's ordinary life is recoverable, but that argument survives in the words of the people who were having it. The window closes with the collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba in 1031.
movements.teaser: Córdoba and al-Andalus, 711 to 1031 — a church arguing out loud with itself about how much of a Muslim world a Christian could live inside, and whether provoking your own execution counted as martyrdom.
voices: Eulogius of Córdoba — priest who chronicled and defended the martyrs, and was executed in 859
Paulus Alvarus — layman, writer and Eulogius's biographer, who lamented that young Christians preferred Arabic learning to their own
Flora and Maria — two of the martyrs, whose imprisonment and death Eulogius recorded at length
Reccafred — the bishop who opposed the martyrs' course and had Eulogius imprisoned
movements.legacy: No continuing community carries the name: Mozarabic Christianity was worn away between the pressure of the Almoravid and Almohad periods and absorption into the Latin church of the northern kingdoms as they advanced. Its liturgy, though, outlived the community that kept it. The old Hispanic rite, which the Mozarabs held on to when the rest of the Latin West adopted Roman usage, was rescued at Toledo around 1500 by Cardinal Cisneros, who had its books printed and endowed a chapel to keep it in use — and Mass in the Hispano-Mozarabic rite is still celebrated there daily.

experienceToday.text: The Mozarabic Chapel, Toledo Cathedral, Spain — where the Hispano-Mozarabic rite is still sung at a daily Mass

movements.name: Cluniac Reform Monasticism
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 4 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) — institutionally rich and immense in scale, with an access flag on its customaries, which are Latin-only. Its end was decided at the gate on a stated fork, 1109 over the alternative 1049, closing the reform's carrying arc whole; the absence of an Era 5 receiver for its twelfth-century peak was flagged forward rather than resolved here.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally (customaries, charters); interior ordinary voice moderate
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Carolingian reform; the establishment Era 4's new orders react against; its 12th-c. peak under Peter the Venerable (to 1156 — first Latin Qur’an, Abelard sheltered) recorded as a continuation note, no receiver entry (approved at the Era 5 gate as a named touch on the Frozen Era 4 record)
movements.why: Reform at a scale nothing before it in the Latin West had reached — a network of houses answering to one abbot rather than to the local lords who had previously owned them. It matters to the atlas in two directions at once: as the Carolingian reform's institutional heir, and as the establishment that the following era's new orders would define themselves against. What it left behind is largely the record of an institution, charters and customaries, rather than of an interior life.
movements.dateRationale: End 1109 (death of Hugh the Great — the reform's carrying arc completes; one boundary crossing, allowed). Alt 1049 (Odilo-to-Hugh hinge) on record; the era-5 receiver gap is flagged to the A1.E5 run (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Foundation Charter of Cluny (910) — trans. in E. F. Henderson, Select Historical Documents (1892), online at the Internet Medieval Sourcebook (Fordham)
sources.note: The constitutional document (exemption, Peter and Paul's ownership, election of abbots); free verified translation at sourcebooks.fordham.edu; also in Rosenwein's reader.

sources.work: John of Salerno, Life of St Odo + Odo of Cluny, Life of Gerald of Aurillac (trans. Gerard Sitwell, St. Odo of Cluny, 1958)
sources.note: The reform's self-portrait: its second abbot's life plus Odo's model of lay sanctity; Sitwell translation verified.

sources.work: Cluniac customaries (Liber tramitis; Bernard and Ulrich of Cluny)
sources.note: The census's named institutional riches — the liturgical machine described from inside. [S: Latin editions (Corpus Consuetudinum Monasticarum); no complete English translation — access flag; status from knowledge.]

sources.work: Barbara H. Rosenwein, Rhinoceros Bound: Cluny in the Tenth Century (Penn, 1982)
sources.note: Standard interpretive study of what Cluniac ritual order meant socially; verified. Her charter work (To Be the Neighbor of Saint Peter, 1989) extends the census's 'charters' leg.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 13: 'Asceticism and its institutions' (Anne-Marie Helvetius & Michel Kaplan)
sources.note: Chapter title/authors verified via search; the monastic-institutional chapter of the era volume.

movements.longDescription: In 909 or 910 — the foundation charter's own year is disputed — a duke of Aquitaine endowed a monastery at Cluny in Burgundy and did something unusual with the deed: he renounced all rights over it, for himself and his heirs, and placed it directly under the pope, so that no local lord or bishop could appoint its abbot or spend its money. Freed from that grip, and led by a run of unusually long-lived and capable abbots, Cluny grew into a network of hundreds of houses across Europe answering to a single abbot, with a life built around an elaborate round of prayer — the community's chief work was the liturgy, sung at a length no earlier Western monastery had attempted. Its abbots reached outward too: Odilo spread the commemoration of all the dead on 2 November and lent his weight to efforts to limit private warfare, and by the eleventh century Cluny's church was the largest in Christendom. Its records are institutional almost throughout — charters, customaries, letters of business — so its inner life is easier to describe from the outside than from within.
movements.teaser: Burgundy and then all of Europe, 909 to 1109 — a monastery deliberately placed beyond the reach of any local lord, which grew into the first continent-wide religious network.
voices: William the Pious, Duke of Aquitaine — whose foundation charter renounced his own family's rights over the house he was endowing
Berno — Cluny's first abbot
Odo of Cluny — second abbot, whose reforming work carried the house's customs far beyond Burgundy
Odilo — abbot for more than fifty years, who spread the commemoration of All Souls and backed efforts to restrain private war
Hugh the Great — abbot for sixty years, under whom the network reached its widest extent and the vast new church was begun
movements.legacy: The order itself dwindled, and its great church was quarried away after the French Revolution, so that only a fragment of what was once the largest church in Europe still stands at Cluny. What it left behind is larger than what survives of it. Its insistence that a monastery answer to Rome rather than to the local lord fed directly into the papal reform of the eleventh century; the commemoration of All Souls on 2 November, which Odilo did most to spread, is still kept across Western Christianity; and the next century's new orders, the Cistercians above all, defined themselves precisely against Cluny's wealth and its long liturgy.

experienceToday.text: Cluny Abbey, Burgundy, France — the surviving transept and towers of the medieval abbey, with its museum, open to visitors

movements.name: St. Thomas Christians of India
movements.informalName: The St. Thomas Christians of India
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 4 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 4 Step 0 run and tiered Marginal/deferred (Tier 3) — real, ancient and distinct, with the entry's own note that its inside voice is thin in every pre-1500 window confirmed rather than softened. Its start was moved to 849, the Tarisappalli/Quilon copper plates, anchoring the window to the era's one dated in-window document.
movements.sourcing: THIN for inside voice in every pre-1500 window: copper plates, epigraphy, liturgy, travelers' notices
movements.relationsSummary: Daughter/partner of the Church of the East
movements.why: Real, ancient, and hard to build honestly — very little of its own voice survives in any window before 1500. What anchors this one is a single dated in-window document, the Quilon copper plates, which is why the window begins where it does rather than at a traditional origin. It holds a place because an Indian Christianity inside the Church of the East's communion, and on nobody else's line, cannot be left off the map merely for the thinness of its own writing.
movements.dateRationale: Start 849 (Tarisappalli/Quilon copper plates — the era's one dated in-window document); anchors the window to its own evidence, keeping the entry's thin-sourcing honesty (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Quilon (Tharisappalli) copper plates, c. 849 CE
sources.note: Royal grant of land and privileges to the Tharisappalli church community under Mar Sapir Iso — the census's 'copper plates' leg and the anchor-document of the era window; existence/date/content verified (incl. recent scholarship, e.g. the Tarisappalli Copperplates study on academia.edu). Specialist editions; no single standard English reader edition.

sources.work: Ishoyahb III, letter to Shem'on of Rev Ardashir on the lapse of the Indian episcopate (c. 650s)
sources.note: Church of the East patriarchal correspondence attesting India's place in (and friction with) the Persian hierarchy — the 'daughter/partner' relation in the census. Quotation verified via GEDSH/reference sites. [S: Syriac edition (Duval, CSCO) with Latin translation; no complete English — access via excerpts in secondary works.]

sources.work: Pahlavi-inscribed 'Persian crosses' (St Thomas Mount, Kottayam, etc.)
sources.note: The census's epigraphy leg — material inside-voice of the community, roughly 7th-9th c. [S: datings and inscription readings debated; details from knowledge, specialist literature only.]

sources.work: Cosmas Indicopleustes, Christian Topography (trans. McCrindle, 1897; online)
sources.note: Outside travelers'-notice attestation of Christians in Male (Malabar) with clergy from Persia — technically just before the era window (c. 550) but the standard attestation bridge into it; translation verified online in the Era 3 pass.

sources.work: A. Mathias Mundadan, History of Christianity in India, vol. 1: From the Beginning up to the Middle of the Sixteenth Century (CHAI, 1984)
sources.note: Standard scholarly history from within the tradition's homeland academy; verified. Honest about how thin the early inside voice is — consistent with the census's THIN flag.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 3: 'Beyond empire I' (Igor Dorfmann-Lazarev)
sources.note: Chapter verified in the vol. 3 TOC. [S: depth of India coverage within the chapter not page-verified; no dedicated India chapter exists in the volume.]

movements.longDescription: On the Malabar coast of India there was, long before any European arrived, a Christian community that traced itself to the apostle Thomas, worshipped in Syriac, and received its bishops from the patriarch of the Church of the East in Mesopotamia — an Indian church inside an Asian communion, on nobody's European line at all. What it left of itself in this period is mostly not writing but objects and documents drawn up by others: granite crosses carved with inscriptions in Pahlavi, the language of Persia, and above all a set of copper plates issued around 849 in which a local ruler grants land and trading privileges to a church at Kollam and names the Christians as a recognised community with standing among their neighbours. Almost nothing survives in which these Christians describe themselves in their own words before about 1500 — which makes them at once one of the oldest continuously existing Christian communities in the world and one of the hardest to hear.
movements.teaser: The Malabar Coast, 849 to 1054 — an Indian church that worshipped in Syriac and took its bishops from Persia, known in this era almost entirely through copper plates and carved stone.
voices: Tradition remembers two bishops, Mar Sabor and Mar Proth, arriving in the ninth century and associated with the church at Kollam, but no individual voice from inside the community survives from this period — what remains of these centuries is documentary and carved rather than personal.
movements.legacy: The community never stopped existing. Its descendants are the St Thomas Christians of Kerala — today divided among several churches, after Portuguese pressure in the sixteenth century and the ruptures that followed, but continuous with this one, and still using Syriac liturgical traditions.
