The objects survive as well: the ninth-century copper plates are preserved in Kerala, and the Pahlavi-inscribed stone crosses still stand in churches at Kottayam and on St Thomas Mount in Chennai.

experienceToday.text: St Mary's Knanaya Church (Valiyapally), Kottayam, Kerala — home to two ancient granite 'Persian crosses' carved with Pahlavi inscriptions

movements.name: Paulicians
movements.statusDescription: The record is genuinely disputed. This entry carries the question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Known almost wholly through hostile heresiology
movements.floorNote: Their opponents accuse them of dualism — of holding that the visible world was made by an evil power rather than by God — and of denying that Christ was divine by nature rather than adopted. Because no Paulician account of their own belief survives, those charges can be neither confirmed nor cleared. The same difficulty attaches to other movements of the period who are known only through the writings of their enemies.
movements.relationsSummary: Deported en masse by Byzantium - also a victim story
movements.why: Not built because the record cannot establish what they themselves confessed. The uncertainty itself is presented honestly.
movements.dateRationale: c. 650-878 (Constantine-Silvanus fl. 650s; fall of Tephrike 878) — matches the numbers to the entry's own '7th-9th c.' claim, correcting a whole-era placeholder; the 970 Philippopolis deportation noted as coda (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Peter of Sicily, History of the Paulicians — trans. in Hamilton & Hamilton, Christian Dualist Heresies in the Byzantine World, c. 650-c. 1450 (Manchester, 1998)
sources.note: HOSTILE SOURCE — the principal Greek account, by a Byzantine envoy; all doctrinal attributions (dualism, adoptionism) come through this and related polemic, exactly as the census's floor note says. Hamilton & Hamilton volume and its Paulician section verified (15 of its 50 source-headings are Paulician).

sources.work: Greek abjuration formulas and the Peter the Higumen / 'Pseudo-Photius' dossier — in Hamilton & Hamilton (1998)
sources.note: The rest of the hostile Greek dossier, translated in the same verified volume. [S: precise contents list of the volume's Paulician headings not itemized this session.]

sources.work: The Key of Truth (ed./trans. F. C. Conybeare, 1898)
sources.note: CONTESTED ITEM — an Armenian text Conybeare claimed as a Paulician manual (adoptionist, non-dualist). Date and attribution are disputed (possibly much later); use only with that dispute stated. [S: scholarly status summary from knowledge; flag matches the census's cannot-confirm-or-clear stance.]

sources.work: Nina G. Garsoian, The Paulician Heresy (1967)
sources.note: The classic critical study; argued the Greek and Armenian source-traditions diverge (Armenian evidence lacks the dualism). [S: not re-verified this session; standard work.]

sources.work: Carl Dixon, The Paulicians: Heresy, Persecution and Warfare on the Byzantine Frontier, c. 750-880 (Brill, 2022)
sources.note: Current monograph; verified. Explicitly recasts the Paulicians as 'broadly conventional Christians' and reappraises the hostile sources — strong support for the census's Contested-Evidentiary status and its deportation/victim framing.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 3: 'Beyond empire I' (Dorfmann-Lazarev); cf. ch. 2 (Louth)
sources.note: [S] Chapter existence verified in TOC, but the Paulicians' chapter placement (Armenian ch. 3 vs Byzantine ch. 2) inferred, not page-verified.

movements.longDescription: The Paulicians appear in the record between the seventh and ninth centuries in Armenia and eastern Anatolia, and almost everything said about them was written by people trying to destroy them. Byzantine heresy-hunters describe a movement that rejected the Old Testament, the cross, the sacraments and the veneration of Mary, and held a dualist view of the world; whether that is what the Paulicians believed, or what their enemies needed them to believe, cannot now be settled. What is not in doubt is what was done to them: imperial campaigns killed and displaced them in large numbers, and the survivors built a fortified state of their own at Tephrike on the frontier, made common cause with the Arabs, and raided Byzantine territory until the fortress fell in 878. Later emperors deported whole Paulician populations to the Balkans.
movements.teaser: Armenia and the Byzantine frontier, c. 650 to 878 — a movement described only by the people who destroyed it, which ended up holding a fortress state of its own against the empire that hunted it.
voices: Constantine-Silvanus — named in Byzantine sources as the movement's founder in the seventh century, and reported killed by the authorities
Sergius-Tychicus — a later leader whose letters are quoted, in fragments, by the same hostile writers
Karbeas and Chrysocheir — commanders of the Paulician state at Tephrike, known from Byzantine military accounts
Every one of these names reaches us through writers who were hostile to them; nothing survives that a Paulician wrote about the Paulicians.
movements.legacy: Nothing institutional survived: the Paulician state ended with Tephrike in 878, and the communities deported into Thrace were absorbed or converted over the following centuries. Their most argued-over legacy is a claim rather than an inheritance — medieval and modern writers have repeatedly linked them to the Bogomils of Bulgaria and through them to the Cathars of the West, but that chain rests on the same hostile heresy-catalogues that describe the Paulicians themselves, and it cannot be demonstrated. An Armenian text called The Key of Truth, published in 1898, was presented as a Paulician manual; its surviving manuscript is centuries later than the movement, and what it proves about these centuries is disputed.

movements.name: Bogomils
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence recorded — dualist cosmology per hostile witnesses (one verified, two carried [S]); own voice unrecovered
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future Step 0 to answer — stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Hostile sources plus later adjacent texts
movements.floorNote: The sources — all of them written by opponents — describe a dualist teaching: that the visible world and the human body were made not by God but by a fallen power. If that description is accurate, it would set the Bogomils outside the Nicene Creed's opening confession of God as maker of all things visible and invisible. No Bogomil statement of their own belief survives to test the charge against, so the question is left open here rather than treated as settled.
movements.relationsSummary: Parent-influence claimed for the Cathars
movements.why: Excluded-in-prospect by the floor's plain reading, pending this era's Step 0. Not a judgment of unimportance.

sources.work: Cosmas the Priest, Sermon (Discourse) Against the Heretics (late 10th c.) — trans. in Hamilton & Hamilton, Christian Dualist Heresies in the Byzantine World (1998)
sources.note: HOSTILE SOURCE — the key near-contemporary account the assignment names; a Bulgarian priest's polemic, incidentally preserving the movement's practices and social appeal. Inclusion and dating (after Tsar Peter, d. 969) verified; a standalone scholarly English translation also circulates on academia.edu (verified).

sources.work: Letter of Patriarch Theophylact of Constantinople to Tsar Peter of Bulgaria (mid-10th c.) — in Hamilton & Hamilton (1998)
sources.note: HOSTILE SOURCE — the earliest official notice of the heresy in Bulgaria, with prescribed anathemas. [S: inclusion in the Hamilton volume from knowledge; the volume itself and its 35 Bogomil source-headings verified.]

sources.work: Euthymius Zigabenus, Panoplia Dogmatica, ch. on the Bogomils (c. 1100) — in Hamilton & Hamilton (1998)
sources.note: HOSTILE + LATER-ADJACENT (just past the era window) — the fullest doctrinal description, from the Constantinople trial of Basil the Bogomil; matches the census's 'later adjacent texts.' [S: inclusion in the Hamilton volume from knowledge.]

sources.work: Dimitri Obolensky, The Bogomils: A Study in Balkan Neo-Manichaeism (Cambridge, 1948)
sources.note: The classic monograph, still the standard narrative; verified. Its 'Neo-Manichaean' frame is what the census's floor note engages — a future Step 0 should weigh newer skepticism about how organized/dualist the movement really was.

sources.work: Yuri Stoyanov, The Other God: Dualist Religions from Antiquity to the Cathar Heresy (Yale, 2000)
sources.note: Modern synthesis of the dualist line including the claimed Bogomil-Cathar link the census records. Stoyanov verified as co-translator of the Hamilton sourcebook [S: this title's details not re-verified this session].

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 6: 'Slav Christianities, 800-1100' (Jonathan Shepard)
sources.note: [S] Chapter verified in TOC; Bogomil coverage within it inferred from its Bulgaria scope, not page-verified.

movements.longDescription: The Bogomils take their name from a Bulgarian priest of the mid-tenth century, and the earliest account of them — a long sermon written against them by another priest, Cosmas — describes a movement of ascetics who rejected almost everything the visible church consisted of: church buildings, the cross, icons, the sacraments, infant baptism and the clergy who administered them. Behind that refusal, the sources report, lay a conviction that the material world and the human body were not made by God at all but by a fallen power, so that the whole apparatus of physical religion was a mistake. They spread from Bulgaria through the Balkans and into Byzantium, where around 1100 their most prominent teacher, a man called Basil, was burned in Constantinople. As with the Paulicians, none of their own writing survives: everything described here is the report of people arguing against them.
movements.teaser: Bulgaria and the Balkans, from the tenth century — ascetics who refused churches, crosses and sacraments as belonging to a world they believed God had not made, and who are described entirely by their opponents.
voices: Bogomil — the Bulgarian priest whose name the movement carries; nothing written by him survives
Cosmas the Priest — their earliest and most detailed opponent, whose sermon against them is the main source for what they taught
Basil the Physician — a Bogomil teacher burned in Constantinople under the emperor Alexios I, around 1100
movements.legacy: The movement continued in the Balkans for centuries — its story runs on directly into the Bogomil communities of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries — before disappearing under Ottoman rule and Catholic and Orthodox pressure alike. Its most discussed legacy is a claimed influence on the Cathars of southern France and northern Italy: medieval writers asserted the connection, and historians still argue about how much of it is real. What it did not leave is a text of its own. Every surviving account of Bogomil belief was written by someone opposing it.

movements.name: Scandinavian Conversion Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 4 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2): rune stones and Adam of Bremen are contemporary witnesses, while the vivid sagas are thirteenth-century retrospectives needing tier care. Its 826–1104 window was left unchanged — the straddle flag raised against it dissolved under the frozen rule as written, 1104 crossing the era boundary exactly once.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: rune stones and Adam of Bremen contemporaneously; the vivid sagas are 13th-c. retrospectives (tier care)
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Anglo-Saxon + Hamburg-Bremen missions; Iceland converted by communal vote at the Althing (1000)
movements.why: The one conversion story in the atlas that a people is recorded as having settled by communal vote — Iceland's Althing decided the question for the whole community in the year 1000. Every other conversion here runs through kings, missionaries, or slow attrition, which is what makes this window distinct rather than merely late. Two mission lines converge on it, the Anglo-Saxon and the Hamburg-Bremen, so it is also where the era's Western missionary reach can be watched arriving.

sources.work: Rimbert, Vita Anskarii / Anskar: The Apostle of the North (trans. C. H. Robinson, 1921)
sources.note: Near-contemporary missionary life (Anskar d. 865, by his successor) — the 826+ Danish/Swedish missions from inside; translation verified, free online (archive.org, Fordham sourcebook).

sources.work: Adam of Bremen, History of the Archbishops of Hamburg-Bremen (trans. F. J. Tschan, Columbia, 1959; repr. 2002 with intro by T. Reuter)
sources.note: The census's named contemporaneous narrative (written c. 1070s, at the era's end), including the famous Book IV description of pagan Uppsala — a Hamburg-Bremen institutional viewpoint, read with that bias in mind; verified.

sources.work: Rune stones (Jelling stones; wider corpus)
sources.note: The census's contemporary material voice — e.g. Harald Bluetooth's Jelling claim to have 'made the Danes Christian' (c. 965). [S: corpus access detail (Rundata / Samnordisk runtextdatabas) from knowledge, not verified this session.]

sources.work: Islendingabok and Kristni saga (trans. Sian Gronlie, Viking Society for Northern Research Text Series 18, 2006)
sources.note: Ari's Book of the Icelanders (c. 1122-33) with the Althing conversion-by-vote account of 1000 that the census highlights; verified, free PDF from the Viking Society (vsnrweb-publications.org.uk). One-century retrospect — much closer than the 13th-c. sagas, but still tier care as the census says.

sources.work: Anders Winroth, The Conversion of Scandinavia (Yale, 2012)
sources.note: Standard modern account; deliberately source-critical about mission narratives and saga retrospectives — same tier discipline as the census; verified.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity, vol. 3, ch. 5: 'Germanic Christianities, 600-1100' (Lesley Abrams); cf. ch. 11: 'The northern frontier' (Ian N. Wood)
sources.note: Both chapters verified in the vol. 3 TOC; Abrams is the scholar of Scandinavian conversion — direct fit.

movements.longDescription: Christianity came north in fits and starts over nearly three centuries. A Frankish monk named Anskar preached in Denmark and at Birka in Sweden in the 820s and 830s, with modest and short-lived results; then came the kings — Harald Bluetooth, who set up a great carved stone at Jelling claiming that he had 'made the Danes Christian', and the two Olafs in Norway, whose methods included force and one of whom was killed in battle and venerated as a saint almost at once. Iceland took a different road: in the year 1000 the question was put to the Althing, the island's assembly, and the pagan law-speaker Þorgeir, after a night's deliberation, ruled that all Icelanders should be baptised, with some old practices tolerated privately for a time — a whole community changing religion by public decision rather than by conquest. The window closes in 1104, when the northern church received its own archbishopric at Lund and stopped being mission territory administered from Germany. The sagas that tell these stories most vividly were written down two centuries later.
movements.teaser: Denmark, Norway, Sweden and Iceland, c. 826 to 1104 — one of the very few conversions anywhere that a whole people is recorded as having settled by public decision at its own assembly.
voices: Anskar — the Frankish monk whose ninth-century missions to Denmark and Sweden opened the north, and whose life was written by his successor Rimbert
Harald Bluetooth — the Danish king who proclaimed on the Jelling stone that he had made the Danes Christian
Olaf Haraldsson (St Olaf) — Norwegian king killed at Stiklestad in 1030 and venerated as a saint almost immediately
Þorgeir Ljósvetningagoði — Iceland's pagan law-speaker, who in the year 1000 gave the ruling that the whole island would become Christian
Adam of Bremen — the German cleric whose history of the archbishops of Hamburg-Bremen is the fullest contemporary description of the Christian north
movements.legacy: These conversions became the national churches of Denmark, Norway, Sweden and Iceland, which have existed continuously ever since — often the same dioceses and the same cathedral sites, reformed rather than replaced at the Reformation. The period left a physical record too: the Jelling stones still stand in Denmark, hundreds of Christian rune stones survive across Sweden, and St Olaf's shrine at Nidaros made Trondheim the great pilgrimage destination of the medieval north. Iceland's later saga writers also preserved the memory of the conversion in the words of the converted rather than of the missionaries.

experienceToday.text: Þingvellir National Park, Iceland — the assembly site where the Althing decided in the year 1000 that Iceland would become Christian, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site

movements.name: The Byzantine Imperial Church (Heraclian & Iconoclast Eras)
movements.informalName: The Byzantine Church of the Crisis Centuries
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 4 Step 0 run as the first half of the era's largest completeness gap — the era-4 continuation of II.13, split at 843 per Mark's two-world steer. Added at the Era 4 gate (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich institutional: Constantinople III acta, Maximus the Confessor's corpus, Nicaea II acta (787); the iconoclast establishment survives mainly in hostile quotation (named problem, shared with III.6)
movements.floorNote: No question (Chalcedonian); carries the monothelete crisis and Constantinople III (680-681) inside its own story
movements.relationsSummary: The church of the crisis centuries: Heraclius's wars, the monothelete compromise and its collapse, Maximus the Confessor's resistance, the iconoclast emperors as rivals inside (Hieria 754, 338 bishops), III.6 as its persecuted monastic counterpart; ends at the Triumph of Orthodoxy (843)
movements.why: Proposed by the Era 4 completeness sweep: the imperial church of 622-843 (Heraclian church, monothelete crisis, Constantinople III, Maximus) had no entry - III.6 covers only its monastic iconophile world from 726. Split from the 843-1054 Macedonian world (III.22) at Mark's steer; provenance chain in the era doc section 1. Tier 1 signal on sourcing; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 622 (Heraclius; era hinge) to 843 (Triumph of Orthodoxy) — split from the Macedonian world at 843 per Mark's two-world ruling (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: This is the imperial church of the empire's worst century and a half. Heraclius recovered the True Cross from Persia in 630 and within a decade had lost Syria, Palestine and Egypt to the Arab armies; his government's attempt to hold the remaining eastern Christians together with a compromise formula — that Christ had two natures but only one will — was pushed as state policy and resisted by a monk, Maximus, who was tried, had his tongue and right hand cut off, and died in exile. Twenty years later a council at Constantinople condemned the formula and vindicated him. Then came iconoclasm: emperors from Leo III onward removed and destroyed religious images, a council of 338 bishops endorsed the policy in 754, the Council of Nicaea reversed it in 787, a second imperial iconoclasm followed, and only in 843 was the matter closed for good. Through all of it the same institution — palace, patriarchate, councils — kept running, which is why this era looks so different depending on whether you stand with the court or with the monasteries.
movements.teaser: Constantinople and the Greek East, 622 to 843 — an empire losing half its territory while arguing, twice over, about Christ's will and about whether God can be painted.
voices: Heraclius — the emperor whose reign opened with the recovery of the True Cross and closed with the loss of the eastern provinces
Maximus the Confessor — the monk who refused the imperial compromise on Christ's will, was mutilated for it, and was vindicated by a council twenty years after his death
Pope Martin I — the bishop of Rome arrested for the same refusal and exiled to the Crimea, where he died
Leo III and Constantine V — the emperors who made the destruction of religious images imperial policy
Patriarch Tarasios — under whom the Council of Nicaea restored the icons in 787
Patriarch Methodios — who, with the empress Theodora, ended iconoclasm for good in 843
movements.legacy: The same institution continued as the Byzantine church of the Macedonian era and through that into the Orthodox churches of today. Its decisions are still binding for most of Christianity: the ruling of the Third Council of Constantinople that Christ has a human will as well as a divine one, and the Second Council of Nicaea's defence of religious images, are both counted among the seven ecumenical councils by Orthodox and Catholics alike, and the canons issued at Constantinople in 692 still shape Orthodox church law. The argument is also still visible in the buildings: in Hagia Eirene in Istanbul the apse carries the plain cross that iconoclast-era decorators set where a figure would otherwise have gone.

experienceToday.text: Hagia Eirene, Istanbul — in the first courtyard of Topkapı Palace, its apse still showing the bare mosaic cross of the iconoclast period

movements.name: The Byzantine Imperial Church (Macedonian Era)
movements.informalName: The Church of the Triumph of Orthodoxy
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 4 Step 0 run as the second half of the era's largest completeness gap — the survey's original 843-1054 draft restored as its own world, split at 843 per Mark's two-world steer. Added at the Era 4 gate (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich institutional: Photius's corpus (Bibliotheca, homilies, encyclicals), conciliar records of 861/867/879-880, imperial legislation; the 1054 exchange documented from both sides
movements.relationsSummary: The church of the restored icons: Photius's two patriarchates and the Photian schism, the Filioque dispute opening, the missions to Bulgaria (864) and the Slavs (parent context of III.7); receives the 1054 schism itself
movements.why: Proposed by the Era 4 completeness sweep: the church that sent Cyril & Methodius and received the 1054 schism had no entry. The survey's original draft window, restored as its own world after Mark's split steer; provenance chain in the era doc section 1. Tier 1 signal on sourcing; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 843 (Triumph of Orthodoxy) to 1054 (the schism itself) (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: With the icons restored in 843, the Byzantine church entered two centuries of confidence: it recovered its learning, sent missions that converted Bulgaria, Moravia and eventually Rus', and put figures back on the walls of Hagia Sophia — the first of them a great gold-ground Virgin and Child in the apse, unveiled in 867, at which the patriarch Photius preached that the imposters who had cast such images down had now been answered. Photius is the age's emblem: a layman raised straight to the patriarchate, an enormous reader who catalogued nearly three hundred books, many of which survive nowhere else, and the man who put in its sharpest form the Eastern objection to the Latin West's addition of one clause, the Filioque, to the Creed. That argument, along with disputes over papal authority and over who had jurisdiction among the newly converted Slavs, hardened across the following century and a half, until in 1054 a papal delegation and the patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated one another inside Hagia Sophia — the conventional date for a division that neither side at the time understood as final.
movements.teaser: Constantinople, 843 to 1054 — icons back on the walls, missionaries sent to the Slavs, and an argument with Rome that ended with two churches excommunicating each other inside Hagia Sophia.
voices: Photius — patriarch, scholar and cataloguer of a vanished library, who framed the Eastern case against the Latin addition to the Creed
Pope Nicholas I — whose claims over Constantinople's affairs Photius refused
Boris of Bulgaria — the ruler baptised in 864, whose choice between Rome and Constantinople was one of the era's sharpest contests
Athanasios the Athonite — founder of the Great Lavra in 963, the first of Mount Athos's great communal monasteries
Michael Keroularios — patriarch at the exchange of excommunications in 1054
Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida — the papal legate who laid the bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia
movements.legacy: The same church continued as the Byzantine church after the schism and, through it, into the Orthodox churches of today. Two of its acts shaped the map permanently: the mission to the Slavs, which made most of eastern Europe Orthodox and Slavonic-speaking, and the rupture of 1054, whose mutual excommunications were only lifted in 1965, when Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras revoked them together. Photius's Bibliotheca preserves summaries of some three hundred ancient books, a great many of which survive in no other form. And the apse mosaic of 867 is still in place in Hagia Sophia.

experienceToday.text: The apse mosaic of the Virgin and Child, Hagia Sophia, Istanbul — unveiled in 867 as the first great figural image set up in Hagia Sophia after iconoclasm ended

movements.name: Bagratid Armenian Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 4 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 4 gate (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate with one first-rank interior voice: Gregory of Narek's Book of Lamentations; Ani cathedral and catholicosate institutionally documented
movements.floorNote: The Armenian church does not accept the Council of Chalcedon's formula of 451 and belongs to the family usually called miaphysite, or Oriental Orthodox. That is a disagreement about how to describe the joining of divinity and humanity in Christ, not about the Nicene Creed, which this church confesses in full.
movements.relationsSummary: The Bagratid revival: catholicosate at Ani by 992, cathedral finished 1001, Gregory of Narek (c. 950-1003); absorbs the story of Caucasian Albania's catholicosate after 705; ends with the fall of Ani (1045)
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: the census's longest spine hole - no Armenian entry between II.4 (ends 554) and IX.27 (1915). The 554-884 gap remains and is disclosed, flagged to A2.d. Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: c. 884 (Bagratid kingdom) to 1045 (fall of Ani); the 554-884 Armenian spine gap is disclosed and flagged to A2.d (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: After two centuries under Arab governors, an Armenian kingdom was restored under the Bagratid dynasty in the 880s, and with it came a burst of church building and writing. The catholicos — the head of the Armenian church — moved his seat to the royal capital of Ani, whose cathedral, finished around 1001 by the architect Trdat, still stands roofless on the plain; Trdat was regarded well enough that he was called to Constantinople to rebuild the dome of Hagia Sophia after an earthquake brought it down. The period's greatest voice, though, was not an architect but a monk. Gregory of Narek wrote a long sequence of prayers, the Book of Lamentations, of such raw self-accusation and longing that Armenians for a thousand years afterwards kept a copy in the house and read it over the sick. The kingdom ended in 1045, when Byzantium annexed Ani; the Seljuk Turks took the city twenty years after that.
movements.teaser: Armenia, c. 884 to 1045 — a restored kingdom that raised the cathedral of Ani, and produced in one monk's book of laments the prayer book Armenians kept by the bed for the next thousand years.
voices: Gregory of Narek — monk and poet whose Book of Lamentations became the Armenian church's most beloved book of prayer
Trdat — architect of Ani's cathedral, called to Constantinople to rebuild the fallen dome of Hagia Sophia
Ashot I — first of the restored Bagratid kings, crowned in 884
movements.legacy: The church itself continued: the same institution carried on into the Armenian kingdom of Cilicia and runs unbroken to the Armenian Apostolic Church of today. Gregory of Narek's Lamentations never went out of use — it is still printed and prayed, and in 2015 Pope Francis declared him a Doctor of the Church, an unusual honour for a figure outside the Catholic communion. Ani itself was abandoned and is now a ruin field on the Turkish side of the closed Armenian border, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016; its cathedral and churches are among the most important surviving works of medieval Armenian architecture.

experienceToday.text: The Cathedral of Ani, Kars province, Turkey — completed around 1001 and still standing in the ruined Bagratid capital, a UNESCO World Heritage Site

movements.name: Syriac Orthodox Christianity under Islam
movements.informalName: The Syriac Orthodox Church under the Caliphs
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 4 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 4 gate (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: Dionysius of Tel Mahre's chronicle tradition, Moses bar Kepha's corpus, Tagrit maphrianate records; West Syriac monasteries (Qartmin, Deir al-Surian) carry the manuscript culture
movements.floorNote: This church does not accept the Council of Chalcedon's formula of 451 and belongs to the family usually called miaphysite, or Oriental Orthodox. The disagreement is about how to describe the joining of divinity and humanity in Christ, not about the Nicene Creed, which it confesses in full.
movements.relationsSummary: The West Syriac church as dhimmi community - patriarch-chronicler Dionysius of Tel Mahre travelled with al-Ma'mun; West Syriac monasticism rides inside, cleanly distinct from Melkite Mar Saba (III.2)
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: the known spine gap - II.2 ends 636 and the next Syriac Orthodox entry is IX.19 (1915). Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: c. 650 (post-conquest reorganization) to 1054 (era end; no single event-end — disclosed) (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: For the West Syriac church the Arab conquest lifted a weight: they had been the losing side under Byzantine emperors who wanted Chalcedon enforced, and under the caliphs they became simply one protected community among others — taxed, but not pressed to change their confession. The centuries that followed were unusually productive. Jacob of Edessa revised the Syriac Bible and wrote the first grammar of his own language; Dionysius of Tel Mahre, patriarch and historian, travelled to Egypt in the caliph al-Ma'mun's own company and wrote a chronicle that later writers mined for centuries; Moses bar Kepha explained the liturgy and the Scriptures for his clergy. The carriers of all this were the monasteries — Mor Gabriel and the other houses of the Tur Abdin plateau, and the Syrian monastery in the Egyptian desert, where monks assembled a library that is now one of the world's great collections of early Syriac manuscripts.
movements.teaser: The Jazira, Syria and Tagrit, c. 650 to 1054 — a church that had been the empire's losing side, and found under the caliphs the room to write its own grammar, chronicles and Bible.
voices: Jacob of Edessa — bishop and polymath who revised the Syriac Bible and wrote the first grammar of Syriac
Dionysius of Tel Mahre — patriarch and chronicler, who travelled to Egypt in the caliph al-Ma'mun's own company
Moses bar Kepha — bishop whose commentaries on the liturgy and Scripture were used for centuries after him
movements.legacy: The same church continued directly into the Syriac Renaissance of the following centuries and exists today as the Syriac Orthodox Church of Antioch, with its own patriarch and a large worldwide diaspora. Its monasteries preserved what would otherwise be lost: the manuscripts gathered at the Syrian monastery in the Egyptian desert are the backbone of the world's collections of early Syriac literature, including some of the oldest surviving Syriac gospel books. Mor Gabriel in the Tur Abdin, founded in 397, is still a working monastery and the seat of a bishop.

experienceToday.text: Mor Gabriel Monastery, Tur Abdin, south-eastern Turkey — founded in 397 and still inhabited, the oldest surviving Syriac Orthodox monastery

movements.name: Makurian Nubian Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 4 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 4 gate (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate by archaeology (Faras murals, bishop lists, Qasr Ibrim documents); thin inside literary voice - disclosed
movements.relationsSummary: Unified Christian Nubia after Merkurios (crowned 697, the 'New Constantine'); Faras cathedral rebuilt 707; the fresco golden age under the peace of the 652 Baqt; picks up 45 years after II.11's 652 end (gap disclosed - the unification decades between Baqt and Merkurios belong to no entry)
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: II.11 ends 652 with no receiver anywhere, and the Faras flowering sits squarely in this window with archaeology-grade attestation. Tier 2-3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 697 (Merkurios crowned) to 1054 (era end); starts 45 years after II.11's 652 end — gap disclosed (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: Between Egypt and the deserts of the Sudan, the Christian kingdom of Makuria held together for centuries under an arrangement no one else had: the Baqt, a treaty struck with Muslim Egypt in 652 that set terms of exchange rather than conquest and was more or less honoured for six hundred years. Under that peace, and especially after Merkurios — whom an Egyptian writer called a new Constantine — took the throne in 697, Nubia built. The cathedral at Faras was rebuilt in 707 and covered, over the following centuries, in wall paintings: enormous saints and archangels, nativities, and portraits of the bishops themselves, several shown with dark skin beside lighter-skinned holy figures. Nubian Christians wrote their own language, Old Nubian, in an alphabet adapted from Coptic. What they did not leave, or what has not survived, is much writing about their inner life; this is a Christianity known mainly by what it built and painted.
movements.teaser: Makuria on the middle Nile, 697 to 1054 — a Christian kingdom that kept a six-hundred-year treaty with Muslim Egypt and covered its cathedral walls with painted saints.
voices: Merkurios — the king crowned in 697 whom an Egyptian chronicler called a new Constantine
Paulos — the bishop under whom the cathedral at Faras was rebuilt in 707
The bishops of Faras — their names and years in office survived written on the cathedral wall, which is why the succession of a church this far south can be reconstructed at all
movements.legacy: Christian Nubia lasted far longer than most people expect, into the fifteenth century in places, before it was worn down and its churches vanished; no Nubian Christian community survives today. What survives is the painting. When the Aswan High Dam was built in the 1960s the cathedral at Faras was about to go under the reservoir, and a Polish archaeological team lifted the murals off its walls. They were divided between Warsaw and Khartoum, and the Warsaw gallery is arranged to reproduce the layout of the church they came from — the only permanent exhibition of medieval Nubian painting in Europe.

experienceToday.text: The Faras Gallery, National Museum in Warsaw — the wall paintings rescued from the cathedral at Faras, hung in the arrangement they had in the church

movements.name: Late Anglo-Saxon Christianity
movements.informalName: The English Church before the Conquest
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 4 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 4 gate (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich: Alfred's own prefaces, the Benedictine Reform documents (Regularis Concordia c. 973), Aelfric and Wulfstan's homiletic corpus, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
movements.relationsSummary: Viking-age survival, Alfred's revival, then the Benedictine Reform (Dunstan, Aethelwold, Oswald) - the English parallel to Cluny; ends at the Conquest (1066, one boundary crossing)
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: no English entry exists after III.4 in eras 4-5 - two-plus centuries of a well-documented national church fall between entries. Start disclosure (Review Round 1, S1): the survey drafted c. 800; the lead thread moved it to c. 793 to meet this run's III.4-end proposal (Lindisfarne) - COUPLED to gate Q3: if Q3 keeps III.4 at 800, this start reverts to c. 800. Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: c. 793 (the Viking break, coupled to III.4's gated end) to 1066 (the Conquest; one boundary crossing) (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: The Viking wars nearly killed English Christianity: monasteries were destroyed, whole dioceses lapsed, and when Alfred of Wessex set out to rebuild he complained that he could hardly find a priest south of the Thames able to translate a Latin letter. His answer was a translation programme — Gregory the Great's Pastoral Care and other essential books put into English so that clergy could read them at all — and the Chronicle begun in his reign is the first sustained history written in English. A century later a second rebuilding, led by the bishops Dunstan, Æthelwold and Oswald, refounded the monasteries on the Benedictine rule and produced an agreed customary for the whole country. The vernacular stayed central throughout: Ælfric wrote well over a hundred sermons in English so that ordinary congregations could hear careful teaching in their own tongue, and Archbishop Wulfstan, preaching in 1014 as the Danish invasions closed in, told the English that their own sins had brought the calamity on them. The Norman Conquest of 1066 ended the church's independent development.
movements.teaser: England, c. 793 to 1066 — a church rebuilt twice, once by a king who could barely find a literate priest and once by monks, and unusual in Europe for preaching and writing in the language people actually spoke.
voices: Alfred the Great — king who launched a programme of translating essential books into English and revived learning after the Viking wars
Dunstan — archbishop of Canterbury and leading figure of the tenth-century monastic reform
Æthelwold — bishop of Winchester, whose house drove the reform and produced the Regularis Concordia, an agreed rule of life for English monasteries
Oswald — bishop of Worcester and archbishop of York, the third of the reforming bishops
Ælfric of Eynsham — monk whose English sermons brought careful teaching to ordinary congregations in their own language
Wulfstan of York — archbishop whose Sermon of the Wolf to the English, preached in 1014, blamed the nation's disasters on its own sins
movements.legacy: The institutions did not vanish at the Conquest — the dioceses, the cathedral communities and the parish network built in these centuries carried straight on into the Norman and later medieval English church, and many English cathedrals still stand where these bishops put them. What is distinctive here is the language: for two centuries England produced Christian literature in the vernacular on a scale unmatched anywhere else in western Europe, from Alfred's translations to Ælfric's sermons to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle. Buildings survive too — late Anglo-Saxon towers and churches, like the decorated tower at Earls Barton, are among the oldest working parish churches in England.

experienceToday.text: All Saints' Church, Earls Barton, Northamptonshire — a late Anglo-Saxon tower of about 970, still a working parish church

movements.name: Georgian Revival — Tao-Klarjeti and Athos
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 4 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 4 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 4 gate (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Thin-to-moderate: Giorgi Merchule's Life of Grigol (951) is a real inside source; translation culture; Iviron's Athonite founding documented
movements.relationsSummary: Grigol Khandzteli rebuilds Georgian monasticism from Khandzta (c. 782); Iviron founded on Athos 980-983; hands to the Georgian Golden Age (IV.15) - continuesAs candidate for the A4 walk
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: spine gap between II.10 (ends 609) and IV.15 (starts 1000). Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: c. 780 (Khandzta's founding) to 1000 (hands to the Georgian Golden Age, IV.15) (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: After the Arab conquests reduced the old Georgian kingdoms to a handful of mountain principalities, the rebuilding of Georgian Christian life happened in the highland province of Tao-Klarjeti, where a monk named Grigol founded the monastery of Khandzta around 782 and, over a very long life, seeded a whole district with monasteries. What makes him unusual for a figure of this period is that we can hear about him from inside: a Georgian monk called Giorgi Merchule wrote his life in 951, and it contains the famous sentence defining Georgia itself as the land where the liturgy is celebrated in the Georgian tongue. The movement also went abroad. Georgian monks were in Palestine, on Sinai and near Antioch, and between 980 and 983 they founded Iviron on Mount Athos, which became a translation house moving books between Greek and Georgian in both directions — one of them, a Georgian retelling of a story ultimately of Indian origin, passed into Greek as Barlaam and Josaphat and from there into most of the languages of Europe.
movements.teaser: Tao-Klarjeti and Mount Athos, c. 780 to 1000 — Georgian monks who rebuilt their church from a mountain province and then went abroad and turned a corner of Athos into a translation house.
voices: Grigol Khandzteli — the monk who founded Khandzta around 782 and seeded Tao-Klarjeti with monasteries
Giorgi Merchule — his biographer, writing in 951, whose Life of Grigol is a rare inside account of this world
John the Iberian and John Tornike — the Georgian founders of Iviron on Mount Athos, between 980 and 983
Euthymius the Athonite — abbot of Iviron and a prodigious translator between Georgian and Greek
movements.legacy: The same tradition runs straight on into the Georgian Golden Age of the following centuries and into the Georgian Orthodox Church of today. Its most visible legacy is Iviron itself, still one of the twenty ruling monasteries of Mount Athos, and the body of translated literature its monks produced, which gave the Georgian church a full library in its own language. In Tao-Klarjeti many of the churches these monks built still stand, ruined or converted, in what is now north-eastern Turkey.

experienceToday.text: Iviron Monastery, Mount Athos, Greece — founded by Georgian monks between 980 and 983 and still one of Athos's twenty ruling monasteries

movements.name: Post-Aksumite Ethiopian Christianity
movements.informalName: The Ethiopian Church in the Silent Centuries
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 4 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 4 Step 0 run with St-Thomas-pattern honesty about its thin window. Added at the Era 4 gate (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: THIN - the thinnest window of any era-4 candidate: no contemporary inscriptions; survival under Coptic metropolitans institutionally attested; the Gudit invasion tradition (c. 960) rests on late, hostile accounts - disclosed
movements.relationsSummary: The church between Aksum's decline and the Zagwe: survives in isolation under Coptic metropolitans; would close the spine II.9 (ends 615) to IV.9 (starts 1137) - continuesAs candidates for the A4 walk
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep as a spine-closing entry with honest thinness: whether a thin entry or a named-gap register serves honesty better is an open gate question. Start c. 615 precedes the era boundary by design (handoff from II.9's gated end) - a Q7-class case, disclosed. Tier 3 / register question; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: c. 615 (handoff from II.9's gated end; start-before-era under the standing rule) to 1137 (Zagwe rise = IV.9's start; one boundary crossing) (Era 4 gate, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: Aksum had been one of the great powers of the late-antique world, minting its own coins, its kings Christian since the fourth century. Then the trade that sustained it moved away, the coinage stopped, and Ethiopian Christianity went quiet for something close to five hundred years — one of the least documented stretches in the whole history of any ancient church. What can be said with confidence is small but decisive: the church survived, its centre shifted south into the highlands, and it went on receiving its chief bishop from the Coptic patriarch in Alexandria, a link that would last into the twentieth century. Later Ethiopian tradition fills the silence with the story of a queen remembered as Gudit, who is said to have destroyed churches around the year 960, but that account comes from much later and largely hostile sources and cannot be verified. When the record resumes under the Zagwe kings in the twelfth century, there is a functioning church with monasteries, a liturgy in Ge'ez and its own saints — which tells us the intervening centuries were not empty, only silent.
movements.teaser: The Ethiopian highlands, c. 615 to 1137 — five near-silent centuries in which a church lost its empire, moved into the mountains, and simply kept going.
voices: No individual figure from this period can be named with confidence. It is the least documented stretch of Ethiopian Christian history, and the names later tradition supplies — including the queen remembered as Gudit — cannot be checked against contemporary sources.
movements.legacy: Everything later Ethiopian Christianity is rests on the fact that this church did not die. The same institution continues directly into the Zagwe period — the age of the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela — and on into the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church of today, one of the largest ancient churches in the world. The link with Alexandria that these centuries kept alive held until 1959, when the Ethiopian church finally received a patriarch of its own; and what was carried through the silence — worship in Ge'ez, a distinctive monasticism, a liturgical calendar unlike anyone else's — is still what marks Ethiopian Christianity out.

movements.name: Cistercian Monasticism
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) — rich across the whole range the project asks for: formation documents, Bernard's sermons, Aelred on friendship, the lay-brother world and the chapter statutes. Its 1300 end sits at the era boundary as structural scoping under the continues-cap convention, not as a claim that the tradition stopped there.
movements.sourcing: RICH: formation documents, Bernard's sermons, Aelred on friendship, lay-brother world, chapter statutes
movements.relationsSummary: Reform child of Cluny; shapes later mysticism
movements.why: The one Era 5 entry rich across the whole range the project actually asks for: how a house was founded, what it taught its novices, what its abbots preached, what its lay brothers did, and how its chapters governed. Very few traditions anywhere in the atlas can be read at all five of those levels. It is also the reform of a reform — Cluny's own child, founded in reaction to what Cluny had become.

sources.work: Narrative and Legislative Texts from Early Citeaux (ed./trans. Chrysogonus Waddell, Studia et Documenta 9, 1999)
sources.note: Verified. Latin/English facing texts of Exordium Parvum, Exordium Cistercii, Carta Caritatis - the census's formation documents and the statute tradition's root, in the movement's own words. Berman-debate caution: authenticity/dating of the founding narratives is contested (see secondary).

sources.work: Pauline Matarasso (trans.), The Cistercian World: Monastic Writings of the Twelfth Century (Penguin Classics, 1993)
sources.note: Verified. Bernard's letters, Song of Songs sermons, the Apologia, William of St Thierry, Vita Prima selections, exemplary stories - Bernard's voice plus communal texture in one in-print volume.

sources.work: Aelred of Rievaulx, Spiritual Friendship (trans. Braceland, Cistercian Fathers 5); with Walter Daniel, Life of Aelred
sources.note: The census's named friendship text; the Life gives an abbot seen up close by his own monk. [S] edition details from knowledge, not verified this session.

sources.work: Chrysogonus Waddell (ed.), Cistercian Lay Brothers: Twelfth-Century Usages, with Related Texts (Studia et Documenta 10, 2000)
sources.note: Verified via JEH review. The conversi's regulated world - the order's ordinary/manual-labor half, the census's lay-brother leg made concrete.

sources.work: Janet Burton & Julie Kerr, The Cistercians in the Middle Ages (Boydell, 2011)
sources.note: Current standard survey. [S] not individually verified this session. Read with Constance Berman, The Cistercian Evolution (2000), which argues the founding documents are later constructions.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 4 'Monastic and religious orders, c.1100-c.1350' (B. P. McGuire)
sources.note: Chapter verified in TOC; direct fit.

movements.longDescription: In 1098 a group of monks walked out of the great Burgundian abbey of Molesme because they thought Benedictine life had grown too comfortable — Cluny and the other rich houses above all — and settled in a marshy clearing called Cîteaux to keep the Rule of St Benedict as plainly as they could: bare churches, simple food, no elaborate liturgy, and their own hands in the fields. Within a generation the reform had a constitution, the Carta Caritatis, binding every daughter house to the mother house through annual visitation and a yearly general chapter, and after Bernard of Clairvaux arrived in 1113 the order spread across Europe at extraordinary speed. Much of the actual labour was done by lay brothers, the conversi, who took vows but lived a separate, largely manual life alongside the choir monks on farms called granges. The order never ended, and its writers — Bernard on the Song of Songs, Aelred of Rievaulx on friendship — stayed among the most-read spiritual authors of the Latin West for centuries afterward.
movements.teaser: Burgundy and then all of Europe, 1098 to 1300 — monks who walked out of a rich abbey to keep Benedict's Rule plainly, and ended up building one of the best-organized institutions in medieval Christendom.
voices: Robert of Molesme — the abbot who led the founding group out to Cîteaux in 1098
Alberic — Cîteaux's second abbot, who secured papal protection for the fragile new house
Stephen Harding — the English third abbot, under whom the Carta Caritatis gave the order its constitution
Bernard of Clairvaux — the order's most famous voice, whose sermons on the Song of Songs and vast correspondence made him the most listened-to churchman in Europe
Aelred of Rievaulx — abbot in Yorkshire, whose Spiritual Friendship argued that friendship between monks was itself a road to God
The conversi — the lay brothers who did most of the order's manual work and left few names of their own, though their customs and daily round were written down in detail
movements.legacy: The order is still here: Cistercian and Trappist houses keep the same rule today. Its buildings became a style of their own — the bare, unpainted, superbly proportioned church that architects still simply call Cistercian, of which Fontenay in Burgundy survives almost complete. Its writers stayed in circulation for centuries; Bernard's sermons on the Song of Songs and Aelred's Spiritual Friendship shaped nearly every later Western tradition of contemplative prayer and warm, affectionate devotion. And the granges left a mark on European farming, water management and land clearance that outlasted the monks who worked them.

experienceToday.text: Marmagne, Burgundy, France — the Abbey of Fontenay, founded from Clairvaux in 1118 and one of the most complete surviving Cistercian abbeys in Europe

movements.name: Carthusian Life
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2). The run took the entry's own question — whether its defining silence leaves enough breadth for a full tradition — as the honest reason it is not Tier 1, and read its deliberately few personalities as the formation logic rather than as a sourcing failure.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: strong formation texts (Guigo I & II); deliberately few personalities - which IS the formation logic
movements.relationsSummary: The desert revived inside the Latin West
movements.why: A real question rides on this one: whether a life built on silence leaves breadth enough to carry a whole tradition. Its formation texts are strong exactly where its personalities are few, and that scarcity is the formation logic rather than a gap in the record — the desert revived inside the Latin West. It holds a place because a tradition that deliberately produces almost no public voice is a real kind of Christian life, and the difficulty of representing it is part of what it is.

sources.work: Guigo II, The Ladder of Monks and Twelve Meditations (trans. Colledge & Walsh, 1978; Cistercian Studies 48)
sources.note: Verified. The lectio divina ladder - the tradition's most influential formation text.

sources.work: Guigo I, Meditations (trans. A. Gordon Mursell, Cistercian Studies 155, 1995)
sources.note: Founder-generation interior voice: aphoristic self-scrutiny, no system. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: Guigo I, Consuetudines Cartusiae (Customs, c. 1127)
sources.note: The census's 'formation logic' as legislation: cell, silence, capped community size. [S] Latin/French only (Sources Chretiennes 313); no complete standard English - access flag.

sources.work: Adam of Eynsham, Magna Vita Sancti Hugonis (Life of Hugh of Lincoln) (trans. Douie & Farmer, Oxford Medieval Texts, 2 vols)
sources.note: Lived Carthusian texture through the order's one very public member, written by his own chaplain. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: Gordon Mursell, The Theology of the Carthusian Life in the Writings of St. Bruno and Guigo I (Analecta Cartusiana 127, 1988)
sources.note: [S] from knowledge. The thinness of English scholarship mirrors the order's deliberate silence - itself a fact worth stating in the era document.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 4 'Monastic and religious orders, c.1100-c.1350' (B. P. McGuire)
sources.note: Chapter verified in TOC.

movements.longDescription: In 1084 Bruno of Cologne, who had been a leading master of the schools at Reims, gave up his career, took six companions into a high, hard valley in the Alps above Grenoble, and built a life with almost nothing in it: each man in his own cell with a small garden, meeting the others only for the night office, part of the Mass, and a weekly walk. Guigo I, the fifth prior, wrote the customs down around 1127 — cell, silence, and a strict cap on how many could live in any one house — and Guigo II's Ladder of Monks, a short account of reading, meditating, praying and resting in God, became one of the most widely used descriptions of prayer in the Western church. Deliberately, the order produced almost no public figures; the one great exception was Hugh, prior of the English charterhouse at Witham and then bishop of Lincoln, whose chaplain wrote him up in unusual detail. The Grande Chartreuse is still a working monastery, and the order has kept substantially the same shape ever since — a traditional saying has it that the Carthusians were never reformed because they were never deformed.
movements.teaser: The Alps above Grenoble, from 1084 onward — hermits who built a monastery out of separate cells and near-total silence, then kept it almost unchanged for nine hundred years.
voices: Bruno of Cologne — master of the schools at Reims, who gave up his career to found the first charterhouse in 1084
Guigo I — fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, who wrote down the order's customs and left a book of unsparing private meditations
Guigo II — author of The Ladder of Monks, the short treatise on reading, meditation, prayer and contemplation that became the West's standard map of prayer
Hugh of Lincoln — the order's one very public member, a Carthusian prior who became an English bishop and was written up at length by his own chaplain
movements.legacy: The order is still living and still small, which is exactly what it intended. Its longest reach is Guigo II's Ladder of Monks: the four-step pattern of reading, meditating, praying and resting in God passed into the general devotional vocabulary of the West and is still taught today, often by people who have never heard of the Carthusians. The charterhouse plan — a great cloister ringed by individual cells and gardens — became a recognisable building type across Europe, and several former charterhouses now serve as museums and galleries. The liqueur the monks of the Grande Chartreuse still make has kept the name in ordinary circulation long after most people forgot what it belonged to.

experienceToday.text: Saint-Pierre-de-Chartreuse, France — the Museum of the Grande Chartreuse at La Correrie, two kilometres below the monastery itself, which remains closed to visitors

movements.name: Canons Regular / Victorine School
movements.informalName: The Canons Regular and the Victorines
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — rich textually, moderate in community texture, with its distinctiveness from the Cistercian and university traditions named as the real test it would have to pass. Both dates were corrected at the Freeze from numbers that matched nothing to 1108 and 1246, and the Premonstratensians were routed inside this canons-regular family rather than given their own entry.
movements.sourcing: Rich textually; community texture moderate
movements.relationsSummary: Bridge between cloister and the schools; the Premonstratensians (Norbert’s reformed canons, 1120/21) ride inside this canons-regular family’s story
movements.why: Its distinctiveness from the Cistercian and the university traditions is a real test it has to pass — it sits between them by design. The canons regular are the bridge between cloister and schools: a life under rule that nonetheless teaches, and a theology of contemplation worked out inside Paris rather than away from it. That position is what makes it worth an entry, and it is also exactly what makes the entry contestable.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1108 (William of Champeaux settles at Saint-Victor — the school's actual beginning; the old 1100 matched nothing); end 1246 (death of Thomas Gallus, last major Victorine thinker; alt 1173 on record) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Hugh of St Victor, Didascalicon (trans. Jerome Taylor, Columbia, 1961; newer trans. Harkins in Victorine Texts in Translation)
sources.note: The school's program: all the arts ordered to wisdom. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: Richard of St Victor, The Twelve Patriarchs, The Mystical Ark, Book Three of the Trinity (trans. Grover Zinn, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1979)
sources.note: Verified. Contemplative theology built on communal reading.

sources.work: Liber ordinis Sancti Victoris (the abbey's customary)
sources.note: The census's community-texture leg: offices, discipline, hospitality in daily detail. [S] Latin only (CCCM 61) - access flag; matches the census's 'community texture moderate'.

sources.work: Victorine Texts in Translation (ed. Feiss et al., New City Press/Brepols, multi-volume)
sources.note: Modern annotated corpus incl. Hugh on love and formation and Adam of St Victor's liturgical sequences - the school's sung, ordinary face. [S] series details from knowledge.

sources.work: Paul Rorem, Hugh of Saint Victor (OUP, 2009)
sources.note: [S] not individually verified this session; standard one-volume entry to the school.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 4 (McGuire); cf. ch. 5 'The theological framework' (L. Smith)
sources.note: Both chapters verified in TOC; the entry's cloister-vs-schools distinctiveness question sits between them.

movements.longDescription: Canons regular were clergy who lived in community under a rule — usually the Rule of St Augustine — but who, unlike monks, kept working in the world: serving churches, running hospitals, teaching. The most influential of their houses was the abbey of Saint-Victor on the left bank of Paris, where the master William of Champeaux withdrew from the schools in 1108 and where his successors built a way of learning that refused to choose between the classroom and the cloister. Hugh of St Victor argued in the Didascalicon that every art and science, rightly ordered, leads toward wisdom; Richard of St Victor mapped the stages of contemplation more carefully than anyone in the Latin West had yet done; Adam of St Victor wrote the sequences the abbey sang. The school's line ran down to Thomas Gallus, who died in 1246, and the abbey itself no longer stands.
movements.teaser: Paris and the abbey of Saint-Victor, 1108 to 1246 — clergy under a rule who would not choose between the cloister and the classroom, and worked out a theology of contemplation in the middle of a university town.
voices: William of Champeaux — the Paris master who withdrew to Saint-Victor in 1108 and began the school there
Hugh of St Victor — the school's greatest teacher, whose Didascalicon ordered all learning toward wisdom
Richard of St Victor — his successor, author of the West's most careful account of the stages of contemplation
Adam of St Victor — poet of the liturgical sequences the abbey sang, the school's ordinary, singing face
Norbert of Xanten — founder in 1120 of Prémontré, the reformed canons who carried this way of life across northern Europe
Thomas Gallus — the last major Victorine thinker, who died in 1246
movements.legacy: The abbey is gone, but the way of life is not: canons regular still exist, and Norbert's Premonstratensians remain an order today. The Victorines' real bequest was intellectual. Hugh's insistence that the arts and sciences belong inside the search for God, and Richard's stage-by-stage analysis of contemplation, were read and quarried by nearly everyone who wrote on prayer in the later Middle Ages — Bonaventure most of all — and the abbey's sequences stayed in the liturgy long after the school that composed them had gone quiet.

movements.name: The Franciscan Movement
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1), immense in scale, with its famous layered-hagiography problem carried rather than resolved — the tier system exists for exactly that. Its lay third order was routed inside its own story at the Freeze, and the shape of its Era 6 receiver, which carries only the Fraticelli splinter and the Observant reform, was flagged forward as an open gap.
movements.sourcing: RICH, with a famous layered-hagiography problem - exactly what the project's tier system exists for
movements.relationsSummary: Sibling-rival of the Dominicans; parent of Observants and Spirituals; its lay third order (Order of Penance, 1221) rides inside its own story
movements.why: One of the largest movements in the atlas by any measure, and the clearest case anywhere of the problem the project's tier system was built for — the sources about Francis were rewritten repeatedly, by his own order, within living memory of him. What arrived with the friars was a Christian life lived in the streets of the new towns rather than behind walls, which is why it and the Dominicans stand as siblings and rivals at once.

sources.work: Francis's own writings (Testament, both Rules, Canticle of the Creatures, letters), in Francis of Assisi: Early Documents, vol. 1 (ed. Armstrong, Hellmann & Short, 1999; free online)
sources.note: Verified. The founder's undisputed first-person layer, kept distinct from all hagiography.

sources.work: The layered hagiography: Francis of Assisi: Early Documents, vols. 1-3 (1999-2001) - Celano's Lives, Legend of the Three Companions, Assisi Compilation, Bonaventure
sources.note: Verified. The census's famous layered-hagiography problem, printed in datable layers with the apparatus to work the tier system.

sources.work: Clare of Assisi: Early Documents (ed. Regis Armstrong, rev. 2006)
sources.note: Verified. Clare's letters to Agnes of Prague and her Form of Life (the first monastic rule written by a woman) - the movement's female branch in its own voice.

sources.work: Scripta Leonis, Rufini et Angeli (writings of Brother Leo and companions; ed./trans. Rosalind Brooke, Oxford Medieval Texts, 1970)
sources.note: The companions' counter-memory against the official portrait; central evidence in the poverty dispute. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: Augustine Thompson, Francis of Assisi: A New Biography (Cornell, 2012)
sources.note: Deliberately source-critical, layer by layer - pairs with the census's tier-care note. [S] not individually verified this session.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 3 'Religious poverty and the search for perfection' (Kienzle); cf. ch. 4 (McGuire)
sources.note: Both chapters verified in TOC.

movements.longDescription: Francis of Assisi was a cloth merchant's son who gave away his inheritance, took the gospel's instructions to the apostles as a literal rule of life, and began preaching and caring for lepers in the towns of central Italy; by 1209 others had joined him and Pope Innocent III gave the group verbal approval. What made the movement new was that it did not withdraw behind walls — the friars owned nothing, begged, worked, and preached in the streets of the fast-growing commercial towns. Clare of Assisi built the movement's women's branch and wrote her own Form of Life, the first monastic rule known to have been composed by a woman, and a third order let married lay people live a version of the same discipline without leaving ordinary life. Within a generation of Francis's death in 1226 the order was quarrelling bitterly over how literally his poverty had been meant — a fight that eventually split it into Spirituals and Conventuals, and that also produced repeated rewritings of his own life story, by his own brothers, within living memory of him.
movements.teaser: Assisi and then most of the known world, from 1209 — a merchant's son who took the gospel's poverty literally, and an order that began arguing about what he meant almost before he was buried.
voices: Francis of Assisi — the founder, whose Testament, Rules and Canticle of the Creatures survive in his own words
Clare of Assisi — founder of the movement's women's branch and author of the first monastic rule known to be written by a woman
Brother Leo — Francis's companion and secretary, whose recollections preserve a counter-memory to the order's official portrait
Thomas of Celano — the first biographer, commissioned to write Francis's life and then commissioned to write it again
Bonaventure — minister general and theologian, whose authorized life of Francis was meant to settle the quarrel over him
movements.legacy: The Franciscans are still one of the largest religious families in the world, in several branches, with a lay third order alongside them. Beyond the order, the movement changed the ordinary furniture of Western devotion: the Christmas crib, which Francis is credited with staging at Greccio in 1223; the Stations of the Cross, spread through Europe largely by Franciscans; an affectionate attention to Christ's humanity and to the poor; and a strand of Christian language about creation — the Canticle of the Creatures, with its brother sun and sister moon — that is quoted constantly to this day. The basilica raised over Francis's tomb at Assisi carries some of the most famous fresco cycles in European art.

experienceToday.text: Assisi, Italy — the Basilica of Saint Francis, built over his tomb from 1228 and frescoed by Cimabue, Giotto and Simone Martini

movements.name: The Dominican Order
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a rich base — constitutions, formation treatises, and sworn canonization-inquest testimonies, which give it an unusually direct evidentiary footing for the era.
movements.sourcing: Rich: constitutions, canonization-inquest sworn testimonies, formation treatises
movements.relationsSummary: Sibling-rival of the Franciscans; parent of the German convent-mysticism tradition
movements.why: Its evidence has an unusually direct footing for the period: the canonization inquests preserve sworn testimony — people describing under oath what they saw — which almost nothing else in the era offers. Its constitutions are the other side of the same thing, a religious order designing itself deliberately and in writing, with a preaching purpose stated first and the structure built to serve it. Its downstream reach includes the German convent-mysticism tradition, one of the atlas's few routes to women's own theological writing.

sources.work: Simon Tugwell (ed.), Early Dominicans: Selected Writings (Classics of Western Spirituality, 1982)
sources.note: Verified. Jordan of Saxony's Libellus, the Nine Ways of Prayer, Humbert of Romans' Treatise on the Formation of Preachers (the census's formation-treatise leg), and the early constitutions in appendix (the constitutions leg).

sources.work: The canonization process of St Dominic (Bologna and Toulouse, 1233), in F. C. Lehner, Saint Dominic: Biographical Documents (1964)
sources.note: The census's sworn-testimony leg: friars and lay witnesses under oath on what Dominic actually did. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: Jordan of Saxony, letters to Diana d'Andalo (trans. Gerald Vann, To Heaven with Diana!, 1960)
sources.note: The master general's correspondence with the Bologna nuns - the order's women's side and its interior register. [S] translation details from knowledge.

sources.work: Gerard de Frachet, Vitae Fratrum (Lives of the Brethren, c. 1260)
sources.note: Communal self-portrait in anecdote: dormitory, road, deathbed - ordinary texture. [S] English (Conway, 1924) from knowledge.

sources.work: M. Michele Mulchahey, 'First the Bow is Bent in Study': Dominican Education before 1350 (PIMS, 1998)
sources.note: The formation system as system. [S] not individually verified this session.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 4 (McGuire); cf. ch. 9 'The Word and its diffusion' (Jansen)
sources.note: Both chapters verified in TOC; preaching is the order's reason for existing.

movements.longDescription: Dominic de Guzmán was a Spanish cathedral canon who, travelling through Languedoc, concluded that the church was losing the argument with dissenters because its own preachers arrived on horseback with baggage while their opponents walked and fasted. His answer was an order built backwards from a purpose: friars trained in theology, living poor and mobile, whose stated reason for existing was preaching. Approved in 1216, the Order of Preachers wrote itself a constitution of unusual sophistication — elected superiors, representative chapters, and a clause stating that the rule did not bind under sin, so that it could never get in the way of study — and planted itself immediately in the new universities at Paris and Bologna. Its convents of women, in the German lands especially, became one of the very few settings in medieval Europe where women wrote theology and were read.
movements.teaser: Toulouse, Paris and Bologna, from 1216 — an order built backwards from a single purpose, and the rare medieval institution that put its whole reason for existing into its own name.
voices: Dominic de Guzmán — the Castilian canon who founded the order and was canonized within thirteen years of his death
Jordan of Saxony — his successor as master general, who wrote the order's account of its own beginnings and whose letters to the Bologna nun Diana d'Andalo survive
Diana d'Andalo — the Bolognese woman who founded the convent of St Agnes and to whom Jordan wrote
Humbert of Romans — master general and author of a detailed treatise on how to form a preacher
Gerard de Frachet — compiler of the Lives of the Brethren, the order's portrait of itself in dormitory and roadside anecdotes
movements.legacy: The Dominicans are still here, and much of what they built outlasted the century: the constitutional machinery of elected superiors and representative chapters, a permanent commitment to study as itself a form of religious life, and the university theology that Albert the Great and Thomas Aquinas produced inside the order and that still anchors Catholic thought. Their German convents fed the mystical writing associated with Meister Eckhart, Johannes Tauler and Henry Suso. The order also supplied the church with much of its inquisitorial personnel, which belongs to the same inheritance and is not separable from it. The rosary's spread through Europe was carried largely by Dominicans, though the traditional story that Dominic himself received it is legend rather than history.

experienceToday.text: Bologna, Italy — the Basilica of San Domenico, where Dominic is buried in a shrine carved by Nicola Pisano, Niccolò dell'Arca and the young Michelangelo

movements.name: Athonite & Comnenian Byzantine Monasticism
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) as the era's Orthodox monastic anchor and the parent of hesychasm. One sourcing nuance was carried rather than smoothed over: Symeon the New Theologian's corpus is Constantinopolitan — the entry's Comnenian half — not Athos proper. Its c. 963 start, which precedes the era, stands under the adopted start-before-era rule.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: founders' typika, Symeon the New Theologian's corpus
movements.relationsSummary: Heir of the iconophile tradition; parent of hesychasm
movements.why: The Orthodox monastic anchor of the era, and the world hesychasm comes out of — the practice that shapes Eastern spirituality from this point forward has its roots in the houses covered here. Athos is unusual in the atlas as a place that has held the same purpose continuously since this window opened, a rare fixed point on a map mostly made of things that ended. Its founders' typika are constitutional documents in the plainest sense: what a house was for, written down by the people founding it.

sources.work: Byzantine Monastic Foundation Documents (ed. Thomas & Constantinides Hero, Dumbarton Oaks, 5 vols, 2000; free online)
sources.note: Verified. The founders'-typika leg complete in English: Athanasios's Great Lavra documents, the Evergetis typikon, Pantokrator, and more - legislation, liturgy, diet, and charity in lived detail.

sources.work: Symeon the New Theologian, The Discourses (trans. deCatanzaro, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1980)
sources.note: Verified. Catecheses actually preached to his monks - formation as delivered, plus the era's boldest claim of direct experience of God. Nuance flag: Symeon's corpus is Constantinopolitan, the entry's 'Comnenian' half rather than Athos proper.

sources.work: Symeon the New Theologian, Hymns / Divine Eros (trans. Daniel Griggs, SVS Press, 2010)
sources.note: The same claim in first-person poetry. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: Holy Men of Mount Athos (ed./trans. Greenfield & Talbot, Dumbarton Oaks Medieval Library, 2016)
sources.note: Lives of the mountain's founders incl. Athanasios of Athos - Athonite hagiography in facing-page translation. [S] volume details from knowledge, not verified this session.

sources.work: Rosemary Morris, Monks and Laymen in Byzantium, 843-1118 (CUP, 1995)
sources.note: Standard study of the monastic world's social ecosystem: patrons, property, holy men. [S] not individually verified this session.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, ch. 4 'The rise of hesychasm' (Krausmuller); cf. ch. 3 'The culture of lay piety in medieval Byzantium' (Gerstel & Talbot)
sources.note: Chapters verified in TOC. [S] fit is partial - hesychasm crests after this window; assignment to era review.

movements.longDescription: In 963 the monk Athanasios, with the backing of a Byzantine emperor, founded the Great Lavra on the mountainous peninsula of Athos in northern Greece, and the loose scatter of hermits already living there began to take the shape it has kept ever since: a self-governing federation of monasteries, each running on a written charter, a typikon, in which its founder set down exactly what the house was for, down to the diet, the liturgy and the charity. In Constantinople in the same period Symeon the New Theologian preached to his monks that God can be known directly and consciously, in experienced light, and was pushed out of his monastery for pressing the claim so hard. Between them the Athonite houses and the capital's monasteries carried the disciplines of interior prayer that the following century would gather up and name hesychasm.
movements.teaser: Mount Athos and Constantinople, 963 to 1300 — a mountain of monasteries governed by their founders' written charters, and the monks who insisted God could be known directly and not merely believed in.
voices: Athanasios the Athonite — founder of the Great Lavra in 963 and effectively the organizer of Athonite monasticism
Symeon the New Theologian — abbot in Constantinople whose sermons and hymns claimed direct experience of God, and who was exiled for insisting on it
The founders of the Evergetis monastery in Constantinople — whose typikon was copied and adapted more widely than any other, from Athos to the Slavic lands
movements.legacy: Mount Athos never stopped. Its monasteries have been continuously occupied since this period, still governed by their own charters, and it is one of the very few places on the whole map of Christian history where a visitor can find something doing today what it was doing a thousand years ago. The prayer practices formed here fed directly into hesychasm and the Palamite theology of the next century, and from there into the whole later devotional life of Orthodoxy — the Jesus Prayer, and eventually the Philokalia. Athonite typika were adapted by Georgian, Serbian, Bulgarian and Russian founders, exporting a model of monastic government across Eastern Europe.

experienceToday.text: Mount Athos, Greece — the Great Lavra, founded in 963 and still the senior monastery of the mountain; entry requires a permit and is open to men only

movements.name: The Beguines
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1), and named the flagship for the marginalized-voices duty the census sets itself: Hadewijch, Mechthild of Magdeburg and Marguerite Porete are first-person women's voices, the rarest commodity in the atlas, all in verified modern translation. Its 1310 end, Porete's burning, crosses the era boundary once as a principled straddle rather than an artifact.
