movements.sourcing: RICH in first-person women's voice - the rarest commodity in the whole atlas (Hadewijch, Mechthild, Porete)
movements.relationsSummary: Lay women's movement outside every standard structure; suppression pressure is part of its own story
movements.why: This is where the census's own duty toward marginalized voices actually pays out. Lay women in no order and under no rule, living a religious life outside every standard structure the era provided — and, unusually, writing about it themselves, so the atlas can hear the thing described from inside rather than only from the authorities who found it irregular. The suppression that eventually came for them belongs to the same story and not to an epilogue.

sources.work: Hadewijch, The Complete Works (trans. Mother Columba Hart, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1980)
sources.note: Verified. Visions, letters, and poems in Middle Dutch - a beguine directing other women's formation, in her own voice. Spine text 1 of 3.

sources.work: Mechthild of Magdeburg, The Flowing Light of the Godhead (trans. Frank Tobin, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1998)
sources.note: Verified. Begun as a beguine, finished at Helfta; includes her defense of writing as an unlettered woman. Spine text 2 of 3.

sources.work: Marguerite Porete, The Mirror of Simple Souls (trans. Ellen Babinsky, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1993)
sources.note: Verified. The movement's boldest theology and its martyrdom (1310) - the suppression pressure the census names, carried in one book's fate. Spine text 3 of 3; crossover with the Free Spirit entry.

sources.work: Jacques de Vitry, Life of Marie d'Oignies, in Mary of Oignies: Mother of Salvation (ed. Mulder-Bakker, Brepols, 2006)
sources.note: The sympathetic clerical outside view that won the movement its first toleration; hagiographic-frame flag. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: Walter Simons, Cities of Ladies: Beguine Communities in the Medieval Low Countries, 1200-1565 (Penn, 2001)
sources.note: Verified. The standard social history - courtyards, labor, and rents behind the mystics.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 20 'On the margins of religious life... beguines and beghards' (Simons); cf. ch. 19 'Mysticism and transcendence' (Hollywood)
sources.note: Verified in TOC; the volume's co-editor writing on this exact movement - strongest reference fit in the era.

movements.longDescription: From the late twelfth century, women in the towns of the Low Countries and the Rhineland began living religious lives without joining any order: no lifelong vows, no rule, no enclosure. They kept their own property or worked — often in cloth — lived alone or in walled courtyard communities called beguinages, prayed, and nursed the sick and the dying. Some of them wrote, and that is what makes them extraordinary on any map of medieval Christianity: Hadewijch's visions and letters, Mechthild of Magdeburg's Flowing Light of the Godhead, Marguerite Porete's Mirror of Simple Souls are among the very few medieval accounts of a religious life told from the inside by the women actually living it. Because they fitted no category, they attracted suspicion: Porete was burned in Paris in 1310, and in 1312 the Council of Vienne moved against the beguine life itself.
movements.teaser: The towns of the Low Countries and the Rhineland, c. 1190 to 1310 — women who lived a religious life under no rule and no vows, wrote about it in their own words, and were finally condemned for fitting nowhere.
voices: Marie d'Oignies — the movement's first widely known figure, whose life was written by a sympathetic churchman and helped win the beguines early toleration
Jacques de Vitry — the cleric who wrote that life and defended the movement at Rome
Hadewijch — a beguine of the Low Countries whose visions, letters and poems in Middle Dutch guided other women's formation
Mechthild of Magdeburg — who began The Flowing Light of the Godhead as a beguine and finished it at the convent of Helfta, defending along the way her right to write as an unschooled woman
Marguerite Porete — author of The Mirror of Simple Souls, burned at Paris in 1310 for refusing to withdraw it
movements.legacy: The beguinages themselves outlasted the suppression by centuries: whole courtyard quarters in Bruges, Leuven and other Flemish towns still stand, lived in and intact, and are now protected as world heritage. The writing survived too, though not always under its author's name — Porete's Mirror circulated anonymously for six hundred years and was read as an orthodox devotional classic until scholars identified it as hers in the twentieth century. Hadewijch and Mechthild are read today as major theologians in their own right, and the movement as a whole has become one of the standard reference points in the history of women's religious life.

experienceToday.text: Bruges, Belgium — the Princely Beguinage Ten Wijngaerde, founded in 1244, still standing around its garden

movements.name: The Waldensians
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), and named the map's clearest dissent-that-survived thread. Its evidence splits by period — inquisition registers early, genuine internal literature later, with the Liber Antiheresis flagged Latin-only and its representativeness contested. The 1300–1517 gap its continuing thread jumps was flagged to the succession walk rather than closed here.
movements.sourcing: Hostile-source problem early (inquisition registers), genuine internal literature later
movements.floorNote: No plain-reading doctrinal question - discipline, not doctrine, was the charge
movements.relationsSummary: The map's clearest 'dissent that survived' thread - joins the Reformed tradition in 1532
movements.why: The map's clearest thread of dissent that survived. Almost every medieval movement the church condemned is now known only through the records of the people who condemned it; this one lasted, kept its own literature, and in 1532 joined the Reformed tradition — so a single line of protest can be followed from twelfth-century Lyon into the Reformation without a break. The charge against it was discipline rather than doctrine, a distinction the entry keeps visible because it changes what the condemnation was actually about.

sources.work: Valdes's Profession of Faith (1180) and the early Waldensian dossier, trans. in Wakefield & Evans, Heresies of the High Middle Ages (Columbia, 1969; repr. 1991)
sources.note: Volume verified. The founder's own orthodox confession - evidence the charge was discipline (unauthorized preaching), matching the census floor note. [S] precise Waldensian contents not itemized this session.

sources.work: Durand of Osca, Liber Antiheresis (c. 1190s; ed. Selge, 1967)
sources.note: The earliest inside theological text, from the first generation; its author later reconciled with Rome - representativeness contested, flag carried. [S] Latin only; no English - access flag.

sources.work: Bernard Gui, Inquisitor's Guide, Waldensian section (trans. Janet Shirley, 2006), plus 13th-c. inquisition registers
sources.note: HOSTILE flag. How the persecutors described practice; depositions preserve ordinary believers' voices no inside text records. [S] translation details from knowledge.

sources.work: Euan Cameron, Waldenses: Rejections of Holy Church in Medieval Europe (Blackwell, 2000)
sources.note: Source-critical standard; warns against reading later Waldensian identity back into the 1170s. [S] not individually verified this session.

sources.work: Gabriel Audisio, The Waldensian Dissent: Persecution and Survival, c.1170-c.1570 (CUP, 1999)
sources.note: The survival arc to the 1532 Reformed union that the census's relations line names. [S] not individually verified this session.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 12 'Christians and heretics' (Biller); cf. ch. 3 (Kienzle)
sources.note: Verified in TOC; Biller is the leading Waldensian specialist.

movements.longDescription: Around 1173 a rich merchant of Lyon named Valdes gave away his property, had parts of Scripture translated into the language people actually spoke, and began preaching in the streets. His confession of faith was entirely orthodox; what he would not do was stop preaching without a licence, and in 1184 the bull Ad abolendam condemned him and his followers for exactly that. Driven out of the cities, the movement survived in the Alpine valleys between France and Italy for three and a half centuries of intermittent persecution, with its own travelling ministers and its own books. In 1532 its representatives met the Reformers at Chanforan and threw in with the Reformed tradition — which is why a single line of protest can be followed from twelfth-century Lyon into the Reformation without a break.
movements.teaser: Lyon and the Alpine valleys, from about 1173 — a merchant who gave away everything to preach, condemned not for what he believed but for preaching without permission, and a movement that outlived everyone who condemned it.
voices: Valdes of Lyon — the merchant who gave away his wealth, commissioned Scripture in the vernacular, and would not stop preaching
Durand of Osca — a first-generation Waldensian whose theological defence of the movement survives, and who later reconciled with Rome
Bernard Gui — the Dominican inquisitor whose handbook describes Waldensian practice from the outside, and whose registers preserve the words of ordinary believers recorded nowhere else
movements.legacy: The Waldensian church is still here. Having joined the Reformed tradition at Chanforan in 1532, it survives as the Waldensian Evangelical Church, based in the same Piedmontese valleys and now united with Italy's Methodists — one of the very few medieval movements condemned by Rome that never disappeared and never had to be reconstructed out of its enemies' files. Its long habit of vernacular Scripture and lay preaching anticipated, and then joined, the Reformation.

experienceToday.text: Torre Pellice, Italy — the Waldensian Cultural Centre Foundation and its historical museum, in the Alpine valleys where the community survived

movements.name: Zagwe Ethiopian Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — moderate in sourcing here and richer in the next era, so its work in this window is holding the spine. At the Freeze a stated fork was decided in favour of ending it at 1270, the Solomonic restoration, with a rename from 'Zagwe & Early Solomonic' to match; that removed a 30-year double-coverage with its successor entry, and the alternative of moving the successor's start was shown and declined.
movements.sourcing: Moderate here, rich next era - a window-setting call
movements.relationsSummary: Continuation of Aksum; formal dependence on the Coptic patriarchate
movements.why: The window was set here deliberately rather than later where the sources bloom: the work this entry does is holding the Ethiopian spine between Aksum and the Solomonic centuries, and it does that by covering years thinner than those on either side. A church in formal dependence on the Coptic patriarchate while carrying an entirely separate political and liturgical life — a relation the atlas has nowhere else.
movements.dateRationale: End 1270 (Solomonic restoration — Yekuno Amlak): fixes a 30-year double-coverage with its continuesAs target V.7 (starts 1270); renamed from 'Zagwe & Early Solomonic' to match the corrected window (the Early Solomonic story belongs to V.7). The move-V.7 alternative was shown and declined — 1270 is V.7's genuine gravity start (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.note: Verified. The Solomonic dynasty's charter myth. Tier care: compiled/redacted early 14th c. - royal ideology at this window's edge, not Zagwe self-description; Budge's translation dated but standard-available.

sources.work: Gadla Lalibela (Life of King Lalibela) (ed./French trans. Perruchon, 1892)
sources.note: Zagwe royal hagiography; existence verified. [S] no English - access flag; the Life postdates the king it praises - tier care.

sources.work: Lalibela's rock-hewn churches (material culture) + land grants and marginalia in gospel books (e.g. the Golden Gospel of Dabra Libanos)
sources.note: The era's most eloquent contemporary witnesses are carved and written into stone and manuscript margins, not narrated - the royal-charters leg. [S] specialist publications only; details from knowledge.

sources.work: Taddesse Tamrat, Church and State in Ethiopia, 1270-1527 (Oxford, 1972)
sources.note: Verified (archive.org). Still the field's standard frame, by an Ethiopian historian.

sources.work: Marie-Laure Derat, L'enigme d'une dynastie sainte et usurpatrice: les rois zagwe (2018)
sources.note: Current Zagwe scholarship revising the Solomonic-propaganda picture; existence verified. [S] French only - access flag.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, 'Church and nation: the Ethiopian Orthodox Tawahedo church (from the thirteenth to the twentieth century)' (Crummey)
sources.note: Chapter verified in TOC; direct fit.

movements.longDescription: After the old Aksumite kingdom faded, a dynasty called the Zagwe ruled the Ethiopian highlands from the twelfth century, and under them the Ethiopian church went on doing what it had done for eight hundred years — with one striking peculiarity of constitution: its head bishop, the abun, was not Ethiopian but a monk sent from the Coptic patriarchate in Egypt, so a wholly independent kingdom kept its senior churchman permanently on loan from another country. The dynasty's most famous achievement is the group of eleven churches cut downward out of solid rock at the town now called Lalibela, after the king who commissioned them, laid out to recall Jerusalem at a time when Jerusalem itself had become unreachable. In 1270 the Zagwe were displaced by Yekuno Amlak, whose line claimed descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba — a claim set out in the Kebra Nagast, compiled in the generations after the takeover and used to justify Ethiopian kingship for the next seven centuries.
movements.teaser: The Ethiopian highlands, c. 1137 to 1270 — a kingdom that carved its churches downward into living rock, ruled by a church whose senior bishop was always a foreigner sent from Egypt.
voices: Gebre Meskel Lalibela — the Zagwe king who commissioned the rock-hewn churches that carry his name and who became a saint of the Ethiopian church
Yekuno Amlak — the ruler who ended the Zagwe in 1270 and founded the Solomonic line
The abuns of this period — Coptic monks sent from Alexandria to head a church whose language and kingdom were not their own, and who left little personal record behind them
movements.legacy: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is one of the largest ancient churches in the world today, and it runs in an unbroken line through this period. Lalibela's churches are not ruins: they are working parish churches, with priests and pilgrims, and remain one of the great pilgrimage destinations of African Christianity. The Solomonic claim launched in these years shaped Ethiopian politics until 1974, when the last emperor to bear the title Lion of Judah was deposed.

experienceToday.text: Lalibela, Ethiopia — eleven churches cut downward out of the living rock in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries and still in use for worship

movements.name: Maronite Christianity
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 5 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Marginal/deferred (Tier 3): thin-to-moderate early, with much of its early history being later reconstruction under polemical pressure — the census's own line, confirmed rather than softened. Its start was decided at a stated fork in favour of keeping 1100 with an Era 4 origin note, rather than backward-extending to c. 685 on tradition-internal evidence.
movements.sourcing: Thin-to-moderate early; much early history is later reconstruction under polemical pressure
movements.floorNote: Contested historiography (monothelete question) is about the past record, not present confession
movements.relationsSummary: West Syriac liturgical family; unique early union with Rome
movements.why: The one Eastern church in the atlas with an early and lasting union with Rome, which makes it structurally unlike anything else in its lane. Its early history is genuinely hard: much of what is told about it was written back into the past under polemical pressure, by people arguing over whether the community had once been monothelete. The entry keeps the distinction that matters — a contested record of the past is not a question about present confession — and accepts a thin early window rather than borrowing the tradition's own later account of itself.

sources.work: Kitab al-Huda (Book of Guidance; Syriac-to-Arabic trans. by Bishop David, 1059; ed. Fahed, 1935)
sources.note: The community's own law-liturgy-theology compendium - the lived internal rulebook. Existence/date verified. [S] Arabic/French only; no English - access flag.

sources.work: Thomas of Kaphartab, Ten Chapters (11th c.)
sources.note: Pre-union Maronite apologetics defending the one-will christology - inside evidence bearing on the contested monothelete historiography (census floor note: about the past record, not present confession). [S] details from knowledge; no English - access flag.

sources.work: William of Tyre on the Maronite union with Rome (1180s), in A History of Deeds Done Beyond the Sea (trans. Babcock & Krey, 1943)
sources.note: OUTSIDE view: the union event through Latin crusader eyes; attestation verified. Hostile-adjacent framing flag - William calls their prior teaching heresy.

sources.work: Kamal Salibi, Maronite Historians of Mediaeval Lebanon (Beirut, 1959)
sources.note: Verified (archive.org). Classic dissection of how later Maronite historians rebuilt the early record under polemical pressure - the census's sourcing note as a monograph.

sources.work: Matti Moosa, The Maronites in History (Syracuse, 1986; repr. Gorgias 2005)
sources.note: Verified. Critical counter-history; itself contested by Maronite traditionalists - the historiography is a live confessional argument on both sides.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, Part III 'East Christianities (eleventh to fourteenth century): Copts, Melkites, Nestorians and Jacobites'
sources.note: Chapter verified in TOC. [S] Maronites unnamed in the chapter title; in-chapter coverage not page-verified - best-available anchor, flagged for era review.

movements.longDescription: The Maronites take their name from a Syriac monk, Maron, and from the monastery built around his memory; by the medieval period they were a distinct church of the West Syriac liturgical family, concentrated in the mountains and gorges of Lebanon, where their monasteries and hermitages were cut straight into the cliffs. Their early history is unusually hard to recover, because much of what is told about it was written down later and under argument — specifically over whether the community had once held that Christ had only one will, a position the wider church had rejected. What is clear is that when the crusaders arrived, the Maronites entered into communion with Rome: William of Tyre describes the union around 1182, and in 1215 the Maronite patriarch Jeremiah al-Amshitti travelled to Rome for the Fourth Lateran Council, after which a papal bull set out the terms of the union.
movements.teaser: Mount Lebanon, consolidating through this era — a Syriac church of cliffside monasteries whose own early history is fought over, and the one Eastern church to enter a lasting communion with Rome in the Middle Ages.
voices: Maron — the Syriac hermit of late antiquity the church is named for
Thomas of Kaphartab — an eleventh-century Maronite writer whose Ten Chapters defends the one-will Christology that later Maronite historians would deny the community had ever held
Jeremiah al-Amshitti — the patriarch who travelled to Rome for the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215
William of Tyre — the crusader archbishop whose history is the main outside account of the union, written from a frankly Latin point of view
movements.legacy: The Maronite Church is very much alive: one of the largest Eastern Catholic churches, the largest Christian community in Lebanon, and with a worldwide diaspora. The union begun here has held for eight centuries and made the Maronites the working model for later Eastern Catholic churches — communion with the papacy alongside a Syriac liturgy and a patriarch of their own. The Qadisha valley, where the monasteries and hermitages are carved into the cliff faces, remains a place of pilgrimage and is protected as world heritage.

experienceToday.text: Northern Lebanon — the Qadisha (Kadisha) Valley, whose cliffside monasteries and hermitages are the historic heart of Maronite monastic life, with the cedar forest above it

movements.name: Military-Religious Orders (Templars, Hospitallers)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — institutionally rich with a thin interior voice, and the Templar trial testimony flagged as coerced rather than read as inside evidence. The entry's own open question, whether this is a tradition or an institution, was left standing for any build to face, alongside the question of holy violence its floorNote names.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally; interior voice thin
movements.floorNote: No creedal question — these orders held the ordinary faith of the Latin church. The hard question they raise is holy violence, and it is a real one.
movements.relationsSummary: Monastic vows fused with arms; Bernard wrote its apologia; the order continues on Rhodes (1310-1517+) - recorded as a continuation note, no receiver entry (approved at the Era 6 gate as a named touch on the Frozen Era 5 record)
movements.why: Whether it amounts to a tradition at all, or only to an institution, is a genuine open test — and its central tension is the hardest kind to hold plainly: monastic vows fused with arms, and defended in its own time by Bernard of Clairvaux. The atlas does not carry it because that fusion was right. It carries it because it happened, at scale and with the church's blessing, and a map that quietly dropped it would be telling a more comfortable story than the record supports.

sources.work: The Rule of the Templars (trans. J. M. Upton-Ward, Boydell, 1992)
sources.note: Verified. Primitive Rule, hierarchical statutes, penances - the fused monastic-military life in regulated detail, down to horses and mess discipline.

sources.work: Bernard of Clairvaux, In Praise of the New Knighthood (De laude novae militiae) (trans. Greenia, Cistercian Fathers 19)
sources.note: The apologia the census's relations line names; the era's theology of holy violence stated plainly - the hard question a build must face. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: Malcolm Barber & Keith Bate, The Templars: Selected Sources (Manchester Medieval Sources, 2002)
sources.note: Verified. Foundation documents, papal bulls, charters, letters from the East, and trial documents - trial testimony carried with a COERCED/HOSTILE flag (torture-extracted, 1307-12).

sources.work: The Hospitallers' Rule and statutes (trans. E. J. King, The Rule, Statutes and Customs of the Hospitallers, 1934)
sources.note: The other order's own legislation, with its 'lords the sick' care obligation - the charitable half of the fusion. [S] edition details from knowledge; old translation - access flag.

sources.work: Malcolm Barber, The New Knighthood: A History of the Order of the Temple (CUP, 1994)
sources.note: Verified. Standard history, foundation to suppression.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 4 (McGuire) + ch. 11 'Christendom and Islam' (Nirenberg)
sources.note: Chapters verified in TOC. [S] no dedicated military-orders chapter identified - split assignment left to era review.

movements.longDescription: In the decades after the First Crusade, two kinds of institution fused into something the church had never authorized before. The Hospitallers began as a hospital in Jerusalem caring for pilgrims — they called the sick 'our lords the sick' — and only later took on a military role; the Templars began as a small band of knights guarding the pilgrim roads, took monastic vows, and were given a rule at the Council of Troyes in 1129. Bernard of Clairvaux wrote their defence, In Praise of the New Knighthood, arguing that a man who killed in this cause was not a homicide but, in his coinage, a malicide — a killer of evil. Both orders grew enormously rich, ran castles, estates and banking networks from the Latin East across Europe, and lost their reason for existing when Acre fell in 1291; the Templars were arrested in France in 1307, made to confess under torture, and suppressed in 1312.
movements.teaser: The Latin East and Iberia, 1120 to 1291 — men who took monastic vows of poverty, chastity and obedience and then went to war, defended in their own time by the most admired churchman in Europe.
voices: Hugh de Payens — the knight who founded the Templars and became their first master
Bernard of Clairvaux — who wrote In Praise of the New Knighthood, the era's most influential defence of holy violence
Gerard — the founder-figure of the Hospital in Jerusalem, remembered as the beginning of the order's care of the sick
Jacques de Molay — the last Templar master, burned in Paris in 1314 after years of imprisonment and forced confession
movements.legacy: One of the two orders is still going. The Hospitallers moved to Rhodes, then Malta, and continue today as the Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a hospitaller body with a legal personality of its own, alongside Protestant orders of St John in Britain and Germany out of which St John Ambulance grew — the medical vocation outlived the military one by many centuries. The Templars did not survive, and their destruction left a very long afterlife in legend and conspiracy writing that has almost nothing to do with the historical order. What both left physically is architecture: castles across the eastern Mediterranean and Iberia, and round churches in Europe built in imitation of the Holy Sepulchre, of which London's Temple Church is the best known.

experienceToday.text: London, England — the Temple Church, consecrated in 1185 as the Templars' English headquarters, with its round nave and its floor of knightly effigies

movements.name: Cathars / Albigensians
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence recorded — dualist theology per the claimed Liber de duobus principiis; the Lyon Ritual as claimed inside practice; docetic Christology at census-claim strength; texts’ status and the movement’s coherence contested in scholarship — disclosed
movements.statusDescription: Carries a named creedal question for a future Step 0 to answer — stated as a question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Inquisition records plus the movement's own surviving ritual
movements.floorNote: By every account we have, they taught that the visible material world was not the good God's making, and that Christ only appeared to have a body — both outside the common Christian creed. Their own voice has not survived to test it against.
movements.relationsSummary: Target of crusade and inquisition - which the map names without softening
movements.why: Excluded-in-prospect by the floor's plain reading, pending this era's Step 0. Exclusion from the conversation set is not endorsement of what was done to them.
movements.dateRationale: Start c. 1143 (Eberwin of Steinfeld's Cologne letter — first solid western description); end 1321 (Bélibaste burned — documented Languedoc Catharism ends; one boundary crossing, allowed) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: The Book of the Two Principles (Liber de duobus principiis, c. 1240s-60s), trans. in Wakefield & Evans, Heresies of the High Middle Ages (1969), p. 511
sources.note: CLAIMED INSIDE, CONTESTED. Inclusion verified. Radical-dualist theology from the circle of John of Lugio (Italy). Non-Catholic authorship broadly accepted, but whether it speaks for 'the Cathars' (esp. Languedoc) is exactly what Pegg and Moore deny.

sources.work: The Cathar Rituals (Occitan Lyon ritual; Latin Florence ritual), trans. in Wakefield & Evans (1969), p. 465
sources.note: CLAIMED INSIDE, CONTESTED. Inclusion verified. The consolamentum liturgy - the census's 'movement's own surviving ritual'. Nuance flag (not override): current scholarship contests whether these are inside texts of a coherent Catharism or of a small literate circle back-projected onto Languedoc.

sources.work: Biller, Bruschi & Sneddon (ed./trans.), Inquisitors and Heretics in Thirteenth-Century Languedoc (Brill, 2011) - Toulouse depositions 1273-82
sources.note: HOSTILE. The only place ordinary believers' voices survive, filtered through interrogation categories; the words 'Cathar'/'perfect' are largely the inquisitors', not the deponents'. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: Rainerius Sacconi, Summa de Catharis (1250), in Wakefield & Evans
sources.note: HOSTILE, INSIDER-TURNED. A former 'heretic' of seventeen years turned Dominican inquisitor - uniquely informed and uniquely motivated; double flag. [S] inclusion not itemized this session (volume verified).

sources.work: Antonio Sennis (ed.), Cathars in Question (York Medieval Press, 2016)
sources.note: Verified. The coherence debate itself: Pegg ('The Paradigm of Catharism; or, the Historians' Illusion'), Moore, Biller, Hamilton, Taylor, Stoyanov face to face - the honest state of the question. For narrative, Barber (2000, traditionalist) vs Moore, The War on Heresy (2012, deconstructionist) [S] neither individually verified.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 12 'Christians and heretics' (Biller)
sources.note: Chapter verified in TOC. Builder caution: Biller is a leading traditionalist party in the live debate - the anchor is not neutral here; read alongside Sennis.

movements.longDescription: From the 1140s, church writers in the Rhineland and then in southern France describe communities with their own ministers, their own initiation rite, and a teaching that the visible material world was not the work of the good God — a dualism that placed them outside Christianity as the councils had defined it. In Languedoc they had noble protection and something close to a parallel church, and in 1209 the papacy launched a crusade against them: two decades of war, then inquisition, then the siege of Montségur in 1244, where roughly two hundred of their ministers walked into a fire rather than recant. The last known Languedoc perfect, Guillaume Bélibaste, was burned in 1321. Almost everything known about them comes from the people who destroyed them, and historians now argue seriously about how much of 'Catharism' was a coherent movement at all and how much was a category assembled by inquisitors out of scattered local dissent.
movements.teaser: Languedoc, c. 1143 to 1321 — a dissenting church with its own ministers and its own initiation, destroyed by crusade and inquisition, and known almost entirely through the records of the men who destroyed it.
voices: Guilhabert de Castres — the most prominent Cathar bishop of Languedoc in the movement's strongest years
Bertrand Marty — the bishop who led some two hundred of his people into the fire at Montségur in 1244
Rainerius Sacconi — a former member of seventeen years who became a Dominican inquisitor and wrote the fullest surviving description of their beliefs: uniquely informed and thoroughly hostile at once
Guillaume Bélibaste — the last known Languedoc perfect, burned in 1321
movements.legacy: Nothing of the movement itself survived; it was extinguished, and no continuing community descends from it. What it left behind belongs mostly to the people who suppressed it — the Albigensian Crusade attached Languedoc to the French crown, and the papal inquisition was built in the 1230s largely to deal with this problem and then became a permanent institution that long outlived its original target. In the modern Languedoc the Cathars have been rediscovered as regional heritage, and ruined hilltop castles are marketed as 'Cathar country', though the ruins standing today are mostly later rebuildings and the popular picture of the movement owes as much to romantic reconstruction as to the sources.

experienceToday.text: Ariège, southern France — the ruined Château de Montségur, above the field where roughly two hundred Cathars were burned in March 1244 (the standing walls are a later rebuilding)

movements.name: Joachimite Current
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: A reading-program more than a community
movements.floorNote: Joachim submitted his writings to Rome, and Rome took him up on it: the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215 condemned his book on the Trinity while leaving his person and his monastery in good standing. The later expectation of a coming age of the Spirit was condemned in its most extreme forms, not in his.
movements.relationsSummary: Where it became communal, it lives inside the Franciscan Spirituals' story
movements.why: Not a candidate tradition on its own; it appears plainly inside the Franciscan tradition's own tensions.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1202 (Joachim's death — the posthumous current is the entry's stated subject; the old 1200 matched nothing) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Joachim of Fiore, selections in Bernard McGinn, Apocalyptic Spirituality (Classics of Western Spirituality, 1979)
sources.note: Verified. Joachim's letters and key texts plus Spiritual-Franciscan material - both ends of the current in one translated volume, with Reeves's preface.

sources.work: Joachim of Fiore, major works: Liber de Concordia, Expositio in Apocalypsim, Psalterium decem chordarum
sources.note: The authentic baseline against which the pseudo-corpus is measured. [S] Latin; critical editions (MGH) and E. R. Daniel's partial Concordia from knowledge - access flag; no complete English.

sources.note: An ex-Joachimite friar's first-person memoir: expectation caught, shared in friaries, pinned to Frederick II, dropped when 1260 passed - communally carried expectation observed from inside; incl. the 1254 Eternal Evangel scandal (Gerard of Borgo San Donnino; hostile commission record = Protocol of Anagni). Bears directly on the c2 question: the current rested on communal expectation more than on Joachim's person, within Franciscan circles - supporting the census's A5 placement. [S] translation and Protocol details from knowledge.

sources.note: Verified. The standard, built exactly on the Joachim-vs-Joachimism distinction the c2 question needs. Mild nuance to census 'reading-program more than a community': Reeves and Salimbene both show episodes of genuinely communal carriage inside Franciscan circles - consistent with the A5 disposition.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4 (chapter assignment open)
sources.note: [S] no dedicated Joachimism chapter identified in TOC this session (a Rusconi contribution may fit); assignment left to era review; cf. ch. 3 (Kienzle) for the Franciscan frame the census points into.

movements.longDescription: Joachim of Fiore was a Calabrian abbot who read history as a pattern with a shape: three ages, of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the third still to come and not far off. He died in 1202, and the current that carried his reading afterwards was never an order or a church — it was a way of reading the Bible and the calendar together, and it spread especially among Franciscans, who found in it a description of their own movement. In 1254 a young friar published an Introduction to the Eternal Gospel that made the claim explicit and scandalous, and it was condemned; the current then fixed on 1260 as the year the new age would open. The year came and went. Some let it go, and some carried the expectation on into the bitter Franciscan quarrel over poverty, where it did most of its later work.
movements.teaser: Calabria and then the Franciscan houses of Europe, 1202 to 1300 — not an order but a way of reading history, which named the year the world would change and kept going after the year had passed.
voices: Joachim of Fiore — the Calabrian abbot whose reading of history the current is named for, and who died in 1202 before any of it happened
Gerard of Borgo San Donnino — the Franciscan whose Introduction to the Eternal Gospel of 1254 made the claim public and was condemned for it
Salimbene de Adam — a friar who caught the expectation, watched 1260 pass, and wrote a candid first-person account of letting it go
Much of the current is anonymous — the texts that actually carried it after about 1240 were written by other hands under Joachim's name
movements.legacy: No community descends from it, and the Florensian order Joachim founded was absorbed long ago. What the current left behind is a habit of mind: the idea that history moves in ages toward a coming age of the Spirit kept resurfacing in Western thought long after anyone was reading Joachim directly — in Franciscan reform movements, in radical politics, and in the recurring modern language of a 'third age' or a new spiritual era. Joachim himself stayed readable enough that Dante placed him in paradise. His abbey at San Giovanni in Fiore still stands and still holds his remains.

experienceToday.text: San Giovanni in Fiore, Calabria, Italy — the Florense Abbey, founded by Joachim and holding his remains

movements.name: 'Free Spirit' Heresy
movements.statusDescription: The record is genuinely disputed. This entry carries the question, not a verdict.

sources.note: HOSTILE CONSTRUCT. The eight-error decree that constituted 'the sect of the Free Spirit' as a juridical object; errors partly extracted, distortedly, from the Mirror. [S] inclusion details from knowledge.

sources.work: Interrogation records of accused beghards and beguines (e.g. John of Brunn; the Schweidnitz interrogations, 1332)
sources.note: HOSTILE. The 'movement' as it exists in the record: answers shaped by the questioners' template. [S] editions/partial translations (incl. in Lerner's apparatus) from knowledge - access flag.

sources.note: Verified. The consensus-setting study the census cites by name: no organized sect - a persecutors' construct over a spectrum of mystical piety. Census fully consistent.

sources.note: Both chapters verified in TOC.

movements.longDescription: In the early fourteenth century the church declared that a sect existed. The decree Ad nostrum, issued at the Council of Vienne in 1312, listed eight errors said to be held by a 'sect of the Free Spirit' — chiefly that a soul perfected in this life becomes incapable of sin and needs neither the church nor the virtues any longer. Interrogators then went looking for people who held them, and found them, because the questions supplied the answers. Modern research, above all Robert Lerner's study of 1972, concluded that no organized sect of this kind ever existed: what existed was a wide spectrum of mystical piety, much of it among beguines and beghards, and a charge that could be laid against any part of it. The movement named here probably was not real; the charge and its victims certainly were.
movements.teaser: The Rhineland and the Low Countries, thirteenth and fourteenth centuries — a heresy that was defined before anyone had been found holding it, and that most historians now think never existed as an organized movement at all.
voices: Marguerite Porete — burned at Paris in 1310, and the one person condemned under this charge who left a substantial book in her own voice; she never used the label, and whether her Mirror of Simple Souls teaches what Ad nostrum condemned is precisely the disputed question

The rest are known only as defendants — men and women like John of Brunn, whose recorded words come out of interrogation and follow the questioners' template closely enough that they cannot safely be read as their own
movements.legacy: Nothing continued, because there was most likely nothing there to continue. What the episode left behind is the charge itself, which stayed available for two centuries afterwards against mystical writing and against religious women living outside enclosure. It also left one of the clearest lessons in the historian's craft: that a heresy can be manufactured out of a decree, a questionnaire and enough pressure. Marguerite Porete's book, once separated from the label, has been read since the twentieth century as a serious work of theology.

Its end was set to 1245, Queen Rusudan's death and the Mongol tributary submission, replacing a round-number 1250.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: chronicles, typika, hymnography, hagiography (Gelati academy)
movements.relationsSummary: Continuation of II.10 - restores the Georgian lane, silent since 622; partner of Byzantine monasticism
movements.why: The Georgian lane's high point and its most substantial window anywhere on the map: a national church with a court behind it, an academy at Gelati, and a body of chronicles, typika, hagiography and hymnography written in its own language. The Caucasus is easy to lose between the Byzantine and Islamic worlds, and this entry is the strongest single argument that it should not be. What closes the window is not a decline but a conquest — the Mongol submission ends the political frame the church had been working inside.
movements.dateRationale: End 1245 (Queen Rusudan's death / Mongol tributary submission — the golden age's actual close; the old 1250 was a round number) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.note: Verified. Annotated English of the medieval corpus via the 13th-c. Armenian adaptation (reaches c. 1125 - coverage flag for the later Golden Age). Complete English of the Georgian corpus (ed. S. Jones, Tbilisi, 2014) exists [S] - details from knowledge.

sources.note: Verified. The hagiography leg in the movement's own voice (George the Hagiorite's Life of John and Euthymios; the Life of George) - and the living bridge to the Athos entry.

sources.note: Volume verified. A Georgian grandee's foundation with its Georgians-only clause - the census's typika leg, in English.

sources.note: The census's hymnography/Gelati leg. [S] specialist/Georgian editions only; attributions traditional - access and tier flags.

sources.note: Verified. Standard English analysis of royal-sanctity ideology (Davit the Builder to Tamar) through monuments - material culture doing work the chronicles cannot.

movements.longDescription: For two and a half centuries Georgia was a real power in the Caucasus, and its church rose with it. David IV, called the Builder, broke the Seljuk hold at the battle of Didgori in 1121, and in 1106 had begun the monastery of Gelati, which was also an academy: philosophy, astronomy, rhetoric and Greek taught alongside the liturgy, with the Neoplatonist Ioane Petritsi among its scholars. Under his great-granddaughter Tamar the kingdom reached its widest extent, its churches were covered in frescoes, and its language was given a literature to match. The age ended not in decline but in conquest — after the Mongol invasions Georgia became a tributary state, and the death of Queen Rusudan in 1245 closes the age.
movements.teaser: Georgia, c. 1000 to 1245 — a mountain kingdom at its height, with an academy at Gelati teaching philosophy beside the liturgy, ended not by decay but by the Mongols.
voices: David IV the Builder — the king who broke the Seljuk hold at Didgori in 1121 and founded Gelati in 1106
Ioane Petritsi — the Neoplatonist philosopher and translator of Proclus who taught at the Gelati academy
Queen Tamar — under whom the kingdom reached its greatest extent, and who was canonized by the Georgian church
George the Hagiorite — the Georgian abbot at Iviron on Mount Athos, who revised the Georgian scriptures and wrote the lives of his predecessors there
Queen Rusudan — Tamar's daughter, whose reign saw the Mongol submission and whose death in 1245 closes the age
movements.legacy: The Georgian Orthodox Church is still the national church of Georgia, in a line running straight through this period. Gelati survives, with its twelfth-century mosaic of the Virgin and centuries of wall painting, and David the Builder is buried at its gate. What the age produced in Georgian — the chronicles, the hymnody, the translations made at Gelati, and beside them Rustaveli's great secular poem — remains the foundation of the national literature; the hymn traditionally attributed to King Demetre I, 'Thou Art a Vineyard', is still sung in Georgian churches and concert halls today.

experienceToday.text: Kutaisi, Georgia — the Gelati Monastery and its academy, founded by David the Builder in 1106, with its mosaics and medieval frescoes

movements.name: Serbian & Bulgarian Medieval Monasticism
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 5 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a moderate-to-rich base with a native genre of its own — the zhitija, or royal saints' lives — alongside typika and chrysobulls, with access flags carried on the non-English editions. Its 1396 end is the era's heaviest overhang at 96 years; the Freeze kept it under the straddle rule's letter rather than capping it, with whether the rule's intent should cap such overhangs left as a standing question.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: typika, royal saints' lives (zhitija - a native genre), chrysobulls
movements.relationsSummary: Children of Byzantium/Athos; carried hesychasm into the Slavic lands; fixes the Slavic lane's Kyiv-to-Moscow jump
movements.why: This is where hesychasm crosses out of Greek into Slavic, which is how it reaches Russia at all — and without this entry the Slavic lane jumps straight from Kyiv to Moscow with nothing in between. It also carries a literary form of its own: the zhitija, lives of royal saints, in which a dynasty writes down its own holiness — a genre with no close parallel elsewhere in the atlas. Hilandar, Studenica, Tarnovo and Rila are the houses that carried both.

sources.work: St Sava of Serbia: Life of St Symeon (Stefan Nemanja) + the Karyes and Hilandar/Studenica typika
sources.note: Founder-family sanctity and legislation in one hand: the zhitija genre's fountainhead and the typika leg (adapted from Evergetis). [S] English access piecemeal (partial translations; Serbian critical editions) - access flag.

sources.work: Domentijan and Teodosije, Lives of St Sava (13th c.)
sources.note: The native royal-saint genre the census names, built around the dynasty's monk. [S] no complete English - access flag.

sources.work: Kiril Petkov, The Voices of Medieval Bulgaria, Seventh-Fifteenth Century (Brill, 2008)
sources.note: Verified. The Bulgarian side's primary corpus in English: inscriptions, charters, seals, graffiti, church records - incl. the Synodicon of Boril (1211, anti-Bogomil - HOSTILE-source crossover with the Bogomil entry) and John of Rila materials. [S] itemization of those two inclusions not page-verified.

sources.work: Royal chrysobulls and charters: Nemanja's Hilandar founding charter; Ivan Asen II's Tarnovo column inscription; monastic land charters
sources.note: The census's chrysobulls leg - kingship and monasticism financing each other on parchment and stone. [S] Serbian-side editions from knowledge (Bulgarian side in Petkov) - access flag.

sources.work: Dimitri Obolensky, Six Byzantine Portraits (Oxford, 1988)
sources.note: Includes a standard scholarly portrait of Sava; frames both churches inside his Byzantine Commonwealth model (a frame, not a verdict). [S] not individually verified this session.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, ch. 1 'The Byzantine commonwealth 1000-1500' (Shepard)
sources.note: Chapter verified in TOC; the Balkans are this chapter's core ground - direct fit.

movements.longDescription: When the Serbian ruler Stefan Nemanja abdicated in 1196 and became a monk, and his youngest son Rastko — already a monk on Mount Athos under the name Sava — joined him there, the two founded Hilandar, a Serbian house on the Holy Mountain. From it the shape of Serbian church life was set: Athonite charters adapted for Serbian monasteries, and a ruling family that produced its own saints and then wrote their lives. Sava secured an autocephalous Serbian church in 1219 and became its first archbishop. In Bulgaria the restored patriarchate at Tarnovo did something comparable, gathering a literary school around it and the cult of hermits like John of Rila. Both churches were the road by which hesychast prayer travelled out of Greek and into Slavonic, and from there eventually to Russia — and Bulgaria was overrun by the Ottoman advance at the end of the fourteenth century, with Serbia following within two generations.
movements.teaser: The Balkans, c. 1170 to 1396 — Serbian and Bulgarian monasteries that took their rule from Mount Athos, wrote their own kings into the calendar of saints, and carried hesychast prayer into the Slavic world.
voices: Stefan Nemanja — the Serbian ruler who abdicated, became the monk Symeon, and died at Hilandar
Sava of Serbia — his son, co-founder of Hilandar, first archbishop of an autocephalous Serbian church from 1219, author of its monastic charters and of his father's life
Domentijan and Teodosije — the monks who wrote the lives of Sava and gave the Serbian royal-saint genre its classic form
John of Rila — the tenth-century Bulgarian hermit whose monastery became the centre of Bulgarian monastic life
Euthymius of Tarnovo — the last medieval Bulgarian patriarch and head of the Tarnovo literary school, who revised the Slavonic liturgical books
movements.legacy: Both churches survive, as the Serbian and Bulgarian Orthodox Churches. So do their buildings, which are among the most visited in the region — Studenica, where Nemanja is buried, and Rila, still Bulgaria's largest monastery — while Hilandar remains one of the twenty ruling monasteries of Mount Athos. The literary legacy outran the politics: the Tarnovo school's revised Slavonic texts, and the hesychast spirituality carried inside them, travelled north and shaped Russian church life for centuries, and the zhitija, the lives of the royal saints, are foundational texts of Serbian literature to this day.

experienceToday.text: Kraljevo district, Serbia — Studenica Monastery, founded by Stefan Nemanja in the late twelfth century, with its white marble churches and Byzantine frescoes
Rila Mountains, Bulgaria — Rila Monastery, the country's largest, built around the memory of the hermit John of Rila

movements.name: The Byzantine Church after the Schism
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run as one of the two Great Schism principals - the pre-banked gap. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich: Cerularius's synodal edict, Anna Komnene's Alexiad, Komnenian synodal records, the Nicaea exile church's documents, Lyons 1274 acta
movements.relationsSummary: The Schism's eastern principal: Cerularius's church, the Komnenian restoration, the 1204 Latin sack and exile to Nicaea, the 1261 return, Lyons union offered and rejected (1274); in tension with the Latin papal church (proposed edge); receiver of III.22
movements.why: Proposed by the Era 5 completeness sweep: one of the two principals of the census's most famous event was absent - IV.6 is monastic only, and III.22 ended 1054 with no receiver. B4 audience demand on record. Tier 1 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 1054 (the Schism) to 1300 (era end; the church continues — era-6 receiver at the A1.E6 run) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: In July 1054 a papal legate laid a bull of excommunication on the altar of Hagia Sophia during the liturgy and walked out; the patriarch, Michael Cerularius, condemned him in return. Neither man believed he had divided Christendom, and for a long time nobody treated the breach as final — but the estrangement between the Greek and Latin churches did not heal, and it hardened catastrophically in 1204, when a crusading army sacked Constantinople, installed a Latin patriarch, and drove the imperial church into exile at Nicaea for nearly sixty years. The Byzantines returned in 1261. In 1274, needing Western help against his enemies, Emperor Michael VIII accepted union with Rome at the Second Council of Lyon; his own clergy and monks refused it, and the union collapsed.
movements.teaser: Constantinople, and Nicaea in exile, 1054 to 1300 — the eastern half of a quarrel nobody at the time thought was permanent, made permanent by a crusader army.
voices: Michael Cerularius — the patriarch at the centre of the events of 1054
Anna Komnene — imperial princess and historian, whose Alexiad is one of the great first-hand accounts of the age and of her father's dealings with Latins and heretics alike
Michael VIII Palaiologos — the emperor who retook Constantinople in 1261 and then accepted a union with Rome that his own church rejected
The monks and lower clergy — collectively the decisive voice against union in 1274, remembered as a body rather than as named individuals
movements.legacy: This is the eastern half of a division that has still not been repaired: the Eastern Orthodox churches today trace their institutional continuity through this church, and the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople remains the first see among them. The sack of 1204 left a memory that shaped Orthodox attitudes to the West for centuries; Pope John Paul II offered an apology for it in 2001, nearly eight hundred years later. And the pattern set in 1274 — union agreed by an emperor and refused by his own clergy and people — would repeat at Florence in 1439 with the same result. The same church continued into the next era through the Palaiologan period.

movements.name: The Latin Papal Church (Gregorian Reform to Innocent III)
movements.informalName: The Roman Church of the Reform Popes
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run as the other Great Schism principal - the church every Latin era-5 entry lived inside, absent in every era. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich: Humbert's bull, Dictatus Papae, Investiture Contest dossiers, Lateran I-IV constitutions, Innocent III's registers
movements.relationsSummary: The Schism's western principal: Leo IX's reform circle, the Investiture Contest, the Lateran councils, the papal monarchy; in tension with the Byzantine church (proposed edge); carries inside its story the era's national churches (England of Anselm and Becket, Capetian France, the Reconquista), the universities and scholastic theology, and the ransom orders (A5 routings)
movements.why: Proposed by the Era 5 completeness sweep: every Latin entry in the era is an order or movement - the church they all lived inside had no entry anywhere. Start c. 1049 (Leo IX) precedes the era boundary under the adopted standing rule, disclosed. B4 audience demand on record. Tier 1 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1049 (Leo IX opens the reform era; start-before-era extension granted at this Freeze) to 1300 (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: In the middle of the eleventh century a circle of reformers around Pope Leo IX set out to free the church from the lay lords who appointed its bishops and sold its offices — and ended by claiming for the papacy an authority no bishop of Rome had exercised before. Gregory VII's Dictatus Papae of 1075 asserted, among much else, that the pope alone could depose an emperor; the resulting Investiture Contest ran for half a century and produced the extraordinary scene of Emperor Henry IV waiting in the snow outside Canossa. What followed was a working papal monarchy: canon law codified, legates everywhere, a run of great councils at the Lateran, and under Innocent III, who reigned from 1198 to 1216, a papacy that arbitrated between kings, authorized the new friars, called crusades, and in 1215 legislated at the Fourth Lateran Council for the whole Latin church — from the definition of the eucharist to the requirement that every Christian confess once a year.
movements.teaser: Rome and all of Latin Christendom, c. 1049 to 1300 — the church every Western order and movement of the age lived inside, remade from a local bishopric into a monarchy that could summon kings.
voices: Leo IX — the reforming pope whose circle set the whole movement going
Humbert of Silva Candida — the cardinal who drafted the reform's sharpest arguments and delivered the excommunication at Constantinople in 1054
Gregory VII — pope of the Dictatus Papae and of the confrontation with Henry IV
Gratian — the canonist whose Decretum, compiled around 1140, gave the Western church a usable body of law
Innocent III — under whom the papal monarchy reached its widest reach, and who summoned the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215
movements.legacy: It never stopped: this is the Roman Catholic Church, and the institutional shape worked out here — a legally defined papal primacy, a professional canon law, a college of cardinals electing the pope, general councils legislating for the whole church — is substantially the shape it still has. Fourth Lateran's requirements of annual confession and Easter communion formed lay Catholic practice for the next seven centuries. So did darker parts of the same programme: the same council imposed distinguishing dress on Jews and Muslims living in Christian territory, and the machinery of inquisition took its permanent form in these decades. The claims made here are also the ones the Reformation would eventually be a protest against. The same institution continued into the next era through Avignon and the Fifth Lateran Council.

experienceToday.text: Rome, Italy — the Archbasilica of St John Lateran, the pope's own cathedral and the setting of the great Lateran councils of 1123, 1139, 1179 and 1215

movements.name: Kievan Rus' Christianity, 1054-1240
movements.informalName: The Church of Kyiv and the Caves
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich with tier care: the Kyiv Caves Paterik and Primary Chronicle are later compilations reaching back into this window; Theodosius's tradition
movements.relationsSummary: III.8's continuation: the Kyiv Caves Monastery world, native metropolitans; ends at the Mongol sack of Kyiv (1240); the 1240-1340 yoke gap to V.8 Muscovy stays disclosed, routed to A1.E6
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: III.8 ends 1054 with no receiver, and the next Rus' entry starts 1340 - this closes most of the Kyiv-to-Moscow jump the census's own notes complain about. Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 1054 (Yaroslav's death — III.8's gated end) to 1240 (Mongol sack of Kyiv); the 1240-1340 yoke gap to V.8 stays disclosed, routed to A1.E6 (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: In the two centuries after Yaroslav the Wise died in 1054, the Christianity that had arrived in Rus' only two generations earlier put down roots of its own. Its centre was the Caves Monastery at Kyiv, begun by a hermit named Anthony in a hillside cave above the Dnieper and turned into a community by Theodosius, its third abbot, who gave it a Byzantine rule and a distinctive emphasis on humility, manual work and care for the poor. Out of that monastery came bishops, chronicles, and a book of stories about its own monks. The church was formally a metropolitanate of Constantinople, usually headed by a Greek, but native metropolitans appeared and a native literature and a native calendar of saints grew up around the princely dynasty. It ended abruptly: the Mongols sacked Kyiv in 1240.
movements.teaser: Kyiv, Novgorod and Vladimir-Suzdal, 1054 to 1240 — a young church growing its own saints, chronicles and monasteries out of a hillside cave, until the Mongols ended it in a single season.
voices: Anthony of the Caves — the hermit who dug the first cave in the hillside above the Dnieper
Theodosius of the Caves — the abbot who made it a community, and whose insistence on humility and manual work set the tone of Rus' monasticism
Hilarion of Kyiv — the first native-born metropolitan and author of the Sermon on Law and Grace, the earliest surviving work of Rus' theology
Nestor — the monk traditionally credited with much of the Primary Chronicle and with early lives of the Rus' saints
Boris and Gleb — the murdered princes who became the first saints canonized in Rus', venerated for refusing to fight back
movements.legacy: The Caves Monastery survived the sack and is still there — the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, with its underground galleries of relics — one of the most important monastic sites in the Orthodox world and, in the twenty-first century, contested ground between rival Ukrainian church jurisdictions. The literature this church produced, the Primary Chronicle above all, is the foundation document of East Slavic history, and the cult of Boris and Gleb, princes venerated precisely for not fighting back, became a distinctive strand in Slavic sanctity. Who inherits Kyiv's legacy — Kyiv, Moscow, or both — is a question with live political weight to this day, and the century of Mongol rule that followed 1240 leaves a real gap in the record between this church and the Muscovy that later claimed it.

experienceToday.text: Kyiv, Ukraine — the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra, the Monastery of the Caves, begun in the eleventh century above the Dnieper

movements.name: Armenian Christianity in Cilicia
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate with a first-rank interior voice: Nerses Shnorhali's corpus (ecumenical letters to Manuel I, prayers, laments); Nerses of Lambron; catholicosate records at Hromkla
movements.floorNote: No question — this church holds the ancient miaphysite confession, the same as the Armenian, Syriac and Coptic churches elsewhere on this map.
movements.relationsSummary: The Armenian church in exile becomes a kingdom's church: catholicosate at Hromkla (1151), Shnorhali's ecumenical correspondence, Levon I crowned 1198; continues the spine from III.16 (1045-1080 gap disclosed); the kingdom itself falls 1375 - era-6 receiver flagged
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: the Armenian spine's next segment - III.16 ends 1045 and the next Armenian entry is IX.27 (1915). Shnorhali is the era's best Armenian inside source. Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1080 (Rubenid consolidation; catholicosate at Hromkla 1151) to 1300 (era end; the kingdom falls 1375 — era-6 receiver flagged) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: After the Seljuk conquest of the Armenian homeland, Armenians resettled in Cilicia on the Mediterranean coast, where a principality grew into a kingdom — Levon I was crowned in 1198 — and the Armenian church went with them. In 1151 the catholicos moved his seat to Hromkla, a fortress above the Euphrates, and there Nerses Shnorhali, 'the Gracious', wrote the finest Armenian religious poetry of the age and conducted a long and remarkably generous correspondence with the Byzantine emperor Manuel I about reuniting the Armenian and Greek churches. The reunion never happened. The Cilician church spent the following century negotiating instead with the Latin crusader states next door — a closeness that some Armenians welcomed and others resented deeply, and that shaped the church's arguments with itself for generations.
movements.teaser: Cilicia, on the Mediterranean coast, c. 1080 to 1300 — an Armenian church in exile that became a kingdom's church, whose greatest poet spent his life writing letters trying to end a seven-hundred-year division.
voices: Nerses Shnorhali — catholicos, poet and hymn-writer, whose letters to Emperor Manuel I are the era's most serious attempt at reunion between the Armenian and Byzantine churches
Nerses of Lambron — archbishop of Tarsus, who pushed the same conciliatory line further and was attacked at home for it
Levon I — crowned king of Armenian Cilicia in 1198, who bound the kingdom closely to the Latin West
Toros Roslin — the illuminator working at Hromkla whose manuscripts are regarded as the summit of Armenian book art
movements.legacy: The Armenian Apostolic Church continues, and this period is a load-bearing part of it: the catholicosate established here still exists as the Catholicosate of Cilicia, now seated at Antelias in Lebanon, one of the two catholicosates of the Armenian church. Shnorhali's hymns and prayers are still sung and prayed, and his long penitential prayer cycle remains one of the most used devotional texts in Armenian. The manuscript illumination produced in Cilicia in these years, Roslin's above all, is among the treasures of medieval art.

experienceToday.text: Gaziantep province, Turkey — Rumkale, the Euphrates fortress the Armenians knew as Hromkla and used as their catholicosate, now reached by boat from Halfeti

movements.name: The Syriac Renaissance
movements.informalName: The Age of Michael and Bar Hebraeus
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich - the strongest eastern attestation of the era: Michael the Syrian's chronicle (the greatest in Syriac), Dionysius bar Salibi's commentaries, Bar Hebraeus's polymath corpus
movements.floorNote: No question — this church holds the ancient miaphysite confession, the same as the Armenian, Syriac and Coptic churches elsewhere on this map.
movements.relationsSummary: The West Syriac church's intellectual summit under Islam and the Crusader interlude; receiver of III.17; the tradition's later medieval decline belongs to era 6
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: III.17 ends 1054 and the next Syriac Orthodox entry is IX.19 (1915). First-rank inside sources across the whole window. Tier 1-2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 1054 to 1300 (era window; Michael the Syrian 1166-1199 and Bar Hebraeus d. 1286 inside) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: The Syriac Orthodox Church lived under Muslim rule, and for a while alongside the crusader states, in the country between the Euphrates and the Tigris — and in exactly this period it produced its best writing in four hundred years. Dionysius bar Salibi commented on the whole Bible and on the liturgy. Michael the Syrian, patriarch from 1166, compiled a world chronicle that remains one of the most valuable historical sources for the medieval Middle East, not least because he quotes at length from earlier writers whose books are otherwise lost. And Gregory Bar Hebraeus, who died in 1286, wrote across nearly everything — history, theology, canon law, grammar, astronomy, medicine, and a collection of jokes — in both Syriac and Arabic, and did it while serving as his church's chief bishop for the eastern provinces under Mongol rule.
movements.teaser: The Jazira and Melitene, 1054 to 1300 — a church living inside other people's empires that answered by writing everything down: a world chronicle, commentaries on the whole Bible, and one polymath who covered nearly every subject there was.
voices: Dionysius bar Salibi — bishop of Amid, who commented on the entire Bible and on the liturgy
Michael the Syrian — patriarch from 1166, whose chronicle preserves whole earlier histories that would otherwise have vanished
Bar Hebraeus — maphrian of the East, historian, theologian, grammarian, astronomer and physician, who wrote in Syriac and Arabic and whose learning was admired well beyond his own church
movements.legacy: The Syriac Orthodox Church continues today, with its patriarchate now in Damascus and a large diaspora. The books written here never went out of use: Michael's chronicle and Bar Hebraeus's histories are still primary sources for anyone working on the medieval Middle East, and Bar Hebraeus's canonical and grammatical works stayed standard in the Syriac churches for centuries. This period is generally reckoned the last great flowering of Syriac letters before the long contraction that followed, which is why later Syriac writers kept looking back to it.

experienceToday.text: Mount Alfaf, near Mosul, Iraq — the Syriac Orthodox monastery of Mor Mattai, long associated with Bar Hebraeus and still maintained by the church

movements.name: The Church of the East under the Mongols
movements.informalName: The Church of Bar Sauma and Yahballaha
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate with a genuine inside travel text: the History of Rabban Bar Sauma and Yahballaha III; Kerait conversion tradition; Prester John material rides inside as labeled legend
movements.floorNote: No question — this church holds the same faith as the wider Church of the East.
movements.relationsSummary: The Nestorian church resurfaces at the Mongol court: Bar Sauma's embassy to Europe (1287), his pupil elected catholicos Yahballaha III (1281-1317); ends at Yahballaha's death (1317, one boundary crossing); the III.1 succession would span a 375-year gap - disclosed, A4's call
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: no Church of the East entry exists after III.1's 845 in any era - the spine's missing revival before the 14th-century catastrophe (era 6's story). Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1220 (the Mongol rise carries the church back into documented view) to 1317 (Yahballaha III's death; one boundary crossing — the 1300+note branch was shown and declined) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: The Church of the East had spread far into Central Asia centuries earlier, and when the Mongols swept west a good many of the peoples they absorbed — the Kerait and the Öngüd among them — were already Christian in this tradition, as were several of the great khans' wives and mothers. For a few decades the church that Latin Europe called Nestorian had extraordinary access: tolerated and sometimes favoured at the Mongol court, and in 1281 a monk who had travelled the whole width of Asia from China was elected its catholicos as Yahballaha III. His teacher, Rabban Bar Sauma, had set out with him on pilgrimage toward Jerusalem and ended up instead as the Ilkhan's ambassador to the West, reaching Rome and the courts of France and England and writing the journey down — one of the very few medieval descriptions of Europe by a traveller from Asia. Yahballaha died in 1317, and the favour did not survive him.
movements.teaser: Central Asia, Persia and China, c. 1220 to 1317 — the church Europe called Nestorian, briefly favoured at the Mongol court, whose head had walked there from China and whose ambassador reached Rome and Paris.
voices: Yahballaha III — catholicos from 1281 to 1317, a monk from the far east of the Mongol world elected to head a church whose politics were not his own
Rabban Bar Sauma — his teacher and travelling companion, sent west as the Ilkhan's envoy in 1287, whose account of Rome and the Frankish courts survives
Sorghaghtani Beki and Doquz Khatun — Christian women of the Mongol ruling house whose position gave the church much of its access at court
movements.legacy: The Church of the East still exists, but this was its last period of long reach. The Mongol elite in Persia turned to Islam within a generation of Yahballaha's death, and the fourteenth century brought the catastrophe — Timur's campaigns above all — that reduced a church once stretching from Cyprus to China to a mountain remnant in Hakkari. Its traces are now mostly archaeological: Syriac gravestones scattered across Central Asia, Christian tomb carvings in the Chinese port cities. The account of Bar Sauma's embassy remains the single most remarkable thing this period produced.

movements.name: The Carmelites
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the Rule of Albert (1206-1214, verified text); thin interior voice this era beyond the Rule - the tradition's great voices (Teresa, John of the Cross) lie downstream in era 7
movements.relationsSummary: The missing fourth mendicant order: hermits on Carmel under Albert's formula vitae, approved as Rule 1247, migration west 1230s-40s; a spine decision here ripples to era 7's Carmelite reform
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: no Carmelite entry exists in ANY era despite the era-7 reform tradition downstream. Tier 2-3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1206 (Albert's formula vitae, 1206-1214 — survey's c. 1200 sharpened on the Rule's own dating) to 1300 (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: Some time between 1206 and 1214 a group of Latin hermits living in a wadi on Mount Carmel above the bay from crusader Acre asked Albert, the patriarch of Jerusalem — who kept his seat at Acre — for a written way of life. What he gave them was short and severe: separate cells, silence, work, daily Mass, and constant meditation on the law of the Lord. As the crusader states contracted the hermits moved west, into England, France and Italy, where a hermit's rule made little sense in a town — so the life was adapted into a mendicant order alongside the Franciscans and Dominicans, and Innocent IV approved the revised Rule in 1247. The order kept the mountain in its name and in its self-understanding, and traced its origins, in its own later retellings, all the way back to the prophet Elijah.
movements.teaser: Mount Carmel and then the towns of Europe, c. 1206 to 1300 — hermits on a Holy Land mountain who lost the mountain, moved to Europe, and had to work out what a hermit is for in a city.
voices: Albert of Jerusalem — the patriarch who wrote the hermits their short rule between 1206 and 1214
Innocent IV — the pope who approved the adapted Rule in 1247, turning the hermits into a mendicant order
The first Carmelites are anonymous — the community that asked Albert for a rule left no names, and the order's own accounts of its earliest years were written much later
movements.legacy: The Carmelites are still here, and their greatest period was still ahead of them: the sixteenth-century Spanish reform that produced Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross grew directly out of this rule, and their writings became the standard vocabulary of Western contemplative prayer. The brown scapular, one of the most widespread Catholic devotional objects, comes from the order — though the story of its being handed to Simon Stock in a vision is a later legend rather than documented history. Albert's Rule itself remains the order's foundation text, one of the shortest and most durable religious rules in the Western church.

experienceToday.text: Haifa, Israel — the Stella Maris monastery on Mount Carmel, the Carmelites' house on the mountain the order is named for

movements.name: Balkan Bogomilism, 1054-1300
movements.statusWord: Floor divergence carried forward from III.13 (register; one verified witness, two [S]; own voice unrecovered)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run as the receiver of III.13's register - the movement demonstrably continues. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Hostile-only, as III.13: Anna Komnene on Basil the physician's burning (c. 1100-1118), Zigabenos's commissioned Panoplia chapter, the Synod of Tarnovo's anathemas (1211, Book of Boril)
movements.floorNote: Everything known about them comes from people writing against them, and by those accounts they held that the visible, material world was not the good God's making — a position outside the common Christian creed. Their own voice has not survived. The Bosnian Church, which older accounts often folded into this movement, is treated separately here; most current scholarship no longer regards the two as the same thing.
movements.relationsSummary: III.13's continuation: Basil burned in the Hippodrome under Alexios I, Zigabenos written against them, Tarnovo 1211 anathematizes them; claimed parent of the Cathars (IV.12) - claim, not established descent
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: III.13 ends 1054 with beyondFloor:true and no receiver while the movement runs demonstrably on. A register draft in the Era 4 pattern - the register carries forward, not a floor re-litigation. End 1300 on the continues-cap convention (the survey's primary c. 1230 corresponds to no event - last source anchor is Tarnovo 1211; both branches disclosed at the gate). Register, not tiered; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 1054 to 1300 (continues-cap convention; the survey's c. 1230 branch was shown and declined — no event; last anchor Tarnovo 1211) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: The Bogomils began in tenth-century Bulgaria and were still there, and in Byzantine territory, throughout this period. What their opponents describe is a movement with no church buildings, no clergy in the ordinary sense, no sacraments as the church understood them, and a teaching that the material world and the institutions of the visible church alike belonged to an evil power. Around the turn of the twelfth century the emperor Alexios I had a Bogomil teacher called Basil brought to Constantinople, drew out his beliefs by pretending to be a convert, and had him burned in the Hippodrome; the emperor's daughter Anna Komnene tells the story, and Alexios commissioned the theologian Euthymios Zigabenos to write the movement up for refutation. In 1211 a synod at Tarnovo anathematized them again. Not one line survives that a Bogomil wrote about themselves.
movements.teaser: Bulgaria, Thrace and Macedonia, 1054 to 1300 — a movement that rejected the visible church entirely, known to us only in the words of the emperors, bishops and synods that hunted it.
voices: Basil the physician — a Bogomil teacher tricked into explaining his beliefs by the emperor Alexios I and burned in the Hippodrome at Constantinople
Euthymios Zigabenos — the theologian commissioned to write against them, whose chapter is the fullest surviving description of their teaching
Anna Komnene — the imperial historian who recorded Basil's interrogation and death
No Bogomil voice survives — every name we have was recorded by an enemy, and nothing written by the movement itself has ever been recovered
movements.legacy: Nothing continued, and almost nothing remains — no buildings, no books, no descendants. Their long afterlife is instead an argument: medieval writers, and many modern ones, have treated the Bogomils as the source of the Western dualist movements, the Cathars especially, and the English word 'bugger' descends by way of 'Bulgar' from that association. Whether any actual line of transmission ran from the Balkans to Languedoc is disputed and probably unprovable. The Bosnian Church, often bundled in with them in older accounts, is now generally handled by scholars as a separate question.

movements.name: The Latin Church of Outremer
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 5 Step 0)
