movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally (patriarchate records, canons of the Holy Sepulchre, pilgrim liturgy); interior devotional voice thinner than the military orders' - disclosed
movements.relationsSummary: A transplanted Latin church with its own hierarchy: patriarchates of Jerusalem (1099, Greek patriarch expelled - the Schism lived on the ground) and Antioch; moves to Acre 1187, falls with it 1291
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: a real church, not just the military orders' backdrop; ends at Acre. Tier 3 signal (interior voice thin); awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 1099 (Latin patriarchate of Jerusalem erected) to 1291 (fall of Acre) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: When the First Crusade took Jerusalem in 1099 the conquerors did not simply add a diocese; they built a whole Latin church on top of an existing Christian landscape, erecting a Latin patriarchate of Jerusalem and expelling the Greek patriarch, and then another at Antioch. For nearly two centuries this transplanted hierarchy ran parishes, cathedrals and an enormous pilgrim traffic to the holy places, with the canons of the Holy Sepulchre at its centre and a distinctive liturgy shaped by processions to the sites themselves. It governed a population that was mostly not Latin — Greek, Syriac, Armenian, Muslim — and its dealings with those communities ranged from workable accommodation to plain dispossession. When Jerusalem was lost in 1187 the patriarchate moved to Acre, and when Acre fell in 1291 the church of Outremer ended with it.
movements.teaser: Jerusalem, Antioch, Acre and Cyprus, 1099 to 1291 — a whole Latin church transplanted onto ground that already had four of its own, which lasted exactly as long as the states that carried it.
voices: Daimbert of Pisa — an early Latin patriarch of Jerusalem, whose quarrels with the kingdom's rulers set the pattern of friction between church and crown
William of Tyre — archbishop, chancellor of the kingdom, and the great historian of Outremer, whose chronicle is the indispensable source for it
Jacques de Vitry — bishop of Acre, preacher and letter-writer, who described the mixed society he found there in unusual detail
The Greek patriarchs of Jerusalem in exile — displaced in 1099 and continuing their line from Constantinople, a standing reminder that this church was built by removing another
movements.legacy: It left no continuing institution in the East: when Acre fell, the Latin patriarchate of Jerusalem became a title without a diocese and stayed that way for more than five centuries, until it was restored as a working see in 1847. What survived instead is stone and story. The church of the Holy Sepulchre, largely rebuilt in this period, is substantially the building pilgrims enter today, and crusader castles and churches from Acre to Cyprus are among the best-preserved medieval buildings in the region. William of Tyre's history became the standard Western account of the crusades for centuries. The long memory of Outremer among Eastern Christians, who experienced it as occupation rather than liberation, is part of the legacy too.

experienceToday.text: Akko (Acre), Israel — the old city, where the Hospitallers' vaulted halls and much of the crusader street plan survive beneath and beside the later Ottoman town

movements.name: Coptic Christianity, Fatimid to Mamluk
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred pending source verification (Era 5 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run with its attestation carried [S] - a named source-base verification is required before any build. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: [S] - carried from standard references, not verified this session: the 13th-century Copto-Arabic golden age (the awlad al-Assal's canon-law and theological compendia, patriarch Cyril III ibn Laqlaq); verification follow-up named
movements.floorNote: No question — this church holds the ancient miaphysite confession, the same as the Armenian, Syriac and Ethiopian churches elsewhere on this map.
movements.relationsSummary: The census's largest spine hole closed: III.3 ends 1013 and the next Coptic entry is VIII.13 (1854); the 1013-1054 remainder belongs to era 4's record (gap disclosed)
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: an ~840-year Coptic silence in the census against a real 13th-century literary golden age. Tier 3 signal, verification-conditioned; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1054 to 1300 — attestation [S]; window and anchors require the named source-base verification before any build (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: By this period Egypt's Christians had lived under Muslim rule for four centuries, and the shape of their life was set by that: a poll tax, stretches of tolerance under the Fatimids alternating with sharp episodes of persecution, and a slow shift out of Coptic and into Arabic as the everyday language. What they did with Arabic is the surprise. In the thirteenth century a single Cairo family, the sons of al-Assal, produced a body of work — canon law, theology, biblical scholarship, philosophy, and Coptic grammars and dictionaries written in Arabic to keep the old language from being lost entirely — that amounted to a renaissance of Coptic learning in a new tongue. Their patriarch for part of that stretch, Cyril III ibn Laqlaq, was a learned and combative man who spent his reign gathering the church's authority into his own hands.
movements.teaser: Egypt, c. 1054 to 1300 — a church losing its own language and answering by writing its whole inheritance down again in Arabic, in what turned out to be its greatest literary century.
voices: The awlad al-Assal — four brothers of one Cairo family, al-Safi, al-Mu'taman, al-As'ad and al-Amjad, whose canon law, theology, biblical scholarship and Coptic grammars are the heart of this period's achievement
Cyril III ibn Laqlaq — patriarch from 1235 to 1243, a cultivated and contentious man who reorganized the church's government around himself
movements.legacy: The Coptic Orthodox Church is very much alive — the largest Christian community in the Middle East — and runs unbroken through this period. The work done here lasted: the al-Assal brothers' canonical collections stayed authoritative in the Coptic church for centuries and were carried south into Ethiopia, where the Fetha Nagast, the law book of the Ethiopian state into the twentieth century, derives from al-Safi's canons. Their grammars and dictionaries are much of the reason the Coptic language is recoverable at all today. The Hanging Church in Old Cairo, which served as the patriarch's seat for most of this period, is still standing and still in use.

experienceToday.text: Old Cairo, Egypt — the Hanging Church of St Mary, built over a Roman gatehouse and the residence of the Coptic patriarchs through most of this period

movements.name: The Humiliati
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 5 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 5 Step 0 run. Added at the Era 5 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Moderate, verified: condemned in Ad abolendam (1184), reconciled by Innocent III (1201) as three orders; rule and order documents survive
movements.relationsSummary: Lay penitential wool-workers condemned alongside the Waldensians and then re-absorbed - the mirror-image of IV.8: same 1184 condemnation, opposite outcome
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: the era's clearest case of dissent reconciled rather than crushed - the counter-story the atlas needs beside the Waldensian thread. Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1170 to 1300 (Ad abolendam 1184 and the 1201 reconciliation inside the window) (Era 5 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.longDescription: In twelfth-century Lombardy, groups of lay wool-workers and weavers began living out a simple, demanding vision of penitence — plain dress, manual labor, and a rejection of the oath-taking and violence expected of feudal society — and called themselves the Humiliati, 'the humbled ones.' In 1184 they were condemned alongside the Waldensians for preaching without official permission, but where the Waldensians' story became one of lasting separation, theirs took the opposite turn: Pope Innocent III reconciled them in 1201, organizing them into three recognized orders — two religious, one for married lay people who stayed in ordinary working life under a shared rule. For roughly two centuries afterward they remained a real presence in northern Italian towns, their rule and community records still surviving, until the movement was formally suppressed by papal bull in 1571.
movements.teaser: Lombardy, c. 1170 to 1300 — lay wool-workers who traded feudal violence and oath-taking for penitence and plain labor, condemned alongside the Waldensians and then, unlike them, welcomed back.

sources.work: Catholic Encyclopedia: Humiliati
sources.note: Overview of origins, rule, papal reconciliation, and 1571 suppression.

voices: No individual founder is named in the record — the Humiliati were fundamentally a lay collective, organized by trade and locality rather than around a founding figure
movements.legacy: No clear record survives of lasting influence beyond their own two centuries — when the order was suppressed by papal bull in 1571, its distinct identity ended with it.

movements.name: The English Mystics and Devout
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) — rich, first-person and vernacular, carrying two women's voices, with the census's own judgment that Margery Kempe's Book may be the atlas's best ordinary-believer document left standing. Its end was moved to c. 1440, when the corpus's last major document was completed, replacing a 1450 that matched nothing.
movements.sourcing: RICH, first-person, vernacular, two women's voices - Julian's Showings; Margery Kempe's Book may be the atlas's best ordinary-believer document
movements.relationsSummary: Carthusians copied and preserved these texts (documented transmission)
movements.why: Two women writing in English about God in the first person, at a point where almost nobody else in the atlas is doing either — Julian of Norwich writing, Margery Kempe dictating, since she could not write. What makes this world matter is less that it produced theology than that it produced testimony: an unpolished, often uncomfortable, unmistakably lived account of religion from people holding no office of any kind. That the texts survive at all is owed to Carthusian copyists, which is documented transmission rather than a guess.
movements.dateRationale: End c. 1440 (Margery Kempe's Book completed c. 1436-38 [S] - the corpus's last major document; the old 1450 matched nothing; keep-1450-as-reception alt was shown) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Julian of Norwich, Showings (trans. Colledge & Walsh, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1978; Short and Long Texts)
sources.note: Verified. The census's first named woman's voice - a lifetime's first-person theological revision in the vernacular. Modern critical alternative: Watson & Jenkins, The Writings of Julian of Norwich (2006) [S] from knowledge.

sources.work: The Book of Margery Kempe (trans. Barry Windeatt, Penguin Classics, 1985)
sources.note: Verified. The census's proposed best ordinary-believer document: an illiterate townswoman's dictated life - pilgrimage, weeping, heresy examinations survived. Mediation flag (not hostile): dictated to two scribes; the priest-scribe's shaping hand is part of the text.

sources.work: The teaching corpus: Richard Rolle, The Fire of Love; Walter Hilton, The Scale of Perfection; The Cloud of Unknowing
sources.note: The movement's formation texts, written for anchoresses, recluses, and devout laity. [S] edition details (Penguin Wolters; Hilton CWS trans. Clark & Dorward 1991) from knowledge.

sources.work: The Carthusian transmission layer: the unique Kempe MS (BL Add. 61823, Mount Grace annotations), the Amherst MS of Julian's Short Text, The Chastising of God's Children; plus Arundel's Constitutions (1409) as counter-pressure
sources.note: The census relations line (Carthusians copied and preserved these texts) as physical evidence, with the vernacular-theology censorship context. [S] manuscript/edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: Bernard McGinn, The Varieties of Vernacular Mysticism 1350-1550 (Presence of God vol. 5, 2012)
sources.note: [S] not individually verified this session. Current standard frame; Nicholas Watson's censorship scholarship named for the Arundel context.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 19 'Mysticism and transcendence' (Hollywood)
sources.note: Chapter verified in TOC (Era-5 recovery). [S] in-chapter coverage of the English vernacular mystics inferred, not page-verified.

movements.teaser: England, c. 1330 to 1440 — hermits, anchoresses and a weeping townswoman who wrote about God in English, in the first person, when almost nobody else did.
movements.longDescription: Across a single century a scattering of English men and women began writing about the inner life of prayer in their own language rather than in Latin — Richard Rolle the Yorkshire hermit with his Fire of Love, Walter Hilton with the Scale of Perfection, and the anonymous author of The Cloud of Unknowing, all writing for recluses and devout lay people rather than for scholars. Two of the voices are women's. Julian of Norwich, an anchoress enclosed in a cell beside a Norwich parish church, spent decades revising an account of sixteen revelations she had received during a near-fatal illness, arriving at the line she is still known for: that all shall be well. Margery Kempe, a brewer's wife and mother of fourteen from Bishop's Lynn who could not write, dictated to scribes a book about her pilgrimages, her uncontrollable public weeping and the heresy examinations she survived — the closest thing the period leaves us to an ordinary believer's own life story. That any of it reaches us at all is largely owed to Carthusian monks, who copied the texts and kept them safe.
voices: Richard Rolle — Yorkshire hermit whose Fire of Love helped make devotional writing in English popular
Walter Hilton — Augustinian canon whose Scale of Perfection became the era's standard guide to the interior life
The anonymous author of The Cloud of Unknowing — never identified, writing for a single young disciple about praying beyond thought
Julian of Norwich — anchoress of Norwich, the first woman known to have written a book in English
Margery Kempe — a Lynn townswoman who could not write and dictated her life instead, producing what is often called the first autobiography in English
movements.legacy: The writings outlived their authors by way of a long silence. Margery Kempe's Book was known only from a few short printed extracts until the single surviving manuscript was identified in a private family library in 1934, and Julian's Revelations circulated quietly among Carthusians and English exiles for centuries before reaching a wide readership in the twentieth. Both are now among the most read of all medieval English religious books; Julian is commemorated each May in the Church of England's calendar, and her cell — destroyed centuries ago, its foundations uncovered after wartime bombing and rebuilt — is again a place people travel to pray in.

experienceToday.text: St Julian's Church, Norwich — the rebuilt cell on the site of Julian's anchorhold, open daily

movements.name: Rhineland Mysticism & the Friends of God
movements.informalName: The Rhineland Mystics and the Friends of God
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a rich base of sermons and sister-books, with one tier-care nuance carried: the sermons survive 'as delivered' only through listeners' transcripts, and the sister-books are collective women's memory rather than individual witness. Eckhart's condemnation stayed where its floorNote puts it — an intra-Catholic language contest, carried rather than resolved.
movements.sourcing: Rich: sermons as delivered to convents; sister-books as collective women's memory
movements.floorNote: Eckhart was condemned over how he said things, not over what the Creed says — and the argument about him has never really been settled.
movements.relationsSummary: Dominican line; feeds Devotio Moderna and (via Theologia Deutsch) Luther
movements.why: The point at which the Dominican line turns into something the whole later West drinks from — Devotio Moderna downstream, and by way of the Theologia Deutsch, Luther himself. Its evidence is unusual in kind: sermons preserved because nuns wrote down what they heard, and sister-books recording a convent's memory of itself rather than any one person's. Eckhart's condemnation belongs inside the story and is carried there, as a contest about language rather than a question about the Creed.

sources.work: Meister Eckhart, The Essential Sermons, Commentaries, Treatises and Defense (trans. Colledge & McGinn, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1981)
sources.note: Verified. Latin and German works with his trial Defense. Eckhart's trial problem carried openly: In agro dominico (1329) condemned 28 out-of-context propositions after his death - a HOSTILE/institutional filter on his memory shaping all later transmission. [S] whether the bull's full text is in this volume not page-verified.

sources.work: Johannes Tauler, Sermons (trans. Shrady, CWS, 1985) and Henry Suso, The Exemplar (trans. Tobin, CWS, 1989)
sources.note: The census's 'sermons as delivered to convents' leg: Tauler preaching to Dominican nuns; Suso's Life of the Servant co-produced with Elsbeth Stagel - a man's interior life reaching us through a woman's editorial hand. Tier nuance: 'as delivered' rests on listeners' transcripts and convent copies. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: The Dominican convent Sister-Books (Schwesternbuecher: Toess, Unterlinden, Engelthal, St Katharinental and kin); study-with-translations: Gertrude Jaron Lewis, By Women, for Women, about Women (PIMS, 1996)
sources.note: The census's 'collective women's memory' leg: nuns writing their own communities' graces, austerities, and deaths. [S] English access piecemeal - access flag.

sources.work: Theologia Deutsch (trans. Bengt Hoffman, The Theologia Germanica of Martin Luther, CWS, 1980)
sources.note: Verified. The anonymous Frankfurt priest's treatise from the Friends of God milieu. Transmission flag: the standard English translates Luther's 1518 edition - the census's feeds-Luther relations line is built into the textual access itself. Rulman Merswin's Friends-of-God literature behind it [S].

sources.work: Bernard McGinn, The Harvest of Mysticism in Medieval Germany (Presence of God vol. 4, 2005)
sources.note: [S] not individually verified this session. Current standard on exactly this ecosystem, Eckhart through the Sister-Books.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 19 'Mysticism and transcendence' (Hollywood)
sources.note: Chapter verified in TOC (Era-5 recovery); direct fit.

movements.teaser: The Rhineland and Switzerland, c. 1300 to 1400 — Dominican preachers who tried to say in German what theology had only ever said in Latin, and the nuns who wrote it down.
movements.longDescription: Along the Rhine a generation of Dominican preachers — Meister Eckhart, Johannes Tauler, Henry Suso — began preaching in German to convents of nuns and to devout lay people, and in doing so had to invent a vocabulary for the inner life that the language did not yet have. Eckhart pushed furthest, speaking of the ground of the soul and of a birth of God within it in terms that got him put on trial for heresy; he died before the case closed, and in 1329 a papal bull condemned twenty-eight propositions drawn from his work, which is how his memory reached everyone who came after. Around Strasbourg and Basel a mixed circle of clergy and laypeople who called themselves Gottesfreunde, the Friends of God, carried the same piety outside the cloister, and out of that milieu came the anonymous Theologia Deutsch. Much of what survives survives because women preserved it: nuns took sermons down as they were delivered, convents compiled sister-books recording their own communities' lives, and Elsbeth Stagel worked with Suso on the book of his own life.
voices: Meister Eckhart — Dominican preacher and master of theology at Paris, tried for heresy at the end of his life and condemned after his death
Johannes Tauler — Eckhart's most widely read successor, preaching to nuns and townspeople at Strasbourg
Henry Suso — wrote the Life of the Servant, an unusually personal spiritual autobiography, together with his correspondent Elsbeth Stagel
Elsbeth Stagel — Dominican nun of Töss, Suso's collaborator, and the writer credited with her convent's sister-book
Rulman Merswin — a Strasbourg banker who gave up his business for the Friends of God and endowed their house on the Green Isle
movements.legacy: Its influence ran far past its own century. The Devotio Moderna in the Low Countries grew in its wake, and the Theologia Deutsch reached Martin Luther, who printed it twice — a partial text in 1516 and a fuller one in 1518 — and wrote that apart from the Bible and Augustine no book had taught him more about God and about himself. Tauler's sermons went on being read by Catholics and Protestants alike for centuries. Eckhart, condemned in his own lifetime, was rediscovered in the nineteenth century and has been read ever since by philosophers, theologians and religious writers well outside the church that condemned him.

movements.name: Devotio Moderna / Brethren of the Common Life
movements.informalName: The Brethren of the Common Life
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a rich base — customaries, the brothers' and sisters' lives, rapiaria and the Imitation — and named a rare both-directions ancestor, feeding Luther's schooling and Jesuit pedagogy alike. Its end was moved to 1517 under the continues-cap convention, replacing a round-number 1500, since its houses ran into the sixteenth century and dissolved under the Reformation.
movements.sourcing: RICH: customaries, brothers' and sisters' lives, rapiaria, the Imitation of Christ
movements.relationsSummary: Parent-influence on both Luther's schooling and Jesuit pedagogy - a rare both-directions ancestor
movements.why: A rare both-directions ancestor — the same movement that schooled Luther also shaped Jesuit pedagogy, so both sides of the sixteenth century's great rupture were formed in part by it. Its own project was smaller and stranger than that inheritance suggests: devout people, many of them lay, living in common without vows and keeping notebooks of what they read. One of those habits produced the Imitation of Christ, which travelled far beyond the houses that made it.
movements.dateRationale: End 1517 (continues-cap: the houses run into the 16th c. and dissolve under the Reformation; the old 1500 was a round non-event; keep-1500+note alt was shown) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Devotio Moderna: Basic Writings (ed./trans. John Van Engen, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1988)
sources.note: Verified. Geert Grote's own writings (incl. Resolutions and Intentions - a layman's self-rule), lives of the Brothers and Sisters, customary material, from Latin and Middle Dutch - founder's voice and communal texture in one volume.

sources.work: Thomas a Kempis, The Imitation of Christ (c. 1418-27)
sources.note: The census's named text and the movement's mass-formation engine - the era's most copied book after the Bible; grown out of the rapiarium practice. [S] standard English edition choice left open - countless editions.

sources.work: The sisters' houses literature: vitae of the Sisters of the Common Life at Deventer (Master Geert's House) and Diepenveen
sources.note: Collective women's memory in the movement's own genre; partly in Van Engen, fuller corpora Middle Dutch only. [S] access flag; edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: Gerard Zerbolt of Zutphen, The Spiritual Ascents, plus the rapiarium practice
sources.note: The movement's method text - interiorized, graded devotion for people in ordinary life - and its distinctive excerpt-book genre. [S] English access details from knowledge.

sources.work: John Van Engen, Sisters and Brothers of the Common Life (Penn, 2008)
sources.note: [S] not individually verified this session. Current standard, by the corpus's own translator.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 26 'Empowerment through reading, writing and example: the Devotio Moderna' (Goudriaan)
sources.note: Chapter recovered via search this session; dedicated chapter - one of the strongest reference fits in the era. Both-directions relations (Luther, Jesuits) reach past 1500 but the movement's own window closes c. 1500 - vol. 6 not needed.

movements.teaser: The Low Countries, c. 1380 to 1517 — devout townspeople who lived in common without taking vows, kept notebooks of what they read, and produced the most copied book of the Middle Ages after the Bible.
movements.longDescription: It began with Geert Grote, a wealthy and worldly Deventer scholar who gave up his career, opened his own house to a group of devout women, and started preaching repentance in the towns of the IJssel valley. After his death in 1384 his followers organized: Brothers and Sisters of the Common Life, living together and supporting themselves by copying manuscripts and other ordinary work, without vows and without leaving ordinary society, alongside a stricter branch of canons at Windesheim. What held them together was less a doctrine than a method — a plain, interior, methodical devotion, and the habit of keeping a rapiarium, a personal notebook of gathered passages to return to. One such gathering, worked up by Thomas à Kempis at a house near Zwolle, became the Imitation of Christ. The houses also took in schoolboys and shaped the Latin schools of towns like Deventer and Zwolle, which is how the movement's formation reached far more people than ever joined it.
voices: Geert Grote — Deventer deacon and preacher whose turn from a wealthy career started the movement
Florens Radewijns — Grote's successor, who gathered the scattered devout into the Brothers of the Common Life
Gerard Zerbolt of Zutphen — set out the movement's graded method of interior devotion for people living ordinary lives
Thomas à Kempis — canon at Mount St Agnes near Zwolle, credited with the Imitation of Christ

No single founding figure holds the women's side of the movement: the Sisters' houses at Deventer and Diepenveen recorded their lives collectively, in books written by and about the community rather than any one member
movements.legacy: The Imitation of Christ never stopped circulating — after the Bible it is the most widely copied and printed Christian book of the era, and it is still in print in dozens of languages. The movement's schooling shaped people who then went in opposite directions: Erasmus was educated at Deventer, Luther spent a school year at Magdeburg in a household connected with the Brethren, and the ordered, interior, personal devotion the movement taught fed into Jesuit formation a century later. The houses themselves did not survive the century they helped bring about; most dissolved during the Reformation.

movements.name: Hesychasm & the Palamite Synthesis
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — theologically rich in Palamas's Triads, the synodal tomoi and Cabasilas as a lay-facing formation voice, but narrower in communal texture than the era's Tier 1 set. The institutional side of its story was placed in the Palaiologan patriarchal entry added at the same gate, and its succession from the Athonite entry, until then carried only in prose, was regularized as an identity link.
movements.sourcing: Rich theologically; Cabasilas is a genuinely lay-facing formation voice
movements.relationsSummary: Heir of Athonite line; parent of the Philokalia line (Eras 7-8)
movements.why: The theological settlement of Eastern Christianity's central practice: what hesychasts on Athos had been doing gets defended, argued and finally received here, and everything the Philokalia later carries runs through it. Its scope is deliberately the movement and its theology — the institution that ruled on it sits in the Palaiologan patriarchal entry instead. Cabasilas is why it is not only a monastic story; he writes about the sacraments for people who are not monks.

sources.work: Gregory Palamas, The Triads (ed. Meyendorff, trans. Gendle, Classics of Western Spirituality, 1983)
sources.note: Verified. In Defense of the Holy Hesychasts (1338-41) - the synthesis's cornerstone in the movement's leading voice.

sources.work: The synodal tomoi of 1341, 1347, 1351 (and 1368), in Norman Russell, Gregory Palamas: The Hesychast Controversy and the Debate with Islam (Translated Texts for Byzantinists, Liverpool, 2020)
sources.note: Verified. The conciliar documents that made hesychasm the Orthodox norm, most first-time English. Flag: victors' records - the anti-Palamite side (Barlaam, Akindynos, Gregoras) is largely untranslated and reaches us mainly through its condemnations [S] access flag.

sources.work: The hesychast method texts: Nikephoros the Monk On Watchfulness, ps.-Symeon's method, Gregory of Sinai - as carried in the Philokalia (vol. 4, trans. Palmer, Sherrard & Ware)
sources.note: The census relations line's Philokalia lineage made concrete, with the tier flag stated: the Philokalia is a 1782 compilation - a later lineage's retrospective canon of these 14th-c. texts. [S] volume/contents details from knowledge.

sources.work: Nicholas Cabasilas, The Life in Christ (trans. deCatanzaro, SVS Press, 1974)
sources.note: Verified. The census's named lay-facing formation voice: sacramental life for people outside the monastery, by a lay theologian of hesychast Thessalonica; his Commentary on the Divine Liturgy beside it [S].

sources.work: John Meyendorff, A Study of Gregory Palamas (1959; Eng. 1964), with Norman Russell, Gregory Palamas and the Making of Palamism in the Modern Age (OUP, 2019)
sources.note: Classic frame plus current corrective on how 'Palamism' was retrospectively systematized. [S] neither individually verified this session.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, ch. 4 'The rise of hesychasm' (Krausmuller)
sources.note: Chapter verified in TOC (Era-5 recovery); this era is the chapter's home ground - direct fit.

movements.teaser: Mount Athos and Thessalonica, c. 1300 to 1400 — monks who repeated a single sentence of prayer until it prayed itself, and the archbishop who argued that what they saw was really God.
movements.longDescription: On Mount Athos monks had long practised hesychia, stillness: sitting alone, controlling the breath, and repeating the Jesus Prayer until it continued of itself — and some of them reported seeing an uncreated light. When the Calabrian scholar Barlaam ridiculed the practice, Gregory Palamas, an Athonite monk who later became archbishop of Thessalonica, answered him in the Triads: God is unknowable in his essence and yet genuinely given in his energies, so what the praying monk meets is God himself and not some created substitute. The argument ran for two decades and was settled by councils at Constantinople in 1341, 1347 and 1351, which vindicated Palamas and made the hesychast position the standard of Orthodox theology. Beside it stands a very different voice: Nicholas Cabasilas, a layman of Thessalonica, who wrote The Life in Christ to show that the same life in God was given through the sacraments to people who would never enter a monastery.
voices: Gregory Palamas — Athonite monk and archbishop of Thessalonica, who gave the practice its theological defence
Gregory of Sinai — carried the hesychast method from Athos into the Balkans
Nicholas Cabasilas — a layman of Thessalonica who wrote about the same life in God for people outside the monastery
Barlaam of Calabria — the scholar whose attack on the hesychasts forced the whole argument into the open
Philotheos Kokkinos — the bishop who wrote up the council's decree, and who later, as patriarch, had Palamas declared a saint in 1368
movements.legacy: It became, and remains, the mainstream of Orthodox theology and prayer. Palamas was declared a saint in 1368, and the second Sunday of Great Lent is still kept in his memory across the Orthodox world. The texts of the hesychast masters were gathered in 1782 into the Philokalia, which carried the practice into Russia and Romania, into the nineteenth-century monastic revival, and — through the anonymous Russian book The Way of a Pilgrim — into the hands of ordinary readers who had never seen a monastery. The Jesus Prayer is prayed today by a great many people who have never heard of the fourteenth-century controversy that defended it.

experienceToday.text: Mount Athos, Greece — the monastic peninsula where the practice took shape, a UNESCO World Heritage Site (visits are by permit and restricted to men)

movements.name: Lollardy
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on the honest mix its sourcing names — hostile trial records that nonetheless preserve ordinary artisans' and women's own stated beliefs, alongside real internal texts. The person-defined check its floorNote ordered was run at this gate and cleared: the movement outgrew Wycliffe, and the beliefs the records preserve are scripture-centred rather than Wycliffe-centred.
movements.sourcing: Hostile trial records preserving ordinary artisans' and women's stated beliefs, plus real internal texts
movements.floorNote: No creedal question: Lollards disputed the church's wealth, its authority and its sacramental teaching, not the Creed. Nor is this simply one man's following — the movement outlasted Wycliffe by well over a century, and what the trial records preserve are ordinary believers' own scripture-centred convictions rather than an Oxford theologian's system.
movements.relationsSummary: Contested influence line to the English Reformation
movements.why: Its records were made by prosecutors and are nonetheless one of the atlas's better windows onto what ordinary English artisans and women actually believed — because to convict someone you first have to write down what they said. That inversion is rare enough to be worth an entry on its own. Whether the line from Lollardy to the English Reformation is a real one is contested, and the entry carries the contest rather than the conclusion.

sources.work: John Wyclif's own corpus: Trialogus (trans. Stephen E. Lahey, CUP, 2013), with the Latin works in the Wyclif Society editions
sources.note: The academic source the movement outgrew - kept distinct from the movement's own texts so the census's person-defined check can actually run. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: Anne Hudson (ed.), Selections from English Wycliffite Writings (CUP, 1978; repr. Toronto MART, 1997)
sources.note: Verified. Twenty-seven texts of 1385-1425 by the movement itself - Twelve Conclusions, Bible tracts, polemic, doctrine - the census's 'real internal texts', mostly anonymous (the anonymity itself evidence of a de-personalized movement).

sources.work: English Wycliffite Sermons (ed. Hudson & Gradon, 5 vols, Oxford, 1983-96)
sources.note: The movement's formation machinery: a complete vernacular preaching corpus for the liturgical year. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: Norman Tanner (ed.), Heresy Trials in the Diocese of Norwich, 1428-31 (Camden 4th ser. 20, 1977)
sources.note: Verified. HOSTILE and COERCED flags both: the persecutors' records, with coerced abjurations - yet preserving ordinary artisans' and women's stated beliefs (Hawisia Moone's recorded confession is a digest of lay Lollard belief), exactly as the census says. Foxe's later martyrology partisan-late [S].

sources.work: Anne Hudson, The Premature Reformation (Oxford, 1988), with Shannon McSheffrey, Gender and Heresy (1995)
sources.note: The field's standard, plus the contested question of women's actual place in Lollard communities. [S] neither individually verified this session.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 28 'Wycliffism and Lollardy' (Ghosh)
sources.note: Chapter verified this session; dedicated chapter - direct fit. The 1380-1520 tail sits within vol. 4's c.1500 horizon; the contested influence-line to the English Reformation is a vol.-6 question left to that era.

movements.teaser: England, c. 1380 to 1520 — artisans and household readers who wanted the Bible in English, and got a century and a half of heresy trials for it.
movements.longDescription: Lollardy grew out of the teaching of the Oxford theologian John Wycliffe — who attacked church wealth and papal authority, denied transubstantiation, and argued that scripture should be available in English — but it quickly became something much wider than him. Its adherents were mostly ordinary people: weavers, smiths, tailors, wives and widows who owned or shared vernacular scripture, met in one another's houses to read it aloud, and doubted images, pilgrimage and the priest's power over the sacrament. The response was severe. Burning for heresy was made law in England in 1401, Archbishop Arundel's constitutions of 1409 forbade unlicensed translation of scripture into English, and Sir John Oldcastle's failed rising in 1414 made Lollardy treason as well as heresy. After that the movement went underground and survived as scattered household networks into the 1520s. Almost everything we know about those households comes from the records their prosecutors kept — because to convict someone you first had to write down what they said.
voices: John Wycliffe — the Oxford theologian whose writings gave the movement its arguments, though it outlived and outgrew him by well over a century
Sir John Oldcastle — the knight whose rising in 1414 failed and turned Lollardy into a political crime; he was executed in 1417
William Sawtrey — a parish priest, the first person burned for heresy in England, in 1401
Hawisia Moone — a Norfolk woman whose confession at the heresy trials of 1428-31, extracted under pressure, is one of the fullest surviving statements of what ordinary Lollards believed
movements.legacy: Whether Lollardy fed directly into the English Reformation is still argued over by historians. What is not in doubt is that Lollard communities in the Chilterns, Essex, Coventry and Kent were still being prosecuted in the 1520s, exactly where and when the first English evangelicals appear, and that some of the same families turn up in both sets of records. Its most concrete survival is physical: around two hundred and fifty manuscripts of the Wycliffite Bible still exist, more than of any other Middle English text — a strange sort of monument for a movement its opponents believed they had stamped out.

movements.name: The Hussite & Bohemian Brethren Movement
movements.informalName: The Hussites and the Bohemian Brethren
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1), and named unique as a functioning non-Roman national church a century before Luther. Two record corrections landed at the Freeze: an origin note recording that its Prague formation (1402–14) precedes Hus's burning, and a fix to its renewal line, which had placed the Moravians at Herrnhut in the wrong era. The absence of an Era 7 entry for its Unitas segment was flagged forward rather than filled.
movements.sourcing: Rich: confessions, hymnody, discipline records
movements.relationsSummary: A functioning non-Roman national church a century before Luther; its Prague formation (1402-14) precedes Hus’s burning (origin note, Era 6 gate); later renewed as the Moravians at Herrnhut (VII.4, Era 8 - era corrected at the Era 6 gate; the era-7 Unitas segment has no entry yet, flagged to A1.E7)
movements.why: A functioning non-Roman national church a full century before Luther — not a suppressed dissent but a country that communed in both kinds, was crusaded against, and kept its own order regardless. It shows that what happened in 1517 was already possible, which changes how the Reformation reads. Its Prague formation runs from 1402, before Hus was ever burned, so the movement is not simply a reaction to his death; the line it opens is renewed later as the Moravians.

sources.work: The Letters of John Hus (trans. Matthew Spinka, Manchester, 1972)
sources.note: Verified. All 105 surviving letters and documents, from Latin and Czech - his own voice, including the Constance prison letters.

sources.work: Peter of Mladonovice, John Hus at the Council of Constance (trans. Spinka, Columbia, 1965)
sources.note: Verified. The eyewitness Relatio by Hus's companion - partisan-sympathetic account carrying the HOSTILE council record (charges, condemnation) embedded within it; both filters flagged.

sources.work: The Four Articles of Prague (1420), Hussite and Taborite manifestos, war songs, and chronicle excerpts, in Thomas Fudge, The Crusade against Heretics in Bohemia, 1418-1437 (Crusade Texts in Translation 9, Ashgate, 2002)
sources.note: Verified. 208 documents from Czech, German, and Latin, most first-time English - the movement's program and its enemies' bulls side by side, hostile items flagged per document.

sources.work: The Unity of Brethren (from 1457): Gregory the Patriarch's letters, the Brethren's confessions, discipline ordinances, and hymnody culminating in the first printed vernacular hymnal (1501); Peter Chelcicky's Net of Faith as its intellectual spring
sources.note: The census's confessions/hymnody/discipline legs in the movement's second, pacifist generation. [S] English access piecemeal (Moravian-tradition scholarship; partial translations) - access flag.

sources.work: Howard Kaminsky, A History of the Hussite Revolution (California, 1967), with Thomas Fudge, Jan Hus: Religious Reform and Social Revolution in Bohemia (2010)
sources.note: The standard and a current entry. [S] neither individually verified this session.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4 (chapter assignment hedged)
sources.note: [S] no dedicated Hussite chapter identified in the recovered TOC this session; nearest anchors ch. 28 (Ghosh - Wyclif's Bohemian reception) and ch. 15 'Sacramental life' (Rubin - utraquism as sacramental claim). 1415-1517 endpoint sits at vol. 4's horizon; the Moravian renewal is Era 7's question.

movements.teaser: Bohemia, 1415 to 1517 — a whole country that took communion in both kinds, was crusaded against five times for it, and kept its own church anyway.
movements.longDescription: Jan Hus preached reform in Czech at Prague's Bethlehem Chapel for more than a decade before the Council of Constance burned him as a heretic in 1415; the shock turned a university movement into a national one. Its emblem was the chalice — the insistence that ordinary lay people, and not only priests, should receive the wine at communion — and its programme was set out in the Four Articles of Prague in 1420. When crusades were called against Bohemia, the Hussite armies under Jan Žižka and then Prokop the Bald beat them one after another, and in 1436 the Compacts of Basel conceded what no other medieval dissent ever won: legal recognition. Out of that settlement two bodies grew. The Utraquist church held the parishes and, under George of Poděbrady, for a time the crown itself; and from 1457 the Unity of the Brethren, a smaller, stricter, pacifist body formed at Kunvald under the influence of the layman Petr Chelčický, which by 1501 had printed what is often called the first hymnbook in a European vernacular.
voices: Jan Hus — preacher at Bethlehem Chapel and rector of Prague university, burned at Constance in 1415
Jakoubek of Stříbro — the theologian who restored the chalice to the laity in 1414, giving the movement its emblem
Jan Žižka — the one-eyed and later wholly blind commander who made the Hussite field armies unbeatable
Petr Chelčický — a layman whose Net of Faith rejected war, oaths and social rank, and shaped the Unity of the Brethren
Gregory the Patriarch — founder of the Unity of the Brethren at Kunvald in 1457
movements.legacy: It did not end in 1517. The Utraquist church and the Unity of the Brethren went on as Bohemia's non-Roman churches for another full century, producing the Kralice Bible and, in Jan Amos Comenius, a last bishop who became one of Europe's great educational reformers, before the Habsburg suppression of the 1620s drove them into exile. Remnants of the Unity survived underground and resurfaced in 1722 at Herrnhut in Saxony as the Moravian Church, which still exists worldwide. In Bohemia the memory never went away: 6 July, the day Hus was burned, is a public holiday in the Czech Republic, and Luther, reading Hus a century later, concluded that 'we are all Hussites without knowing it.'

experienceToday.text: Bethlehem Chapel, Prague — rebuilt on its medieval foundations and surviving walls, where Hus preached in Czech

movements.name: The Ethiopian Monastic Flowering
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) and named the atlas's strongest non-European medieval candidate on its own record — royal chronicles and saints' lives in quantity, with the royal-sponsorship gravity treated as a source condition rather than passed over. One nuance was carried: Zara Yaqob's own writings are simultaneously an inside voice and a persecutor's voice toward the Estifanosites. Its end was capped at 1517, the real break of the Gragn war belonging to the next era.
movements.sourcing: RICH: royal chronicles, saints' lives in quantity (royal-sponsorship gravity needs care)
movements.relationsSummary: Continuation of Aksum/Zagwe - the atlas's strongest non-European medieval candidate
movements.why: No medieval tradition outside Europe reaches the atlas with a stronger documentary case — royal chronicles and saints' lives in quantity, from a continuously Christian kingdom standing inside nobody else's empire. That the court sponsored much of it is a condition on the sources rather than a reason to discount them, and the entry says so. Zara Yaqob is the sharp case: an inside voice, and toward the Estifanosites a persecutor's voice, in the same corpus.
movements.dateRationale: End 1517 (continues-cap for a living tradition; the real break - the Gragn war 1529-43 [S] - is era 7's and would be a forbidden double-straddle from the 1270 start; keep-1500+note alt was shown) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: The royal chronicles: The Glorious Victories of Amda Seyon (trans. Huntingford, Oxford, 1965) and the chronicle of Zara Yaqob (ed./French trans. Perruchon, 1893)
sources.note: The census's royal-chronicles leg, flagged as court production (royal-sponsorship gravity). [S] edition details from knowledge; Zara Yaqob chronicle French-only - access flag.

sources.work: Kebra Nagast (The Glory of Kings) (trans. Budge, 1922; free online)
sources.note: The Solomonic charter myth. Dating debate flagged: received text is an early-14th-c. compilation/redaction claiming ancient authority - the date itself a live scholarly argument and a tier-care case. Link verified in the Era-5 twin's same-day record, not re-fetched this session.

sources.work: The gadl literature of the era's own movements: Gadla Ewostatewos and Gadla Estifanos (Getatchew Haile, The Ge'ez Acts of Abba Estifanos of Gwendagwende, CSCO, 2006)
sources.note: Estifanos translation attested this session. The Estifanosite acts are the persecuted dissenters' own memory of refusing royal-cult conformity under Zara Yaqob - the anti-sponsorship counterweight the census's care note asks for. [S] Ewostatewos editions from knowledge - access flag.

sources.work: Zara Yaqob's own writings: Mashafa Berhan (Book of Light) and Mashafa Milad
sources.note: A reforming king writing theology and enforcing it. Double status flagged: inside voice for the royal reform, HOSTILE source for the movements it condemned (Estifanosites). [S] CSCO editions with Italian/German translations; no standard English - access flag.

sources.work: Taddesse Tamrat, Church and State in Ethiopia, 1270-1527 (Oxford, 1972)
sources.note: Verified in the Era-5 same-day record (archive.org). Still the standard frame for exactly this window, by an Ethiopian historian; current French scholarship (Derat) named as supplement [S].

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, 'Church and nation: the Ethiopian Orthodox Tawahedo church (from the thirteenth to the twentieth century)' (Crummey)
sources.note: Chapter verified in TOC (Era-5 recovery); direct fit - this entry is the chapter's opening ground.

movements.teaser: The Ethiopian highlands, c. 1270 to 1517 — an independent Christian kingdom whose monks argued with its emperors, and often won.
movements.longDescription: When the Solomonic dynasty took the Ethiopian throne in 1270, claiming descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, it did so alongside a monastic expansion that carried churches and monasteries deep into newly conquered regions — the network Tekle Haymanot built in Shewa, and the northern houses founded by the followers of Ewostatewos. The relationship between crown and cloister was contested throughout. The Ewostathians insisted on keeping Saturday as well as Sunday as a Sabbath and were harried for generations before the emperor Zara Yaqob finally conceded the point at a council in 1450; and Zara Yaqob, himself a theological author who reorganized the church and pressed Marian devotion on it, persecuted the monks of Estifanos when they refused the prostrations and observances he demanded. All of it was written down in Ge'ez — royal chronicles, saints' lives, hymns to Mary, and the Kebra Nagast, the book that gave the dynasty its Solomonic charter.
voices: Tekle Haymanot — the monastic founder whose Shewan network of houses carried the church across the expanding kingdom
Ewostatewos — whose insistence on keeping both Saturday and Sunday as Sabbaths made his followers a persecuted movement for a century, until the church conceded
Zara Yaqob — emperor, theological author and church reformer, and the persecutor of the monks who would not conform
Estifanos — leader of the monks who refused the emperor's required observances, and who died in confinement for it
movements.legacy: This is a living church. The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church still keeps the outcome of the Sabbath argument, still sings the Marian hymnody Zara Yaqob's reign promoted, still worships in Ge'ez, and still traces its great monastic houses to the founders of these centuries. The manuscripts of the period — illuminated gospels, gadl lives of the saints, hymn collections — form one of the largest bodies of medieval Christian literature produced outside Europe. The tradition carried on through the wars and upheavals of the century that followed into the church of tens of millions of members it is today.

movements.name: Muscovite Monastic Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) — lives, skete rules and the possessors/non-possessors polemics give it a moderate-to-rich base, with the peasant voice acknowledged as thin. Its monastic frame was kept deliberately and said so at the gate: the 1448 autocephaly rides inside this entry rather than prompting a separate institutional one.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: lives, skete rules, the possessors/non-possessors polemics; peasant voice thin
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Kievan + hesychast lines; parent of the Old Believers' tradition and later renewal
movements.why: This is where Russian Christianity acquires a centre of gravity of its own — the forest hermitages of the north, and with them the possessors-and-non-possessors argument over whether monasteries should own anything, one of the few medieval debates about wealth conducted by the people it actually constrained. The 1448 autocephaly is kept inside this monastic frame deliberately rather than given an institutional entry of its own. Everything later in the Russian line, the Old Believers and the nineteenth-century renewal alike, reaches back through here.

sources.work: Epiphanius the Wise, Life of Sergius of Radonezh (c. 1417-18)
sources.note: The movement's founding hagiography by Sergius's own disciple. Tier care: survives reworked through Pachomius the Serb's redactions (redaction history attested this session). English access abridged (Zenkovsky, Medieval Russia's Epics, Chronicles, and Tales) [S] - access flag.

sources.work: Nil Sorsky, The Authentic Writings (trans. David Goldfrank, Cistercian Studies 221, 2008; alt. Maloney, CWS)
sources.note: Verified. The census's skete-rules leg in the non-possessor leader's own hand: the Predanie, the Ustav, the four authentic letters - the hesychast line transplanted north (census relations made textual).

sources.work: Joseph of Volokolamsk, The Monastic Rule of Iosif Volotsky (trans. Goldfrank, Cistercian, 1983)
sources.note: The possessor side's own legislation - so the census's possessors/non-possessors polemic leg is carried by both parties' texts, not a summary. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: The monastic colonization record: northern founders' lives (Kirill of Beloozero; Zosima and Savvatii of Solovki), foundation charters and land acts; Stoglav (1551) retrospectives
sources.note: Expansion into the Russian north as the movement's lived, economic form. Stoglav-era retrospectives flagged LATE - a century past the window. Peasant voice appears only refracted through monastic land documents (census's 'peasant voice thin' confirmed). [S] editions/access from knowledge.

sources.work: David B. Miller, Saint Sergius of Radonezh, His Trinity Monastery, and the Formation of the Russian Identity (2010)
sources.note: [S] not individually verified this session. Current standard study of cult and colonization together.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 5, 'Russian piety and Orthodox culture 1380-1589' (Stella Rock)
sources.note: Chapter recovered via search this session - direct window fit. [S] chapter number/pages not verified; 1340-1517 endpoint sits inside the chapter's span, so no vol.-6 anchor needed.

movements.teaser: The Russian north, c. 1340 to 1517 — monks who walked into the forest to be alone, and ended up settling a country.
movements.longDescription: Sergius of Radonezh withdrew into the woods north of Moscow in the 1340s to live alone. Within a generation the monastery that grew up around him had sent out disciples who founded dozens more, pushing ever deeper into the northern forests in what later Russians called the northern Thebaid. The texts followed — Epiphanius the Wise's life of Sergius, the skete rules of Nil Sorsky — and so did the art, since Andrei Rublev's Trinity was painted in Sergius's memory for his own monastery. The period also produced the sharpest argument in Russian church history: Nil Sorsky and the non-possessors held that monasteries should own no land and no peasants and should live by their own labour, while Joseph of Volotsk and the possessors held that endowed monasteries could feed the poor, train clergy and carry the church's work. The possessors won it at the council of 1503. In the middle of all this, in 1448, Russian bishops elected their own metropolitan without waiting on Constantinople — the beginning of an independent Russian church.
voices: Sergius of Radonezh — the hermit whose Trinity monastery became the centre of Russian monastic life and, later, of Russian national memory
Epiphanius the Wise — Sergius's disciple and biographer, who wrote the movement's founding life
Stephen of Perm — missionary to the Komi, for whom he devised an alphabet and translated the services
Nil Sorsky — leader of the non-possessors, who wanted monks poor, few and silent
Joseph of Volotsk — leader of the possessors, who wanted monasteries endowed, disciplined and socially useful
Andrei Rublev — monk and icon painter, whose Trinity was made for Sergius's own monastery
movements.legacy: Almost everything that follows in Russian Christianity runs back through here. Sergius's foundation is still a working lavra and a spiritual centre of the Russian Orthodox Church; the hesychast prayer this generation received from the Greeks resurfaced in the elder movement of the nineteenth century; and the argument between possessors and non-possessors about monastic wealth has been re-fought in Russian religious writing ever since. Rublev's Trinity became the most famous icon ever painted.

experienceToday.text: Trinity Sergius Lavra, Sergiev Posad — Sergius's own foundation, still a working monastery and a UNESCO World Heritage Site

movements.name: Observant Reform & Popular Preaching
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on Bernardino's sermon-cycles taken down as spoken, with an access limit noted — the 1427 cycle has no complete English translation. The person-defined question its record carried was cleared at this gate: the movement is multi-founder and multi-order, its legitimacy resting on the Rule strictly observed, with the boundary that Savonarola alone would fail that test kept verbatim. Its dates were anchored to c. 1368 (Brugliano) and 1517 (Ite vos).
movements.sourcing: Rich: Bernardino's sermon-cycles taken down as spoken - near-transcripts of mass lay formation
movements.floorNote: No creedal question. Nor does the movement stand or fall with a single figure: it had many founders across several orders, and its claim rested on keeping the Rule strictly rather than on any leader's person. Savonarola, the one Observant whose following really did gather around himself, is the exception rather than the pattern.
movements.relationsSummary: A merge/split test vs. the mendicant traditions, in the Phase One record's own style; the Spanish observance’s context includes the converso crisis (1391-1492) - carried as context with process honesty, never endorsement
movements.why: Mass lay formation, recoverable almost as it was spoken: Bernardino's cycles were taken down by listeners day after day, so what survives sits close to what a piazza full of ordinary people actually heard. Very little else in the atlas gets that near to preaching as an event rather than as a text. As a movement it is a genuine merge-or-split test against the mendicant traditions it reformed from within — multi-founder, multi-order, resting on the Rule rather than on any one person.
movements.dateRationale: Start c. 1368 (Brugliano - Paoluccio Trinci's documented origin; keep-1400 alt was shown); end 1517 (Ite vos, the Franciscan Observance's institutional terminus, doubling as the era boundary; alt 1498 was shown) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Bernardino of Siena, the 1427 Siena sermon cycle (reportatio of Benedetto di maestro Bartolomeo; standard ed. Delcorno, 1989, Italian)
sources.note: Forty-five vernacular sermons taken down as spoken, audience reactions included - 'virtual tape-recording' status verified this session; the census's near-transcript claim confirmed. Access flag: English in selections only [S] details from knowledge.

sources.work: John of Capistrano: letters, treatises, and eyewitness accounts of the 1451-56 central-European preaching tours
sources.note: Mass preaching at Vienna, Nuremberg, Breslau - carried with the movement's darkness flagged: at Breslau 1453 Capistrano led the trial and burning of Jews on host-desecration charges; those records are HOSTILE, COERCED testimony, and here the movement is the persecutor. [S] largely untranslated (Acta Sanctorum; Hofer) - access flag.

sources.work: The Observance as structure: Observant constitutions and statutes (e.g. the Martinian constitutions, 1430), vicariate records, Bernardino's Latin model-sermon collections
sources.note: The movement's institutional self-organization across Franciscan, Dominican, Augustinian, and Benedictine families - the structure-shaped half of the c2 authority-structure evidence (person-shaped half = the star preachers). Criterion left to the lead thread. [S] Latin editions; details from knowledge.

sources.work: The reform's women in their own words: Colette of Corbie's Constitutions for the Poor Clares; Caterina Vigri of Bologna, The Seven Spiritual Weapons
sources.note: The Observance's female branch as authors, not subjects - a woman legislating a reform, and an Observant Poor Clare's own formation book. [S] English editions from knowledge - access flag.

sources.work: James Mixson & Bert Roest (eds.), A Companion to Observant Reform in the Late Middle Ages and Beyond (Brill, 2015)
sources.note: [S] not individually verified this session. Current standard, cross-order by design - matching the census's merge/split-test relations note; Savonarola treated there inside the Observant frame, per the census floor note (he alone would fail person-defined; the Observance is broader).

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 29 'Observant reform in religious orders' (Roest); cf. ch. 30 'Public purity and discipline' (Rusconi)
sources.note: Both chapters recovered via search this session; a dedicated chapter by the Companion's co-editor - direct fit.

movements.teaser: Italy and Spain, c. 1368 to 1517 — friars who went back to the strict rule, and then preached it to whole cities standing in the square.
movements.longDescription: The Observance began as an argument inside the religious orders: that the Rule should be kept as it was written, not as generations of dispensation had relaxed it. It started small, with Paoluccio Trinci's handful of friars at Brugliano in 1368, and spread across the Franciscans, Dominicans, Augustinians and Benedictines alike, until reformed houses formed rival provinces alongside the unreformed ones. Its public face was preaching. Bernardino of Siena drew whole towns into the piazza for sermon cycles that ran for weeks; the forty-five sermons he preached at Siena in 1427 were taken down as he spoke by a listener in the crowd, asides and audience reactions included, which is about as close as anyone gets to hearing a medieval sermon rather than reading one. John of Capistrano did the same across central Europe. The movement's darker side belongs in the same account: Capistrano's preaching also drove the persecution of Jewish communities, most notoriously at Breslau in 1453.
voices: Paoluccio Trinci — began the Franciscan Observance with a few friars at Brugliano in 1368
Bernardino of Siena — the movement's great preacher, whose Siena sermons of 1427 survive as a listener's near-transcript
John of Capistrano — preached to enormous crowds across central Europe, and led the persecution of Jews at Breslau in 1453
Colette of Corbie — reformed the Poor Clares and wrote constitutions for her own branch of the order
Caterina Vigri of Bologna — Observant Poor Clare, painter and writer, whose Seven Spiritual Weapons is a formation book written by a woman for women
movements.legacy: The Observance won. When Leo X divided the Franciscans in 1517 the Observants took the larger share and the order's leadership, and the reforming impulse ran on into the Capuchins a decade later; the same reformed-against-unreformed pattern shaped the Dominicans and Augustinians too, and Observant houses became a seedbed of the Catholic reform of the following century. Two smaller things passed into ordinary use and outlived the movement: the monti di pietà, low-interest municipal pawn-banks promoted by Observant friars from the 1460s as an alternative to ruinous lending — the one established at Siena in 1472 still trades as a bank today — and the radiant IHS monogram Bernardino held up at the end of his sermons, which became a fixture of Catholic devotional art.

experienceToday.text: Basilica of San Bernardino, L'Aquila — built for Bernardino of Siena in the decades after his death, reopened in 2015 after earthquake repairs

movements.name: Late-Medieval Lay Parish Piety
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 6 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) for reaching the constituency every other tradition reaches only at its edges, on evidence that is rich but oblique — churchwardens' accounts, wills and primers show practice more than interior voice. Its link to Borromean Milan was reclassified at the gate as exemplar-succession rather than identity: the continuesAs field was removed and the relation carried in prose, given the 43-year gap and the region jump.
movements.sourcing: Rich but oblique: churchwardens' accounts, wills, primers - practice more than interior voice
movements.relationsSummary: The ordinary laity as such - the constituency every other tradition reaches only at its edges; its Catholic-reform continuation is EXEMPLIFIED by VI.12 (Borromean Milan) - exemplar-succession carried in prose per the adopted convention (identity continuesAs removed at the Era 6 gate: 43-year gap and region jump)
movements.why: Whether 'the parish' coheres as one bounded tradition is a real and open question — the same plain question the record already asked of Jerusalem's pilgrims. What earns it the attempt is its constituency: the ordinary laity as such, which every other tradition in the atlas reaches only at its edges. Its evidence fits that exactly — what people paid for, left behind, and prayed from, rather than what they said about any of it.

sources.work: Churchwardens' accounts: Morebath (ed. Binney, 1904), All Saints' Bristol (ed. Burgess), Bassingbourn and kin
sources.note: The parish's own financial self-record: lights, images, ales, roof-leads - collective lay agency in ledger form; the record-type behind Duffy's Voices of Morebath (verified this session). [S] individual editions from knowledge - access flag.

sources.work: Books of hours and primers: The Prymer or lay folks' prayer book (ed. Littlehales, EETS, 1895-97) and the mass-market horae
sources.note: The ordinary household's actual prayer equipment, surviving in thousands of worn copies. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: Wills and gild records: bequests for obits, lights, and fabric; the 1389 gild returns; The Lay Folks Mass Book (EETS)
sources.note: Practice documented at the moment of death and in fraternity - the two points where ordinary people wrote themselves down. [S] editions from knowledge.

sources.work: John Mirk, Festial (ed. Powell, EETS, 2009-11)
sources.note: The era's most-copied English sermon collection, written for parish priests preaching to lay congregations - the closest surviving proxy for what the pew actually heard. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: Eamon Duffy, The Stripping of the Altars: Traditional Religion in England, c.1400-c.1580 (Yale, 1992; 2nd ed. 2005), with The Voices of Morebath (2001)
sources.note: Verified. The census's named frame arguing this parish world's vitality, plus the single-parish case study. Builder caution: Duffy's revisionism is a position in a live historiographical argument - carry as frame, not verdict.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 15 'Sacramental life' (Rubin); cf. ch. 21 'Saints and pilgrimages' (Vauchez)
sources.note: Both chapters verified (this session / Era-5 recovery); the parish's sacramental round is ch. 15's ground. The 1517 endpoint and continuesAs line (Tridentine parish renewal) point at vol. 6 for the NEXT era, not this one.

movements.teaser: England, c. 1400 to 1517 — the religion of people who left no writings, reconstructed from what they paid for, prayed from, and left behind in their wills.
movements.longDescription: For most people in late-medieval England, Christianity was the parish: the mass seen from the nave, the yearly round of feasts and processions, the guild you joined, the light you paid to keep burning before an image, the church ale that funded the roof. It was not passive. Churchwardens — ordinary laymen, elected and accountable to their neighbours — collected and spent the money, and their accounts show parishes rebuilding naves, raising towers, buying vestments and hiring carvers on their own initiative. Books of hours, soon printed by the thousand, put the same daily prayers into the hands of any household that could afford them, and sermon collections like John Mirk's Festial tell us roughly what the pew was hearing. Almost none of these people wrote about what they believed. What survives instead is the record of what they did with their money and their time — a different kind of evidence, and in some ways a more candid one.
voices: No founder, leader or spokesman — this is the religion of the ordinary parish, and it reaches us through churchwardens, guild members and will-makers who are named in the records but who wrote nothing about themselves
movements.legacy: Much of it is still standing. The great parish churches of East Anglia, the Cotswolds and the West Country were built or rebuilt in these decades out of ordinary parishioners' giving, and their towers, painted screens and carved roofs are the largest surviving artefact of late-medieval lay religion anywhere. Most of the rest was deliberately taken apart: the English Reformation abolished the guilds and chantries, whitewashed the paintings and broke up the images, so that what we know of the practice comes largely from accounts that record first its purchase and then its destruction. Something like it was built again elsewhere: the intensely parish-centred Catholicism of Carlo Borromeo's Milan, a generation later, ran on the same instincts under very different rules.

movements.name: Taborite Radicalism
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Chronicled largely by opponents and moderate Hussites
movements.floorNote: No creedal question — Tabor stripped worship back to what it could find in scripture, but the argument was about practice and property, not the Creed.
movements.relationsSummary: Radical wing of V.6
movements.why: Not a candidate alone; appears plainly inside the Hussite tradition's story.
movements.dateRationale: String aligned to its own principled numbers (Tabor's founding 1420 to its capitulation 1452); no numeric change (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Taborite manifestos and chiliast articles (1419-20), with the priests' adventist letters, in Fudge, The Crusade against Heretics in Bohemia (Ashgate, 2002)
sources.note: Volume verified. The radicals' own program in English - mountain assemblies, community of goods, the avenging Christ. [S] itemization of included manifestos not page-verified. Enrichment flag vs census 'chronicled largely by opponents': genuine inside texts survive.

sources.work: Nicholas of Pelhrimov (Biskupec), Taborite confession and chronicle (Chronicon Taboritarum)
sources.note: The movement's own bishop defending Taborite doctrine and recording its history - the strongest inside text. [S] Latin editions (Hoefler) only - access flag.

sources.work: Lawrence of Brezova, Hussite Chronicle; John Pribram, The Lives of the Taborite Priests; Aeneas Sylvius Piccolomini's account of Tabor (1451)
sources.note: HOSTILE / MODERATE-HUSSITE flags: the census's named filter - Prague moderates writing against Tabor (Pribram's tract an intra-Hussite heresiology), plus a later outside papal observer. Partial English via Fudge [S] details from knowledge.

sources.work: Howard Kaminsky, A History of the Hussite Revolution (California, 1967)
sources.note: [S] not individually verified this session. Still the standard for Tabor's theology-into-politics arc, built directly on these sources.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4 (hedged, as the Hussite entry)
sources.note: [S] no dedicated Hussite chapter identified this session; same hedged anchor as V.6 - consistent with the A5 placement inside the Hussite story, which this base supports.

movements.teaser: Southern Bohemia, 1420 to 1452 — Hussite radicals who built a town on a hill expecting the world to end, and became the most feared army in Europe instead.
movements.longDescription: In 1420 the most radical wing of the Hussite movement founded a fortified town in southern Bohemia and named it Tábor, after the mountain of the Transfiguration, in the expectation that Christ was about to return and only a few chosen places would be spared. The year passed, the world continued, and the community stayed. Tabor stripped worship down to what it could find in scripture — vernacular liturgy, no vestments, no purgatory, no cult of the saints — elected its own bishop in Nicholas of Pelhřimov, and in its early years held property in common. It also fielded the Hussite wars' most effective army, whose wagon-fort tactics under Jan Žižka and then Prokop the Bald broke crusade after crusade. In the end it was the moderate Hussites of Prague who destroyed it, shattering the Taborite field armies at Lipany in 1434; the town itself surrendered to George of Poděbrady in 1452, and its bishop died in confinement.
voices: Nicholas of Pelhřimov, called Biskupec — the elected Taborite bishop, who defended and chronicled the community's teaching and died a prisoner
Jan Žižka — the Hussite commander who made Tabor's wagon-forts unbeatable, and who also turned on radicals he judged had gone too far
Prokop the Bald — the priest who led the Taborite field armies after Žižka's death
movements.legacy: As a church, nothing continued: Tabor's worship and its community of goods ended with its surrender. Its influence ran two other ways. The wagon-fort tactics its armies perfected were studied and copied across central Europe for a century afterward. And the revulsion of Petr Chelčický and others at what armed radicalism had produced helped push the Unity of the Brethren, founded a few years after Tabor's fall, toward a deliberate and permanent pacifism. The town itself is still there.

experienceToday.text: The Hussite Museum, Tábor — in the old town hall of the town the Taborites founded, with the medieval tunnels beneath it

movements.name: Fraticelli (Spiritual Franciscan rigorists)
movements.statusDescription: Not counted as a candidate tradition of its own — its story is told plainly inside another tradition's, rather than standing alone.
movements.sourcing: Inquisition-era records
movements.floorNote: Declared heretical over poverty doctrine and obedience, not the creed
movements.relationsSummary: Rupture inside the Franciscan family
movements.why: Presented inside the Franciscan tradition's own tensions - an obedience-and-property rupture, told plainly there.
movements.dateRationale: End c. 1466 (the great Fraticelli trial at Rome - documented Fraticelli's effective end; the old 1420 matched nothing; the minimum string-only fix was shown); string corrected to 14th-15th c. (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

sources.work: Angelo Clareno, A Chronicle or History of the Seven Tribulations of the Order of Brothers Minor (trans. Burr & Daniel, Franciscan Institute, 2005)
sources.note: The Spirituals' own martyr-history of their persecution inside the order - the movement's voice, openly partisan (hagiographic frame flagged). Enrichment flag vs census 'Inquisition-era records': genuine internal literature exists. [S] edition details from knowledge.

sources.work: Peter of John Olivi: the usus pauper treatises and the Apocalypse commentary (condemned 1326)
sources.note: The theological wellspring the rigorists carried - the intellectual layer beneath the movement. [S] Latin/partial English (Burr's selections) - access flag.

sources.work: John XXII's bulls: Sancta Romana and Gloriosam ecclesiam (1317-18), Cum inter nonnullos (1323)
sources.note: HOSTILE, INSTITUTIONAL: the papacy constituting 'fraticelli' as a juridical category and declaring absolute-poverty doctrine heretical - the obedience-and-property rupture, matching the census floor note precisely. [S] English access via canon-law collections from knowledge.

sources.work: Inquisition records: the Marseilles friars burned 1318; Bernard Gui's Fraticelli/beguin sections; the Languedoc beguin depositions - English access via Louisa Burnham, So Great a Light, So Great a Smoke (Cornell, 2008)
sources.note: HOSTILE and COERCED flags both: lay men and women who venerated the burned friars as martyrs, known almost only through their interrogations. [S] details from knowledge.

sources.work: David Burr, The Spiritual Franciscans: From Protest to Persecution in the Century after Saint Francis (Penn State, 2001)
sources.note: [S] not individually verified this session. The standard account, built on both the inside literature and the trial record.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 3 'Religious poverty and the search for perfection' (Kienzle); cf. ch. 23 'Repression and power' (Arnold)
sources.note: Ch. 3 verified in the Era-5 recovery; ch. 23 recovered this session. The entry sits exactly between them.

movements.teaser: Italy and Provence, the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries — friars who would not give up absolute poverty after the pope made it a heresy to believe in.
movements.longDescription: The Franciscans had argued for a century about how literally to take Francis's poverty, and in the 1310s and 20s the argument was closed by force. John XXII ordered the strictest friars to conform, had four of them burned at Marseille in 1318 for refusing, and in 1323 declared it heretical to hold that Christ and the apostles had owned nothing at all — turning a devotional ideal into a condemned proposition. Those who would not submit became the fraticelli, 'little brothers', a name their prosecutors used as a legal category as much as a description. They survived for another century and a half in the Marches of Ancona, in Provence and in scattered Italian and Greek communities, supported by lay sympathizers — among them the beguins of Languedoc, who venerated the burned friars as martyrs and were hunted for it. A major trial at Rome in the 1460s effectively ended them.
voices: Angelo Clareno — leader of the surviving rigorists and author of their own history of the order's persecutions
Peter of John Olivi — the theologian of restricted use whose writings the rigorists carried; his Apocalypse commentary was condemned in 1326, decades after his death
Pope John XXII — the pope who made absolute poverty a heresy and gave the fraticelli their name as a category in law
movements.legacy: No community survived and no church descends from them. What survived was the argument. The poverty controversy forced both sides into working out theories of ownership, use and right that fed directly into later Western thinking about property, and the friars who fled the papal court over it — William of Ockham among them — turned the quarrel into political philosophy.
