It also left the beguins of Languedoc, remembered now almost entirely through the interrogations that destroyed them, and it left the poverty question itself, which kept returning inside the Franciscan family every time it reformed.

movements.informalName: The Sects of the Inquisition Records
movements.statusDescription: The record is genuinely disputed. This entry carries the question, not a verdict.
movements.sourcing: Heresiological artifacts in the Free Spirit pattern

sources.note: HOSTILE, COERCED: answers shaped by the questioners' error-template - carried forward deliberately from the Era-5 Free Spirit base (IV.14), because the census names this entry as 'in the Free Spirit pattern'. [S] editions/partial translations (Lerner's apparatus) from knowledge - access flag.

sources.note: HOSTILE CONSTRUCT: the pattern-document that could generate 'sects' on paper - the census's 'heresiological artifacts' phrase made concrete. [S] inclusion details from knowledge.

sources.note: The consensus-setter the census's phrase presupposes (verified in the Era-5 same-day record): such 'sects' are substantially persecutors' constructs. For the Adamite case, modern Hussite scholarship (Kaminsky; Fudge) weighs how much reality sat under the atrocity stories [S].

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 4, ch. 23 'Repression and power' (Arnold); cf. ch. 12 'Christians and heretics' (Biller)
sources.note: Ch. 23 recovered this session; ch. 12 verified in the Era-5 recovery. A repression-record entry anchored to the repression chapter - fit is exact for what this entry actually is. Governing fact: census 'cannot be assessed' - the absence of any inside voice is the primary datum.

movements.teaser: Central Europe, the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries — groups that may have been movements, or may have been what the interrogators already expected to find.
movements.longDescription: Some of the 'sects' in the medieval record are known only from the documents that condemned them. The Bohemian Adamites of 1421 — described as a naked, communal, apocalyptic band on an island in southern Bohemia — appear in the chronicles of people who despised them and in the account of a later outside observer, and the Taborites destroyed them, so no voice from inside survives at all. The wider 'heresy of the Free Spirit' works much the same way: a list of errors condemned at the Council of Vienne circulated among inquisitors as a template, and much of what later depositions 'found' matches that template closely enough that historians since Robert Lerner's work in 1972 have concluded a good deal of it was produced by the questioning rather than discovered by it. Some of these people were certainly real, and some of what they were accused of may well have been true. But the evidence is one-sided, extracted under coercion, and shaped in advance by the questions.
voices: No voice from inside any of these groups survives. Every name we have — John of Brünn, the beguines interrogated at Schweidnitz in 1332, the Adamites of 1421 — reaches us only as a defendant in someone else's record, answering questions written before they were asked
movements.legacy: Nothing institutional survives, and in some cases there may have been nothing to survive: several of these 'sects' may never have existed in the form the records describe. What they left instead is a caution that historians now take seriously — that a confident, detailed list of what a group believed can be an artefact of the procedure that produced it rather than a description of anybody's faith.

movements.name: The Latin Papal Church (Avignon to Fifth Lateran)
movements.informalName: The Church of Avignon, Schism, and Councils
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run as IV.18's receiver - the era's headline gap. Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich: Avignon registers, Schism dossiers from all obediences, Constance and Basel acta, Fifth Lateran constitutions; the era of the papacy's own record-keeping explosion
movements.relationsSummary: Seven popes at Avignon (1309-1377); the Great Western Schism (1378-1417) healed at Constance (Martin V, 1417); Basel and the conciliar contest (Haec sancta, Frequens [S on decree specifics]); the Renaissance papacy; Fifth Lateran closes 16 March 1517. Carries inside its story: conciliarism, the Templar trial, Catherine of Siena and Bridget of Sweden (the Avignon-era prophetic women), the Pragmatic Sanction, and the converso context (1391 pogroms, 1478 Inquisition, 1492 expulsion - carried as context with process honesty, never endorsement)
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: IV.18 ends 1300 with no receiver, and the Avignon-Schism-Constance century - the era's defining institutional drama - had no entry. Tier 1 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 1300 (era boundary; IV.18's gated end) to 1517 (Fifth Lateran's last session, 16 March 1517) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: Avignon, Rome and all of Latin Christendom, 1300 to 1517 — two centuries in which the papacy left Rome, split three ways, was put on trial by its own councils, and came back as a Renaissance court.
movements.longDescription: In 1309 Clement V settled the papal court at Avignon, and for nearly seventy years the popes governed the Latin church from the Rhône rather than the Tiber, building the largest Gothic palace in Europe and an administration to match. The return to Rome in 1377 produced something worse: a disputed election the following year left two popes, an attempt to fix it in 1409 left three, and the schism divided every kingdom, university and religious order in the West for a generation. It was ended not by a pope but by a council — Constance, which removed the rival claimants, elected Martin V in 1417, and declared that a general council holds its authority immediately from Christ. The decades after that were a contest over whether that was true, settled in the papacy's favour by the 1440s. The popes who followed rebuilt Rome, founded the Vatican Library, commissioned the Sistine Chapel and began the new St Peter's. The Fifth Lateran Council, which decreed a programme of reform that changed very little, closed on 16 March 1517 — seven months before Luther's theses.
voices: Boniface VIII — whose claim of papal supremacy over kings in 1302 collapsed the following year at the hands of the French crown
Catherine of Siena — a lay Dominican whose letters pressed Gregory XI to bring the papacy back to Rome
Bridget of Sweden — a widowed noblewoman whose revelations, addressed to popes and kings, made the same demand
Martin V — elected at Constance in 1417, the pope who ended the schism
Julius II — who began the rebuilding of St Peter's in 1506
movements.legacy: This is a continuous institution: the same church, reorganized by the Council of Trent a generation later, is the Roman Catholic Church of today. Its material legacy from these centuries is unmissable — the papal palace at Avignon, the Vatican Library, the Sistine Chapel, the basilica of St Peter's begun in 1506. Its constitutional legacy is quieter and longer-running: the conciliar claim that a general council can judge a pope was defeated but never quite died, resurfacing in Gallicanism, in later Catholic reform movements, and in the arguments around the First Vatican Council four and a half centuries afterward. And the reforms that the fifteenth century's councils repeatedly voted and failed to enforce were still outstanding when Luther wrote.

experienceToday.text: The Palais des Papes, Avignon — the popes' fortress-palace, a UNESCO World Heritage Site open to visitors year-round

movements.name: The Byzantine Church, Palaiologan Era
movements.informalName: The Church of the Empire's Last Century
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run as IV.17's receiver. Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally: the hesychast councils' tomoi (1341/1347/1351), Ferrara-Florence acta (Laetentur Caeli, 1439), Mark of Ephesus's corpus, Gennadius Scholarius's pre-1453 corpus (his patriarchate belongs to VI.17's window); the patriarchal register survives for stretches
movements.relationsSummary: The patriarchal institution of the empire's last century and a half: receives the hesychast councils synodally (V.4 carries the movement and theology - scope split deliberate), signs Florence (1439) and repudiates it at home, falls with the City (29 May 1453); hands to VI.17 (Orthodoxy under the Ottomans, starts 1453) - the clean two-way handoff
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: IV.17 ends 1300 with no receiver; V.4 is the movement, not the institution - the church that ruled on hesychasm and faced Florence had no entry. Tier 1 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 1300 (era boundary; IV.17's gated end) to 1453 (the fall of Constantinople - meeting VI.17's 1453 start, the clean handoff) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: Constantinople, 1300 to 1453 — the church of a dying empire, which in the end chose its theology over its survival.
movements.longDescription: In its last century and a half the Byzantine church governed the shrinking remnant of an empire and still did some of its most consequential work. Synods at Constantinople in 1341, 1347 and 1351 ruled in favour of the hesychast monks and made Gregory Palamas's theology the standard of Orthodoxy. Then came the harder question. With the Ottomans closing in, the emperor and the patriarch went to Italy and in 1439 signed a union with Rome at the Council of Florence, in exchange for military help that never adequately came. Mark of Ephesus refused to sign; at home the union was rejected by monks, by much of the clergy and by the city, and when it was finally proclaimed in Hagia Sophia in December 1452 it was met with open hostility. Five months later, on 29 May 1453, Constantinople fell. The same era produced the Palaiologan revival in art — the mosaics of the Chora church, the painted churches of Mystras — some of the finest work Byzantium ever did, made while the state around it was collapsing.
voices: Gregory Palamas — whose theology the synods of these decades established as the Orthodox standard
Mark of Ephesus — the one Greek bishop at Florence who refused to sign the union, and became Orthodoxy's symbol of that refusal
Bessarion — a Greek archbishop who accepted the union, remained in Italy as a cardinal, and whose library helped carry Greek learning west
Gennadios Scholarios — opponent of the union, and the first patriarch of Constantinople under Ottoman rule
movements.legacy: The patriarchate outlived the empire. Within months of the conquest the sultan installed Gennadios Scholarios as patriarch, and the church became the governing institution of the Orthodox population under Ottoman rule for the next four centuries — a continuous line reaching the Ecumenical Patriarchate of today. The union of Florence was formally repudiated and is still a live memory in Orthodox-Catholic relations. And the scholars who left for Italy, Bessarion among them, carried Greek manuscripts and Greek teaching with them into the Renaissance.

experienceToday.text: Mystras, Greece — the ruined Byzantine city of the Palaiologan era, with its painted churches, a UNESCO World Heritage Site

movements.name: The Waldensians in the Alps
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run as IV.8's receiver - the inherited flag the survey reads as cannot-land-by-silence (the survey's gloss of the Freeze record's general discipline, re-attributed at Review Round 1). Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: The barbes' own manuscript books and the inquisition records of the communities they served [S on specific items]; the 1487 crusade bull and its aftermath documented from both sides
movements.floorNote: No question — the charge against them was always discipline and obedience, not doctrine.
movements.relationsSummary: The scattered communities the barbes circuit on foot; Innocent VIII's 1487 crusade bull and the Cattaneo crusade (1487-88) - survived; the thread the 1532 Chanforan synod (VI.10) receives at the era-7 gate
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: IV.8 ends 1300 and the census's clearest dissent-that-survived thread jumped 232 years by edge alone. Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 1300 to 1517 (era window; the 1487-88 Cattaneo crusade survived inside; VI.10's Chanforan 1532 receives at the era-7 gate) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: The Cottian Alps and beyond, 1300 to 1517 — an outlawed church of scattered households, held together by preachers who walked to them.
movements.longDescription: A century and more after being condemned, the Waldensians had become something no medieval dissent was supposed to be: a durable, organized, underground church. Its members lived openly as ordinary Catholic parishioners and privately as something else, in the high valleys of the Cottian Alps between Piedmont and Dauphiné, and in scattered communities in Provence, in Calabria and Apulia, in Germany and Bohemia. What held it together were the barbes — 'uncles' — itinerant preachers who travelled in pairs, memorized large amounts of scripture in the vernacular, carried small hand-copied books, and worked a circuit of the households. Their existence was known and repeatedly attacked; in 1487 Innocent VIII proclaimed a crusade against them, and the campaign that followed tore through valleys on both sides of the Alps. They survived it.
voices: The barbes are named individually only rarely, and mostly in the records of the people prosecuting them — the church was built so that no single figure held it together, and its continuity rested on the circuit of preachers and the households that sheltered them
movements.legacy: They are the one medieval dissenting movement still here. In 1532, at a synod at Chanforan in the Angrogna valley, the Waldensians of the Alps joined the Protestant Reformation, and the church that resulted still exists as the Waldensian Evangelical Church, based in the same valleys, now in union with Italy's Methodists, with a sister church in Argentina and Uruguay and congregations founded by emigrants in the United States. The valleys themselves keep the memory in place names, in caves and hidden meeting-places, and in a museum network the church runs.

experienceToday.text: Torre Pellice, Italy — the Waldensian Cultural Centre Foundation and its historical museum, in the Alpine valleys the barbes' circuit ran

movements.name: The Church of the East — Timur's Catastrophe and the Hakkari Remnant
movements.informalName: The Mountain Remnant of Asia's Great Church
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 6 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run as IV.22's terminal receiver. Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Thin and partly late [S]: patriarchal succession lists, colophons, Timothy II's 1318 synod records; the catastrophe itself documented mostly from outside
movements.floorNote: No question — the same communion this church has always been in.
movements.relationsSummary: Yahballaha III dies 1317 under the anti-Christian reaction; Timur's campaigns (1380s-1405) destroy the lowland church; the survivors hold the Hakkari mountains - with India (V.23) the one un-destroyed province; the 1552 Sulaqa split falls to era 7's sweep
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: IV.22 ends 1317 and Asia's great church's reduction to a mountain remnant - one of Christian history's largest single catastrophes - had no entry. Tier 3 signal (thin, disclosed); awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 1317 (Yahballaha III's death - IV.22's gated end) to 1517 (era end; the 1552 Sulaqa split is era 7's) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: From Mesopotamia to the Kurdish mountains, 1317 to 1517 — the collapse of the most widely spread church in the medieval world into a handful of highland valleys.
movements.longDescription: For centuries the Church of the East had been the most geographically extensive church on earth, with metropolitan provinces running from Baghdad across Central Asia to India and China. It ended within a lifetime. When the patriarch Yahballaha III — a monk born far to the east among the Öngüd — died in 1317, the Mongol rulers of Persia had already turned to Islam and made Christians a persecuted minority in Mesopotamia; then Timur's campaigns between the 1380s and 1405 destroyed the lowland dioceses outright, along with much of the population that had sustained them. What survived did so by geography: communities in the Hakkari mountains and around Lake Van and Urmia, where the patriarchate relocated and where, over the fifteenth century, the office became hereditary within a single family, passing from uncle to nephew. The one province Timur never reached was the community on the Malabar coast of India, which went on receiving bishops from a patriarch who now governed from a mountain village.
voices: Yahballaha III — the last patriarch of the church's Mongol-era expansion, who died in 1317 as the persecutions closed in
Timothy II — patriarch in the years just before the collapse, whose synod of 1318 is among the last acts of the old order
Beyond the patriarchs, the people of this era reach us mainly as names in manuscript colophons — scribes recording who they were, where they were copying, and what was happening around them
movements.legacy: The remnant endured. The hereditary patriarchate that formed in the mountains split in 1552, when part of the church entered communion with Rome, and the two lines run to the present as the Assyrian Church of the East and the Chaldean Catholic Church. Their Syriac liturgy and their manuscript tradition are carried now by communities largely dispersed by the persecutions and displacements of the twentieth century. And the Indian province that outlasted the catastrophe became the St Thomas Christians of Kerala, whose descendants number several million.

movements.name: Terminal Christian Nubia (Late Makuria and Dotawo)
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 6 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run as III.18's terminal receiver. Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Archaeology-grade at both ends (Barshambu's 1317 stela in the converted throne hall; the Gebel Adda letter naming King Joel, 1484; Faras and Tamit inscriptions); inside literary voice thin - the III.18 disclosure pattern
movements.relationsSummary: The Nubian story's actual end: Dongola's throne hall becomes a mosque (1317), Makuria fragments, the successor kingdom of Dotawo persists to King Joel (documented 1484), then the record falls silent (a possible Queen Gaua c. 1520s carried as live-scholarship nuance)
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: III.18 ended 1054 with no receiver and the story's real end - a church dying slowly over four centuries - had no entry anywhere. Start 1054 precedes the era by 246 years; the defining gravity-window (1317, 1484) is this era's - the standing-rule extension is Mark's to grant. Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 1054 (III.18's gated end) to c. 1484 (King Joel of Dotawo, the last documented; Gaua c. 1520s carried as nuance). Era-6 slot ruled at the Freeze under a standing-rule extension; the III.18 succession FIELD is withheld (4->6 forbidden) - the relation is this entry's named register line (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: The Middle Nile, 1054 to about 1484 — the slow ending of a Christian kingdom that had held the Nile above Egypt for eight hundred years.
movements.longDescription: Christian Nubia had been a going concern since the sixth century: kingdoms with cathedrals and bishops, a literature in Old Nubian, Greek and Coptic, and treaties that kept Muslim Egypt at a distance. Its ending took four centuries and left an unusually physical record. In 1317 the throne hall of the royal palace at Dongola was converted into a mosque, and the stone that records it is still legible. Makuria fragmented after that, and a smaller successor kingdom, Dotawo, persisted downstream around Gebel Adda and Qasr Ibrim, still issuing documents in Old Nubian, still with a king and a bishop. The last of them anyone can name is King Joel, documented in 1484. After that the record simply stops — no conquest, no massacre, no final synod; just documents that cease, and a population that over the following generations became Muslim.
voices: Almost no one from these centuries speaks to us directly. The names we have — King Joel of Dotawo, the bishops in their epitaphs, the officials in the Old Nubian documents from Qasr Ibrim — are names on deeds and tombstones rather than voices, and no Nubian account of the church's own ending survives
movements.legacy: No church continued and no community carried the tradition forward. What survived is material, and was very nearly lost as well: when the Aswan High Dam was built in the 1960s an international rescue campaign lifted the wall paintings out of the cathedral at Faras before the reservoir covered it, and exceptionally dry conditions at Qasr Ibrim preserved a large archive of Old Nubian, Greek, Coptic and Arabic documents. Because of that salvage, a Christian civilization that left no descendants is better documented now than it was a century ago, and its painting can be seen in museums in Warsaw and Khartoum.

experienceToday.text: The Faras Gallery, National Museum in Warsaw — the rescued wall paintings from Faras cathedral, the only permanent display of medieval Nubian painting in Europe

movements.name: The Franciscan Order — Spirituals Crisis to the Great Division
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run - the inherited Franciscan-shape flag resolved as the order's own era-6 entry (the A5-inside-V.14 alternative stays stated). Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Rich: the poverty-controversy dossiers (Quorundam exigit 1317, Cum inter nonnullos 1323), Observant and Conventual records, Ite vos (1517); Clareno and Olivi's internal literature beyond the inquisition record
movements.floorNote: No question — the poverty condemnations were about obedience and property, not the Creed.
movements.relationsSummary: The order between IV.4 (ends 1300) and the 1517 division: the Spirituals crisis (Marseille burnings 1318), Conventual/Observant polarization, Leo X's Ite vos (29 May 1517) splitting the family in two; V.12 Fraticelli and V.9's Franciscan wing are its two named wings
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: the order itself vanished from the census between 1300 and the Capuchins' era while its two wings (V.9, V.12) hung A5-shaped around a missing center. Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 1300 (era boundary; IV.4's end) to 1517 (Ite vos, 29 May 1517 - the Great Division) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: Across Latin Christendom, 1300 to 1517 — two centuries in which Francis's order argued with itself about poverty until the pope cut it in two.
movements.longDescription: By 1300 the Franciscans were an enormous international order with universities, libraries and buildings, and a founder who had told them to own nothing. The strain broke in the 1310s and 20s. The Spirituals, who wanted the Rule kept to the letter, were ordered to conform; four were burned at Marseille in 1318 for refusing; and in 1323 John XXII declared it heretical to teach that Christ and the apostles had owned nothing at all, which put the order's own official self-understanding on the wrong side of the law. The minister general Michael of Cesena fled the papal court with William of Ockham rather than accept it. The argument did not end so much as change shape, into a long polarization between Conventuals, who accepted the order's endowments and urban convents, and Observants, who from 1368 built up reformed houses keeping the Rule strictly. Leo X ended the pretence of a single order on 29 May 1517, dividing the family formally in two.
voices: Ubertino da Casale — the Spirituals' most forceful advocate at the papal court
Angelo Clareno — led the surviving rigorists and wrote their own history of the order's persecutions
Michael of Cesena — minister general, who defied John XXII over poverty and fled Avignon in 1328
William of Ockham — the philosopher who left with him, and who turned the poverty quarrel into a theory of rights and of the limits of papal power
Pope John XXII — who closed the poverty question by declaring one side of it heretical
movements.legacy: The order is still here, and still divided along the line drawn in 1517: the Order of Friars Minor and the Conventual Franciscans both date their separate legal existence from that bull, and the Capuchins broke away from the Observants a decade later, making three. Beyond the family, the poverty controversy left a real intellectual inheritance — the arguments about use, ownership and right worked out in it, above all by Ockham, fed into later Western thinking about property and about the limits of authority. And the Observant reform that grew out of the crisis became one of the main engines of Catholic renewal in the century that followed.

movements.name: The Bosnian Church (Krstjani)
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 6 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run - the question Era 5 routed here, carried with the identification debate honest. Status fork (plain candidate [lead lean] vs Contested-Evidentiary) is Mark's; the c. 1230s start fork has BOTH branches open (standing-rule extension, or start 1300 + origin note if declined). Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Largely external (papal condemnations, Ragusan records); Gost Radin's 1466 testament is the one great inside document - and it reads orthodox, a cross drawn down its margin
movements.floorNote: The old identification of the krstjani as Bogomil dualists has been rejected by most scholarship since the 1970s, so this is not a case of a church known to have departed from Nicene belief. What they actually held is still debated; that the church existed, with its hierarchy of djed, gost and starac and its own monastic houses, is not in doubt. It is treated here as a Slavonic-rite church standing between Rome and Orthodoxy, with the ambiguity acknowledged rather than resolved.
movements.relationsSummary: The autonomous church of medieval Bosnia - condemned by Rome as heretical, defended by its own kings, ending with the Ottoman conquest (Bosnia falls 1463; Radin's testament 1466); NOT folded into the Bogomil register, per the Era 5 ruling and current scholarship
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: a real, organized, autonomous church that the census carried only as a question inside someone else's register debate. Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: c. 1230s (standing-rule extension granted at the Freeze, as drafted) to 1463 (the Ottoman conquest of Bosnia; Radin's testament 1466 just past) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: Medieval Bosnia, c. 1230s to 1463 — an independent church whose members called themselves simply Christians, and whose beliefs are still argued over.
movements.longDescription: Between Catholic Hungary and Orthodox Serbia, medieval Bosnia had a church of its own. Its members called themselves krstjani, Christians; it used a Slavonic liturgy, and it had its own hierarchy headed by a djed, a 'grandfather', with gosts and starci under him and communities called hiže, houses, scattered through the countryside. Rome repeatedly condemned it as heretical and periodically sent friars against it, while Bosnia's own rulers protected and made use of it. What its members actually believed remains genuinely disputed: the long-standing identification of them with Bogomil dualism has been rejected by most historians since the 1970s, and the one substantial document written from inside — the will of Gost Radin, made in 1466 — reads like conventional Christianity, with a cross drawn down its margin. Bosnia fell to the Ottomans in 1463, and the church did not outlast the kingdom.
voices: Gost Radin — a senior figure of the church and a courtier, whose testament of 1466 is the only substantial document written from inside it
Ban Kulin — the ruler at whose court, in 1203, an abjuration was made that stands at the disputed beginning of the whole story
Beyond a handful of djeds and gosts who witnessed royal charters, the church's members are anonymous
movements.legacy: Nothing continued. After the Ottoman conquest the krstjani disappear from the record within a generation or two, absorbed into Islam, Catholicism and Orthodoxy, and no later church claims descent from them. What remains is inscriptional and archaeological: charters and grave inscriptions naming djeds and gosts, and the stećci, the great carved limestone tombstones of medieval Bosnia and its neighbours — though those were raised by Catholics and Orthodox as well, and the once-popular idea that they are specifically a Bosnian Church monument is no longer accepted. The church's other legacy is the argument about it, which became part of Bosnian national self-understanding in the twentieth century and is still running.

experienceToday.text: Stećci medieval tombstone graveyards — 28 necropolises in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia, inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site

movements.name: Armenian Christianity after the Kingdom (Sis to Etchmiadzin)
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 6 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run as IV.20's receiver segment. Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Thin after Shnorhali's generation; colophons rich [S] - the era's Armenian voice survives mostly in scribes' margins
movements.floorNote: No question — the ancient miaphysite confession, unchanged.
movements.relationsSummary: The kingdom falls (Sis 1375; Levon V dies in exile 1393); the catholicosate remains at Sis until a national council elects a catholicos at Etchmiadzin (1441) - the national spine relocates home, Sis continuing as a second catholicosate; the 1441-1915 hole to IX.27 stays the spine's longest named gap
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: IV.20 ends 1300 and the kingdom's fall + the see's return home - the spine's defining relocation - had no entry. Ends at 1441, a genuine gravity end. Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 1300 (era boundary; IV.20's gated end) to 1441 (the catholicosate returns to Etchmiadzin - the national spine relocates home) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: From Cilicia to Ararat, 1300 to 1441 — a church that lost its kingdom and moved its see back to where it had started.
movements.longDescription: The Armenian kingdom of Cilicia on the Mediterranean spent the fourteenth century under pressure from Mamluk Egypt and from Latin Europe at the same time: repeated attempts to seal a union with Rome, pressed by kings who needed western help, were resisted by clergy and people who saw the church's independence at stake. The kingdom fell in 1375 when the Mamluks took Sis, and its last king died in exile in Paris in 1393. The catholicosate stayed at Sis for two more generations, increasingly cut off from the great majority of Armenians living far to the east under other rulers, until in 1441 a national council meeting at Vagharshapat elected a catholicos at Etchmiadzin — the church's original see, left behind nearly a thousand years earlier — and the centre of Armenian church life moved home. Sis did not surrender its own succession, so the church has had two catholicosates ever since. Much of what we hear from Armenians of this period comes from colophons: the notes scribes wrote at the ends of the manuscripts they copied, recording who they were and what was happening around them.
voices: Levon V — the last king of Armenian Cilicia, who died in exile in Paris in 1393
Grigor Tatevatsi — theologian of the monastic university at Tatev, whose teaching stiffened Armenian resistance to union with Rome
Kirakos of Virap — elected catholicos at Etchmiadzin in 1441, first of the restored line
The scribes of the colophons — mostly anonymous copyists whose notes at the ends of manuscripts are this era's fullest Armenian account of itself
movements.legacy: Etchmiadzin has been the Mother See of the Armenian Apostolic Church ever since 1441, and remains so today. The see at Sis, whose holder did not move, kept its own succession and continues as the Catholicosate of Cilicia, based since the 1930s at Antelias in Lebanon — the two sees still in communion with one another. The manuscripts of these centuries, colophons and all, form the core of the Matenadaran collection in Yerevan, and the colophon habit has left historians one of the most detailed running records of ordinary catastrophe and survival anywhere in the medieval world.

experienceToday.text: Etchmiadzin Cathedral, Vagharshapat, Armenia — the Mother See the church returned to in 1441, a UNESCO World Heritage Site

movements.informalName: The Maronites of Lebanon and Cyprus
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 6 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run as IV.10's receiver - closing the dead-end with the thread's own defining event inside the window. Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: Thin-to-moderate, much of it Rome-side [S]: the Florence union act (1445), Fifth Lateran reception (1516); the patriarchal archive's era-6 layer not verifiable this session
movements.floorNote: No question — the monothelete dispute is an argument about the church's early history, not about what Maronites confess now.
movements.relationsSummary: Mamluk raids on Kesrwan (1305 [S]); the union with Rome - the tradition's own 'unique early union' identity - formalized at Florence's last public act (the Cyprus Maronites, 7 Aug 1445) and affirmed during Fifth Lateran (1516)
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: IV.10 dead-ended at 1300 in every later era while the union that defines the tradition was formalized in this very window. Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 1300 (era boundary; IV.10's gated end) to 1517 (era end; the union formalized inside - Florence 1445, Fifth Lateran reception 1516) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: Mount Lebanon and Cyprus, 1300 to 1517 — a mountain church that turned a long-claimed friendship with Rome into a formal, permanent union.
movements.longDescription: The Maronites were a Syriac-speaking church of the Lebanese mountains, with a patriarch based in the Qadisha valley and communities on Cyprus as well. The fourteenth century opened badly, with Mamluk campaigns against the Kesrwan around 1305 that displaced Christian populations, and for most of the period the church survived largely by remoteness — monasteries and rock-cut hermitages tucked into a gorge that armies found expensive to enter. Its relationship with Rome, claimed since the crusader period, was made explicit in this window: at the Council of Florence, in an act of 7 August 1445, the Maronites of Cyprus were formally received into union with the Roman church, and the relationship was affirmed again during the Fifth Lateran Council in 1516. Unlike almost every other Eastern church, the Maronites hold that they were never out of communion with Rome at all — a self-understanding that this era's documents put on paper.
voices: Named individuals are scarce in this window: the patriarchs of the period are known mainly from succession lists and from the Roman documents addressed to them, and the era's Maronite voice survives chiefly in liturgical manuscripts and scribes' notes rather than in personal writing
movements.legacy: It is a living church. The Maronite Church remains in full communion with Rome, is the largest Christian body in Lebanon, and has a worldwide diaspora; its patriarch still carries the title of Antioch, and the Syriac liturgy of these centuries is still in use in developed form. The Qadisha valley stayed the patriarchate's refuge for centuries afterward, and its monasteries and hermitages are still there.

experienceToday.text: Ouadi Qadisha (the Holy Valley) and the Forest of the Cedars of God, Lebanon — the gorge that sheltered the Maronite patriarchate and its monasteries, a UNESCO World Heritage Site

movements.name: St Thomas Christians, 1300-1517
movements.informalName: The Malabar Church before the Portuguese
movements.statusWord: Researched — deferred, richer window later (Era 6 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 6 Step 0 run with St-Thomas-pattern honesty. No continuesAs from III.11 - the eras are non-adjacent; the 1054-1300 gap stays a named register. Added at the Era 6 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-02).
movements.sourcing: THIN, better than the prior window: MS Vatican Syriac 22 copied at Cranganore 1301 (oldest dated Syriac manuscript from India, naming Yahballaha III); 14th-c. travelers' notices [S]; the 1490 delegation and 1504 bishops' letter [S]; da Gama 1498
movements.floorNote: No question — the same communion this church has always been in.
movements.relationsSummary: The community between III.11 (ends 1054) and VI.18 (starts 1599): a dated inside colophon opens the window, real correspondence with the catholicos closes it; with the Hakkari remnant (V.17), the province Timur never reached; the 1517-1599 gap to VI.18 goes to era 7's sweep
movements.why: Proposed by the completeness sweep: this window is materially better-attested than the 1054-1300 stretch era 5 declined (a dated inside document at its first year). Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: 1300 to 1517 (era window; the 1301 Cranganore colophon opens it, the 1490/1504 correspondence [S] closes it; both adjacent gaps stay named) (Era 6 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)
movements.teaser: The Malabar coast, 1300 to 1517 — an Indian church worshipping in Syriac and governed from Mesopotamia, in the last two centuries before Europe arrived.
movements.longDescription: On the pepper coast of south-west India there had been Christians for longer than anyone could document, who traced their founding to the apostle Thomas, worshipped in Syriac, and belonged to the Church of the East, receiving their bishops from its patriarch far away in Mesopotamia. In this window they come into focus. A Syriac manuscript copied at Cranganore in 1301 — the oldest dated Syriac manuscript from India — names the patriarch Yahballaha III in its colophon, showing the link intact. Socially the community was no marginal minority but an established, high-status trading group with privileges from Hindu rulers and a headman of its own. By the late fifteenth century, with the church's Mesopotamian heartland shattered, the connection had to be actively maintained: a delegation travelled to the patriarch around 1490 asking for bishops, and the bishops who came back wrote home in 1504 describing the community — and the arrival of Portuguese ships.
voices: Yahballaha III — the distant patriarch named in the 1301 Cranganore colophon, the era's clearest evidence that the link to Mesopotamia held
Mar Jacob — one of the bishops sent from Mesopotamia after the delegation of about 1490, who served in Malabar into the Portuguese period
The community is otherwise largely anonymous in this window: its record survives in manuscript colophons and in letters written about it rather than by it
movements.legacy: The community is still here. The centuries after 1517 brought Portuguese pressure, the Synod of Diamper in 1599 and the Coonan Cross revolt of 1653, which between them divided the St Thomas Christians into the several churches they remain — Syro-Malabar and Syro-Malankara Catholics, the Malankara Orthodox and Jacobite Syrian churches, the Mar Thoma Church and others — together numbering several million people in Kerala and around the world. Syriac is still used liturgically among them, and the claim of apostolic origin from Thomas that this era's documents already take for granted is still the community's defining self-description.

movements.name: Lutheran Wittenberg & Its Congregations
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) — rich in both directions, with Luther's corpus on one side and the congregations' own lived record on the other, including women's voices in verified modern editions (Argula von Grumbach, Katharina Zell). The visitation records carry a care note: what they show about ordinary knowledge is itself a live scholarly debate. The Augustinian Hermits were routed into this entry's record as Luther's seedbed rather than given an entry of their own.
movements.sourcing: RICH at every level - including visitation records showing what villagers actually knew (disillusioning and honest)
movements.relationsSummary: Child of late-medieval piety and its protest; rival of Rome, sibling-rival of the Reformed; the Augustinian Hermits are its seedbed (Luther’s own order [S]) — their Reformation-lands houses dissolved into this story, the Catholic remainder continuing in the Tridentine orbit

Very few entries in the atlas let a movement's ideal and its ordinary reception be checked against each other so directly. Its lay record also includes women publishing under their own names in the 1520s, which almost nothing else this early can show.

movements.longDescription: Wittenberg was a small Saxon university town when one of its theology professors, an Augustinian friar named Martin Luther, began arguing in public about indulgences, penance and the authority of Scripture — and within a few years a movement had grown around him that reorganised worship, emptied monasteries, and put the Bible, a catechism and a hymnbook into ordinary German households. What that looked like from the pew is documented unusually well: from 1527-28 the Saxon churches sent visitors out to examine parish after parish, and their reports are frank about how little many villagers actually knew. The movement settled its own arguments in writing — the Augsburg Confession of 1530, then the Book of Concord of 1580 — and the churches shaped by it spread north and east across Germany and Scandinavia, where they remain.
movements.teaser: Saxony and then northern Europe, 1517 to 1580 — a university town's quarrel over indulgences that ended with catechisms, hymnbooks and a new confession of faith in ordinary households.
voices: Martin Luther — Wittenberg theology professor whose 1517 protest began the movement, and whose catechisms and hymns shaped its ordinary worship
Philipp Melanchthon — Luther's colleague, author of the Augsburg Confession (1530) and of the instructions that sent visitors out to inspect Saxon parishes
Katharina von Bora — former nun who married Luther and ran the household that became the movement's most-watched model of a pastor's family
Argula von Grumbach — Bavarian noblewoman who published pamphlets under her own name in the 1520s defending the evangelical cause
Katharina Schütz Zell — Strasbourg pastor's wife who published devotional writing, hymn collections and open letters in her own name
movements.legacy: It became the Lutheran churches — an ongoing communion of tens of millions across Germany, Scandinavia, the Baltic and North America, and, through later missions, Africa and Asia. Its most durable everyday bequest is less doctrinal than liturgical and musical: congregational hymn-singing in the local language, the small catechism learned by heart at home, and a tradition of church music that runs from Luther's own tunes through to Bach.

experienceToday.text: The Luther museums in Lutherstadt Wittenberg, Germany — Luther's own house and Melanchthon's, a UNESCO World Heritage site

It also holds one of the best ordinary-life archives in Christian history: Geneva's consistory registers set down, week by week and name by name, what a city's church actually did about the ordinary conduct of ordinary people. Enormous downstream reach and granular evidence of daily practice rarely sit together anywhere on the map.

movements.longDescription: Two Swiss city-states, a generation apart, worked out what a whole town would look like if its church were rebuilt from Scripture: Zurich under Huldrych Zwingli from 1519, which stripped images and the Mass out of its churches; and Geneva after 1536 under John Calvin, whose Ecclesiastical Ordinances of 1541 gave the city pastors, teachers, elders and deacons, and a consistory that met every week. Geneva's consistory registers survive, and they are startlingly ordinary — quarrels between neighbours, absent husbands, people who had not been to church — which makes this one of the best pictures anywhere of what a church actually did about the daily conduct of ordinary people. From these two cities the Reformed pattern travelled: Scotland, France, the Netherlands and English Puritanism all trace back here.
movements.teaser: Zurich and Geneva, 1519 to 1650 — two small cities that rebuilt church and civic life out of Scripture, and kept the minutes.
voices: Huldrych Zwingli — Zurich's people's priest from 1519, whose preaching and public disputations carried the city into reform
Heinrich Bullinger — Zwingli's successor, who steadied Zurich for four decades and corresponded with Protestants across Europe
John Calvin — the French exile who gave Geneva its church order, its catechism, and the Institutes
Theodore Beza — Calvin's successor at Geneva and co-author of the metrical psalter the Reformed world sang
Marie Dentière — former abbess turned Genevan reformer, who published in her own name arguing that women could speak about Scripture
movements.legacy: Reformed and Presbyterian churches worldwide descend from these two cities, and so do four traditions this map carries separately — the Scottish Kirk, the Huguenots, the Dutch Reformed and English Puritanism. Beyond doctrine the everyday inheritance is a style: plain whitewashed interiors with the pulpit at the centre, congregational psalm-singing in the language people spoke, and church government by elected elders rather than by bishops.

experienceToday.text: The International Museum of the Reformation, Geneva — beside St Peter's Cathedral, in the old cloister where the city voted for reform
The Grossmünster, Zurich — Zwingli's own church, still open to visitors

movements.name: The Anabaptist Movements
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on a rich base read with genre care — the Martyrs Mirror and the Hutterite Chronicle alongside the movement's own hymnody, with the court testimonies flagged as coerced rather than taken as plain inside voice. Its end was moved to 1650, bringing the Dordrecht Confession (1632) back inside its own window; the previous 1600 had stranded it.
movements.sourcing: RICH in ordinary inside voice: court testimonies, prison hymns, the Martyrs Mirror, Hutterite Chronicle
movements.floorNote: The mainstream of the movement held the historic creeds' teaching about God and Christ, though Menno Simons and the Dutch wing taught a distinctive doctrine of Christ's heavenly flesh that their neighbours disputed. The era's anti-Trinitarian groups are a separate story, told elsewhere on this map.
movements.relationsSummary: Persecuted by Lutheran, Reformed, and Catholic traditions alike - a loud tension in the sources; parent of the free-church line
movements.why: Persecuted by Lutheran, Reformed and Catholic authorities alike — the one movement of the era that all three of its neighbours agreed to suppress, which by itself says something the confessional histories do not. Its inside voice is unusually ordinary: prison hymns, court testimony, a martyrology the communities kept for themselves. The whole free-church line descends from it, so a large share of later Protestantism traces back to people their own century treated as criminals.
movements.dateRationale: End 1650 (continues-cap; living; the Dordrecht Confession 1632 [S] rescued in-window — the old 1600 stranded it; alt c. 1632 was shown) (Era 7 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-02)

movements.longDescription: In January 1525 a handful of men in Zurich, impatient with how slowly their own city's reform was moving, baptised one another as adults — and were hunted for it. Anabaptists held that baptism belonged to those who could confess faith for themselves, that the church was a voluntary body rather than a whole society, and, for most of them, that a Christian could neither swear oaths nor take up the sword; Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed authorities alike treated this as sedition and executed them by the hundreds. The survivors regrouped: Hutterite communities holding goods in common in Moravia, and in the Low Countries the congregations gathered by a former priest, Menno Simons, whose name their descendants still carry.
movements.teaser: Swiss lands, Moravia and the Low Countries, 1525 to 1650 — believers who baptised one another as adults and were hunted for it by every other church of their century.
voices: Conrad Grebel — Zurich radical, among the first to be re-baptised in January 1525
Felix Manz — drowned in the Limmat at Zurich in 1527, the movement's first martyr at Protestant hands
Michael Sattler — former Benedictine prior, principal author of the Schleitheim Articles of 1527 and executed that same year
Menno Simons — Dutch priest who left his parish in 1536 and gathered the scattered congregations that took his name
Anneken Jans — executed at Rotterdam in 1539, whose testament written for her infant son survives in the movement's own martyr book
movements.legacy: The movement survives directly: Mennonites, Amish, Hutterites and Brethren all descend from it, and the wider free-church principle — that membership is a voluntary adult commitment and that the church should not be an arm of the state — became one of the most widely adopted Protestant ideas in the world. Its martyr book, the Martyrs Mirror of 1660, is still printed and still read aloud in Amish and Mennonite homes.

experienceToday.text: The Täuferhöhle near Bäretswil, Switzerland — the cave in the hills outside Zurich where hunted Anabaptists met to worship, reachable on a short marked walk
The Menno Simons monument at Witmarsum, Friesland — freely accessible, on the site where he is said to have preached to his congregation

movements.name: The English Reformation & Elizabethan Settlement
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) — the Prayer Book as lived formation, with churchwardens' evidence continuing from the late-medieval parish entry's base. Its end was extended at the Freeze to 1650 so that it carries the Stuart century itself rather than leaving a 47-year micro-entry, the Elizabethan-close alternative having been shown and declined; the absence of any Church of England entry between 1650 and 1815 was flagged forward.
movements.sourcing: Rich: liturgy (BCP), martyrology, visitation, wills tracking belief-change across decades
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Lutheran/Reformed influences on native soil; parent of Anglican and dissenting lines; extended at the Era 7 gate to carry the Stuart century (1604 Hampton Court to the Westminster Assembly [S]) - the C7 scope-fix
movements.why: The clearest case in the atlas of a reformation carried by a book of prayer rather than by a confession of faith — what changed English religion is what people were required to say together, week after week. Its evidence lets that change be tracked from below: wills written in the same parishes across decades register what ordinary people believed about the dead as the formulas they used shift under them. The entry now carries the Stuart century as well, so it holds the whole arc rather than stopping at Elizabeth.

movements.longDescription: England's Reformation began as a king's quarrel — Henry VIII's break with Rome in the 1530s — and only afterwards became a change in what people believed, swinging hard toward Protestantism under Edward VI, back to Rome under Mary I, and settling under Elizabeth I into a church that kept bishops and cathedrals while preaching a Protestant gospel. What actually altered English religion was less a confession of faith than a book: the Book of Common Prayer, first issued in 1549 and revised in 1552, 1559 and 1662, which fixed the words the whole country was required to say together, week after week. The change can be watched from below in churchwardens' accounts and in the wills of ordinary people, whose formulas about the soul and the dead shift decade by decade — and the settlement held, uneasily, until the civil wars of the 1640s broke it open again.
movements.teaser: England, the 1530s to 1650 — a reformation carried less by a confession of faith than by a book of prayer the whole country had to say aloud together.
voices: Thomas Cranmer — Archbishop of Canterbury and chief architect of the Book of Common Prayer, burned at Oxford in 1556
Elizabeth I — whose settlement of 1559 fixed the shape of the English church for centuries
John Jewel — Bishop of Salisbury, whose Apology of 1562 defended that settlement to the rest of Europe
Richard Hooker — its theologian, author of Of the Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity from 1593
John Foxe — martyrologist whose Acts and Monuments gave English Protestantism its memory of the Marian burnings
movements.legacy: It became the Church of England, and through it the worldwide Anglican Communion. Its most far-reaching bequest is verbal: the cadences of the Book of Common Prayer and of the King James Bible of 1611 shaped English-language worship, and phrases from both — 'till death us do part', 'ashes to ashes, dust to dust' — passed into ordinary speech far beyond any church. The dissenting traditions that later broke away from it, Puritan, Congregational and Baptist, are equally its children.

movements.name: The Scottish Reformation & Kirk
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2), on kirk-session discipline records the census rates denser still than Geneva's. Its distinctness from its Genevan parent — a national-covenantal formation logic of its own — stands as the real uniqueness test any build would have to pass.
movements.sourcing: RICH - kirk-session discipline records even denser than Geneva's
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Geneva; distinct national-covenantal formation logic (a real uniqueness test)
movements.why: Its kirk-session records are denser still than Geneva's, which makes this the atlas's single best archive of church discipline as actually administered — parish by parish, and mostly over quite small matters. Its real test is distinctness from its Genevan parent, and the honest answer is a formation logic of its own: national and covenantal, a whole people bound rather than a city governed. Whether that suffices to make it a separate tradition rather than a Genevan province is precisely what a build would have to argue.

movements.longDescription: In 1560 the Scottish Parliament abolished papal authority and adopted a Reformed confession of faith, and the church that followed set out to remake a whole nation rather than a single city: a minister and a school in every parish, and in each parish a kirk session of elders meeting to deal with quarrels, drunkenness, broken promises and sexual misconduct. Those session registers survive in extraordinary quantity, which makes Scotland the best-documented case anywhere of church discipline as it was actually administered — usually over small matters, among neighbours who then had to go on living beside each other. The Kirk's covenanting instinct, the idea of a whole people bound to God by public oath, came to a head in the National Covenant of 1638 and in the conflicts that followed it.
movements.teaser: Scotland, 1560 to 1650 — a church that set out to reform an entire nation parish by parish, and wrote down what it found there.
voices: John Knox — preacher and polemicist, the Reformation's loudest Scottish voice and the author of its partisan first history
Andrew Melville — who pressed the Kirk toward a fully presbyterian government in the decades after Knox's death
Archibald Johnston of Wariston — lawyer, co-drafter of the National Covenant of 1638, and a relentless diarist of his own conscience
movements.legacy: It became the Church of Scotland, and through emigration and mission the worldwide Presbyterian family. Its ambition of a school in every parish left Scotland unusually literate for its time, and its habit of government by elected elders sitting in courts of the church — session, presbytery, assembly — was carried onto every continent. Metrical psalm-singing in the Scottish manner is still heard in Gaelic congregations today.

experienceToday.text: John Knox House on Edinburgh's Royal Mile — a 1470s townhouse and museum, now part of the Scottish Storytelling Centre

movements.name: The Huguenots
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 7 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on synod acts, memoirs, martyrologies and refugee narratives. Its start was moved to 1559, the first national synod at Paris and the church's own organizational birth, replacing a soft 1550s.

Its distinctive genre is the refugee narrative — people writing about what it was to leave, which the atlas has very little of otherwise. It begins with an act of self-organization rather than a ruler's decision, which sets it apart from most of the era's other national Reformations.

movements.longDescription: France's Protestants organised themselves before any ruler told them to: in 1559 delegates met secretly in Paris to adopt a confession of faith and a book of discipline, creating a national church inside a Catholic kingdom. What followed was nearly a century of civil war and precarious tolerance — the St Bartholomew's Day massacres of August 1572, the Edict of Nantes in 1598 that gave them legal existence and fortified towns, then the slow erosion of that edict until Louis XIV revoked it in 1685. Rather than convert, several hundred thousand left, carrying their trades, their psalters and their memory of what it was to flee into England, the Dutch Republic, Prussia, Switzerland, South Africa and the American colonies.
movements.teaser: France, 1559 to 1685 — a church that organised itself in secret, survived a century of civil war, and then scattered across the world rather than convert.
voices: Gaspard de Coligny — Admiral of France and the Huguenots' leading noble protector, killed at the outset of the St Bartholomew's Day massacre in 1572
Philippe Duplessis-Mornay — statesman and theologian, the movement's chief negotiator and apologist
Charlotte Arbaleste de Mornay — his wife, whose memoirs record her own escape from the 1572 massacre
Jean Crespin — Genevan printer whose martyrology gathered the letters and last words of executed French Protestants
movements.legacy: The tradition still exists in France, in the united Protestant church that grew out of it, and the dispersion left permanent traces abroad: Huguenot surnames, silk-weaving and watchmaking trades, and congregations founded in London, Berlin, Amsterdam, Cape Town and Charleston. The English word 'refugee' comes from the French réfugié, a word that came into use for them.

experienceToday.text: The Musée du Désert in the Cévennes, France — the memorial museum of Huguenot persecution and clandestine worship, in the farmhouse country where it happened

That echo across the whole width of the atlas is worth drawing for its own sake. It is also the era's counter-case — the Reformation seen from the side that stayed, and paid for staying.
