movements.longDescription: In 1796 a Norwegian farmer's son named Hans Nielsen Hauge had a religious experience while working in his father's field, and set out on foot to tell people about it — which was against the law, because Norway's Conventicle Act reserved religious meetings to the parish clergy. He wrote thirty-three books and tracts, walked thousands of miles, and founded mills, paper works and trading businesses to support the network of "friends" that grew around him; the state answered by arresting him in 1804 and keeping him in prison and under prosecution for most of the following decade. The movement long outlasted the man: after his death in 1824 the friends' societies went on meeting and trading, and in 1842 the Conventicle Act itself was repealed.
movements.teaser: Norway, 1796 to 1842 — a farmer's son who walked the country preaching without a licence, wrote thirty-three books, built factories to pay for it, and spent most of a decade in prison.
voices: Hans Nielsen Hauge — lay preacher, author of thirty-three books, industrial entrepreneur, and prisoner of the state church for most of a decade

Beyond Hauge himself the movement was deliberately lay and collective — the "friends" ran their own societies, businesses and meetings, and it is those local networks rather than any named successor that carried it on after his death
movements.legacy: Haugean piety became one of the permanent layers of Norwegian Lutheranism: a lay preaching culture, a network of mission societies and prayer houses, and a suspicion of clerical monopoly that outlived the law it was reacting against. Norwegian emigrants carried it into the American Midwest, where Haugean congregations became one of the founding strands of Norwegian-American Lutheranism. In Norway today Hauge is honoured about equally as a revivalist and as an entrepreneur, which would have puzzled almost nobody who knew him.

experienceToday.text: Hans Nielsen Hauge's Memorial Museum, Rolvsøy, Fredrikstad — his birthplace, a protected building from around 1730, with a visitor centre and guided tours

movements.longDescription: After the Napoleonic wars a wave of personal religious awakening ran through the Protestant churches of Switzerland, France, the Netherlands and Germany — in Geneva against a comfortable rationalist establishment, in the Netherlands to the point of secession from the state church in 1834, everywhere with an insistence that faith had to be felt and not merely inherited. What distinguished it was what it built. Johann Hinrich Wichern's Rauhes Haus for street children in Hamburg (1833) grew into the Inner Mission, a whole programme of organized Christian social work; at Kaiserswerth in 1836 Theodor and Friederike Fliedner founded a deaconess motherhouse that trained women as nurses and teachers, and one of its visitors in 1851 was Florence Nightingale. By the time the generation was over, awakened piety in these countries had turned into a permanent network of hospitals, orphanages, schools and training houses.
movements.teaser: Switzerland, France, the Netherlands and Germany, 1815 to 1880 — an awakening that turned personal conversion into hospitals, orphanages and the first Protestant order of nursing sisters.
voices: Johann Hinrich Wichern — founder of the Rauhes Haus in Hamburg and of the Inner Mission, who argued that social work was the church's own business
Theodor and Friederike Fliedner — founders of the Kaiserswerth deaconess motherhouse in 1836, which trained women for nursing, teaching and prison visiting
César Malan — Geneva preacher and hymn-writer, dismissed by the city's church for the fervour of his preaching
Adolphe Monod — the Réveil's greatest French preacher, whose deathbed addresses were taken down and published
Félix Neff — evangelist and practical reformer among the isolated Protestant villages of the French Alps
Isaac da Costa and Guillaume Groen van Prinsterer — the Dutch Réveil's poet-polemicist and its political thinker
movements.legacy: The German Diakonie — the Protestant social-service network the Inner Mission became — is still one of the largest welfare providers in Europe, and the deaconess model spread across the Protestant world and into the professionalization of nursing. The Dutch secession of 1834 grew into a major strand of Reformed Christianity in the Netherlands and, through emigration, in North America. And Wichern left one thing almost everyone has met without knowing it: he made the first Advent wreath at the Rauhes Haus in 1839, so the children in his care could count the days to Christmas.

experienceToday.text: Das Rauhe Haus, Hamburg — Wichern's institution of 1833, still a working diaconal organization on the same site

movements.longDescription: In the 1830s and 40s, thousands of Americans across denominations followed Baptist farmer William Miller's calculation that Christ would return around 1844 — and when the date passed without incident, in what believers still call the Great Disappointment, most walked away disillusioned. A determined remnant didn't: they reread their calculations, concluded the date had marked something other than Christ's visible return, and built lasting communities around that reinterpretation, most enduringly the Seventh-day Adventist Church and a cluster of related Adventist bodies. What makes the story unusual is how openly it was told — the movement wrote down its own failed prediction and its own morning-after reckoning with it — and that same instinct for self-documentation carried into its later history, including its own internal debate over the Trinity in its earliest decades, formally settled in its 1931 statement of belief.
movements.teaser: New England and beyond, 1831 to 1906 — a movement that dated Christ's return, watched the date pass in silence, and chose to write down its own disappointment rather than pretend it never happened.
voices: William Miller — the Baptist farmer-turned-preacher whose calculations sparked the movement
Hiram Edson — reinterpreted the 1844 date's meaning the morning after the Great Disappointment, in a vision on his own farm
Joseph Bates — convinced the movement's other founders to keep the seventh-day Sabbath
Ellen G. White — the movement's central prophetic voice, whose visions and writings shaped its lasting institutions
movements.legacy: This ferment became an ongoing denomination — the Seventh-day Adventist Church, now a global body of tens of millions, along with smaller related Adventist bodies that trace back to the same movement.

experienceToday.text: The William Miller Farm, Low Hampton, New York — his restored home, the chapel he built, and Ascension Rock, open for tours

movements.longDescription: At a small monastery in the forest near Kozelsk, south of Moscow, a hermitage founded in 1821 became the centre of something Russian Orthodoxy had never had at this scale: elders — startsy — who kept the door open to anyone who walked up to it. Peasants, students, landowners and novelists queued outside the cell of Father Ambrose, and the elders who could not see everyone answered by letter, leaving thousands of pages of spiritual direction addressed not to monks but to ordinary people trying to live ordinary lives. They were also publishers: from the 1840s, with the Slavophile thinker Ivan Kireevsky, Optina ran a press that put the Greek ascetic fathers into Russian and made a monastic literature available to laypeople for the first time. Dostoevsky came in 1878 after the death of his small son, and turned what he found there into the elder Zosima.
movements.teaser: Russia, 1821 to 1906 — a forest monastery where monks kept a door open to anyone who knocked, and answered by letter the thousands who could not come.
voices: Leonid of Optina — the first of the elders, who brought the practice of eldership to the hermitage in the 1820s
Macarius of Optina — his successor, and the driving force behind the monastery's publishing work
Ambrose of Optina — the most sought-after of them all, who received visitors daily for decades and whom Dostoevsky met
Ivan Kireevsky — Slavophile philosopher and lay collaborator who helped the monastery become a publishing house
Theophan the Recluse — not an Optina monk, but the bishop whose Russian Philokalia and vast correspondence belong to the same renewal
movements.legacy: The Soviet state closed Optina in 1918 and killed or scattered its monks, but the monastery was returned to the church in 1987 and is active again, receiving thousands of pilgrims a year, with the elders now canonized. The books it printed did more travelling than the monks: the Philokalic spirituality it made available in Russian carried into the émigré theology of twentieth-century Paris and from there into English, and The Way of a Pilgrim, with its Jesus Prayer, became one of the very few Orthodox devotional books widely read in the West — J. D. Salinger built a novel around it in 1961.

experienceToday.text: Optina Pustyn, near Kozelsk, Kaluga region — the monastery of the elders, returned to the church in 1987 and receiving pilgrims again

movements.longDescription: It began as an argument about when to hold memorial services for the dead — Saturday, as tradition had it, or Sunday, as convenience on Mount Athos had made usual — and the monks who insisted on the older practice were nicknamed for the boiled wheat, kollyva, served at those services. The quarrel was small; what came out of it was not. Its leaders argued for frequent communion against a general practice of receiving perhaps once or twice a year, and in 1782 published in Venice the Philokalia, an anthology of Greek ascetic writers on prayer that became one of the most influential books ever printed in Orthodoxy. Under Ottoman rule they also did something with few parallels anywhere in Christian history: they prepared, pastorally and deliberately, people who expected to be executed for refusing to convert, and then wrote up their deaths in a New Martyrologion in 1799. For their trouble the Kollyvades were driven off Athos and scattered through the islands.
movements.teaser: Mount Athos and the Greek islands, 1750s to 1860s — monks mocked over a quarrel about boiled wheat, who published the book that reshaped Orthodox prayer.
voices: Nicodemus the Hagiorite — the movement's great editor and compiler, co-editor of the Philokalia and author of a handbook of spiritual counsel
Macarius of Corinth — bishop and co-editor of the Philokalia, and the movement's advocate of frequent communion
Athanasios Parios — its most combative theologian and defender in the controversy
Kosmas Aitolos — itinerant preacher who founded hundreds of village schools across Greek lands and was executed in 1779; he wrote almost nothing, and survives in what his hearers wrote down
movements.legacy: The Philokalia went straight out of Greek: Paisius Velichkovsky translated it into Slavonic in 1793, Theophan the Recluse into Russian later in the century, and English translations in the twentieth century put it into the hands of readers with no Orthodox background at all. Frequent communion, the practice the Kollyvades were mocked for, is now ordinary across most of the Orthodox world. The movement is generally read as the seed of the modern Greek Orthodox revival, and its leading figures have since been canonized by the church that once expelled them.

experienceToday.text: Mount Athos, Greece — the monastic republic where the dispute began; visits require a permit and, by the peninsula's own ancient rule, are open to men only

movements.longDescription: The Coptic Orthodox Church entered the nineteenth century poor, largely untaught, and reduced in the eyes of most outsiders to a survival — and then in 1854 a young patriarch took office and spent seven years changing that. Cyril IV founded schools, including one for girls at a time when that was nearly unheard of in Egypt, brought in a printing press, built a library, and set about educating clergy who had mostly learned the liturgy by ear. He died suddenly in 1861, not yet fifty, in circumstances still argued about. What he started did not stop: an elected lay communal council from 1874, a Coptic press and newspapers from the 1870s, and the schools that would eventually produce the twentieth-century Sunday School movement out of which the modern Coptic renaissance came.
movements.teaser: Egypt, 1854 to 1906 — seven years of a reforming patriarch, and a church long counted out beginning to teach itself again.
voices: Cyril IV — patriarch from 1854 to 1861, remembered by Copts as the Father of Reform, who founded the schools and imported the press

Much of what followed him ran through institutions rather than individuals — the elected lay council of 1874 and the Coptic newspapers of the 1870s onward — and the reformers behind them are far less well documented in accessible sources than the patriarch himself
movements.legacy: Everything the modern Coptic Church is known for was made possible here. The Sunday School movement that grew out of Cyril's schools, formally organized from 1918, produced the generation of teachers, monks and bishops who repopulated the desert monasteries and led the church through the twentieth century, and the Coptic diaspora carried that renewal to Europe, North America and Australia. The Coptic Orthodox Church remains the largest Christian community in the Middle East.

experienceToday.text: The Coptic Museum, Old Cairo — the world's largest collection of Coptic Christian art and manuscripts, in the middle of Coptic Cairo's ancient churches

movements.longDescription: In 1830 a young man in western New York named Joseph Smith published the Book of Mormon — which he said he had translated from golden plates shown to him by an angel — and on 6 April that year organized a church around it. Its members were driven out of Ohio, then Missouri, then Illinois, where a mob killed Smith in the Carthage jail in 1844; under Brigham Young most of them crossed the plains from 1847 and settled the Salt Lake valley, laying out towns, irrigation systems and eventually a territory largely of their own making. The nineteenth-century church practised plural marriage openly from 1852, which brought decades of federal prosecution before its president formally renounced the practice in 1890 and Utah entered the Union six years later. Its members documented themselves relentlessly: the Relief Society's minute book, Eliza R. Snow's poems and trail diaries, and Emmeline B. Wells's newspaper make up one of the fullest records any nineteenth-century American religious community left behind.
movements.teaser: New York to the Great Basin, 1830 to 1906 — a new scripture, a church driven west across a continent, and a desert territory built very largely from scratch.
voices: Joseph Smith — founder, translator and publisher of the Book of Mormon, killed by a mob in Illinois in 1844
Emma Hale Smith — his wife, first president of the Relief Society, and compiler of the church's first hymnbook
Brigham Young — who led the migration west in 1847 and organized the Utah settlements
Eliza R. Snow — poet, hymn-writer and Relief Society leader, one of the movement's most influential women
Emmeline B. Wells — editor of the Woman's Exponent from 1877 to 1914 and a leading Utah suffragist
movements.legacy: It is a large and growing worldwide church, headquartered in Salt Lake City, with millions of members on every continent and one of the most extensive volunteer missionary programmes of any religious body. Its genealogical archives, built for its own theological reasons, have become a resource used by family historians of every background in the world. And its settlement pattern is still legible on the ground: grid-plan towns, irrigation canals and ward meetinghouses across the American Intermountain West.

experienceToday.text: The Church History Museum, Salt Lake City — the church's own museum of its nineteenth-century origins and migration, opposite Temple Square, free to enter

movements.longDescription: In the early 1870s a young Pittsburgh clothing merchant named Charles Taze Russell gathered a small circle to study the Bible without reference to inherited denominational teaching, and in 1879 began a magazine, Zion's Watch Tower and Herald of Christ's Presence. Around the magazine grew an international network of readers who called themselves Bible Students, distributed Russell's six-volume Studies in the Scriptures by the million, worked door to door as colporteurs, and gathered for annual conventions from 1893. The movement was built on printing and personal distribution from the very start, which is why its record of itself is unusually complete for a body of its size. The name Jehovah's Witnesses, and the tightly centralized organization the movement is known for today, came later — after Russell's death in 1916, under his successor Joseph Franklin Rutherford.
movements.teaser: Pittsburgh and outward, 1870s to 1906 — a Bible study circle that became a printing house, and a magazine that built a worldwide readership on foot, door by door.
voices: Charles Taze Russell — founder, editor of Zion's Watch Tower from 1879, and author of the six-volume Studies in the Scriptures

The colporteurs — the ordinary readers who sold and gave away the movement's literature full time, and whose reports in the magazine are its own account of how it actually grew
movements.legacy: It became one of the most recognizable religious movements in the world: several million active members in nearly every country, still organized around door-to-door work and one of the largest religious publishing operations anywhere, in hundreds of languages. Its members' refusals — of military service, of flag salutes, of blood transfusions — produced a long series of court cases, and some of the resulting judgments, particularly in the United States, became landmark free-speech and religious-liberty precedents that now protect everyone.

movements.longDescription: Mary Baker Eddy was a New England woman in poor health for most of her early life who, after a recovery in 1866 that she attributed to reading the Gospels, spent nine years working out what she had understood and published it in 1875 as Science and Health with Key to the Scriptures. Around the book she organized a church in 1879, a college to train practitioners, and a set of periodicals that carried the healing testimonies of ordinary members. Its congregations have no ordained clergy, no sacraments and no sermons in the usual sense: two lay readers read aloud from the Bible and from Eddy's book, the same lesson in every branch church in the world on any given Sunday. Eddy governed the movement closely through the Manual of The Mother Church, written in 1895, until her death in 1910 — and the practitioners who did most of its actual work were, then as later, overwhelmingly women.
movements.teaser: New England and outward, 1875 to 1906 — a church with no clergy and no sermons, built around one book and the healings its readers reported.
voices: Mary Baker Eddy — founder, author of Science and Health, and the movement's governing authority to the end of her life

The practitioners — the mostly female healers whose printed testimonies in the church's own periodicals are the movement's characteristic literature and the main record of how ordinary members experienced it
movements.legacy: It is an ongoing denomination, much smaller now than at its height, with branch churches and reading rooms in many cities and its landmark complex in Boston. Its most widely felt legacy is a newspaper: The Christian Science Monitor, founded by Eddy in 1908 in her late eighties, became a respected international daily that has won multiple Pulitzer Prizes and is read by people with no connection to the church at all. Its position on medical treatment has also been the subject of repeated legal and public debate over the years, particularly where children are concerned.

experienceToday.text: The Mary Baker Eddy Library and the Mapparium, Boston — the church's library and its 1935 stained-glass globe, open to the public

movements.longDescription: John Thomas was an English doctor who emigrated to America in 1832, nearly drowned in a shipwreck on the way, and resolved that if he survived he would work out the Bible's teaching for himself rather than take it on anyone's authority. He concluded that most of what the churches taught had been added long after the apostles, and set out the alternative in Elpis Israel in 1848. His followers organized as "ecclesias" — small congregations with no clergy, where members taught and presided in turn — and in 1864 adopted the name Christadelphians, brothers of Christ, largely so they could claim conscientious-objector status in the American Civil War. Robert Roberts, a Scottish printer's apprentice who became the movement's second great figure, gave them a magazine that has run continuously since 1864 and a written confession, the Birmingham Statement of Faith, that they still use.
movements.teaser: Britain and North America, 1848 to 1906 — a doctor who set out to start the Bible again from scratch, and small lay congregations who took a new name so they could refuse to fight.
voices: John Thomas — English physician and emigrant whose Elpis Israel (1848) set out the movement's whole reading of Scripture
Robert Roberts — his younger colleague, who founded The Christadelphian magazine in 1864 and drafted the statement of faith the community still uses
movements.legacy: It continues as a small worldwide body — tens of thousands of people in autonomous ecclesias across Britain, North America, Australia, Africa and elsewhere — with no clergy, no central headquarters, the same statement of faith, and a magazine published without a break since 1864. Its tradition of conscientious objection outlasted the war it was named for: Christadelphians were among the recognized objectors in both world wars, and their case files are part of the legal record of conscience in Britain and the United States.

movements.longDescription: In 1830 and 1831, people in the fashionable London congregation of the Scottish preacher Edward Irving began speaking in tongues and prophesying — something almost nobody in Britain had expected to see again — and Irving was deposed by his presbytery for his teaching and died in 1834, before the movement that bears his name had really taken shape. What emerged was a church built on the conviction that Christ was about to return and had restored the apostolate to prepare for it: twelve men were called as apostles, and around them grew a fourfold ministry, church buildings on a near-cathedral scale, and one of the richest liturgies composed in the nineteenth century. Because the apostles were held to be irreplaceable, no successors were ordained. As they died, the church's ministry simply ran out, and when the last of them died in February 1901 its congregations entered what they called the time of silence — continuing to worship, with nobody left who could ordain anyone.
movements.teaser: Britain, 1832 to 1901 — a church that expected the world to end, restored twelve apostles to meet it, and then quietly ran out of clergy when the last of them died.
voices: Edward Irving — the Scottish preacher whose London congregation was where it began, deposed in 1833 and dead in 1834; the movement is named for him although he was never one of its apostles
Mary Campbell and Margaret Macdonald — the young women in western Scotland whose 1830 prophecies and tongues touched the whole thing off, and whose words survive only in other people's accounts
John Bate Cardale — the London lawyer called as the first of the twelve apostles, and the principal author of the church's liturgy
Henry Drummond — banker, politician and patron, on whose Albury estate the prophetic conferences met
Francis Valentine Woodhouse — the last surviving apostle, who died on 3 February 1901, after which no more ordinations were possible
movements.legacy: The liturgy outlived the church that wrote it: scholars of worship studied it long after the congregations fell silent, and it drew on Eastern, Roman and Anglican sources in a combination nobody else had attempted. Its buildings survive and are still in use by other congregations — the great church in Gordon Square, London, is Grade I listed. And a German branch that broke away in 1863 precisely because it wanted to keep calling new apostles became the New Apostolic Church, which today has millions of members, mostly in Africa and Europe. The original body itself has no ministry left and, by its own theology, cannot acquire one.

experienceToday.text: The Church of Christ the King, Gordon Square, London — built 1850-54 as the Catholic Apostolic Church's central church, Grade I listed and still in use for worship

movements.longDescription: John Humphrey Noyes taught that a Christian could be wholly free of sin in this life, and in 1848 he gathered a community at Oneida in upstate New York to live as though the kingdom had already arrived. They held property in common, replaced marriage with what they called complex marriage — in which every member was in principle married to every other — submitted to a formal system of group criticism, and from 1869 ran a selective breeding programme they named stirpiculture. They also worked hard and paid their way, manufacturing animal traps, silk thread and eventually tableware. Outside campaigning and internal strain finished it: Noyes left for Canada in 1879, and in 1880 the community voted itself out of existence, reorganizing on New Year's Day 1881 as a joint-stock company.
movements.teaser: Upstate New York, 1848 to 1881 — a community that believed sin was already over, abolished marriage among themselves, and finally voted itself into a cutlery company.
voices: John Humphrey Noyes — founder and, to the end, the community's sole governing authority
Tirzah Miller — his niece, whose diaries are the fullest surviving inside account by a member, and show the pressure of that authority as well as the life
John Mears — the Hamilton College professor whose public campaign against the community in the late 1870s helped bring the outside pressure that ended it
movements.legacy: As a religious body it left nothing — no successor community, no continuing church, no doctrinal descendants. As a business it left a great deal: Oneida Limited became one of the best-known tableware manufacturers in the world, and its flatware sat on ordinary tables for generations without the faintest hint of where it came from. The Mansion House the community built still stands and is a National Historic Landmark, run as a museum and inn.

movements.statusDescription: Outside the Constitution's own sense of a Christian movement — named and explained, never silently dropped.
movements.floorNote: Neither Spiritualism nor New Thought is a confessionally Christian movement in the sense this atlas maps. They grew up alongside nineteenth-century Christianity, borrowed a good deal of its vocabulary, and overlapped with it socially — but they are not traditions within it. They are named here only because visitors often ask where they belong.
movements.why: Outside the atlas's scope entirely - named only because participants will ask.
movements.dateRationale: Start corrected to 1848 (the Fox sisters at Hydesville [S]) — the previous numerics were an era-window fill artifact; end 1906 era cap (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.note: CONTEXT-ONLY per census floorNote (outside the atlas's scope; named because participants will ask). Insider-chronicle advocacy flag; the confession/recantation double flag; women's leadership structurally central. [S] editions from knowledge.

sources.note: Context-only. Posthumous-editing tier flag on Quimby; the Eddy-Quimby dependence controversy noted as contested, no position taken (cross-ref christian-science). [S] editions from knowledge.

movements.longDescription: In March 1848 two young sisters in a farmhouse at Hydesville, New York, said they were communicating with the dead through rapping sounds, and within a few years séances, mediums and spirit circles had spread through the United States and Britain, drawing in reformers, grieving families and scientists who wanted to test the claims. Running alongside it, and partly overlapping, was New Thought: a family of teachers descended from the Maine healer Phineas Quimby who held that mind governs matter and that right thinking heals. Both borrowed Christian vocabulary heavily and grew in the same nineteenth-century soil as the revivals, but neither is a Christian tradition, and this atlas names them only because visitors reasonably ask where they fit. Spiritualism's public credibility took a heavy blow in 1888, when Margaret Fox declared before an audience in New York that she and her sister had produced the original raps by cracking their toe joints — a confession she withdrew a year later.
movements.teaser: North America and Britain, 1848 to 1906 — table-rapping in a New York farmhouse and a mind-over-matter gospel, both grown up beside the churches without belonging to them.
voices: Margaret and Kate Fox — the sisters at Hydesville in 1848, whose rappings started it, and whose later confession and retraction have been argued over ever since
Andrew Jackson Davis — the self-taught seer whose writings supplied Spiritualism with much of its theology before the Fox sisters made it a movement
Emma Hardinge Britten — medium, lecturer and the movement's first serious chronicler
Phineas Quimby — the Maine clockmaker and mental healer at the head of the New Thought line
Emma Curtis Hopkins — the teacher who trained most of New Thought's founding generation
Charles and Myrtle Fillmore — founders of Unity in 1889, the largest of the New Thought bodies
movements.legacy: Spiritualist churches still exist in Britain and the United States, and the effort to test their claims scientifically produced the Society for Psychical Research in 1882 and, indirectly, a whole field of investigation. New Thought became ongoing denominations — Unity, Religious Science and their relatives — but its far larger legacy escaped religion altogether: its language of mind over circumstance runs straight into twentieth-century positive-thinking, self-help and prosperity literature read by millions who have never heard of Quimby.

movements.name: Korean Catholic Origins
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Strong (Tier 1) on martyrs' letters and trial records — a pre-missionary church documented by the missionaries who finally reached it. Its 1886 end was kept with its rationale written for the first time, the France–Korea treaty ending the persecution era, and the 1886–1904 seam was disclosed forward to the next gate rather than absorbed here.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: martyrs' letters and trial records; the pre-missionary church documented by the missionaries who finally reached it
movements.relationsSummary: Self-founded by lay Confucian scholars before any priest arrived - a world-history singular of lay initiative; ~10,000 martyrs; precursor-sibling of Korea's Protestant story
movements.why: A world-history singular: a church founded by lay Confucian scholars who read their way into Christianity out of books and organized a community before any priest had ever arrived. Nothing else in the atlas begins that way. What follows is some ten thousand martyrs, and a record made largely of their own letters and trial testimony — a church that existed before any missionary arrived, and was written up by the ones who eventually did.
movements.dateRationale: End 1886 kept, principled: the France-Korea treaty ending the persecution era [S]; the 1886-1904 seam disclosed to era 10 (IX.2’s origin lines); start 1784 (Yi Sung-hun’s Beijing baptism [S], incoming-class) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: The self-evangelized church's own documents: Chong Yak-chong, Chugyo yoji (c. 1798-1801, vernacular han'gul catechism); the community's letters to Beijing and Rome (1784-, incl. the 1811 letter to the Pope); Yi Byeok's Essence of Sacred Doctrine
sources.note: The lay church teaching itself in its own hand. Yi Byeok attribution debated - tier flag [S]. English access chiefly via Baker & Rausch. [S] editions from knowledge.

sources.work: The Hwang Sa-yong silk letter (1801)

sources.work: The persecution records: Sinyu (1801), Kihae (1839), Pyongo (1846), Pyongin (1866) interrogation and execution records in the Choson annals and police archives
sources.note: HOSTILE/COERCED flags at full strength - the martyrs' testimony through the persecutor's pen, under torture; ~10,000 martyrs per census. [S] archival details from knowledge.

sources.note: Double filter (hostile court + hagiographic compilation); Daveluy carries the census's 'documented by the missionaries who finally reached it' leg - missionary-compiler filter. [S] details from knowledge.

sources.note: Chapter number verified this session; Grayson is the Korea hand - direct fit.

movements.longDescription: Korea is the only country in the world where the Catholic Church began without a missionary. In the late eighteenth century a circle of Confucian scholars near Seoul studied Chinese-language Catholic books, convinced themselves, and sent one of their number, Yi Sung-hun, to Beijing to be baptized in 1784; he came home and baptized the others, and a church of several thousand people existed before a priest had ever set foot in the country. It was written in Korean from the start — Chong Yak-chong's catechism was in the vernacular script rather than in the scholarly Chinese of the elite — which is part of why it reached women, servants and the poor as fast as it reached the literati. The Choson state read it as treason against the Confucian order, and the church spent a century under persecution, with something on the order of ten thousand Korean Catholics killed in successive purges between 1801 and 1866, until a treaty with France in 1886 finally brought the killing to an end.
movements.teaser: Korea, 1784 to 1886 — the one church in the world that converted itself out of books, and then paid for it with some ten thousand lives.
voices: Yi Sung-hun — sent to Beijing by his study circle and baptized there in 1784, he came home and baptized the rest
Yi Byeok — one of the founding scholars of the circle, credited with the earliest Korean writing on the faith
Chong Yak-chong — author of the first Korean-language catechism, written for people who could not read Chinese; executed in 1801
Kang Wan-suk — a noblewoman and catechist who ran much of the underground church in Seoul, executed in 1801
Andrew Kim Taegon — the first Korean-born Catholic priest, executed in 1846 at the age of twenty-five

Hwang Sa-yong — author of the 1801 letter on silk, intercepted before it reached Beijing, which lay in the state tribunal's archive for nearly a century before the church recovered it, and is now in the Vatican
movements.legacy: It became one of the largest and most active Catholic communities in Asia — several million people in South Korea today, in a church that still traces its beginning to laypeople rather than clergy and takes considerable pride in the fact. In 1984 Pope John Paul II canonized 103 of its martyrs in Seoul itself rather than in Rome, and further beatifications followed in 2014. The execution grounds are now national shrines, and the martyrs' letters and trial testimony remain among the most vivid first-person religious documents anywhere in nineteenth-century Asia.

experienceToday.text: Jeoldusan Martyrs' Shrine, Seoul — the riverside cliff where Catholics were executed in 1866, now a church and museum holding the martyrs' relics and records

movements.name: Laestadianism & the Nordic Revivals
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on sermons, movement periodicals and later oral histories, with the Sami dimension named as carrying real marginalized-voice value. Its end was aligned to the 1906 era cap, replacing a round-1900 artifact, and a scope note recorded that the Swedish low-church revivals sit inside its Nordic plural deliberately rather than by accident.
movements.sourcing: Moderate: sermons, movement periodicals, later oral histories; the Sami dimension adds real marginalized-voice value
movements.relationsSummary: Child of Pietism's long line in the Lutheran north; spoken-absolution practice; living communities today. Scope note (Era 9 Freeze): the Swedish low-church revivals (Rosenius/EFS 1856, Waldenström/Mission Covenant 1878 [S]) sit inside this entry’s Nordic plural DELIBERATELY, not accidentally.
movements.why: A revival that took root among the Sami as well as among Nordic settlers, which gives it marginalized-voice value the region's other awakenings do not carry. Its distinctive practice is spoken absolution between ordinary believers — forgiveness declared face to face rather than from a pulpit — an unusual thing for a Lutheran movement to have made central. Its communities are still living, and the plural in its title is deliberate: Sweden's low-church awakenings belong inside this entry rather than beside it.
movements.dateRationale: End aligned to the 1906 era cap (living; round-1900 artifact replaced); start 1844 (Laestadius and Milla Clementsdotter [S]) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

movements.longDescription: Lars Levi Laestadius was a Swedish Lutheran pastor and a serious botanist, of partly Sami descent, serving parishes in Lapland that were being destroyed by alcohol — and in 1844 a conversation with a young Sami woman he called Mary changed his preaching entirely. What followed spread through the Sami and Finnish north: fierce sermons in the local languages, an end to drinking, and intense emotional expression in meetings that startled outsiders. Its most distinctive practice is confession and spoken absolution between ordinary believers — forgiveness declared face to face by a neighbour rather than pronounced from a pulpit. It was never only his: the same century brought Paavo Ruotsalainen's awakening in Finland and, in Sweden, the low-church revivals of Carl Olof Rosenius and P. P. Waldenström, and the plural in this entry's name is deliberate.
movements.teaser: Lapland and the Nordic north, 1844 to 1906 — a revival among Sami and Finnish parishes where ordinary believers forgave each other's sins out loud.
voices: Lars Levi Laestadius — pastor, botanist and preacher, of partly Sami descent, whose sermons set the revival going
Milla Clementsdotter — the young Sami woman whose 1844 conversation with Laestadius he credited with changing everything; her own words survive only in his account of them
Juhani Raattamaa — the lay schoolmaster who became the movement's real organizer and the architect of its practice of spoken absolution
Paavo Ruotsalainen — the unlettered Finnish farmer at the centre of Finland's own awakening
Carl Olof Rosenius — Swedish lay preacher and editor whose journal Pietisten carried the low-church revival across Sweden
Paul Petter Waldenström — theologian and preacher behind the Swedish Mission Covenant of 1878
movements.legacy: Laestadian communities are alive across northern Finland, Sweden and Norway and among emigrant descendants in the American upper Midwest, now divided into several distinct and generally conservative branches. It is one of very few European revival movements with a substantial indigenous constituency, and Sami has remained a language of its preaching. The Swedish revivals in the same entry left their own institutions — the mission society Rosenius helped inspire and the Mission Covenant Church, whose American cousin became the Evangelical Covenant Church.

experienceToday.text: The Laestadius Museum and cottage, Pajala, Sweden — the rectory and cabin where Laestadius lived from 1851 until his death in 1861, with his herb garden

movements.name: Plymouth Brethren & Dispensational Formation
movements.statusWord: Researched — viable, secondary (Era 9 Step 0; c2 cleared on the community limb)
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on movement periodicals, Darby's vast corpus, assembly records and Müller's narratives. Its person-defined check was run at this gate as the criterion's ninth live application and cleared on the community limb — the 1848 Open/Exclusive division shows the body was never reducible to Darby — with the Exclusive wing's later Darby-centrism named as the honest counter-note. Its end was aligned to the 1906 era cap, replacing a round-1900 artifact.
movements.sourcing: Rich: movement periodicals, Darby's vast corpus, assembly records, Mueller's narratives
movements.floorNote: There is a fair question about a movement so shaped by one man's mind: was it a tradition, or Darby's following? The 1848 division answers it — the movement split into Open and Exclusive Brethren and both halves went on, which a body reducible to its founder could not have done. The honest counter-note is that the Exclusive wing afterwards centred itself heavily on Darby's own authority.
movements.relationsSummary: Child of evangelical dissent; via Scofield reshaped how millions read Scripture; influence on the Bible-institute tradition
movements.why: Its influence is out of all proportion to its size — by way of Scofield's reference Bible, a framework worked out in small assemblies reshaped how millions of people read Scripture, and much of modern popular prophecy belief runs back through it. Its own life is well documented in movement periodicals, assembly records and Müller's narratives. The 1848 Open and Exclusive division is also why it clears the person-defined test: a body that split in two and continued in both halves was never reducible to Darby.
movements.dateRationale: End aligned to the 1906 era cap (living; round-1900 artifact replaced); start 1827 (Dublin gatherings [S]) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.note: The census's named leg - answered-prayer bookkeeping as an ordinary-facing genre. [S] editions from knowledge.

sources.note: Title recovered this session; [S] chapter number not recovered; no dedicated Brethren chapter surfaced. Flagged for era review.

movements.longDescription: In the late 1820s a handful of dissatisfied Christians in Dublin — among them a dentist, a lawyer and a young Anglican curate named John Nelson Darby — began meeting to break bread together with no ordained clergy, no denominational name and no set liturgy, and assemblies on the same pattern spread through Britain and then the world. Darby also worked out a way of reading the Bible that divided history into distinct dispensations, kept Israel and the church permanently separate, and expected Christ to remove the church before a final tribulation — a scheme almost unknown before him and enormously consequential after. Alongside the theology ran an equally characteristic practice: George Müller ran orphanages in Bristol for thousands of children on the principle of never asking anyone for money and publishing the accounts. In 1848 the movement split over how far assemblies were answerable to one another, into the Open and Exclusive Brethren, and both halves carried on.
movements.teaser: Dublin, England and then the world, 1827 to 1906 — a few people breaking bread without clergy, whose way of reading prophecy went on to shape how millions read the Bible.
voices: John Nelson Darby — former Anglican curate, the movement's dominant mind and the architect of dispensationalism
Anthony Norris Groves — dentist, missionary to Baghdad and India, and the author of the movement's earliest internal criticism of Darby
George Müller — who housed and educated thousands of orphans in Bristol without ever soliciting a donation, and published the books to prove it
Benjamin Wills Newton — the Plymouth leader whose clash with Darby precipitated the 1848 division
J. G. Bellett — one of the original Dublin circle, and its most sympathetic memoirist
movements.legacy: Open and Exclusive assemblies exist worldwide to this day, and Müller's Bristol work continues as a charitable trust with a museum in one of the original orphan houses. But the movement's real reach is elsewhere: Darby's dispensational scheme, packaged in the notes of the Scofield Reference Bible from 1909 and taught in the Bible institutes, became the default end-times framework of American evangelicalism and lies behind most popular prophecy writing and preaching of the last hundred years — read by millions who have never heard of the Brethren.

experienceToday.text: The George Müller Museum, Ashley Down, Bristol — in one of the original orphan houses, telling the story of the 17,000 children who lived there; free entry

movements.name: The Sunday School & Bible-Institute Movement
movements.informalName: The Sunday School and Bible-Institute Movement
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on a rich institutional record with teachers' and students' memoirs. Its own ecology question — whether this is a tradition, or a set of formation technologies operating inside other traditions — was left standing as a genuine test. Its c. 1900 end was kept and stated as a judgment rather than a default, the entry making no living-continuation claim that would call for an era cap.
movements.sourcing: Rich institutionally, with teachers' and students' memoirs
movements.relationsSummary: Lay formation technologies at industrial scale (Raikes 1780; Moody 1886); ecology question: movement-as-tradition vs. technology-inside-traditions - a genuine Step 0 test
movements.why: A genuine open test sits at its centre: is this a tradition of its own, or a kit of formation methods that other traditions simply ran inside themselves? Either way, it is where a very large share of ordinary Christians in the industrial age actually learned the faith: Sunday schools reaching children by the million, Bible institutes training the workers who staffed the mission movement. Leaving it off the map would mean leaving off the machinery by which most people were formed.
movements.dateRationale: End kept c. 1900 STATED (living:false — no cap claim; round-1900 trio member, judged not defaulted); start 1780 (Raikes) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

movements.longDescription: In 1780 a Gloucester newspaper proprietor named Robert Raikes hired four women to teach the town's factory children to read on Sunday — their one free day — and then publicized the results in his own paper. The idea travelled with extraordinary speed, and by the middle of the nineteenth century Sunday schools were teaching literacy along with religion to millions of working-class children in Britain and America, staffed overwhelmingly by unpaid women volunteers and organized by unions that supplied lessons, prizes and books at industrial scale. A century after Raikes the same instinct produced the Bible institute: schools like D. L. Moody's in Chicago, opened in 1886, that took ordinary lay people rather than university graduates and trained them in a year or two as evangelists, teachers and missionaries. Together they are the machinery by which most ordinary Christians of the industrial age actually learned the faith.
movements.teaser: Britain and North America, 1780 to about 1900 — the machinery by which most ordinary Christians of the industrial age learned to read, and learned the faith.
voices: Robert Raikes — the Gloucester newspaperman who hired the first teachers in 1780 and then advertised the results into a movement
Thomas Stock — the curate who worked with Raikes on the first school and is easily the more forgotten of the two
D. L. Moody — the evangelist whose Chicago institute of 1886 became the model Bible school
Emma Dryer — the educator who did much of the founding work behind Moody's institute, and whose part in it is thinly documented compared with his
movements.legacy: Sunday school became a near-universal feature of Protestant congregational life worldwide and stayed there; the graded, standardized lesson series invented in the 1870s is still the shape of most children's curricula. Historians credit the movement with a substantial share of working-class literacy in nineteenth-century Britain, for many children the only schooling they got. The Bible institutes turned into colleges, and their graduates staffed the twentieth-century missionary agencies, radio ministries and publishing houses that carried evangelical Christianity around the world.

experienceToday.text: Gloucester, England — the city where Raikes started, with St Mary de Crypt church and the surviving schoolroom, and Raikes's own house still standing in the old centre

movements.name: The Student Volunteer Movement & Edinburgh 1910
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on SVM records, volunteers' diaries and letters, and conference reports. Its record is unusually personal for a movement of institutions: volunteers' own diaries and letters sit alongside the conference reports. It takes its name from an event falling just past the era line, inside the single crossing the rules allow, and the record says so rather than hiding it.

movements.longDescription: In the summer of 1886 a hundred students at a conference in Massachusetts signed a declaration that they were willing and desirous to become foreign missionaries, and over the next thirty years the Student Volunteer Movement they founded put something on the order of twenty thousand young Americans and Britons on ships, under the watchword "the evangelization of the world in this generation." Its summit was the World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh in 1910, where twelve hundred delegates met to plan the work as one enterprise instead of a hundred competing ones. Two of the very few non-Western delegates used their few minutes to say the necessary thing: V. S. Azariah of India asked the room, to its face, for friends rather than masters, and Cheng Jingyi of China told it that the Chinese church wanted to be one church and had no use for European denominational divisions. Both were right, and it took the rest of the century to act on it.
movements.teaser: North America, Britain and the world, 1886 to 1920 — a generation of students who volunteered by the thousand, and the conference where they were told, politely, to let go.
voices: John R. Mott — the movement's organizer and the chairman of Edinburgh 1910, later a Nobel Peace Prize laureate
Robert Wilder — one of the original hundred, who toured the campuses and turned a conference pledge into a movement
Grace Wilder — his sister, whose part in the movement's origins is real and recorded almost entirely through other people
J. H. Oldham — Edinburgh's secretary, whose continuation work turned a conference into an institution
V. S. Azariah — Indian delegate, later the first Indian Anglican bishop, whose Edinburgh address asked Western missionaries for friendship rather than supervision
Cheng Jingyi — Chinese delegate whose short speech for a united, non-denominational Chinese church is the most quoted thing said at the conference
movements.legacy: Edinburgh's continuation committee became the International Missionary Council in 1921 and fed into the World Council of Churches in 1948: the modern ecumenical movement dates its own beginning to that room. The same generation's evangelistic energy went the other way, into the independent missionary agencies that multiplied through the twentieth century, so that one gathering is claimed as an ancestor by two movements that spent the following century largely apart. The Student Volunteer Movement itself never recovered from the First World War and had effectively ended by mid-century.

movements.name: Indonesian Christianity
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on mission records read with gravity, the Batak church's own records and revival testimonies. Its open-ended present tail was segmented at 1906 under the census's segment discipline, leaving the era-10 segment — the 1965–71 Timor revival and the HKBP's growth — for that era's own gate to create rather than inherited by silence.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: mission records (with gravity), the Batak church's own records, revival testimonies
movements.relationsSummary: Nommensen and the HKBP (among the largest Lutheran bodies on earth); the 1965-71 Timor revival; one of the largest Christian communities in the Muslim-majority world - previously absent entirely
movements.why: One of the largest Christian communities in the Muslim-majority world, and the census previously had no entry for it at all. The Batak church that came out of this window is among the largest Lutheran bodies anywhere on earth — a fact most maps of Lutheranism would not lead anyone to expect. Its own church records and revival testimonies sit beside the mission archive, so the tradition can be read partly in its own voice rather than only in its founders'.
movements.dateRationale: Present-tail segmented: the era-9 segment caps at 1906 per the census’s segment discipline; the era-10 segment (the 1965-71 Timor revival, HKBP growth) is the A1.E10 gate’s to create; start 1861 (Nommensen [S]) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: The Batak church's own records: the HKBP 1881 church order, synod minutes, congregation registers; Batak teachers' and pastors' writings and church press; first evangelists' accounts
sources.note: An indigenous church's institutional self-record growing inside then beyond the mission. First-evangelist accounts [S]. [S] Batak/Indonesian and German archives - access flag.

sources.work: Mission records WITH gravity: Nommensen's letters and reports (Rheinische Missionsgesellschaft archives, Wuppertal); the Joseph Kam-era Moluccan records; Minahasa mission records
sources.note: The census's own '(with gravity)' flag made structural: mission filter AND the Dutch-colonial frame around a German mission, both flagged. [S] archives - access flag.

sources.work: The indigenous-initiative leg: Kiai Sadrach's Javanese communities (c. 1870s-90s) - the mission's hostile-suspicious file AND the community's own practice and continuity
sources.note: Both-pens flag; the archipelago's clearest in-window case of Christianity on indigenous terms. [S] details from knowledge (Partonadi's study - see secondary).

sources.work: Revival testimonies: Toba conversion-era and mass-movement testimonies (1880s-1900s, largely through mission transcription); the 1965-71 Timor revival flagged as past this era's window
sources.note: WINDOW FLAG: the census relations line's Timor revival is in-entry (1861-present) but past c. 1914 - staged for the era-10 run, not built here. Transcription filter on the Toba layer. [S] details from knowledge.

sources.note: The standard (largely by Indonesian scholars) and the Sadrach recovery. [S] neither individually verified this session.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8 (chapter assignment hedged): nearest ch. 32 (Francisco, Filipino Christianity) and ch. 34 (Stanley) - both numbers verified
sources.note: [S] no Indonesia/Netherlands-Indies chapter surfaced in the recovered TOC. Flagged for era review.

movements.longDescription: Christianity had been present in the eastern Indonesian islands since the Portuguese and the Dutch East India Company, but the churches that matter most today were built in the nineteenth century and, very quickly, by Indonesians. German missionaries reached the Batak highlands of North Sumatra in 1861, where Ludwig Nommensen spent more than fifty years; the church that grew there gave itself a written order in 1881 and is now among the largest Lutheran bodies anywhere in the world. Further west, in Java, a Javanese teacher known as Kiai Sadrach gathered thousands of followers into congregations that kept Javanese forms, Javanese leadership and Javanese ways of teaching — which the Dutch missions regarded with deep suspicion at the time, and which is now read as the archipelago's clearest early case of Christianity on local terms. Almost everything written about all of this in the period was written by the missions; the churches' own records are what let it be read the other way round.
movements.teaser: Sumatra, Java and the eastern islands, 1861 to 1906 — churches planted by foreign missions and rebuilt, almost at once, on Indonesian terms.
voices: Ludwig Ingwer Nommensen — German missionary among the Toba Batak from 1862 until his death in 1918, buried at Sigumpar in North Sumatra
Kiai Sadrach — Javanese teacher who built a large network of congregations on Javanese terms, and was distrusted by the Dutch missionaries for it
Joseph Kam — the Dutch pastor whose work in the Moluccas from 1815 revived the older island churches left over from the Company era

The Batak evangelists and teachers — the local preachers who did most of the actual spread of the church into the highlands, recorded in the church's own registers rather than in the mission's published accounts
movements.legacy: Indonesia now has one of the largest Christian populations of any Muslim-majority country in the world, numbering in the tens of millions, and the Batak church founded in this window counts several million members on its own — a fact that would surprise most people's mental map of where Lutherans live. The universities, schools and hospitals that grew out of the mission remain, one of them carrying Nommensen's name. The great Timor revival of 1965 to 1971, one of the largest recorded in the twentieth century, belongs to the next chapter of the same story.

experienceToday.text: The Batak Christian Protestant Church (HKBP), North Sumatra — the church founded in this window, still one of the largest in Indonesia and a member of the World Council of Churches

movements.name: Northeast India Revivals & the Mar Thoma Reform
movements.informalName: The Northeast India Revivals and the Mar Thoma Reform
movements.statusDescription: Reviewed at the Era 9 Step 0 run and tiered Viable, secondary (Tier 2) on church records, revival accounts and hymnody in local languages. Its present tail was segmented at 1906 on the same discipline applied to the Indonesian entry, and a scope note was recorded naming what it does not carry: this entry holds the reform wing of 1889, while the Malankara Orthodox majority after the court verdict has no row — a named absence left for a later gate, with the backward 1665–1836 gap likewise disclosed.
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich: church records, revival accounts, hymnody in local languages
movements.relationsSummary: Mar Thoma: an ancient-rite church with evangelical reform, honestly extending the St. Thomas lane; indigenous hill revivals made these among the most Christian regions on earth. Scope note (Era 9 Freeze): this entry carries the REFORM wing of 1889; the Malankara Orthodox/Jacobite majority after the court verdict has no row — a named absence for a later gate; VI.18’s 1665 end leaves the 1665-1836 gap disclosed backward.
movements.why: Two things the atlas has nowhere else, joined across a bridge lane. Mar Thoma is an ancient-rite Eastern church that reformed itself along evangelical lines and kept both, which extends the St Thomas story honestly rather than replacing it; the hill revivals in the Khasi, Mizo and Naga country made those among the most thoroughly Christian regions on earth, in languages that got their first written hymnody out of the same process. The entry also names what it does not carry: on the other side of that division, the Malankara Orthodox majority has no row of its own yet.
movements.dateRationale: Present-tail segmented: the era-9 segment caps at 1906 (the Khasi revival 1905-06 at the boundary [S]; the Mizo revivals are era 10’s); the era-10 segment is the A1.E10 gate’s to create; start 1836 (Abraham Malpan’s reform liturgy [S]) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)

sources.work: The Mar Thoma reform's own documents: Abraham Malpan's revised liturgy (1836ff.); the reformers' 1836 memorial; Mathews Mar Athanasius's records; synod records and service books; the Travancore Royal Court litigation record (to 1889)
sources.note: An ancient-rite church's own liturgical-textual act of reform; the court record under ADVERSARIAL-LEGAL flag. [S] Malayalam/Syriac sources - access flag.

sources.work: The hill revivals' own record: Khasi revival (1905-06, Mairang) and Mizo revival (1906ff.) accounts; hymnody in local languages (Khasi and Mizo revival hymns; lengkhawm zai); indigenous evangelists' and converts' accounts
sources.note: The census's named local-language hymnody leg - indigenous composition, not translation: the revivals' own theological voice; accounts partly self-recorded, partly mission-transcribed (filter flag). Indigenous accounts [S]. [S] editions from knowledge.

sources.work: Church records WITH mission filters: Welsh Calvinistic Methodist records (Khasi/Mizo hills); American Baptist records (Naga hills, Assam); presbytery/assembly and association minutes
sources.note: Missionary-pen flag on the early layers; indigenous-majority governance visible by the window's end; the colonial-administration frame (Inner Line, expeditions) flagged around the record. [S] archives (Aberystwyth; ABHS) - access flag.

sources.work: Robert Eric Frykenberg, Christianity in India: From Beginnings to the Present (OUP, 2008), with Frederick S. Downs, History of Christianity in India vol. V pt. 5: North East India (CHAI, 1992)
sources.note: The standard covering both wings and the standard regional study. [S] neither individually verified this session.

sources.work: Cambridge History of Christianity vol. 8, ch. 29 'Christians and religious traditions in the Indian empire' (Frykenberg)
sources.note: Chapter number verified this session; direct fit for both wings.

movements.longDescription: In 1836 a teacher at the seminary in Kottayam, Abraham Malpan, revised the Syriac liturgy that Kerala's St Thomas Christians had used for centuries — cutting what he judged unscriptural and putting the service into Malayalam so ordinary people could follow it. The reform divided the ancient community, and after decades of argument and litigation a royal court verdict in 1889 separated the two parties for good: the reforming wing carried on as the Mar Thoma Syrian Church, an Eastern church that kept its ancient rite and its evangelical conscience together, while the larger body continued as the Malankara church. A thousand miles to the northeast, in the Khasi, Mizo and Naga hills, small congregations planted by Welsh and American missions caught fire on their own — village preachers and singers carried revival through the hills, most famously the Khasi awakening of 1905-06, and hill languages received their first written hymnody out of the same process, composed rather than translated.
movements.teaser: Kerala and the hill country of northeast India, 1836 to 1906 — an ancient Syriac church reforming its own liturgy at one end of India, and hill villages singing their first hymns in their own languages at the other.
voices: Abraham Malpan — the Kottayam seminary teacher whose 1836 revision of the Syriac liturgy began the Mar Thoma reform
Mathews Mar Athanasius — the reform party's metropolitan, consecrated in 1842, who carried it through its first decades of conflict
Thomas Jones — the Welsh missionary who gave the Khasi language its written form in the 1840s
Edwin W. Clark — the American Baptist who, with Naga converts, began the mission in the Naga hills in 1872
movements.legacy: The Mar Thoma Syrian Church is still here, with dioceses in India and among Indian communities abroad, and its annual Maramon Convention on the sandy bed of the Pamba river remains one of Asia's largest Christian gatherings. The hill churches did more than survive: Mizoram and Nagaland are today among the most thoroughly Christian regions on earth, Presbyterian and Baptist respectively, and the revival hymnody composed in those years is still what their congregations sing.

movements.name: Orthodoxy after 1821 — the National Churches
movements.informalName: The Millet Church Breaks into Nations
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich institutionally: the Greek autocephaly acts (1833; Tomos of 1850, verified), the Exarchate firman (1870, verified), the 1872 council acta (verified); parish texture thinner
movements.relationsSummary: VII.18 ends at Gregory V’s hanging; this receives the break-up: Greek autocephaly (1833/Tomos 1850), the Bulgarian Exarchate (1870) and the 1872 phyletism condemnation (A5 inside, named), Serbia 1879, Romania 1885 [S]; the one-church-or-national-siblings split test is this entry’s own Step 0 question; VIII.12 stays separate per the E8 seam ruling
movements.why: Receiver of VII.18 (seamless at 1821). Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1821 (Gregory V hanged — seamless to VII.18’s legal tail); end 1906 era cap (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Under Ottoman rule the Orthodox of the Balkans had been governed as a single religious community answering to the Patriarch of Constantinople. The Greek revolt of 1821 — which opened with the hanging of Patriarch Gregory V at the gate of his own residence — broke that arrangement apart, and as each new nation won independence its church claimed self-government: Greece declared its church self-governing in 1833 and was formally recognized by Constantinople in 1850, Bulgaria won an imperial decree creating a national exarchate in 1870, Serbia was recognized in 1879 and Romania in 1885. In 1872 a council at Constantinople condemned phyletism — organizing the church by ethnic nation rather than by place — even as national churches went on multiplying anyway. What the century produced was not one church breaking up so much as a family of them, each with its own synod, its own language of worship, and its own claim on a people.
movements.teaser: Greece, the Balkans and Constantinople, 1821 to 1906 — Orthodoxy under one Ottoman roof breaking into national churches, each new nation claiming a church of its own.
voices: Gregory V of Constantinople — the patriarch hanged at the gate of his own residence in 1821, whose death opened the century
Theoklitos Pharmakidis — the churchman who argued for and drafted the 1833 declaration of Greek self-government
Konstantinos Oikonomos — his opponent, who defended the Patriarchate's authority and the older canonical order
Antim I — first exarch of the Bulgarian Exarchate created in 1870
movements.legacy: These are the churches that make up Orthodoxy today: the Church of Greece and the Bulgarian, Serbian and Romanian patriarchates all date their modern independence to this century, and the pattern they set — a self-governing church per nation — became the normal shape of the Orthodox world. So did the argument the 1872 council started. Wherever Orthodox jurisdictions overlap on the same ground, as they do throughout the diaspora, the question of whether a church is defined by place or by people comes straight back.

movements.name: The Catholic Church of the Long Nineteenth Century
movements.informalName: The Church of Pius IX and Leo XIII
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Rich: Vatican I acta (definitions promulgated 18 Jul 1870, verified), the encyclical corpus (Mirari Vos, Syllabus, Rerum Novarum [S]), the devotional revolution’s own literature [S]
movements.relationsSummary: The Roman hole’s fourth recurrence closed: Gregory XVI to Leo XIII — 1854 [S], the Syllabus [S], Vatican I (verified), the Papal States’ end, the Kulturkampf [S], Rerum Novarum [S], Lourdes and the ultramontane wave [S]; A5 home for the missionary-Catholic frame, the US immigrant church, the 1850 English restoration [S]
movements.why: Receiver of VII.19 — without it era 9 carries an Anglo-Catholic revival, a Korean church, and a Haitian concordat with no Rome for any of them to be in communion with. Tier 1 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.19); end 1906 era cap; Vatican I 18 Jul 1870 verified in-window (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Between the fall of Napoleon and the eve of the First World War, the Catholic Church lost a state and gained a papacy. Gregory XVI and then Pius IX met the liberal century head-on: Pius defined the Immaculate Conception in 1854, catalogued the errors of the age in the Syllabus of 1864, and in July 1870 saw the First Vatican Council define papal infallibility — weeks before Italian troops entered Rome and ended the Papal States. Stripped of territory, the papacy grew in reach instead: bishops and ordinary Catholics looked to Rome as never before, new congregations of sisters and brothers staffed schools and hospitals across the world, and mass devotion gathered around Marian apparitions like Lourdes in 1858. Under Leo XIII the church that had spent decades condemning the modern world began to negotiate with it, most consequentially in Rerum Novarum (1891), which put the church on the side of a worker's right to a living wage and to organize.
movements.teaser: Rome and the Catholic world, 1815 to 1906 — a papacy that lost its last territory in the same weeks it was declared infallible, and grew in reach as it shrank on the map.
voices: Pius IX — the longest-reigning pope, who defined the Immaculate Conception, issued the Syllabus of Errors, and lost the Papal States
Leo XIII — his successor, who opened the church's engagement with industrial society in Rerum Novarum (1891)
Bernadette Soubirous — the Pyrenean girl whose 1858 visions made Lourdes the century's great pilgrimage site
John Henry Newman — the English convert whose theology of conscience and of doctrinal development ran alongside, and sometimes against, the century's Roman current
Nicholas Wiseman — first archbishop of Westminster after the Catholic hierarchy was restored in England in 1850
movements.legacy: This is the Catholic Church still recognizably in place — a worldwide body governed from Rome, with the papacy at its centre in a way earlier centuries would not have recognized. Vatican I's definition remains binding doctrine; Rerum Novarum founded the tradition of Catholic social teaching that every pope since has extended; Lourdes still receives millions of pilgrims a year. The century also left a fracture line, in the Catholics who could not accept 1870 and became the Old Catholics, and a set of questions the church would only take up again at the Second Vatican Council.

movements.name: The Victorian Church of England
movements.informalName: The Established Church of the Long Century
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Rich [S-heavy]: the parties’ own organs, Essays and Reviews (1860 [S]), the Gorham dossier [S], Lambeth 1867 [S], parish-revival records
movements.relationsSummary: VIII.5 is a movement inside this church: the parties [S], the crisis of faith, the first Lambeth Conference (1867 [S]) — the Communion becoming a communion; renewal-inside relation with VIII.5 named both directions
movements.why: Receiver of VII.20 — prevents the establishment-church anomaly recurring in Anglican form. Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.20); end 1906 era cap (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: The Church of England entered the nineteenth century as a comfortable establishment and left it a contested one. Three parties argued for its soul — evangelicals who had inherited the awakening's fervour and its campaigns against slavery and squalor, high churchmen who rediscovered the church's catholic inheritance, and broad churchmen who wanted room for the new biblical criticism and the new geology. The quarrels went to law: the Gorham case of 1850 over what baptism does, the storm over the essayists of 1860 who applied critical methods to Scripture, ritual prosecutions that put clergymen in prison over vestments and candles. Underneath the controversies the church rebuilt itself, in thousands of new buildings and slum parishes at home and in a mission network abroad that by 1867 had produced enough overseas bishops that a first Lambeth Conference had to be called to hold them together.
movements.teaser: England and its empire, 1815 to 1906 — an established church arguing with itself over Rome, over Darwin and over the Bible, while quietly turning into a worldwide communion.
voices: Charles Simeon — the Cambridge evangelical whose long ministry shaped a generation of parish clergy
Lord Shaftesbury — the evangelical layman behind the century's factory, mining and child-labour reforms
Samuel Wilberforce — bishop of Oxford, the era's great diocesan organizer and Darwin's most famous public sparring partner
Frederick Denison Maurice — theologian of the broad church and of Christian socialism, dismissed from his professorship over his view of eternal punishment
John William Colenso — bishop of Natal, whose critical work on the Pentateuch and defence of his Zulu converts split the colonial church
Charles Longley — archbishop of Canterbury, who convened the first Lambeth Conference in 1867
movements.legacy: The Church of England is still established in England, and the conference it improvised in 1867 became the standing instrument of an Anglican Communion of tens of millions across the world. The parties formed in this century are still recognizable as evangelical, Anglo-Catholic and liberal, and so are their arguments — only now conducted across the whole Communion rather than inside one country's church. The century also left the physical church most English people picture: Victorian gothic parish buildings, surpliced choirs and hymnbooks, all of them inventions of this period rather than inheritances from before it.

movements.name: The Russian Church — the Synodal Century
movements.informalName: The Church of Filaret and Pobedonostsev
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich institutionally: Filaret’s catechism and the Synodal Bible (1876 [S]), synodal records, the missionary societies’ archives [S]; John of Kronstadt’s parish corpus fits here [S-heavy: anchors carried from standard references, not verified this session]
movements.relationsSummary: Receiver of VII.21: Filaret of Moscow, Pobedonostsev’s ober-procuracy [S], the Altai and Japan missions (Nikolai from 1861 [S]), the 1905 toleration edict and pre-council movement [S]; renewal-inside relation with VIII.11 (Optina) named both directions; tension-partners: the Belokrinitsa hierarchy (1846 [S]) and the Stundist ferment; Alaska (VIII.47) is this church’s mission
movements.why: Receiver of VII.21 — without it VIII.11 is renewal inside a missing church. Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.21); end 1906 era cap (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: For this whole century the Russian Orthodox Church had no patriarch. It was governed by a Holy Synod whose chief lay officer, the ober-procurator, answered to the tsar — an arrangement that produced both an immense institution and a cramped one. Metropolitan Filaret of Moscow gave Russia its standard catechism and pressed for decades for a Bible in modern Russian, finished in 1876 over long resistance; missions went out to the Altai peoples, to Alaska and to Japan; monasteries and their elders drew crowds, and a parish priest, John of Kronstadt, became the most sought-after confessor in the empire. But under Konstantin Pobedonostsev, ober-procurator for a quarter-century, the church was also the instrument of a policy of religious uniformity that pressed hard on Old Believers, Eastern Catholics and evangelicals alike. When toleration was finally decreed in 1905, the church immediately began preparing the council that would give it back its own head.
movements.teaser: Russia, 1815 to 1906 — a church with no patriarch, run by a lay official of the tsar, that produced a Bible, a missionary empire and a famous parish priest while waiting a century to govern itself again.
voices: Filaret (Drozdov) of Moscow — metropolitan for nearly half a century, author of the church's catechism and champion of the Russian Bible
Makary (Glukharev) — founder of the Altai mission, who translated Scripture into the languages of Siberian peoples
Nikolai (Kasatkin) of Japan — sent to Hakodate in 1861, he built a Japanese Orthodox church staffed by Japanese clergy
John of Kronstadt — the parish priest whose eucharistic preaching and charity drew the whole empire to a naval town
Konstantin Pobedonostsev — the lay ober-procurator whose long tenure defined the era's policy of religious uniformity
movements.legacy: The Bible Filaret fought for is still the Russian Orthodox Church's standard translation, and the missionary churches begun in this period — in Japan, in Alaska — are still there. Its deepest legacy is the council it spent the century waiting for: the preparatory work of 1905-06 became the Moscow Council of 1917-18, which restored the patriarchate just as the revolution arrived that would try to destroy it.

movements.name: Armenian Christianity — the Zartonk Century
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the 1863 Constitution’s own text (verified), the National Assembly records [S], the Evangelical split’s documents [S]
movements.relationsSummary: The Zartonk: the Armenian National Constitution (1863, verified — lay representation limiting patriarchal power); the Armenian Evangelical Church (1846 [S]) and Protestant millet (1850 [S]) — the mission-era split inside the era’s own story; the Hamidian massacres (1894–96 [S]); ends at the 1906 cap — 1906–1915 left to era 10 (the fork was shown)
movements.why: Receiver of VII.24 — the VI.28 precedent’s third link; declining re-opens the 1815–1915 hole (conditional flag banked). Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.24); end 1906 era cap RULED over the 1915 branch — 1906-1915 left to era 10 (IX.27 receives) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Zartonk — awakening — is what Armenians call their nineteenth century: a revival of language, schools, printing and civic life carried largely inside the church, because under Ottoman rule the church was the nation's legal body. Its central document is the Armenian National Constitution of 1863, which seated lay delegates in a national assembly and limited what the Patriarch of Constantinople could do alone, an unusual experiment in giving a laity formal power over its own hierarchy. The century also divided the community: converts of American missionaries were expelled from the Apostolic Church and organized as the Armenian Evangelical Church in 1846, recognized by the Ottoman state as a separate Protestant community in 1850, while an Armenian Catholic patriarchate continued alongside.
