And it ended in blood — the Hamidian massacres of 1894-96 killed tens of thousands and emptied whole districts.
movements.teaser: Constantinople, Anatolia and the Caucasus, 1815 to 1906 — a national awakening carried by a church, which wrote its people a constitution and then watched the massacres begin.
voices: Mkrtich Khrimian, called Hayrik — editor, bishop, patriarch of Constantinople and later catholicos, the era's great popular voice for the Armenian peasantry
Nerses Varzhapetian — patriarch of Constantinople, who took the Armenian case to the Congress of Berlin in 1878
Grigor Odian — among the young Constantinople intellectuals who drafted the Armenian National Constitution of 1863
movements.legacy: The Armenian Apostolic Church remains the national church of Armenia and of a diaspora this century's emigrations began; the Armenian Evangelical Church founded in 1846 and the Armenian Catholic Church are both still here, small and continuous. The habit of lay representation written into the 1863 constitution survived into the Apostolic Church's later governance. And the awakening's institutions — its schools, presses and newspapers — carried a national literature and a national self-understanding that the catastrophe of the following decade would scatter across the world but not extinguish.

movements.name: The Old Catholic Churches — Utrecht to the Union
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the Declaration of Utrecht (1889, verified), Döllinger’s corpus [S], the churches’ own synodal records [S]
movements.relationsSummary: VII.25’s continuation: Vatican I rejected; Döllinger excommunicated 1871 [S]; Reinkens consecrated by Utrecht 1873 [S]; five bishops sign the Declaration of Utrecht (24 Sep 1889, verified) — the Union founded; the 1815 start keeps segment continuity (the 1870-formation branch was shown)
movements.why: Receiver of VII.25 — the same should-not-live-in-a-relations-line logic that seated its parent. Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 RULED over the 1870 formation-event branch (segment continuity with VII.25; the pre-1870 Utrecht line carried, not a head-gap); Declaration of Utrecht 24 Sep 1889 verified in-window (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: There had been a small church at Utrecht out of communion with Rome since an eighteenth-century quarrel over Jansenism left it electing its own archbishops. It stayed a Dutch curiosity until 1870, when the First Vatican Council defined papal infallibility and a body of German, Swiss and Austrian Catholics — professors, priests and laypeople, with the church historian Ignaz von Dollinger at their head — refused to accept it. Excommunicated, they needed bishops, and Utrecht had them: Joseph Hubert Reinkens was consecrated for the German Old Catholics in 1873 by a bishop of that line. In 1889 five bishops signed the Declaration of Utrecht, binding these churches into a union that professed the faith of the undivided church of the first thousand years and rejected the papal claims of 1870 — and then went on to drop compulsory celibacy for clergy and to put the liturgy into the language of the people.
movements.teaser: The Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland, 1815 to 1906 — Catholics who could not accept the pope's 1870 infallibility, and an old Dutch church that had bishops to spare.
voices: Ignaz von Dollinger — the Munich church historian whose refusal of the 1870 definition made him the movement's intellectual founder; excommunicated in 1871
Joseph Hubert Reinkens — first bishop of the German Old Catholics, consecrated by the see of Utrecht in 1873
Hermanus Heykamp — bishop of Deventer, the Utrecht-line bishop who consecrated him
Eduard Herzog — first bishop of the Christian Catholic Church of Switzerland
movements.legacy: The Union of Utrecht is still there: a small communion of national churches in the Netherlands, Germany, Switzerland, Austria, Poland and the Czech lands. Its most consequential work turned out to be ecumenical. The Bonn conferences Dollinger convened in the 1870s were among the first modern meetings of Old Catholic, Anglican and Orthodox theologians at one table, and in 1931 the Old Catholics and the Church of England entered full communion by the Bonn Agreement — one of the earliest such agreements between separated Western churches, and a model for many since.

movements.name: Nineteenth-Century Methodism
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Rich [S-heavy]: connexional minutes, the Primitive Methodist magazine record [S], the 1844 split dossiers [S], ecumenical conference records from 1881 [S]
movements.relationsSummary: Receiver of VII.5 — whose children (VIII.4, VIII.6) had rows while the church did not: British Wesleyan consolidation [S]; the Primitive Methodists A5 INSIDE (Mow Cop 1807, formed 1811–12 [S] — female itinerants, the working-class connexion); the US family’s 1844 North/South slavery split [S]; the Black Methodist handoff (AME 1816, AME Zion 1821 [S]) named toward VIII.1
movements.why: Receiver of VII.5; the flag-9 Primitive Methodists land inside. Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.5); end 1906 era cap; Primitive Methodists (Mow Cop 1807, connexion 1811-12 [S]) A5 inside (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: A movement that began as a society inside the Church of England spent the nineteenth century becoming a worldwide family of churches, and dividing as it grew. In Britain the Wesleyan connexion consolidated into a respectable denomination, and those who found it too respectable went their own way: the Primitive Methodists, born at an open-air camp meeting on Mow Cop in 1807 and a settled connexion by 1811-12, took the gospel into the pit villages behind working-class preachers, a striking number of them women. In America, Methodism became the largest Protestant body in the country and then split down the middle over slavery in 1844 into northern and southern churches that would not reunite for nearly a century; Black Methodists, refused equal standing, had already built churches of their own — the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816, the AME Zion Church in 1821. By 1881 the family was scattered enough that it needed a world conference simply to speak to itself.
movements.teaser: Britain, North America and the mission fields, 1815 to 1906 — a revival grown into a worldwide church, divided by class at one end of the Atlantic and by slavery at the other.
voices: Hugh Bourne and William Clowes — the Staffordshire preachers whose 1807 camp meeting on Mow Cop began the Primitive Methodists
Jabez Bunting — the administrator who shaped, and centralized, British Wesleyan Methodism for a generation
Richard Allen — founding bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816
James Varick — first superintendent of the AME Zion Church
William Taylor — the itinerant preacher, later missionary bishop, whose work ran from the California goldfields to India and Africa
movements.legacy: Methodism became one of the largest Protestant families in the world: the United Methodist Church and British Methodism, the AME, AME Zion and CME churches, and Methodist churches across Africa and Asia all descend from this century's expansion. Its machinery outlasted it too — the class meeting, the itinerant preacher, the connexional conference. So did its conviction that holiness is meant to be practical and available now, which passed through the Holiness movement into Pentecostalism and from there into a very large share of world Christianity.

movements.name: Nineteenth-Century Baptists
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate-to-rich [S]: association minutes, Spurgeon’s corpus [S], the 1845 SBC founding documents [S]
movements.relationsSummary: Receiver of VII.16: Spurgeon [S]; the SBC formed 1845 in the slavery split [S]; Landmarkism [S]; the downgrade controversy [S]; the era’s most consequential Baptist stories (Black Baptist — VIII.1; missions — VIII.7) already carried elsewhere, said honestly
movements.why: Receiver of VII.16 — the genuine-call draft (the least census-distinctive of the big-church tails, stated); awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.16); end 1906 era cap; distinctiveness caveat on the record (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Baptists began the century as a scattering of self-governing congregations and ended it as one of the largest Protestant families in the English-speaking world, without ever agreeing to be governed from anywhere. In London, Charles Haddon Spurgeon preached weekly to thousands at the Metropolitan Tabernacle and published sermons that sold in the millions; late in life he broke with the Baptist Union over what he called the Down-Grade, convinced his fellow ministers were quietly giving up the doctrines they had been ordained to preach. In America the family split in 1845, when Baptists in the South, refused a slaveholding missionary appointment, formed the Southern Baptist Convention. Running alongside was Landmarkism, which held that only true Baptist congregations were churches at all and traced an unbroken Baptist succession back to the apostles.
movements.teaser: Britain and North America, 1815 to 1906 — congregations that answered to no bishop, arguing their way into becoming one of Protestantism's largest families.
voices: Charles Haddon Spurgeon — London's Metropolitan Tabernacle preacher, whose printed sermons reached a worldwide readership
James Robinson Graves — the editor and controversialist who gave Landmarkism its shape
William Bullein Johnson — first president of the Southern Baptist Convention, formed at Augusta, Georgia, in 1845
John Clifford — the Baptist Union leader who stood on the other side of Spurgeon in the Down-Grade dispute
movements.legacy: The bodies formed in this century are still the shape of Baptist life: the Southern Baptist Convention became the largest Protestant denomination in the United States, and the Baptist Union of Great Britain and its counterparts continue. Spurgeon's sermons have never gone out of print, and the Down-Grade Controversy became a template for the fundamentalist-modernist battles of the century after. Two of the era's most consequential Baptist stories are told elsewhere in this atlas — the Black Baptist churches of America, and the overseas mission movement that Baptists largely began.

movements.name: Nineteenth-Century Quakerism — the Separations
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Rich for the separations (both sides’ own minutes and epistles [S]); the abolition/women’s-rights overlap documented in Friends’ own records [S]
movements.relationsSummary: VII.1 ends 1815 living; the Hicksite separation (1827–28 [S]) is the family’s defining century event; Gurneyite/Wilburite divisions [S]; the pastoral-system revival [S]; the E8 window-honesty applied: this segment is the honest home for the separations
movements.why: Receiver of VII.1 (mild segment lean per the survey). Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.1); end 1906 era cap; the Hicksite separation 1827-28 [S] is the century event (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: The Society of Friends came into the nineteenth century intact and left it in pieces. In 1827-28 the American yearly meetings tore apart over Elias Hicks, a Long Island farmer and travelling minister who held that the Inward Light, not the Bible or a doctrine of atonement, was the heart of the faith; those who followed him and those who opposed him became separate bodies meeting in separate houses. Within twenty years the evangelical side divided again, between followers of the English banker-minister Joseph John Gurney and the conservative John Wilbur. Out of the Gurneyite stream came something Friends had never had — revival meetings, planned worship and paid pastors — so that by the century's end some Quaker meetings still sat in silence while others sang hymns and listened to a sermon. Through all of it Friends kept up the work they were best known for: abolition, prison reform, and the women's rights movement several of them helped to launch.
movements.teaser: North America and Britain, 1815 to 1906 — a people known for silence dividing three ways over what the silence was for, while leading the fights against slavery and for women's rights.
voices: Elias Hicks — the travelling minister whose preaching on the Inward Light precipitated the separation of 1827-28
Joseph John Gurney — the English evangelical Friend whose teaching shaped the largest branch of American Quakerism
John Wilbur — his conservative opponent, whose followers kept to the older quietist discipline
Lucretia Mott — Hicksite minister and abolitionist, a principal organizer of the 1848 Seneca Falls women's rights convention
Levi Coffin — the Indiana Friend whose house was one of the busiest stations on the Underground Railroad
movements.legacy: All three streams are still here: the pastoral, evangelical Friends who are now the majority of Quakers worldwide — most of them in Kenya and Latin America — the unprogrammed liberal meetings, and the small conservative bodies that kept the older ways. Friends' public work outlasted their divisions. The peace testimony survived the separations intact, the relief agencies that grew from it were jointly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1947, and the Quaker practice of seeking the sense of a meeting rather than counting votes has been borrowed far outside the Society.

movements.name: American Unitarianism & Universalism — the Consolidations
movements.statusWord: Floor Question carried — VII.27’s two-thread separation re-carried (Unitarian beyondFloor at own-confession strength; Universalist arguably floor-clean), the Transcendentalist third thread named Outside-A4-adjacent (Era 9 Step 0)
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Rich own record: Channing’s 1819 sermon [S], the AUA’s founding (1825, verified), Emerson’s 1838 Address [S], convention records [S]
movements.floorNote: Two different questions here, and they get different answers. The Unitarian side placed itself outside the Nicene creed's confession of the Trinity by its own explicit teaching — that is the movement's own account of itself, not an outsider's charge. The Universalist side is a separate case: its defining claim was about the scope of salvation rather than about the doctrine of God, and much of it would sit comfortably inside Nicene bounds. A third strain, the Transcendentalists, moved past the question of Christian doctrine altogether.
movements.relationsSummary: AUA organized 25 May 1825 (verified); Channing’s Baltimore sermon (1819 [S]); the Transcendentalist strain pulling past the register question [S]; Universalist conventions [S]; register-cap convention applies
movements.why: Receiver of VII.27 — else the register lane’s American thread goes silent at 1815 while alive. Register; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1819 (Channing’s Baltimore sermon [S]; AUA organized 25 May 1825, verified); end 1906 register-cap convention (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Two movements that had grown up separately in New England spent this century turning themselves into organized denominations. In 1819 William Ellery Channing preached an ordination sermon in Baltimore that gave liberal Congregationalists both a name and a platform, and in 1825 they founded the American Unitarian Association; the Universalists, who taught that God would in the end save everyone, built their own conventions on a separate track. Within a generation the Unitarian side produced a third thing it had not expected: Ralph Waldo Emerson left the ministry and told Harvard's divinity students in 1838 to look for religion in intuition and nature rather than historical revelation, and the Transcendentalists carried that further than most of their elders wanted to go. What held the movements together was less a shared creed than a shared refusal of creeds, along with a strong practical bent — toward schools, prisons, asylums and abolition.
movements.teaser: New England and the mid-Atlantic, 1819 to 1906 — liberal churches that made a principle of having no creed, and organized themselves anyway.
voices: William Ellery Channing — whose 1819 Baltimore sermon named and defined American Unitarianism
Hosea Ballou — the Universalist preacher whose Treatise on Atonement (1805) shaped the movement's theology
Ralph Waldo Emerson — Unitarian minister turned essayist, whose 1838 Divinity School Address broke with historical Christianity
Theodore Parker — the radical Unitarian preacher and abolitionist who pushed the movement's boundaries hardest
Dorothea Dix — the Unitarian reformer whose campaigns transformed the treatment of the mentally ill
movements.legacy: Both bodies survived, and in 1961 merged into the Unitarian Universalist Association, still a functioning denomination in North America. Their wider mark is out of proportion to their numbers: the Transcendentalists' essays became a permanent part of American literature, and the causes the movement threw itself into — abolition, public education, humane treatment of prisoners and the mentally ill — long outlived the theological arguments that produced them.

movements.name: The Ruthenian Greek Catholic Church — Polotsk to Galicia
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate [S]: the Polotsk acta (1839, verified as event), Galician diocesan records [S], Sheptytsky’s early corpus [S]
movements.relationsSummary: The Synod of Polotsk (1839, verified) dissolves the Union in the Russian Empire — ~1.5M transferred (verified); Chełm follows 1875 [S]; Austrian Galicia the survival zone and national engine (Sheptytsky from 1900 [S]); VIII.31’s natural tension-partner
movements.why: Receiver of VII.28 — declining re-opens a 1815–1946 gap with the century’s largest forced church-dissolution inside it. Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.28); end 1906 era cap; Synod of Polotsk 12 Feb 1839 verified in-window (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Millions of Belarusians and Ukrainians worshipped in the Byzantine rite while in communion with Rome, an arrangement dating from a union of 1596. In the Russian Empire it was abolished by decree: at the Synod of Polotsk in February 1839, bishops led by Joseph Semashko declared their church reunited with Russian Orthodoxy, and roughly a million and a half people were transferred with a stroke of the pen; the remaining eparchy of Chelm followed in 1875, with resistance in some villages broken by force. What survived did so under Austrian rule in Galicia, where the Greek Catholic Church became not only a church but the institutional backbone of Ukrainian national life — its clergy the schoolteachers, editors and co-operative organizers of a people who had almost no other leadership. At the turn of the century Andrey Sheptytsky took the metropolitan see of Lviv and began the long tenure that would carry the church through everything the next fifty years brought.
movements.teaser: Belarus, Ukraine and Austrian Galicia, 1815 to 1906 — an Eastern church in communion with Rome dissolved by decree in one empire and turned into a nation's backbone in the other.
voices: Joseph Semashko — the bishop who engineered the Synod of Polotsk in 1839 and led his church into the Russian Orthodox Church
Andrey Sheptytsky — metropolitan of Lviv from the turn of the century, who made the Galician church a national institution
Markiyan Shashkevych — the Greek Catholic priest and poet whose writing helped begin the Ukrainian literary revival in Galicia
The villagers of Pratulin — thirteen Greek Catholics killed in 1874 for refusing to surrender their church, later beatified as martyrs
movements.legacy: The Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church is the largest Eastern Catholic church in the world today, and everything it survived afterwards — Soviet liquidation in 1946, four decades underground, its re-emergence in 1989 — rested on the Galician base built in this century. In the lands where the union was dissolved by decree, it never came back. The church's habit of carrying a national culture as well as a liturgy, formed here, is still one of the most distinctive things about it.

movements.name: Philippine Catholicism — Gomburza to the Aglipayan Schism
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate [S]: the secularization dossiers [S], Gomburza records (1872 [S]), the Revolution’s church documents [S], the IFI’s founding texts [S]
movements.relationsSummary: VII.29’s promised continuation, sharpened: the secularization controversy [S]; the Gomburza executions (1872 [S]); the Revolution’s church question [S]; the Iglesia Filipina Independiente proclaimed 1902 [S] — window-orthodox, with the era-10 drift note carried for the register’s next act
movements.why: Receiver of VII.29 (the VI.19 chain’s third link). Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (segment continuity with VII.29); end 1906 era cap; the Aglipayan proclamation 1902 [S] in-window (its doctrinal drift is era 10’s, window-noted) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Spanish friars had run the Philippine church for three centuries, and the century's great church fight was over whether Filipinos could run their own parishes. The secularization campaign — transferring parishes from Spanish religious orders to diocesan clergy, most of them native-born — turned into a national grievance, and in 1872, after a mutiny at the Cavite arsenal, three priests who had championed it were garrotted: Mariano Gomez, Jose Burgos and Jacinto Zamora, remembered ever since by the single name Gomburza. Their execution did more for the independence movement than their campaign ever had; Jose Rizal dedicated his second novel to their memory. When Spanish rule ended, part of the church went with it: in 1902 the labour organizer Isabelo de los Reyes proclaimed an Iglesia Filipina Independiente and named the former revolutionary chaplain Gregorio Aglipay its head, and for a few years a substantial minority of Filipino Catholics followed it.
movements.teaser: The Philippines, 1815 to 1906 — three priests garrotted over who should run the parishes, and a national church proclaimed thirty years later in the ruins of Spanish rule.
voices: Pedro Pelaez — the Manila cathedral canon who first pressed the case for Filipino priests in Filipino parishes
Mariano Gomez, Jose Burgos and Jacinto Zamora — the three priests executed in 1872, remembered together as Gomburza
Gregorio Aglipay — the priest and revolutionary chaplain who became the first head of the Iglesia Filipina Independiente
Isabelo de los Reyes — the writer and labour organizer who proclaimed the independent church in 1902
movements.legacy: The Iglesia Filipina Independiente is still a functioning church, and since 1961 has been in full communion with the Episcopal Church and the wider Anglican Communion. The Catholic Church it broke from remained the country's majority faith and, over the following decades, got what the secularization campaign had asked for: a Filipino hierarchy drawn from Filipino clergy. Gomburza became a national memory more than a churchly one — three priests' names on monuments and in schoolbooks, taught as the beginning of a country.

movements.name: The Church of the East & the Chaldean Consolidation
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Thin-to-moderate [S]: succession records, mission archives (ABCFM Urmia 1834 [S]; Canterbury’s mission 1886 [S])
movements.relationsSummary: The formation center era 8 lacked: John Hormizd confirmed as Chaldean patriarch (1830 [S]) — the modern Chaldean Catholic Church consolidates; the Qudshanis line continues as the Assyrian Church of the East [S]; NO continuesAs back to Frozen VI.30 (165-year gap — the E8 named-gap disclosure is the bridge, restated here); IX.19 receives the family forward
movements.why: The flag-12 segment with the story-center the gap lacked. Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815; end 1906 era cap; John Hormizd confirmed 1830 [S]; NO continuesAs back to VI.30 (165-year gap — the E8 named-gap disclosure is the bridge) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: The Church of the East — the church that once sent bishops from Baghdad as far as China — entered this century reduced to the mountains and plains of the Ottoman-Persian borderland and divided between rival patriarchal lines, one in communion with Rome and one not. In 1830 Rome confirmed John Hormizd as patriarch of Babylon, consolidating the Chaldean Catholic Church as a single body; the line that stayed independent kept its seat in the mountain village of Qudshanis in Hakkari, its patriarchate passing from uncle to nephew, and its people came to be known as the Assyrian Church of the East. Both then found themselves courted by outsiders. American Congregationalist missionaries settled at Urmia in the 1830s and gave the region a printing press and schools in the spoken Syriac of the day; from 1886 the Archbishop of Canterbury sent a mission expressly instructed to strengthen the ancient church rather than convert its members.
movements.teaser: Mesopotamia, the Hakkari mountains and Urmia, 1815 to 1906 — the oldest missionary church in Asia, reduced to two patriarchates and a mountain village, and rediscovered by Western missions.
voices: John Hormizd — confirmed patriarch in 1830, the figure in whom the modern Chaldean Catholic Church consolidated
Joseph Audo — Chaldean patriarch who resisted Roman centralization over his church's jurisdiction, including at the First Vatican Council
Justin Perkins — the American missionary who established the Urmia press and printed Scripture in the spoken Syriac of the region
movements.legacy: Both churches are still here, and both are now largely churches of exile. The Chaldean Catholic Church remains the largest Christian body native to Iraq. The Assyrian Church of the East, driven out of the Hakkari mountains during the First World War, spent most of the twentieth century with its patriarch abroad and only returned the seat to Erbil in 2015. The Urmia press left a quieter legacy: printing Scripture and schoolbooks in the language people actually spoke helped make modern Aramaic a written literary language, which it has remained.

movements.name: The Confessional Lutheran Revival & the Emigrations
movements.region: Prussia, Saxony, Bavaria; N. America; Australia
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Rich: the Prussian Union documents (1817, verified), the emigration records (1838 sailing, verified), the Missouri Synod’s founding (1847, verified) and Der Lutheraner [S], Erlangen corpus [S]
movements.relationsSummary: The Prussian Union (1817, verified) forces merger; the Old Lutherans refuse and are persecuted [S]; the Saxon emigration (1838, verified) and the Missouri Synod (1847, verified); Neo-Lutheranism and Erlangen [S]; Löhe’s Neuendettelsau [S]; Australian Lutheranism’s same root [S] — a confession-defined COUNTER-shape to the awakening entries
movements.why: The sweep’s biggest Protestant hole: still-living communions on three continents with no row. Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1817 (the Prussian Union, verified — the confession-defining provocation); end 1906 era cap; Saxon emigration Nov 1838 and Missouri Synod 26 Apr 1847 verified in-window (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: In 1817 the king of Prussia ordered his Lutheran and Reformed subjects into a single united church. Many Lutherans complied; some would not, holding that a confession of faith is not something a state can merge. These Old Lutherans were fined, had their services broken up and their pastors imprisoned — and rather than conform, whole congregations emigrated. Some went to South Australia in 1838 under Pastor August Kavel; a Saxon company sailed for Missouri the same year and had to depose its own leader for immorality within months of landing. Out of that chastened remnant, under the young pastor C. F. W. Walther, came the Missouri Synod of 1847: a church that made subscription to the Lutheran confessions the condition of fellowship, and built its own schools, seminaries and German-language press to keep them. In Germany the same instinct produced a scholarly renewal at Erlangen, and at Neuendettelsau, Wilhelm Lohe's training of pastors and deaconesses for emigrant congregations overseas.
movements.teaser: Prussia, Saxony and Bavaria, then Missouri and South Australia, 1817 to 1906 — Lutherans who would not let a king merge their confession, and sailed rather than sign.
voices: Johann Gottfried Scheibel — the Breslau theologian whose refusal of the Prussian Union made him the Old Lutherans' first leader
C. F. W. Walther — the Saxon emigrants' pastor, first president of the Missouri Synod and editor of Der Lutheraner
Martin Stephan — the Dresden pastor who led the Saxon emigration of 1838 and was deposed by his own colonists soon after arrival
August Kavel — who led Prussian Old Lutherans to South Australia in 1838
Wilhelm Lohe — the Bavarian pastor whose Neuendettelsau institutions sent pastors and deaconesses to emigrant churches on three continents
movements.legacy: The churches this produced are on three continents still: the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod and the Wisconsin Synod in North America, the Lutheran Church of Australia, and the independent Lutheran churches of Germany. Their parochial schools became one of the largest Protestant school systems in the United States. The wider legacy is a pattern rather than an institution — a church defined by a written confession rather than by a state, a nation or a revival, which became one of the standing options in Protestant life and remains an argument Protestants have with each other.

movements.name: Malagasy Christianity — the Self-Carried Church
movements.informalName: The Church that Grew under Persecution
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Real inside voice: martyr accounts (Rasalama 1837, verified), Malagasy hymnody [S], the memorial churches [S]; LMS archives as the outside frame
movements.relationsSummary: LMS arrives 1818/1820 [S]; first baptisms 1831 (verified); Ranavalona I bans Christianity (1835, verified) and Rasalama is martyred (1837, verified) — the church then GROWS for 25 years with no missionaries; Ranavalona II converts (1869); French conquest ends the window (1895–96 [S]); VIII.21’s exact kin-shape
movements.why: The era’s clearest missing self-carried church — not inside VIII.7’s named wings. Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1818 (LMS arrival window [S]; first baptisms 1831 verified); end 1895 principled (the French conquest [S]) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: The London Missionary Society reached Madagascar in 1818, and its most consequential work turned out to be alphabetical: within a decade Malagasy had a written form, a printing press and, by 1835, a complete Bible. Then the door slammed. Queen Ranavalona I banned Christianity in 1835 and expelled the missionaries; Rasalama, the first Malagasy martyr, was speared in 1837, and for the next quarter-century believers were hunted, enslaved, and thrown from the cliff at Ampamarinana above the capital. The church did not merely survive the persecution — it grew through it, without foreign clergy, on the Bible it had been left and hymns its own people wrote, and when the missionaries were allowed back they found far more Christians than they had left behind. Ranavalona II was baptized in 1869 and burned the royal talismans, and the church became the establishment it had once been martyred by, until the French conquest of 1895 ended the kingdom that housed it.
movements.teaser: Madagascar, 1818 to 1895 — a church whose missionaries were expelled and whose members were speared and thrown off cliffs, and which was larger at the end of the persecution than at the start.
voices: David Jones and David Griffiths — the Welsh missionaries who gave Malagasy its written form and its first complete Bible
Rasalama — the first Malagasy Christian martyr, speared in 1837
Rafaravavy — the noblewoman who survived the first wave of persecution, escaped the island, and carried the church's story abroad
Ranavalona I — the queen whose 1835 edict outlawed Christianity and began the persecution
Ranavalona II — the queen baptized in 1869, who burned the royal talismans and made the kingdom Christian
movements.legacy: Christianity is still the majority faith of Madagascar, and the churches grown from this period remain among the island's largest institutions. In Antananarivo four memorial churches stand on the sites where believers were killed, built by the people who had survived them. The story travelled further than the island did: the Malagasy persecution became one of the most retold missionary narratives of the nineteenth century, a standard illustration in sermons and mission magazines wherever the question was whether a church could hold together with no clergy and no protection at all.

movements.name: East African Christianity & the Uganda Martyrs
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: the martyrs’ double-communion record (1885–87, verified; canonized 1964), the Baganda evangelists’ wave [S], CMS/White Fathers archives
movements.relationsSummary: Krapf 1844 [S]; UMCA 1857 [S]; CMS and White Fathers reach Buganda 1877/1879 [S]; the Uganda Martyrs — Anglican AND Catholic pages executed 1885–87, Lwanga burned at Namugongo (1886, verified); the 1900 Agreement’s Christian kingdom [S]; forward kin: IX.3 (Balokole) is this story’s era-10 child
movements.why: Outside VIII.7’s named wings; formation-grade with double-communion witness. Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1844 (Krapf at Mombasa [S]); end 1906 era cap; Lwanga and companions 3 Jun 1886 verified in-window (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Christianity came back to East Africa along the coast first — Johann Ludwig Krapf landed at Mombasa in 1844 and began the language and mapping work later missions relied on — and then inland to the kingdom of Buganda, where Anglican missionaries arrived in 1877 and French Catholic White Fathers in 1879. Their converts were largely young men of the royal court, and when the kabaka Mwanga II turned on them between 1885 and 1887 he killed both kinds together: Anglican and Catholic pages executed side by side, the largest group burned alive at Namugongo on 3 June 1886 under the leadership of Charles Lwanga, who is said to have arranged his own pyre. Persecution did what it often does. The church grew, and Baganda converts carried it outward as evangelists into the surrounding kingdoms faster than any mission society could have, so that by the agreement of 1900 that settled Buganda's relations with Britain, it was a Christian kingdom.
movements.teaser: The East African coast and the kingdom of Buganda, 1844 to 1906 — Anglican and Catholic converts burned together at Namugongo, and a church that spread out of their ashes across the region.
voices: Johann Ludwig Krapf — the German Lutheran in Anglican service whose 1844 landing at Mombasa opened inland East Africa to mission
Joseph Mukasa Balikuddembe — first of the martyrs, killed in 1885 for rebuking the kabaka
Charles Lwanga — leader of the Catholic pages, burned at Namugongo on 3 June 1886 and canonized in 1964
James Hannington — first Anglican bishop of Eastern Equatorial Africa, killed on the road into the kingdom in 1885
Mwanga II — the kabaka whose persecution of 1885-87 created the martyrs
Apolo Kivebulaya — a Muganda convert who spent his life as an evangelist among the peoples west of the kingdom
movements.legacy: Uganda became one of the most heavily Christian countries in Africa, and the martyrs are honoured on both sides of the division that produced them — canonized by the Catholic Church in 1964, commemorated in the Anglican calendar, with shrines of both communions at Namugongo that draw enormous crowds every 3 June. The pattern set here mattered as much as the memory: African Christians carrying the faith to neighbouring peoples on their own initiative is how Christianity actually spread across this region, and the revival that swept these same churches from the 1930s grew out of the same soil.

experienceToday.text: The Basilica of the Uganda Martyrs at Namugongo, Uganda — built over the place where Charles Lwanga and his companions were burned, with the Anglican martyrs' shrine nearby

movements.name: The Taiping Heavenly Kingdom
movements.informalName: The Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace
movements.statusWord: Floor Question (register) — new-revelation and sonship claims at own-text strength [S]; person-defined ground plain; shelf ruled REGISTER over Outside-A4 at the Era 9 Freeze; ended 1864
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: The movement’s own printed scriptures and edicts [S — own-text strength]; hostile Qing and missionary accounts flagged; modern scholarship (Spence [S])
movements.floorNote: Hong Xiuquan claimed to be God's second son and the younger brother of Jesus Christ, and the kingdom's own printed scriptures rest on that claim. Both the claim and the authority built on it sit outside anything the historic creeds confess — recorded here as a description of what the movement's own texts say, not as a verdict on the people caught up in it.
movements.relationsSummary: Hong Xiuquan founds the God Worshippers; the Heavenly Kingdom declared 1851, Nanjing taken 1853, falls 1864; ~20 million dead (verified) — the century’s largest Christianity-adjacent movement and its largest catastrophe; VIII.7’s China wing needs this row to point at
movements.why: Participants will ask; the row exists so the map answers honestly. Register; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1850 (the God Worshippers’ rising); end 1864 (the Kingdom falls) — both the movement’s own dates; register shelf RULED over the Outside-A4 branch (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Hong Xiuquan was a village schoolteacher in Guangdong who failed the imperial examinations four times. After one failure he collapsed into a delirium and saw visions he could not interpret until, years later, he reread a Christian tract handed to him in the street; from it he concluded that the old man in his vision had been God the Father, the elder brother beside him Jesus Christ, and that he himself was God's second son, sent to sweep China clean of demons. The God Worshippers he and his cousin Feng Yunshan gathered in Guangxi became an army. They proclaimed the Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace in 1851, took Nanjing in 1853 and held it for eleven years — banning opium, alcohol and footbinding, destroying idols and ancestral tablets, holding land in common, and printing their own scriptures alongside the Bible. The war fought to destroy them was among the deadliest in human history, with estimates of the dead running to twenty million, and when Nanjing fell in 1864 Hong was already dead and the kingdom went with him.
movements.teaser: Southern China, 1850 to 1864 — a failed examination candidate who concluded he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ, and the kingdom founded on that conviction, which cost perhaps twenty million lives.
voices: Hong Xiuquan — the examination candidate turned Heavenly King, who identified himself as the younger brother of Jesus Christ
Feng Yunshan — his cousin and closest colleague, who built the God Worshippers into a mass movement in Guangxi
Yang Xiuqing — the East King, who claimed to speak with the voice of God the Father and dominated the kingdom until he was killed in 1856
Hong Rengan — the Heavenly King's cousin, who had lived among Protestant missionaries in Hong Kong and returned in 1859 with a programme for modernizing the kingdom
Issachar Jacox Roberts — the American Baptist missionary with whom Hong studied for a few months in 1847, and who declined to baptize him
movements.legacy: The Heavenly Kingdom left no church. Its institutions were destroyed with it in 1864 and no continuing body traces its descent from Hong Xiuquan. What it left instead was consequence. The Qing dynasty was permanently weakened by the war and by the regional armies raised to win it; the lower Yangtze countryside took generations to recover; and Chinese officials and villagers alike had been handed a reason to associate Christianity with rebellion and mass death, a suspicion that later missionaries met everywhere they went. Later Chinese revolutionaries, Sun Yat-sen among them, looked back on the Taiping as forerunners, and the movement remains a fixture of Chinese historical memory and museum display.

movements.name: Japanese Christianity — the Hidden Christians’ Emergence & the Meiji Church
movements.informalName: The Church that Survived Two Centuries in Hiding
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Real inside voice: the 1865 Ōura declaration (verified to the day), Kakure oral tradition [S], the bands’ records [S], Uchimura’s corpus [S]
movements.relationsSummary: 17 Mar 1865: Urakami villagers reveal themselves at Ōura (verified — ~30,000 hidden believers surface); the final Urakami persecution to 1873 [S]; the Kakure who stayed separate [S]; the Protestant bands and Uchimura’s Mukyōkai (1901 [S]); Nikolai’s Orthodox mission from 1861 [S — the start fork shown]
movements.why: The Japan lane went silent when VI.13’s wing was named un-continued; 1865 is the reveal the whole hidden-church story waits on. Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1865 RULED over the 1861 Nikolai branch (the Ōura revelation of 17 Mar 1865, verified — the reveal the hidden-church story waits on); end 1906 era cap (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: On 17 March 1865, weeks after a French church opened in Nagasaki's foreign settlement, a group of villagers from nearby Urakami came in, and one woman quietly told the priest that the hearts of all present were the same as his, and asked where the statue of Mary was. They were descendants of Christians driven underground in the 1600s, who had kept baptism, prayers and a liturgical calendar for over two hundred years without a single priest. In the months that followed tens of thousands more made themselves known. The government's ban was still in force, and the Urakami villagers were deported and held until 1873; when it was lifted, a Christianity of three kinds grew quickly in Meiji Japan — Catholic parishes rebuilt around the emerging hidden communities, Protestant bands of samurai-class students at Yokohama, Kumamoto and Sapporo, and a Russian Orthodox mission that Nikolai of Japan had begun in 1861 and staffed largely with Japanese clergy. Not all the hidden Christians rejoined: some, the Kakure, kept the tradition exactly as they had received it, and remain separate to this day.
movements.teaser: Nagasaki and Meiji Japan, 1865 to 1906 — villagers who walked into a new church and revealed that their families had kept the faith for two and a half centuries without a priest.
voices: Bernard Petitjean — the French priest at Oura to whom the Urakami villagers revealed themselves in 1865
Nikolai (Kasatkin) of Japan — the Russian monk who arrived at Hakodate in 1861 and built a Japanese Orthodox church
Niijima Jo — who left Japan illegally to study in America and returned to found Doshisha in Kyoto
Uchimura Kanzo — Sapporo Band convert who founded the Non-Church movement, a Christianity without clergy or sacraments
movements.legacy: Christianity in Japan stayed small — roughly one per cent of the population then and now — but its institutions outlasted the century: Doshisha and other mission-founded universities, the Orthodox cathedral in Tokyo that Nikolai built, and a Catholic community around Nagasaki that is still the largest in the country. The hidden Christians' story became the basis of a UNESCO World Heritage listing of Nagasaki-region sites in 2018, and it has had a long literary afterlife, most famously in Endo Shusaku's novel Silence.

experienceToday.text: Oura Church, Nagasaki — the church where the hidden Christians revealed themselves in 1865, a National Treasure of Japan and open to visitors
Hidden Christian Sites in the Nagasaki Region — the villages, islands and churches inscribed together as a UNESCO World Heritage property in 2018

movements.name: The Haitian Church — Rupture to Concordat
movements.informalName: The Church of the First Black Republic
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Thin and outside-pen-weighted, said so [S]: concordat documents (1860, verified), state records, later church histories
movements.relationsSummary: Schism from Rome across the whole post-independence period (verified — no Rome-trained clergy; the state runs the church; the Catholic-Vodou creole field forms in the vacuum); the Concordat signed 28 Mar 1860 (verified) — the story’s own resolution; start 1804 precedes the era once, disclosed (the story is indivisible)
movements.why: The marginalized-voices duty argues against another deferral — the first Black republic’s church story carried nowhere. Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1804 RULED over the 1815 branch (one disclosed pre-era reach — the story is indivisible); end 1860 RULED over the era-cap branch (the Concordat of 28 Mar 1860, verified — the story’s own resolution, the VII.22-1787 pattern) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: When Haiti declared independence in 1804 as the first Black republic, its church was cut adrift. Rome would not recognize the new state, the French clergy had fled or been killed, and for more than half a century no properly appointed bishop and almost no seminary-trained priest arrived. The state filled the gap, appointing its own clergy, and the parishes were served by men of irregular standing — some genuine priests under suspension, some who had simply assumed the title. In that long vacancy Haitian religious life took the shape it has largely kept: Catholic sacraments, feast days and saints woven together with Vodou practice inherited from West Africa, held by most Haitians as one thing rather than two. The rupture formally ended on 28 March 1860, when Haiti and the Holy See signed a concordat restoring a regular hierarchy — and began a much longer argument about what to do with everything that had grown up in the meantime.
movements.teaser: Haiti, 1804 to 1860 — the first Black republic's church, left for fifty-six years without Rome, a bishop or a seminary, and what grew in the gap.
voices: Fabre Geffrard — the president whose government concluded the 1860 concordat that restored Haiti's ties with Rome

The clergy of the schism years are poorly recorded — most of the men who served Haitian parishes between 1804 and 1860 arrived without appointment and left little written trace, and what record survives was largely written by outsiders
movements.legacy: The hierarchy the 1860 concordat established is still the framework of the Haitian Catholic Church, the country's largest institution. The creole religious world formed during the schism is also still there, and the church's relationship to it — stretches of quiet accommodation alternating with campaigns to stamp it out, most violently the anti-superstition drives of the 1940s — has been one of the defining questions of Haitian religion ever since.

movements.name: The Alaskan Mission — Herman’s Decades & Veniaminov
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate: Veniaminov’s own journals and Aleut translations [S], Herman’s Spruce Island record [S], post-1867 native-clergy records [S]
movements.relationsSummary: Veniaminov reaches Unalaska (1824, verified) — Aleut/Tlingit alphabets and translations [S]; Herman’s hermit decades (d. 1836 [S]); Innocent made bishop (1840, verified); after the 1867 sale the church STAYS — a native church under its own clergy [S]; VIII.31’s mission, the renewal-relation named
movements.why: Flag 4’s fork resolved toward the own entry conditioned on VIII.31 existing (else the A5 branch is hostless). Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1824 (Veniaminov at Unalaska 29 Jul 1824, verified); end 1906 era cap; the church stays after the 1867 sale [S] (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: Russian Orthodoxy reached Alaska with the fur trade, and two very different men made it stay. Herman, a lay monk who had come with the first mission in 1794, spent his last decades alone on Spruce Island near Kodiak, running a school and an orphanage for Alutiiq children and quarrelling with the trading company over its treatment of them. In 1824 a young married priest, Ioann Veniaminov, arrived at Unalaska and did the work of a linguist: he devised an alphabet for Aleut, translated the Gospel of Matthew and a catechism into it, and wrote an account of the islands and their people that scholars still use. Widowed, he became a monk, was made bishop in 1840 as Innocent, and rose eventually to be Metropolitan of Moscow. What the two of them built proved unexpectedly durable — when Russia sold Alaska in 1867 and the Russians went home, the church stayed, in the hands of Alaska Native clergy and lay readers who kept the services going in their own languages.
movements.teaser: Kodiak, the Aleutians and the Alaskan mainland, 1824 to 1906 — a hermit monk, a priest who wrote the Aleut alphabet, and a church that stayed on after the empire that brought it sold the territory and left.
voices: Herman of Alaska — the lay monk of Spruce Island, defender of the Alutiiq against the fur company; canonized in 1970 as the first saint of Orthodox America
Ioann Veniaminov, later Saint Innocent — priest at Unalaska from 1824, creator of the Aleut alphabet, then bishop of Alaska and finally Metropolitan of Moscow
Iakov Netsvetov — the first Alaska Native priest, who served the Yukon mission for twenty years
Tikhon (Bellavin) — bishop of the American diocese at the turn of the century, later patriarch of Moscow
movements.legacy: Orthodoxy is still a living Alaska Native tradition, with dozens of parishes serving villages across the Aleutians, the Kodiak archipelago and the Yukon-Kuskokwim delta, many of them keeping services in Yup'ik, Aleut and Tlingit alongside English. The mission also became the root of Orthodoxy in North America as a whole: the diocese Veniaminov founded moved its seat to San Francisco and then to New York, and is the ancestor of today's Orthodox Church in America. Herman's grave on Spruce Island is still a place of pilgrimage.

experienceToday.text: The Church of the Holy Ascension, Unalaska, Alaska — the parish Veniaminov served, and a National Historic Landmark
Spruce Island, Alaska — Saint Herman's hermitage and grave, a pilgrimage site for Orthodox Christians

movements.name: Nineteenth-Century Latin American Catholicism
movements.informalName: The Church of the New Republics
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate [S]: the patronato dossiers [S], the Reforma-era records [S], the 1899 Plenary Council acta [S], Brazil’s religious question [S]
movements.relationsSummary: A whole-continent silence in the century it became independent: the patronato fights and Rome’s slow recognition [S]; liberal/clerical conflict and the Reforma [S]; Romanization and the 1899 Latin American Plenary Council [S]; Brazil’s imperial church [S]; VII.17’s partial-continuation stays PROSE (the E8 ruling’s own logic — no identity write)
movements.why: Era 9 carried NO Latin American row at all. The devotional-register alternative was shown. Tier 2 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1815 (window; the independence century); end 1906 era cap; NO continuesAs from VII.17 (the E8 prose-continuity ruling’s own logic — edge/prose, not identity) (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: The Spanish crown had run the church in its American empire under a papal grant, appointing the bishops and collecting the tithes. When the colonies won independence the new republics claimed exactly the same right, and Rome — which had backed the crown — took decades to recognize either the governments or their nominees, leaving dioceses vacant and seminaries shut for a generation. What followed was a long fight between liberals and clericals over land, schools, cemeteries and marriage: sharpest in Mexico, where the Reform laws of the 1850s stripped the church of its property and drove it out of public life, and loudest in Brazil, where two bishops were tried and imprisoned in the 1870s. Rome answered by tightening its grip, importing European clergy and religious orders, rebuilding seminaries on Roman lines, and in 1899 summoning the bishops of the whole continent to Rome for a first Latin American Plenary Council. Underneath all of it the devotional life of ordinary Catholics — confraternities, patronal feasts, pilgrimage shrines, household saints — carried on much as before, often with very few priests.
movements.teaser: Spanish America and Brazil, 1815 to 1906 — a church that lost its king, waited a generation for Rome to recognize its bishops, and was fought over by every new republic.
voices: Benito Juarez — the Mexican president whose Reform laws separated church and state and confiscated the church's property
Gabriel Garcia Moreno — the president of Ecuador who consecrated his republic to the Sacred Heart and governed it as a Catholic state
Vital Maria Goncalves de Oliveira and Antonio de Macedo Costa — the Brazilian bishops tried and imprisoned in the religious question of the 1870s
Leo XIII — who convened the first Latin American Plenary Council at Rome in 1899
movements.legacy: This is the century that made Latin America's church what it is: a Roman-aligned hierarchy laid over a much older popular Catholicism, with far fewer priests per head than Europe had, and a long habit of arguing with the state. The 1899 council was the first time the continent's bishops met as a single body, and the continental conferences that followed — Rio in 1955, Medellin in 1968 — grew from that precedent. Latin America is still home to the largest share of the world's Catholics.

movements.name: Ethiopian Christianity — Tewodros to Menelik
movements.informalName: The Church of the Re-founded Empire
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate [S]: royal chronicles [S], the Boru Meda settlement records (1878 [S]), mission-era accounts flagged outside-pen
movements.relationsSummary: The stale-lane find: VI.25 ends 1650 and IX.20 begins 1900 — the re-foundation century carried nowhere: Tewodros II (1855–68 [S]); Yohannes IV and the Council of Boru Meda (1878 [S] — the Tawahedo settlement); Menelik and Adwa (1896 [S]); ends 1900 seamless to IX.20; NO continuesAs back to Frozen VI.25 (205-year gap — disclosure bridges); the 1650–1855 Gondarine gap stays named
movements.why: The segment that halves the Ethiopian lane’s silence. Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1855 (Tewodros II [S]); end 1900 seamless to IX.20; NO continuesAs back to VI.25 (205-year gap — disclosure bridges); forward continuesAs to IX.20 written at this Freeze (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: After a century in which Ethiopia's emperors were figureheads and the regional lords ruled, a provincial soldier crowned himself Tewodros II in 1855 and set out to remake the empire — and its church, whose lands he seized and whose clergy he tried to bring under his hand, until his quarrel with Britain ended with a redcoat army at Magdala and his suicide in 1868. His successor Yohannes IV settled a doctrinal argument that had divided Ethiopian theologians for two centuries: at the Council of Boru Meda in 1878 he ruled for the Tewahedo position on how Christ's divinity and humanity are united, and enforced it as the empire's single teaching. Menelik II then did what no other African ruler managed in that century — at Adwa in 1896 he destroyed an invading Italian army and kept his country independent — and Ethiopia entered the twentieth century as an ancient Christian state that had never been colonized, its church still receiving its head, the abun, from the Coptic patriarch in Egypt.
movements.teaser: Ethiopia, 1855 to 1900 — an emperor who fought his own church, a council that settled a two-century argument about Christ, and the only African army to defeat a European one and keep its country.
voices: Tewodros II — the emperor who re-founded the empire and broke with the church over its lands and privileges
Abuna Salama III — the Egyptian-appointed metropolitan who clashed with Tewodros and pressed for a single doctrinal settlement
Yohannes IV — who convened the Council of Boru Meda in 1878 and made the Tewahedo formula the empire's one teaching
Menelik II — victor at Adwa in 1896, who kept Ethiopia independent and expanded it far to the south
Empress Taytu Betul — Menelik's consort, a force in the Adwa campaign and in the church's affairs alike
movements.legacy: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church is one of the largest of the ancient Oriental Orthodox churches, and both things this century settled are still in place: the Tewahedo doctrine ruled at Boru Meda, and the independence Adwa secured. The one arrangement that did change came later — the church received its first Ethiopian bishops in 1929 and its own patriarch in 1959, ending sixteen centuries of taking its head from Alexandria. Adwa itself became a byword far beyond Ethiopia, a rallying point for Pan-Africanism and, in the Caribbean and the Americas, for movements that looked to Ethiopia as the image of an Africa that had never been conquered.

movements.name: Dutch Neo-Calvinism & the Secession Churches
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Rich own record [S]: the Afscheiding acts (1834 [S]), Kuyper’s corpus [S], the CRC’s records (1857 [S]), the 1892 union documents [S]
movements.relationsSummary: The Afscheiding (1834 [S]); the CRC in North America (1857 [S]); Kuyper — the Doleantie (1886 [S]), the Free University (1880 [S]), the 1892 GKN union [S] — a confession-defined formation family distinct from VIII.9’s awakening frame (the VIII.41 logic)
movements.why: The C15 counter-shape logic applied to the Dutch world. Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1834 (the Afscheiding [S]); end 1906 era cap (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: In 1834 a village pastor in Groningen, Hendrik de Cock, was suspended for preaching the old Reformed doctrines against what he took to be the liberalism of the national church, and his congregation walked out with him. The Afscheiding that followed was a secession of mostly poor and rural people, who were fined and had soldiers billeted on them for holding illegal services; many emigrated, and in 1857 their American cousins founded what became the Christian Reformed Church in North America. Fifty years after de Cock, Abraham Kuyper — journalist, politician, theologian — led a second and larger secession, the Doleantie of 1886, and in 1892 brought most of the two streams together. Kuyper's idea was always bigger than a church: that Christ's claim covers every sphere of life, each with its own proper authority, so believers should build their own schools, university, newspaper and political party rather than either withdraw from society or dissolve into it. He founded the Free University in Amsterdam in 1880 and served as prime minister of the Netherlands from 1901 to 1905.
movements.teaser: The Netherlands and the American Midwest, 1834 to 1906 — Calvinists who walked out of the national church twice, and then built a university, a newspaper and a governing party.
voices: Hendrik de Cock — the Groningen pastor whose 1834 suspension began the Afscheiding
Guillaume Groen van Prinsterer — the historian and politician whose anti-revolutionary politics prepared the ground Kuyper built on
Abraham Kuyper — theologian, newspaper editor, founder of the Free University, and prime minister of the Netherlands from 1901 to 1905
Herman Bavinck — the movement's systematic theologian, whose Reformed Dogmatics is still in use
Albertus Van Raalte — who led a colony of Seceders to Michigan in 1847
movements.legacy: The churches are still here: the Dutch Reformed families at home, most of them since 2004 inside the Protestant Church in the Netherlands, and in North America the Christian Reformed Church with its schools and colleges. Kuyper's larger idea travelled furthest. Sphere sovereignty and a Christian worldview applied to scholarship, politics and the arts became a standing tradition in Reformed thought and shaped a great deal of evangelical higher education in North America. It also travelled in a direction Kuyper's heirs still argue about, supplying vocabulary that South African theologians later adapted in defence of apartheid.

movements.name: Russian Evangelicals — Stundists to the Baptist Union
movements.statusDescription: Proposed by the Era 9 Step 0 run; ADOPTED at the Era 9 Freeze (Mark, 2026-08-03).
movements.sourcing: Moderate [S]: the movement’s own hymnody and congregational records [S], persecution dossiers under Pobedonostsev [S]
movements.relationsSummary: The Stundist movement in Ukraine (1860s [S]); Pashkovites in Petersburg (1874 [S]); the Russian Baptist Union (1884 [S]); persecution under Pobedonostsev [S] — the direct ancestors of IX.12’s Initsiativniki, with no era-9 row; VIII.31’s tension-partner
movements.why: The 80-year ancestry carried rather than disclosed as a gap. Tier 3 signal; awaiting the gate.
movements.dateRationale: Start 1860 (the Stundist movement, 1860s [S]); end 1906 era cap; the direct ancestors of IX.12’s Initsiativniki (Era 9 Freeze, Mark, 2026-08-03)
movements.longDescription: In the 1860s Ukrainian peasants working alongside German colonists in the southern provinces began meeting for the Bible studies their neighbours called Stunden, hours — reading the Scriptures for themselves in the Russian translation then appearing. Reading became conversion, and conversion became congregations. The movement then met a second one coming from the opposite end of society: from 1874 in St Petersburg, aristocrats converted under the preaching of the English evangelist Lord Radstock gathered around Colonel Vasily Pashkov, who opened his house for meetings that servants and nobles attended together. The strands joined in a Russian Baptist Union in 1884, and the state answered with everything it had — Pashkov exiled, meetings broken up, children removed from Stundist parents, families deported — since leaving the Orthodox Church was a crime as well as a sin. The toleration decree of 1905 gave them their first legal breathing space in forty years.
movements.teaser: Ukraine and Russia, 1860 to 1906 — peasants who read the Bible in their own language and aristocrats who read it in a palace, and both of them breaking the law.
voices: Nikita Voronin — baptized in the river at Tiflis in 1867, conventionally counted the first Russian Baptist
Ivan Ryaboshapka and Mikhail Ratushny — among the earliest Ukrainian Stundist leaders
Lord Radstock — the English evangelist whose 1874 mission converted a circle of the Russian aristocracy
Vasily Pashkov — the guards colonel who opened his St Petersburg house to preaching and was exiled for it in 1884
Konstantin Pobedonostsev — the Holy Synod's chief lay officer, who directed the state's campaign against them
movements.legacy: These congregations are the ancestors of Russian and Ukrainian evangelical Protestantism as it now exists. The Baptist and Evangelical Christian unions descended from them survived the Soviet century, went through their own painful split in the 1960s between those who registered with the state and those who refused, and are today, with the Pentecostals, the largest Protestant presence across the former Soviet Union. Emigrants carried the tradition abroad as well, into Slavic Baptist communities in North and South America and Germany that are still identifiably from this root.
